LESSON – 1
GEOGRAPHICAL FEATURES AND
SOURCES OF TAMIL NADU
Learning Objectives
After learning this lesson you will be able to
 Understand the physical features of Tamil Nadu
 Learn about the classification of the land and
 Know the sources for the study of Tamil Nadu History.

1.1 Introduction
The general description of the Geography of Tamil Nadu, the land lying between Tirupatihill and the cape- comerin are explained. In Tamil Nadu, the land is traditionally divided into
five geographical regions (tinai): they are the mountainous regions (kurinchi) which include the
forest areas, fertile plains (marudam), coastal region (neidhal), pastoral region (mullai) and
arid region (palai). The history of the past can be written only on the basis of relevant and
reliable sources available; the sources may be grouped into inscriptions, numismatics,
archaeology and literature.
Tamilagam
Tamilagam is named after the name of the people who speak Tamil Language. The
southern most part of Tamilagam called kumara-kandam or lemuria was devoured by the Indian
Ocean. Tamil Nadu is bound by the Western Ghats on one side, and the Coromandel Coast on

the other.The Western and Eastern Ghats bind the Deccan Plateau in Tamil Nadu. While the
Western Ghats tend to be steep and high, the Eastern Ghats are lower and their slopes gentler.
1.2 Geography and History
It is true to say that “Geography governs History”. The geographical features of a country
like its mountains and rivers, its climate and natural resources determine in a large measure
the nature of the social and economic life of its people. The people’s standard of life as well as
their social customs and institutions bear the imprint of the geographical features of the land in
which they live. It is obvious that in moulding the human factor itself, the influence of the
geographical features has a vital share.
Generally speaking, it may be said that the geographical, no less than the human factor

has an important part to play in moulding history. For instance, the long history of the commercial
relations of South India with countries on either side of the ocean was primarily the result of
South India’s geographical position. Geography and human history thus shape each other,
and their relationship is complex.

3
1.3 Frontiers of Tamilagam
Naturally, therefore a history of the early Tamils has to be preceded by a consideration of
the principal geographical features of Tamilagam. The exact extent of Tamilagam has varied
from age to age. A legendary account states that in the age of the so-called First Tamil Sangam,
extended farther into the south and the east than the present confines of Tamil Nadu and that
it comprised forty nine major divisions. The traditional conception during the age of this Sangam
was that Tamilagam comprised that part of Peninsular India, which stretched south from
Venkadam (Thirupati) to Kanyakumari. The land stretching south from the Konkan along the
west coast, now comprising the Kerala state was a part of Tamillaagam throughout the early
period of South Indian History. Tolkappiyanar explains about Sen Tamil Chernta Pannirunilam.

But he does not specify the twelve units of Sen Tamil Nadu, there is an old venba which says
that Sen Tamil Nadu consists of Twelve regions.
It is beyond dispute that Tamilagam of Historical times extended southwards from the
Tirupati hill down to Kanyakumari, surrounded by sea on the three other sides. Thus it formed
the southernmost part of the South Indian Peninsula.
1.4 Classification of the land
To understand the subject the following divisions are made namely the mountainous
region, Rainfall, Rivers, Flora and Fauna and Minerals.
1.4.1 The mountainous region
The mountainous regions lie in the western part of Tamil Nadu. The western Ghat and
the Eastern ghats run parallel to the West and East coasts of Peninsula. Both the Ghats meet
at Doddabedda and the continuation of these Ghats goes up to Cape Comerin. The Palghat
gap connects the highlands of Kerala and Coimbatore.

Western Ghats:
All the rivers that flow towards Tamil Nadu, originate from the Western Ghats. Ooty,
Kunoor, Kotagiri, Erkad and Kodaikkanal are some of the important hill stations existing on
these hills. They are summer resorts. The Palani, Anaimalai, Kodai, Sabari, Podiyil etc. are

4
important places on the southern part of this Ghat. Western Ghats offer access between the
Carnatic, the Deccan Plateau, and the Malabar Coast.
Eastern Ghats:
The Eastern Ghats running by the side of the East coast are different from the Western
Ghats in their nature and formation, particularly in respect of height, productivity and scenery.
They possess little of the magnificence of the Western Ghats; the Eastern Ghats are scattered,
broken and of much lower altitude. But they are older than the Western Ghats. They are
running southwards from Orissa along the coast and then near about Madras they take a
south-westerly direction meeting the Western Ghats at the Nilgiris. Isolated masses of hills like
the Palani and the Shevroy hills, in and near the Salem district, branch off from the main range.
1.4.2 Rainfall

Tamilagam has depended largely on rainfall for the successful pursuit of agriculture. The
South-West monsoon gives scanty rain to the eastern side, because the South West monsoon
winds do not blow across this region. On the whole, the South-West monsoon is the heaviest
in the northern region of Tamil Nadu, and generally it decreases towards the south.
The North-East monsoon starting from October to mid-December provides the heaviest
rainfall for Tamil Nadu, the average rising from 40" to 50". Generally the maximum rainfall of
the year in Tamil Nadu occurs in the period from mid-October to mid- November
Generally the total rainfall is more inadequate, and hence artificial irrigation is employed
especially in regions which are far removed from the major river systems of the country.
1.4.3 Rivers
Fortunately, the rivers, though small in number, supply a substantial amount of water

needed for cultivation. The Kaveri, the Palar, the river Vellar, the Vaigai and Tamiraparani are
some of the important rivers which rise in the Western Hills and irrigate the eastern slopes and
later merge in the Bay of Bengal.

5
The Kaveri:
The most prominent river of Tamilagam is unquestionably Kaveri, celebrated in Tamil
literature and history. It is said that Karikalan constructed a dam across the river kaveri. The
Cauvery River, originating in the Coorg district of the neighboring state of Karnataka, is the
lifeline of the state. The lush Coromandal plains are irrigated by the Cauvery and its Thanjavur-
Nagapattinam delta is called the granary of Tamil Nadu. It bifurcates into two branches called
Kollidam and Kaveri
Palar
The river Palar originates from Nandidrug in Karnataka, and running through the North
Arcot District, falls into the Bay of Bengal near Sadras in the Chengleput district. It helps the
irrigation of some areas of Chengleput district.
Vellar
This river draining the southern slopes of the Shevaroys and Kalrayans and the northern

slopes of the Pachamalais enters the sea just north of the Kaveri delta. It flows through
Bangalore, Salem and Cuddalore.
Vaigai
The Vaigai raises from the Palani hills and flows through the rown of Madurai. Due to the
construction of certain dams in modern times, water from the Western ghats has been diverted
into the Vaigai, and as a result the volume of water flowing through this river has been augmented.
Tambraparani
The Tambraparani is the biggest of the rivers in the southernmost region. It flows through
the Tirunelveli district. It derives directly the benefit of the South-west monsoon and it irrigates
a large part of the Tirunelveli district.
All these rivers fall into the Bay of Bengal. All the rivers have been used for irrigation.
The Gulf of Mannar is famous for pearl fisheries.

6
Rivers were used for commerce and trade. Dams have been constructed across the
rivers and they are also used for hydro-electric utility. Rivers are sacred and people worshipped
them. They also formed the backbone of the Dravidian civilization.
The coastal region
The coastal regions of Tamil Nadu (the ‘Coromandal’ coast) have a few natural harbours,
and these areas have had links with the Romans, Arabs, and the Chinese since ancient times.
Their port cities are scattered along the coastline. The Satavahanas, the Pallavas and the
Cholas had strong navies, and for a time the Cholas colonized nations east of the Bay of
Bengal.
1.4.4 Flora and Fauna
Agriculture has been the main occupation of Tamil Nadu. The total cropped area of present
Tamil Nadu is about 16 million acres. Out of the 16 million acres under cultivation in the present

Tamil Nadu 38% is devoted for the cultivation of rice, other crops cultivated consisted of Cholam
(11%) Kambu (9%), Ragi (5%), Varagu (4%) and 13 % consisted of commercial crops such as
groundnut and cotton. A small percentage of land is devoted for the cultivation of tobacco,
sugarcane and vegetables.
On the western slopes of Western Ghats are found a number of flora and fauna. Tea,
coffee, Cardamom, Cinchona, Bamboos, Rose-wood etc are found. A variety of fruits are also
cultivated and they are exported. Many wild animals are living in the Ghats. Vedanthangal
nearer to Madras is noted for its bird sanctuary with thousands of acquatic birds.
1.4.5 Minerals
Tamil Nadu has a fair distribution of certain minerals. Llignite, Iron, Cromite, Aluminium,
Bauxxite, Copper, Graphite etc are some of the resources of Tamil Nadu. Lignite is found in

Neyveli. Iron, Cromite, Aluminium etc are found in Salem district. Pearl fishing is popular in
Tuticorin. Salt is also taken from Tuticorin and Marakkanam. Recently petroleum is found in
Tanjavour district.

7
Special features of Tamilagham
Varieties of beautiful sculptures are found in the temples. Bronze images of Tamil Nadu
are world famous. People of different races and communities are living in this land. The situation
of Tamilnad is the extreme south of peninsula has saved it from the cultural and political influences
brought by Kushans, Afghans, Turks, Mughals etc in the north; with the exception of the Muslim
invasions in the 14th century and a brief Government of Madurai Sultanate, Tamil Nadu
successfully retained the essentials of ancient culture of Tamil Nadu. The fertility of the soil, the
regularity of the monsoons, the never failing rivers like kaveri, the rich quality of minerals and
the excellent flora and fauna lead the land to great prosperity
1.5 Sources
The history of any country can be reconstructed only on the basis of relevant source

material. The sources for the study of History of Tamil Nadu may be grouped into epigraphical
data, numismatics, archaeology and literature.
1.5.1 Literary Sources
The literary sources can be divided into Indigenous literature and foreign literature. The
Indigenous literature can be divided further into Tamil literature and Non-Tamil literature.
Tamil Literature
Literary sources include books written in the past, religious literature, poetry, travelogues,
biographies, and other kinds of literature. From these, historians can learn about the social,
economic and religious conditions of their times. Literary sources thus supplement the
archaeological sources of knowledge about the past.
Books were written on palm-leaves before paper became common. Palm leaf manuscripts
are collected in places like the Sarasvathi Mahal Library at Thanjavur, established by Nayak

Kings in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
The following are some of the main literary sources of the history of Tamil Nadu.

8
The oldest Tamil literature belongs to the first and second centuries CE. Sangam literature
may be considered as the more valuable and most reliable source of history of Sangam Age.
The whole of Sangam literature Consisted of Tolkaippiyam, Pattupattu, Ettutokai,
Patheninkilkanakku, Twin Epics namely Silapathikaram and Manimegalai and Perundevanar
Bharatham are of most useful for the purpose.
For the study of the Pallava period the Hymns of the Devaram written by Appar, Sambandar
and Sundarar explains about the Socio-economic and Religious conditions of the Pallava age.
The religious conflict, the great famine, and the Pallava chalukya conflict can be studied through
these works. The Naliyira Divya Pravandam of the Alvars is a religious work. We infer information
about the war materials used by the Pallavas and Rashtrakutas from Nandikkalambatgam, a

work dedicated to Nandivarman III, and the pandikkovai. The Bharatha Venba mentions about
the battle of Tellaru. Thus these literary works serve as the useful source material for the study
of the Pallava History.
In the Chola period many Tamil works were written. Periyapuranam of sekkilar,
Kalingathuparani of Jayamkondar, Ottakkuttar’s Muvarula, Kulothungan chola Pillai Tamil were
some of the literary works which serve as a source material for the study of the cholas
The pandikkovai and Periyapuranam throw light for the study of the Pandyas, The Divya
suri-Charitha and the Guruparamparai are other contemporary Vaishnavite works. Thiruvilaiyadal
Puranam of Paranjothi also gives some historical information.
The Non- Tamil literature
The Ramayana and Mahabharatha explain about the society of the Pandyas. Avanthi

sundari kathasara of Bharavi and Matavilasaprahasana of Mahendravarman are some of the
Sanskrit works which explains about the Pallava History. Gangadevi’s Madura Vijayam or
Kambana Raja Vijayam is the Sanskrit works. A detailed description of Kumarakumban’s
expedition is narrated in the Madura Vijayam.
Foreign Literary works
Amomg the foreign writers Megasthenese, Strabo, Pliny and Ptolemy of the west and
Pan Kou, Fahien, Hiuen Tsang of the East are prominent and their accounts besides Periplus
and Peutingerian Tables are very useful.

9
The earliest direct notice of south India is probably found in the work of Megasthenes,
the Greek who visited the Magadhan Empire. Megasthenes mentions about the Pandya
kingdom. Another Greek historian, Strabo, explains about trade between southern India and
Europe via Egypt. Periplus of the Erythraean Sea is a book on trade between India and Rome
in the ancient period. The author is unknown. He describes about the western coast of India
and trading conditions here. After this period, Chinese travelers, Fahien and Hiuen Tsang
describes about southern India.
From the ninth century onwards, there were Arab travelers and geographers who refer to
the southern India. Ibn Batuta, the Moroccan traveller of the fourteenth century, wrote of his
travels in South India and describes about the religion and society of the Tamils. .

From the fourteenth century, there are many European accounts. Some of these writers
were Benjamin of Tuleda and Marco Polo. Marco Polo travelled through southern India on his
way back from China to Europe in the late thirteenth century.
The rise of Vijayanagar in the fourteenth century is mentioned by many European writers.
The Italian Nicolo Conti and Portuguese Duarte Barbosa visited Vijayanagar in the fifteenth
century and wrote about their experiences. Several other traders and missionaries left records
of their travels in India.
Many of the Arabic and Persian historical works were written under the patronage of
Muslim rulers of the Deccan. Ferishta, who lived in 16th- and early 17th century, wrote a
comprehensive history of Islamic rule in India, and touched upon the extreme south also.
Abdul Razzak, a Persian ambassador in the Vijayanagar court, wrote down his observations of

the administration and society of that time.
1.5.2 Archaeological Sources
The archaeological sources can be classified into three divisions namely Epigraphy and
Copper plate, Numismatics and Monuments.

10
Epigraphy
Epigraphy is the study of inscriptions on rocks, pillars, temple walls and copper plates.
Inscriptions are the main source for reconstructing the history and culture of ancient civilizations.
The Rocks
Inscriptions of Ashoka, Hathikumpha inscription of King Kharavela of Kalinga etc are
found outside the Tamil country, these inscriptions mentions about the Tamil rulers.
The Pillars
Allahabad Pillar inscription of Samudragupta refers to 12 rulers of South India which
mentions about the ruler Vishnugopa of Kanchi.
The Caves
Tiruppargundram, Nagamalai, Anaimalai, Kilkuyilkudi, Tirukkovalur Kudimiyamalai etc
are some of the places where inscriptions are found and they give reference about the Sangam
period.
During the Pallava and the Pandya period number of caves were carved out throughout
their empire. Mandagapattu, Mahendravadi, Trichy, Sittannavasal, Mamalapuram are some of

the caves of the Pallavas. From Mandagapattu inscription we come to know that prior to the
Pallava period temples were constructed with the help of the perishable materials like timber,
Marter, wood etc. The Rathas of the Mamalapuram also bear inscriptions of the Pallava and
the chola period.
Temples
Kanchi, Mamalapuram, Tanjavur, Gangaikonda Cholapuram , Darasuram, Madurai ,
Tanjavur etc. are the places were big and small temples are found with plenty of valuable
historical inscriptions. They give information about the expeditions, method of ad,omistration
(Utiramerur), and the social and economic life of the people.
Copper Plates
The Copper plate was used for inscribing matters. They are found in Prakrit, Sanskrit
languages. Hirahadahalli, Gunapadeya, Mayidavelu are some of the Pallava copper plates:

11
Velvikudi, Talavoypuram, Sinnamannur, Sivakasi copper plates describe about the Pandyas.
Thiruvalangadu, Karanthai, Anbil, Largen Leydon are some of the Chola copper plates.
Numismatics
It is a study of coins. During the Sangam period, the Romans settled here and issued
coins. The coins of this age are found in Arikkamedu, Madurai and other places. The coins of
Vijayanagara rulers, the Nayaks, the Sultanate etc. give information about their social and
economic conditions.
Monuments
From the temples we infer their architecture style. The Kailasanatha temple,
Vaikundaperumal temple etc reveal the Pallava’s style. The descriptions of various Gods are
also identified from the sculptures of these temples. Different poses of the dancing girls are
found on the eastern gopura of the Chidambaram temple.
The excavations at Arikkamedu, Poompuhar, Kodumanal and other places reveal the

overseas commercial activities of the Tamils. Thus the archaeological monuments give more
information for reconstructing the history of Tamil Nadu.
1.6 Summary
To understand the history of Tamil Nadu we use literature, Inscriptions, Numismatics and
Monuments as source material. The fertility of the soil, the regularity of the monsoons, the
never failing rivers like kaveri, the rich quality of minerals and the excellent flora and fauna lead
the land to great prosperity

2.1 Introduction
Scholars regard the Sangam period as the “Classical Age” of the Tamils. Some scholars
consider the sangam age as the “Golden Age” of the Tamils, which marked a unique epoch in
the history of Tamilaham. The physical features of ancient Tamilaham landscape with its
mountains and rivers have induced the ancient Tamils to divide the landscape on the basis of

15
geographical set up. The hilly regions were called Kurinchi, the forest area was known as
Mullai, the fertile regions of river-valleys are called as Marutham, the seashore is known as
Neithal and the waste land and the sandy desert are called as Palai. These fivefold divisions of
the land gave an impetus to the development of culture. Sangam literature reflects the matter
of great historical importance.
Ancient Tamil Civilization
The term “Tamilakam” appears to be the most ancient term used for designating the
Tamil territory. According to the Tolkappiyam “the virtuous land in which Tamil is spoken as the
mother tongue lies between the northern Venkata hill and the southern Kumari. The
Silappadikkaram defines the Tamilakam as “The Tamil region extends from the hills of Vishnu
(Tirupati) in the north to the oceans at the cape in the south. In this region of cool waters were

the four great cities of Madurai, Uraiyur, kanchi and Puhar with the roaring waters (of Kaveri
and the ocean)”. These ancient texts do not clearly define the eastern and western boundaries
of the Tamilakam. Scholars assume that these boundaries were the seas, which may explain
their omission from their ancient definitions. The ancient Tamilakam thus included the present
Kerala.
While excavating a site linked to the Sangam period, archaeologists have unearthed
remnants of a civilization in Tamil Nadu whose drainage system resembles that of the Indus
Valley Civilization. Around 3000 ancient artefacts have been found from Keezhadi Pallai
sandhaipudur village in the Shivaganga district. The artefacts include swords, arrows, other

16
iron and copper weapons. Further a particular note about the drainage system which is
underground and lay with “baked clay pipe lines” similar to those of Harappan civilization.
According to Archaeological Survey of India, the site is over 2500 years old, (more than
500 BC) and belongs to the ancient Pandyan era. This means that there was a flourishing
Dravidian civilization was in existemce.
Ancient brick Structure
2.2 Division of Lands
The Sangam Age in Tamil Nadu witnessed prosperity in all spheres of life. The Tamil
people had a common language and culture in the Sangam Age. But they lived in five different
Natural landscapes. These natural landscapes or geographical regions were called as Thinais.
Sangam literature referred about the fivefold division of land and they were known as Kurinji,

Mullai, Marudham, Neydal and Palai. Each Thinai was grograpphically distinct from the other.
Moreover each thinai region reflected their social characteristics. The life of the people in
these divisions differed according to their regions.
Kurinji - It refers to the hilly region. The people in this region were known as Vettuvar
(Hunter) and Kuravar. Their main occupation was hunting. Occasionally they also cultivated
vegetables and fruits and gathered honey. Their deity was Murugan or Seyon.

17
Mullai- It is the pastoral area. They domesticated animals. The people of this region
were known as kovalar or Ayar. They produced dairy products like milk, curd and Ghee. They
worshipped Thirumal or Mayon.
Marudham- This region refers to fertile and agricultural lands. People in this region were
referred as Vellalars because their profession was agriculture. They were familiar with the
Irrigation methods also. They worshipped Indra or Rain God.
Neidal- Coastal area is the region of Neidal. People were called as Meenavar or
Parathavar. (Fisherman) Their main occupation was fishing.Their chief deity was varunan or
the sea God
Palai- refers to Desert region. Among these five regions the first four regions are of
permanent nature and the fifth region cannot be considered to be so. The Mullai and kurinchi

regions by nature’s blessings are of interchangeable into palai region and vice versa. The
people of this region were known as Maravar of Kallar. Highway robbery and warfare were
their occupations. Korravai or Kali was the chief Goddess worshipped by them.
2.3 Caste system
The Tamil society during the Sangam period was broadly divided into several groups. In
the beginning of the Sangam Age, the Tamil society was not organized on the basis of the
Vedic caste system, namely Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, vaisyas and Sudras. However, the earliest
of the Sangam literature, Tolkappiyam mentions about the fourfold divisions were prevalent in
the Sangam society namely, Anthanar, Arasar, Vaislyar and Vellalar, it may be said that this
classification roughly corresponds to the Vedic Social division. Arasar were the ruling class. .

Anthanars played a significant role in the Sangam polity and religion. Vanigar”s profession was
trade and commerce. And the vellalas were agriculturists. Another Sangam work, Purananuru
mentions the names of ancient Tamil tribes such as Thudiyan, Pannan, and Kadamban. Other
tribal groups like Parathavar, Panar, Eyinar, Kadambar, Maravar and Pulaiyar were also found
in the Sangam society. Ancient primitive tribes like Thodas, Irulas, Nagas and Vedars lived in
this period. These divisions indicate the complex social structure prevalent in the Sangam
Age. The social order of the people was based on the region in which they lived or on the
occupation which they had adopted

18
The four-fold division was known to them and this was mentioned in the poem Purananuru.
V.Kanakasabai has a classification of caste. Ulavar, Ayar artisans like goldsmiths etc., Padai-
Achis (armed men), Valaiyar (fishermen), pulaiyar (official slaughters). There is no warrant for
such a division in society.
The concept of upper classes was quite well established in the days of Silappadikaram
where it is said that the Goldsmith being a kamala walked at a distance from the higher class
prople walking along the street among whom Kovalan the vaisya, was one.
The Brahmins
Brahmins played a prominent role in the Tamil society ever since the coming of the
Aryans into South India. They are mentioned in practically in every text in sangam literature
i.e., Tolkappiyam, the Ten Idyls, the Eight Anthology and the Eighteen Minor Works. Brahmins

had composed major and minor poems: they had played the role of patrons also. They had
been ambassadors, priests, ascetics, householders, merchants and judicial advisors. Thus
they have contributed to the enrichment of Tamil Culture.
The Brahmins are called Andanar or Parppar or Maraiyavar. Acording to Thiruvalluvar
Andhanar is otherwise called Aravar, because they assume justice and kindness towards all
creatures. Parppar means a ‘seer’: “Maraiyavar’ means those who study and teach the Marais
or the Vedas. Tolkappiam mentioned the duties of Parppar and they were Learning, Teaching,
Performing sacrifices, giving presents and Receiving presents.
Tolkappiyar also speaks of the Arivar. They are the wise men who know the past, the
present and the future, i.e. are omniscient. Agastya, the famous sage is included among these
ascetics by Nachchinarkkiniyar.

The Andanar were recruited for service in the royal court as purohits and probably as
astrologers. Some of them served as judicial advisers, and were employed as ambassadors.
The Andanar lived in particular parts of the town or village. Their quarters were called
Parppana Cheri .They were famous for their clean surroundings and hygienic environment.
Their residential area could be easily recognized. The housewife in the Andanar family was a
dutiful and industrious lady whose charity was proverbial like that of Arundadi.

19
It is strange that couple of references in the whole of the sangam literature has led many
scholars to conclude that the Tamil Brahmin of the sangam Age was a meat-eater and a wine
drinker, The sources which are supposed to support them are poems 113 and 119 of Purananuru
and Kapilar’s Inna Narpadu one of the eighteen minor works of the sangam literature. According
to K.A.N.Sastry ‘Apparently Brahmins ate meat and drank toddy without incurring reproach’.
Scholars have come to a conclusion that the Brahmins after their Gurukulam’s education
neglected non-vegetarian food.
In all walks of life the Brahmins had high respect and reward. The Brahmins helped the
kings for performing the sacrifices and the conduct of state affairs, particularly in the
administration of justice. The kings treated them with great courtesy. Thus the Tamil Brahmins

of the Sangam Age enjoyed considerable respect in the society.
Other Communities
The kings of Sangam Age were the natives of Tamilaham in every sense. The Tamil
kingdoms were founded by Dravidian immigrants. It is clear that they were not Aryan
immigrants.The king’s duties were well recognized. The occupational or professional order in
the long -run became birth based. Among these, Vellala the agriculturist were highly respected
by all other communities, as the daughters of Velir, the Vellala chiefs were given in marriage to
the Tamil Kings i.e. the celebrated Pari, Anji, Kari, Or Pehan etc.The vellalars are introduced as
Ulavar (Cultivator) who owned the curved plough and led a virtuous life. They condemn killing
and abhor stealing: perform their duties to the heavenly Gods and offer oblations.
Tolkappiar calls the commercial community as Vaisyas. The merchant community was

the backbone of national economy. Basically they were traders dealing in the eight varieties of
grams, dhal, millets. According to Thirukural the merchant community had a high standard of
honesty. They won’t take anything more than what should they get, and won’t give anything
less than what they should give and thus they regard the goods of others equal to that of their
own. They have developed the foreign trade during the sangam age. They were the owners
of the big vessels which were used for their trade. They lived in luxurious houses and led a high
life.

20
The natural occupation of the coastal region was fishing and the people who had adopted
fishing as their occupation was called ‘Minavar”after the Tamil word “Min”that is the people who
lived on fishing. They were also called as “Paradavar”. They were also mentioned in the sangam
literature as”Valainar” and “Nuliyar”. According to Pattinappalai they built boats small and big
and carried on their trade along the sea coasts. Gradually they became sailors, who took their
trade to Arabia and Af rica in the west, and Burma and China in the east
.Perumpanarruppatai.speaks about their large houses in the broad streets approaching the
sea shore.
There were other innumerable communities. The Umanar were the manufactures and
sellers of salt. Blacksmith rendered their effective service for the heroic society. He was known

as Kollan with the famous title Karungaikkollan (meaning the strong armed smith). The
goldsmith, were called as Porkollan. Silapathikaram mentions about Porkollar for Goldsmith.
He was the dealer in gold and manufacturer of jewels and ornaments. They were treated as
low-born persons.
The Carpenter was a busy craftsman .The art of building was known to them. Wood
carvings and wood works were in their houses. Purananuru explains about their skill. The
carpenters made vehicles and bedsteads, planks and doors, chariots and boats. The weavers
were the next importance to the agriculturist and they were famous in foreign countries for their
fine production of textile goods. The tailors were known as Tumiyaakarar. The shepherds and
cowherds were a very important and large community: They represented the pastoral regions
in the land and cattle were their wealth.

The vedars were the hunters and they accompanied the king on the hunting expedition.The
cobbler who was treated as a “low born” not only made and mended shoes but he manufactured
the” Pari” the large leather can be used for drawing water for irrigation Such was the Tamil
Sangam social structure.
2.4 Occupations
Agriculture was the main occupation of the sangam people. It was considered to be a
noble profession. Tirukural says that agriculture alone provides the means of catering to the

21
elementary needs of mankind and other professions depend directly or indirectly on agriculture.
Apart from Varagu ,Tinai were also cultivated.
Cattle breeding were another important occupation of the Sangam age. Milk and Milk
products were used by the Tamil people hence they showed keen interest in cattle rearing.
Milk, curd, ghee, butter were taken to the nearby region for sale. The women folks were the
vendors of milk products.
Weaving was a prominent occupation of the Sangam people. They developed great skill
in manufacture nice variety of cotton and silk clothes. Silappadikkaram refers about 32 varieties
of cotton cloth. Dyeing of the cloth was skillfully done. Well designed bordered silk cloth was
a common feature.
The skill of blacksmith was also very much in demand in the Sangam Age in making toys,

utensils, agricultural implements, weapons of warfare and all the construction of buildings and
ships.
During the Sangam age the Toddy Tapping was also an important occupation. Pattinapalai
mentions various kinds of toddy namely pilimattu, matu, and naravu and it explains that ‘pili’
was tapped from the spathe of palmyra tree. Toddy was generally known as ‘kal’. The term
‘teral’ which denoted money, also was used as the synonym for toddy.It is also offered to
‘natukal’, the memorial stone, during worship. Hence the toddy tapping also was an important
and profitable occupation of those days.
The natural occupation of the coastal region was fishing and the people who had adopted
fishing as their occupation was called ‘Minavar”after the Tamil word “Min” that is the people
who lived on fishing.
The Brahmins discharged their six fold functions. These were the study of the Vedas,

conducting Vedic sacrifices, officiating priests in sacrifices giving gifts to others and receiving
gifts. They were highly respected by the rulers and also by the rich and the poor people. They
were liberally donated by the kings. Some Brahmins took secular functions also. Thus they
had been ambassadors, priests, ascetics, householders, merchants and judicial advisors

22
There were other occupational groups also. The Umanar were the manufactures and
sellers of salt. Blacksmith, the goldsmith, the cobbler and the carpenter were treated as lowborn persons.
2.4.1 Slavery
There was no trace of the existence of slavery in the Sangam age. Megasthenes said
that slavery as an institution was never known to India: as he had never seen an open market
for the sale of slaves. V.Kanakasabai says “slavery was ever unknown amongst the Tamils and
this is strong evidence of their superior civilization in the early period”. V.A.Smith also remarks
“Slavery is said to have been unknown amongst the Tamils”.
But N.Subramaniyam concludes in a reasonable way that there might have been slavery
but in disguise. He puts forth the following in support of his view: Purananuru mentions the
term “”Adiyurai” which means “Adimai “Silappathikaram mentions the term ‘Urimai Surram”

which means “Adimai” since the foot note says “Adimaittirli” Thiruttondar Purnam mentions
directly the word “Adimai”.
These evidences seem to proper and appropriate. He also says that unconditional
submission of a subject to the king, of a disciple to his guru and of the wife to her husband also
indicates the slavery in a philosophical way.
In addition to these things the system of bonded labour that is “Pannaiyal” system which
existed till recently may be considered as evidence.
However we have to give margin that there is no direct evidence in the Sangam classics
to show that there existed the institution of slavery .
2.4.2 Dwellings
Primitive men lived in the natural caves and worshipped Nature via Sun, Moon, cloud
and even Lightening. But in course of time people felt the need of a dwelling place, and gradually

he began to build houses so as to protect himself from the horrors of the Sun, Rain and even
cruel animals etc.

23
No doubt the Sangam classics reveal that the ancient Tamils were far advanced in this
aspect also. They were well trained in the art of brick and mortar. We hear about the cloud
capped storied buildings of Pukar from Pattinappalai
People lived in two kinds of houses-those built of mud and others built of bricks. According
to the literary evidence the second category of houses were built of Suduman, which means
burnt mud. The poor lived in thatched houses covered with leaves of gross of the coconut or
Palmyra.
A Sangam classic speaks of the large houses with spacious front-yards. They used to
have double doors. Invariably the royal buildings had the tiger mark, the royal emblem of the
Chola kings. There were small tanks and cattle sheds in the spacious front yard of the large
houses.
There were huge and lofty storied buildings with many halls big and small

With a narrow passage between the main entrance and the next inside door: and there
were much elevated piles around the buildings which were provided with long ladders with
close set rungs. There were windows to allow the breeze in .Literary work speaks about the
storied buildings with huge circular pillars, where numerous guests were fed in the spacious
kitchen halls and the surplus was kept ready for the newcomers. It is also said that there were
grain stores in the interior parts of the houses.
2.4.3 Food and drink
The diet system of the ancient Tamils was not much different from that of the present
days. Primarily it may depend upon the flora and fauna of the land. The diet of the Tamils was
simple but a great importance was attached to it, as it is the life sustainer. The sangam people
ate both vegetarian and non vegetarian food. Cooked rice was the staple food of the ancient

tamils and it continued through the ages without much change.
There are vast paddy fields with one crop or the other always. The land is cultivated
throughout the year with alternative crop plants. There is ample evidence from sangam classics
to show that milk was in use, and sometimes the rice was cooked with milk. Curd and buttermilk

24
also had their due places in the meals and they were popular in those days too. Ghee was
used invariably by the middle and high class people. Ghee was used in the performance of
sacrifices.
Eating of mutton was always accompanied by drinking of Toddy and ginger. The king ate
and drank in the company of his guests and relatives. The sangam people used betel leaves
also. In addition to this they used slaked lime and areca nut.
2.4.4 Dress
A variety of clothing was used by the people during this age, including those made of
cotton and silk. People living in hilly and deserted areas wore dresses made of foliage and
flowers. Sheaths of grassy weeds (Korai) were used for making dress by the hill and forest
area people. Skins of animals and barks of trees were also used. Men of the poorer classes
wore only one piece of cloth around the waist. Women covered their upper body with a kind of

dress called kachchu. Among the higher classes, men wore two pieces; one around the waist
and the other, the upper cloth, thrown over the shoulders. Women of sophisticated society
wore half sari, made of the finest cotton and silk fabrics, with embroidery.
The cotton dress was more popular among all Tamils and the silk also was in use, perhaps
by the rich. A sangam literary work mentions about the dress of those days. It speaks about
the cotton, silk and foliage dresses. It says that the ladies by mistake were the cotton, cloth of
their husband instead of their own silk sarees. It shows that the silk was used invariably by
ladies and the ancient Tamils were well trained in fine cotton weaving and in silk too. Pattinappalai
mentions also about the use of foliage dress by the paratavar women. This is clear evidence

to show that in ancient times the foliage dress was in use among the maids and ladies on
festive and ceremonial occasions.
2.4.5 Ornaments
Ornaments were very popular among the ancient Tamils and there were numerous varieties
of them and especially the married women were crazy for such ornaments. But one should not
think that all the maids and ladies wore all kinds of ornaments mentioned in Sangam classics.

25
Particular ornament worn by particular individual depended on the social and economical
conditions of the person concerned. Pattinapalai provides details of ornaments worn by ancient
Tamils, and it refers wherever necessary by the common term ilai (ornaments), such as nerilai
(proper ornament), pasilai (special or gold ornament) and murrilai (complete set of ornaments).
Ilai is a common name for the ornaments as they are made of gold and studded with diamonds.
However mention is made about two particular ornaments namely kulai and toti.Kulai means
an ear ring but here the ‘kotunkulai’ may be said as an ear ornament such as modern ‘jimikki’
and ‘pontoti’ means in this context may mean the goldern bracelet as it is worn by putalvar
(son). From the above mentioned information we come to know that the Sangam people lead
a civilized life.
2.4.6 Amusements, Pastimes and Games

The amusements, pastimes and games of the ancient Tamils varied from place to place.
In the towns the people had less time for leisure due to their social activities whereas the rural
people had spent their leisure time in many ways. In the Mullai region, the bull fighting was very
common. In villages cock-fighting and goat-fighting were popular. Wrestling was also known to
the Sangam Tamils.
Kuravar boys used to make bows and arrows with twigs and thorns. Horse and elephant
riding was the pastime of few people. On the full moon day, which is specially intended for
Varunan the sea-god, the dark skinned paratavar folk, neglected their usual work of fishing in
the wide cold sea, ate and drank, and enjoyed playing with their black mates, who wore garments
of green leaves
To train the youngsters in warfare the villages had organizations, called Paravai and

Muranakalari, Porvila Pundodai Vilavu were celebrated in honour of the distinguished youngsters.
Panar and Viraliyae, skilled in Music and dance respectively provided entertainment to
the kings chieftains and the public.
Youngsters took the game of football. Kalangadudal was a favorite game of the girls.
Swinging on a pole-suspended by ropes was another pastime of the girls. Boys and girls
delight in erecting fancy structures and dolls with sand imitating the cries and pranks of birds
was one of the amusements. Tiny carts and toys were also used.

26
This reminds us in the ancient days, women used to wear around their waist green
leaves plaited with colorful flowers. This kind of fanciful attire was considered a decorative
garment, and was used by maids, on extraordinary occasions such as festivals. And it is
evident that the full moon day was set apart for offering prayers to Varunan the sea-God by the
Paradavar folk; hence their womenfolk presented with garment of foliage
It is evident, in those days both men and women used to drink but the drinks were quite
different from each other; the women used to wear silk, but the men were contended with
cotton.
2.4.7 Festivals
There were many festivals celebrated in the Sangam age and references can be found in
the sangam classics. Marudam region Tamils used to worship Indra as their God. Hence they

celebrated a festival known as “Indra Vizha”. We are able to get detailed information about this
festival from the Tamil epics Silappadkkaram and Manimekalai and it says how the chola rulers
celebrated this festival in a grand manner. There was a belief that if they celebrate a festival to
Lord Indra they will have a good rain and also their difficulties and dangers are removed
Lord Murugan is the favourite God of the Sangam Tamils. The sangam Tamils used to
celebrate Kartigai festival. There was a reference in the literary work about this festival. The
literary work Ahananuru says that the Kartigai festival is celebrated during the full moon day of
the Tamil month of Karthigai. The literary works Thirumurugatrupadai and Purananuru explains
about the khandashati vizha. Accordingly the legend says that the lord Murukan destroyed
kadamba Asura king Sruabadma.

We have a reference about the festival of Pongal. It is known as harvest festival and they
used to celebrate this festival in order to thank the God Sun. They used to celebrate this
festival in the month of Thai.
Maduraikanchi speaks about the Thiruvonam festival. According to that on Thiruvonam
the birth star of Lord Vishnu, a group of stars which are brigh together and resemble like an
eagle. Hence this incident was celebrated for ten days by the Pandya rulers.

27
Thus we can say many festivals which were celebrated by the Sangam Tamils even now
we follow in Tamil Nadu
2.4.8 Marriage
During the Sangam age, marriage was very simple and natural. The coming together of
man and woman constituted marriage. “Manam” means in Tamil marriage.
There was not a much difference in the system of ritualistic marriage what we follow now
to the Sangam age marriage rituals. Silappadikaram gives a graphic picture of the marriage
between kovalan and kannagi. The bride was on the eve of completing 12 years and the
bridegroom 16 years. This was an arranged marriage by their parents. The sacred “Tali “(which
the bride was to wear around her neck throughout her wedded life) was taken round for all to
bless it: the grand old Brahmins conducted the marriage of Kovalan and Kannagi (as chaste as

Arundhati). The system of wearing Tali is a peculiarly non-Aryan practice. It is indigenous to
Tamilaham. Later on it was incorporated by the Brahmins into their ritualistic pattern.
In those days early marriage was practiced. After ritualistic marriage became fully
established the practice of arranged marriage automatically followed.
2.4.9 The Courtesans (Parathaiyar)
The courtesans are mentioned in many places in the Sangam literature especially in the
Aham literature. They were known as “Parattaiyar or Kanigaiyar”. During the Sangam age, a
courtesan was a woman who had sexual relationships with rich and powerful men for money.
Their profession was prostitution. They were of two kinds. The professional prostitutes were
who earned a living by the profession and did not get attached to any particular customer. They
were known as Cheri parattaiyar.

There were others who though belonging to that community set their heart upon a particular
person and lived in love with him but were not married at any time. They were known as Kadar
parattaiyar and they were just unmarried spouses. Kovalan lived with Madhavi on those terms
only.

28
These courtesans found in large numbers in the palace of the king. They were the king’s
body-guards and servants. They served as maids of the queen. They accompanied the king
even to the battlefield; these courtesans lived in a separate suburb called “Parattaiyar Cheri”.
These courtesans were greatly accomplished in fine arts especially in the art of dancing,
music and drama. Prizes were given to the best dances. Madhavi won the prize from the king,
and that started the affair between Kovalan and Madhavi.
The favourite courtesans of the kings received special honours and treatment. During
the Sangam age it was considered necessary that this class of persons should not be
discouraged from their ancestral profession.
2.4.10 Hospitality
Thiruvalluvar wrote much about hospitality in his Thirukkural. Hospitality was considered

as an essential duty of a house – holder, and hence they gave a warm welcome to their guests
and provided delicious food. Cordiality to neighbours also was considered as a duty of a house
– holder.
Malaipatukadam narrates how sangam Tamils invited their guests warmly and used to
share their food with the guests. Even if the guests came late at night they were sure to get
food and shelter. Charity was an allied virtue of the ancient Tamils: feeding the poor was
believed to be sacred duty. Hence the ancient Tamils were more hospitable and charitable.
Pattinappalai explains that there were public feeding houses in Pukar and the large quantity of
“Kanchi” the rice water drained from the cooked rice was flowing through the street like a
rivulet. Besides all these, the foreigners who had diverse tongues, stayed in Pukar on trade

purposes, led a free and happy life as they received kind hospitality from the Tamils.
Thus the hospitality of the ancient Tamils is proverbial. It was in high order and the
tradition is continuing even today.
2.4.11 Funeral practices
During the Sangam age the Tamils followed four methods to dispose the dead. The
methods were Cremation, Urn Burial, Exposing for vultures and jackals to eat and simple

29
burial. The cremation ground or the burning ghat was Sudukadu, while the rest were known as
Idukadu. Of these cremation seems to have been the most usual practice and this we inferred
from Naladiyar.
The urn burial was done by putting the dead body in a large pot and burying the pot deep
in the ground upside down. The urn was called “Mudumakkal tali”- meaning “the urn of the
departed ones”. Sati was practiced during this period.
Epic Silappadikaram mentions about the customary for certain post-mortem rites to be
performed.
After cremation, brick tombs of various shapes were raised by the relatives of the dead.
Epic Manimekallai mentions about such construction of tombs. It is different from “Nadukal”which
was raised for the warriors who had fallen in battle.
2.4.12 Customs and Practices
The sangam literature gives a detailed description about the various customs and practices

of the people of the Sangam Age. In the Sangam Age people lived mostly in villages, leading a
simple and contended life. The ideal of the house holder was to sustain society by feeding the
ascetics and bachelors. Thiruvalluvar wrote much about hospitality in his Thirukkural.
During festival time they used to organize feeding the public and they used to distribute
good and tasty food. Every person was to take care of the parents, the elder brother, the
teacher and the king as the “Five Great Ones” to be primarily respected. Tirukural says that it
was a Duty of a father “to make the son take the first seat in the assembly of the wise ones” In
turn it was the duty of the son to conduct himself as to earn a very good name and fame for his
father. Pisir Andaiyar says that the main reason why .hair on his head not turned grey in spite

of his old age was that the youngsters in his house never crossed him. For a wife, the husband
was more worthy of worship than anybody else,
Guests were treated well and while the guests were leaving the inmates used to walk
along with them “Seven Steps”. Another custom was that the practice of setting apart some
food for the crow before one began to eat. The shepherdess lighted the fire at home with a

30
stick which was violently rubbed against a wooden frame: this was the only way they know to
make fire. The practice of scrubbing the floor with cow dung paste was quite common in those
days. In course of time it acquired the religious significance.
The young girls were entrusted with watching the drying grains in front of their houses as
they were not engaged otherwise. Perhaps this may remind us that the young maids were sent
to the tinai (millet) field for watching the ear of corn (katir).
Another practice was the determination of the hour of the day. It was determined by them
in a variety of ways. One such way was to find out the position of the sun. Another way was by
observing the dropping away of water from the water basin set up for the purpose. Another way
was by observing the blossoming of flowers. The dawn was no doubt announced by the unfailing

cock. Many of the traditions of the Sangam age continued and survived in the later periods and
some exist even today.
2.5 Beliefs and Superstitions
The Tamils had many beliefs and like most ancients were to a great measure Superstitious.
They believed in the significance of dreams which they thought would always come true. They
felt that the exact time when a dream would be realized depended on the Jamam (the quarter
of the night) in which it occurred. A dream of the first quarter of the night was expected to be
effective in a year: that of the second quarter in eight months: that of the third quarter in in
three months and that of the last quarter in ten days. For instance the dreams of Kannagi and
Kooperundevi become true very early. The following were considered as bad Omens by the
Sangam Tamils and it was referred in Purananuru; i.e. the hooting of birds as bad omen, the

falling of burning logs in all directions, riding a pig, seeing oneself naked and oneself taking oilbath.
According to Ahananuru, the Tamils had profound faith in certain other omens also. The
lizard creeping along the steep wall was watched for the direction from which it hooted. It was
known as “Asariri. Kalithogai says that in those days journeys were undertaken on auspicious
days. The same literature mentions that it was considered lucky if the left eye of a girl or the
right one of a man quivered violently. According to Silappadikaram if the planet “Velli” (Venus)

31
appeared in the south it was a bad omen. The cawing of a crow was taken to portend the arrival
of guests,
The Sangam Tamils believed in ghosts and spirits and feared. Kuruntogai speaks that
Tamils believed that the nature of next birth of a man was decided by the thoughts of his last
moments in this birth. Untouchability prevailed during this time. They believed in the efficacy of
Margosa leaves and white mustard as protective against the influence of ghosts-Pey: women
applied ney and white mustard to the hair on heads of children to protect them from evil influences
Left was inauspicious during this period. The bride after her marriage entered the motherin-law’s house placing her right foot on it.The dancer ascended the placing her right foot first
on it.
The husband must not leave the company of his wife for fifteen days after the start of

menstrual flow for her: but is not to seek union with her during the menses period. Scientific
enquiry would show that this was not mere belief but the result of careful observation. It was
customary for the women, after the child-birth to go to the public tank for bathing. During the
period of “impurity”, they were “unapproachable” and must not touch the domestic utensils.
2.5.1 Status of women
Status of Women
The Sangam literature describes the position of women in ancient Tamil Society. In the
Sangam Age women were treated with respectable position. However, male chauvinism
prevailed. The natural feminine qualities such as Achacham, Madam and Naanam were insisted
in the Sangam literature. Tolkappiyar credits the womanhood with the virtues of self-restraint,
mental peace, uprightness, uttering only purposeful words, and discrimination between good

and evil. These qualities made it clear that woman were expected to occupy a more passive
role in the society. Chastity was the most important virtue of Tamil women. They considered
Karpu much more important for them than life itself. They were highly devoted towards their
husbands. Chaste women were greatly respected in the society. The women were given
freedom to choose their life partners during the Sangam period.

32
According to the Sangam literature, a woman had to play different roles in the family
such as a dutiful wife, responsible mother and an ideal hostess to guest.
Women had no rights on property and, in general, were subordinate to men. However,
women mixed freely in the business and amusements of social life. In towns and cities, women
of lower classes were employed as hawkers, vendors, shopkeepers or servants in rich
households and in the villages; they worked in the fields and gardens along with men and
shared their hardships. The ladies of the higher classes were more confined to their homes,
but they were not secluded from society.The treatment of women in Pattinappalai is highly
commendable. In the text we find references to the young maids with shining forehead and
guiltless look are entrusted to watch the drying grains in front of the spacious houses. They

unmindingly scare away the guilt fowls by throwing away their golden ear-ring. This shows
clearly the gold ornaments were in much use among the Tamils during the Sangam age and
also they were very rich.
Women’s education was also insisted during the Sangam Age. We come to know a few
women like Avvaiyar, Ponmudiar, Kakkaippatiniyar and Nachchellaiyar, whose verses are found
in the Sangam literature. The most exquisite and soul-stirring pieces contributed by the Tamil
poetesses of Sangam period have been praised as the repositories of poetic excellence and
fertile wisdom.
2.5.2 Sati
The loving wife was a lucky one if she predeceased her husband: but if she had the
misfortune to survive him, her position become miserable. She could either perish with him on
the funeral pyre or survive to lead the humiliating life of a widow.

The practice of Sati was there in the sangam age: but this term Sati is not used in the
sangam age. Tolkappiam speaks about “Tippaidal” (falling into flames) this means that
“Tippaidal” was the most usual form of self-immolation. It must be said that there is no instance
of compelling the widow to perform sati. Sangam literature including Tirukural does not mention
about the practice of Sati.

33
In some cases women commits Sati on the death of their husbands. Kopperundevi, who
died the moment she saw her husband roll to his death, belongs to the first category.
Peunkoppendu, the wife of Bhuda-p-pandiyan, who died on the funeral pyre of her husband,
falls into the second category. Women who live widowed life relate to the lowest category of
women. Kopperundevi left the mundane world along with her lord. The ancient Tamils raised
monuments over the remains of women who committed sati. Sensitive women tried to avoid
the degraded life after the husband’s death. Hence they followed self immolation. Moreover,
for those women life had lost all meaning with the death of her husband.
2.5.3 Family
The basic unit of the ancient Tamil society was the family. A group of families constituted
the different strata of the Tamil society. Hence, the household life of the Tamil people played an

important role in the development of Tamil culture. Domestic life has been patronized as a
supreme state in the life of every human-being. Love and virtue are the important qualities of
the householders and they are considered as the symbol of the family life.
An excellent wife is a blessing to the family and that has bearing the good children are
considered as a precious ornament. The wife is known as the “illuminator” of the family. There
are number of pictures of the sweet home in the sangam literature which bear ample testimony
to the significance attached to the family life.
One could not find a parallel to this type of reverence and respect shown to the family life
in any other ancient civilizations of the world.
2.5.4 Widowhood
From the epic Manimekalai we understand that it was not every woman whose husband

predeceased her followed self immolation. The life of a widow was to be that of an ascetic. It
was a life of Nonbu (Penance). It was a degraded life: for a woman life was not worthwhile after
her husband’s demise. It was known as Kaimmai, the condition of being reduced or bereaved:
and a woman so bereaved was a Kaimpen.

34
She was prescribed a kind of diet to follow. The widow had to serve symbolic, sacrificial
food for the departed soul of her husband and she was to clean, scrub and wash the floor of the
house The Tamil literary work says that “the weeping widow washed the ground with her tears”.
Naturally the rigours of a widowed life drove a few loving and sensitive women to prefer to
death to a life of such humiliation.
2.6 Education
The value and importance of education were fully realized by the Tamils of the sangam
age. Tirukkural provides an elaborate exposition of the value of learning. The sangam classics
show that education was popular among all classes of people as the poets invariably belong to
different classes. The patinenkil kanakku works indicate that educational activities had continued
to be steady even after the Sangam age. Parents were keen in the education of their children.

Ponmutiyar a sangam poetess says that it is the duty of the father to educate his son.
Pattinappalai reveals that in Pukar, there were many eminent scholars who had hoisted flags
so as to invite other great scholars for debate. This shows that education was much appreciated
by all classes and hence there were many scholars and poets
The student began their education in the young age. They were the personal disciples of
the teacher. The students wrote on dried and cut palm leaf bits. The leaves are called “Olai”
and the bundle of leaves was a “Suvadi” The teacher was paid either in cash or in kind by the
students. The students gave their manual labour and wealth to the teacher. During the Sangam
age much of the teaching was oral. The teacher was given great respect. In view of the above
facts, it is clear that education was popular among all people and poets represented all
communities.

2.7 Fine Arts
Painting
Fine arts took fine shape during the sangam age. The Tamils of the Sangam age paid
proper attention for the painting. Sangam classics reveal that the figures of Gods and natural
sceneries were painted on the walls as well as on canvas. Pattinappalai refers to the paintings

35
of Goddess Tirumakal on the wall, and the tiger, the royal emblem on the doors. It also hints
about various figures painted on the walls. It is sure that there might have been literature on
painting. Manimekalai mentions about “Oviyac cennul”. It says that the painter will create the
figure to draw in his mind first then draw it and finally paint it. The unpainted drawing was called
“Punaiya Oviyam”. The painting in Tamil was called “Oviyam” and the painter was called “Oviyan”.
Sculpture
Sculpture was a familiar plastic art for the Sangam Tamils. The artists were called
“Mannittaral”, experts in stucco work. The sculptors were called “Sirpasarigal. Since they have
used perishable material for making sculptures, there is no concrete evidence about the Sangam
paintings and sculptures. We have reference from the literary work Silappadikkaram which

speaks about the dolls and images as Pavai. These images were worshipped in the temple of
those days.
Dance and Drama
Dance and Drama could not function without music. It was the soul of the other two fine
arts. Dance was performed by both men and women. Attan Atti was a damcer. He was the
celebrated husband of Adi Mandi, a daughter of karikal chola. Natanam was the term used for
dance in Sanskrit, and Natakam was the term used for drama. . A Kuttan was a male dancer,
and a Kutti was a female dancer.
In the sangam period the dancing had attained a high degree of excellence and was
cultivated with great enthusiasm. There were many kinds of dances such as Vallikkuttu,
Kuravaikkuttu and so on. This art was well developed during the sangam age and the dance
performance exhibited by Matavi was quite different from those of Vallikkuttu, etc., and far

advanced. She received the Royal Award of 1008 kalanchu pon which was the custom of those
days.
Drama was an “attempt to represent on the stage a story” of course to the accompaniment
of Music. It was otherwise called Natakam. Among the dramas Kuravai Kuttu, Kumarikkuttu
and Tunangai kuttu were famous during this period.

36
Music
The Tamils of the Sangam age had acquired a remarkable skill in Music. They took great
delight in enjoying music both vocal and instrumental. They were very much interested to
witness either a dance performance or a play. This can be ascertained from the concept of
“Muttamil” that is Iyal, Isai and Natakam.
Pattinappalai shows that the citizens of Pukar were used to gather at a common place to
enjoy music and witness dramas. The term “isai” itself denotes that the music melt the minds of
the people. Whenever we think of Tamil music we have to think about the “pan” the melody of
Tamil isai. The Tamils of the sangam age were far advanced in Music. They had separate pan
for every region, namely kurincippam for kurinci region, pancuram for palai region, marutappan
for marudham region and cevvalippan for neytal region. In the same way they had separate

yal (stringe instrument) for the five regions and they were called with the names of the respective
regions, but vilari Yal for neytal region. There were seven tunes called Kura, tuttarn, kaikkoli,
ulal, Ili, vilari and taram, each representing the seven strings of Yal. It was also restricted that
a particular pan should be sung only in a particular time and there were appropriately adjusted
musical tunes suited to various occasions such as marriage, religious functions, coronation or
war.
Musical Instruments
There were numerous musical instruments in Tamilakam. A sangam literature mentions
about the Kulal, yal, Mulavu and Murasu. The most prominent Kulal of the Sangam age is
identified with the present flute. There were various types of Yal. The Mulavu (tabor) and the
mulavu (drum) are the leather instruments. The mracu had played a prominent part in the
royal activities.

Thus these evidences show clearly that the Tamils of the sangam age acquainted a
remarkable skill in the field of music.
In view of the facts we have seen so far, it is clear that the fine arts such as Music, Dance
and Drama as well as Painting and Sculpture were well developed during the Sangam age.

37
2.8 Summary
Thus the social order of the people was based either on the region in which they lived or
on the occupation which they had adopted. The occupational or professional order in the long
run became birth-based. Sangam Age people had a well- organized social life. They lived in
both towns and rural areas.
