3.1 Introduction
The Sangam economy was very simple. The Tamil society had enjoyed an affluent
economy during the Sangam Age. Agriculture, industry, trade and commerce made the Sangam
Tamils almost self-sufficient. Exports were also made to the other parts of the world.
3.2 Agriculture
Agriculture
During the Sangam age and even afterwards agriculture was the main occupation of the
Tamils. In the beginning the people cultivated some coarse varieties of paddy and other grains
such as millets. Gradually the methods of cultivation had improved and during the sangam
age, it had become well developed. The agriculturists in Sangam Age had maintained a
respectable status among the people. Tirukkural, the scripture of the Tamils, praises the nature
and importance of agriculture in an entire chapter.

Agriculture alone can save the mankind from the pangs of hunger and hence almost all
the people have to depend either directly or indirectly on agriculturists. They alone can be
generous as they have a good stock of grains always with them and the word “Velanmai” which
denoted agriculture first, later denoted the hospitality. Pattinappalai speaks in detail about the
public feeding twice.Ilango adigal says that the appeasement of the man’s appetite and the
sustenance of the king’s prowess depend on the agriculture.
The Palar, the Pennar, the Kaveri, the Vaigai and the Tamraparani – to mention only the
larger among the Tamil rivers sustained the fertility of the land. The delta region was very
fertile. Pattinappalai says that cultivation was going on throughout the year without any interval,
and hence the fields were always with one crop or the other. Paddy cultivation yielded an

40
enormous and surplus return. This helped the people to be self-sufficient in food, their vital
need: and the surplus grains helped them to get sufficient money for their other necessary
expenses and also improved their economic condition to some extent, besides improving the
economic condition of the country also.
3.2.1 Cattle Rearing
Cattle are closely connected with agriculture. Bulls and Buffaloes are much needed for
agriculture. Besides this the milk and the milk-products are used as food. In those days there
was a separate class of people set apart for the purpose. They were called ayar, Itaiyar, koval
and Potuvar. Their main occupation was dairy farming and other allied works which provided
their livelihood. The sale of milk and milk-products helped the people to improve their economic
condition.
3.2.2 Hunting

Hunting was the profession for the people who lived in the hilly tract and forest areas. It
was also treated as a sport by the rich living in other parts of the country. Meat formed part of
the daily food of the majority of the people and hunters had a good earning in those days.
Besides, they had extract honey and ivory.
3.2.3 Fishing
Fishing was an important occupation as it yielded much profit. The peple who were
engaged in fishing were called as ‘minavar’ and ‘valaiyari’. They engaged themselves in pearlfishing and collecting conch-shells, which fetched a fair fortune. They earned much by fishing
and it was also an important occupation.
3.2.4 Salt Manufacture
Salt was manufactured in coastal areas .Pattinappalai explains that salt was sold in
exchange of paddy which was used as a measure of value then and the boats were used for

the purpose. The people engaged in the salt trade were called “umanar”. Building of boats and
other industries flourished during the sangam age

41
3.2.5 Textile industry
Apart from agriculture, spinning and weaving were the most important and widely practiced
crafts. Spinning was done by patient women in spare time.Uraiyur and Madurai were famous
for weaving. The Periplus mentions the fineness of Tamil Textile Fabrics especially those of
Uraiyur. We have abundant references in contemporary Tamil literature about the beauty and
fitness of the textile products. The art of weaving attained a high degree of perfection. Weaving
of complex patterns on both cotton and silk are mentioned in the Tamil Literature.
1) Cotton Clothes
There were varieties and grades with regard to cotton fabrics.
The cotton clothes were so nicely woven which looked like the slough of the snake or a
cloud or smoke or stream. There were important centers of cotton textiles and saris. Uraiyur

deserves special mention in this regard. Even today it ranks as the foremost centre of cotton
saris.
2) Silk Industry
Silk Industry was also flourished and foreigners were interested in buying silk clothes.
Silk clothes were variously known as Kosikam, Pithakam, Sunnam, Pedakam, Panakam,
Vanadai, Ponneluttu, Kaththulam etc. Kanchipuram was a popular centre of silk clothes and
saris. Even today it is famous for silk. Pattukkottai was yet another center which seems to have
attracted the Chinese traders. Embroidery cloth was used by them during the Sangam period.
3) Dyeing
Dyeing was a widespread ancillary industry to weaving: and the blue dye for the lenon
cloth was a favourite colour with the consumers. The excavations conducted at places like
Arikamedu and Uraiyur and from that they found about dyeing vats built with several course of
bricks.

Thus we can conclude that next to Agriculture Textile industry provided employement
opportunites and also developed the foreign trade.

42
3.2.6 Sugarcane Industry
Pattinappalai reveals that there were sugarcane presses, where the juice was boiled and
jaggery and sugar were prepared. The fragrant smoke coming out of the boiling juice made the
lily flowers grown in the nearby fields, to grow pale and fade. This shows that the ancient
Tamils were carrying on this industry as one of the main cottage industries which yielded them
much profit.
3.2.7 Pottery
Potters and their produce are mentioned in the Sangam literature. The art of making
pottery was flourished as a cottage industry in the Sangam period. There were different ceramic
industries prevalent and the techniques and methods employed in the industry were perfectly
in tune with the demands of the people. Majority of the people commonly used these vessels.
Due to demand supply has become more. Hence many people engaged in this profession.

The art has reached perfection during the Sangam Age. But in the post sangam period these
vessels slowly and steadily replaced by those made of metals like iron, copper, tin, lead etc.
However, they continued to be used by the poor and in the rural even today.
3.2.8 Metal Carving and Cutting
The Tamils developed advanced techniques in the field of metal carving and cutting.
Metals like gold, silver, copper and iron were used in this industry. Ornaments were made out
of both gold and silver. Bangles, beads and vessels were made out of copper. Iron was the
most popular and common metal and was used for making objects of many kind. Agricultural
equipment and articles of warfare were made out of iron. Iron was available in plenty in the
country at that time. In the same manner gold mines were reported to have been identified in
the Nilgris and the adjoining areas

Blacksmith rendered their effective service for the society. He was known as Kollan
with the famous title Karungaikkollan (meaning the strong armed smith). The goldsmith, were
called as Porkollan. Silapathikaram mentions about Porkollar for Goldsmith. He was the dealer
in gold and manufacturer of jewels and ornaments. They have organized themselves into
occupational group and lived in a separate block of quarters. . They were treated as low-born
persons.

43
3.2.9 Stone Cutting and Carving
Stone Cutting and Carving was a yet another cottage industry and provided employment
opportunity to the people. The semi-precious stones like Quartz, Jasper, beryl, crystal etc:
where used for making beads and studs. We are able to get their beads and semi-precious
stones from the excavation sites. From literary source we come to know that these ornaments
were sent to North India.
3.2.10 Beads and Bangle-making Industry
Beads and bangles were manufactured in a large scale out of gold, copper, glass, ivory
and terracota.Shells beads and bangles were popular with women folk of the Sangam age,
Bangles reached beyond seas and thus it led to the development of trade contacts.
3.3 Trade
Literature provides information about the extensive trade carried on those days in
Tamilakam. It explains about the articles imported or exported at the Pukar port. Further in

those days they had the trade with barter system.
3.3.1 Inland Trade

44
The inland trade was in a flourishing condition in the sangam age. Most of the trade was
carried on by barter. Paddy got in barter of salt. Other commodities were also sold in barter.
Peddlers used to sell paddy, millets, vegetables, liquor, etc. and occasionally clothes and
ornaments also. The exchange of essential commodities such as paddy, salt, vegetable, etc.
on a barter basis was Common in those days, especially in villages. Side by side there were
bazaars and markets in towns and cities, where the monetary system was prevalent. We learn
from sangam classics that the indigenous coins of Tamils were in use. Sangam classics
reveal that paddy and salt were used as a measure of value. In early days, paddy and salt were
given as wages.
There were bazaars markets in town. The bazaar or market is mentioned as “Angadi”.

There were Nalangadi (day bazaar) and Allangadi (evening or night bazaar). In these markets
such large varieties and large quantities of goods were sold and purchased. Crowds thronged
into the markets for busy transactions. Silappadikaram gives a detailed description of the markets
in the city of Puhar.
In Madurai people of many countries speaking many languages crowded for busy
transactions. Especially foreigners who had come from outside Tamilaham made wholesale
purchase of Tamilian goods for sale elsewhere. In the Allangadi or evening bazaar in Madurai
the following people were busy in selling and buying; Namely the grocers, the sellers of couchbangles, goldsmiths, appraisers of gold articles, sellers in foreign cloth, other textile dealers,
sellers of copper wares, painters, and dealers in perfumes , flowers and sandal paste.

The following commodities were sold in the bazaar of Puhar: i.e. dyes, Scented powder,
sandal paste, flowers and aromatic wood like ahil were sold in abundance .Silapathikaram
reveals that flowers were greatly in demand especially during festivals and more particularly
during the festival of Indra.
Normally textile dealers, sellers of perfumes, flowers sandal paste, scented-powder, sellers
of salt, oil mongers, dealers in bronze and copper wares, carpenters, goldsmiths, artists like
painters and sculptors, dealer in dolls, lapidaries, those that sold false hair or fashionable wigs,
traders in sheep, fish and mutton and sellers of cakes and vegetable edibles thronged the

45
bazaar. Pattinappalai mentions the market place as ‘avanam’ and flags were flying in front of
the shops indicating the sale of particular commodities and the poem also mentions the sale of
salt, tasty victuals, fried fish and meat and toddy. The traders lived in separate streets. There
were warehouses near the bazaar.
The merchants functioned often in a body. Apart from the tendency to associate as
‘guilds’ and ‘chambers of commerce” the wandering hawkers literally went about in large numbers
together. Such merchant bodies were called “Vanikachchattu” Such caravan of traders moved
from place to place for business. They were escorted by the warriors. In spite of these protective
measures, they were not free from danger from robber gangs.
The pearl of the Pandya kingdom has been a much desired article in the kingdoms of the

Gangetic Valley. The Arthasastra of Kautilya mentions few commodities as coming from the
land of the Pandyas namely Pearl and cotton fabric from Madurai.
Thus the Sangam people had brisk internal trade. The wholesalers, retailers and hawkers
had indulged themselves in brisk trade. Barter system prevailed in internal trade. The business
people sold their goods by openly announcing the profits that they were aiming at. Honest
trade led to increased trade and the increased trade led to the increased prosperity. Integrity in
trade was accepted as a general principle.
3.3.2 Foreign Trade
From early times Tamilaham carried on an extensive trade with foreign countries. The
great secret of her foreign trade is her possession of certain commodities which have always
been in great demand in foreign markets: pepper, ginger and rice among food products: sandal

wood, almug among trees: cardamom, cinnamon and turmeric among stimulating spices: Ivory
and pearls for luxurious ornaments: cotton fabrics for dress: monkeys, deer and peacocks
among favourite domesticated animals and birds, cheetahs, and tigers and elephants among
the wild animals. These articles were in great demand in the crowded bazaars of foreign lands.
It is certain that there was a well –developed maritime trade in Tamilaham during the Sangam
age.

46
1) Hebrews
The most ancient trade contact Tamilaham had was with the ancient land of Hebrews.
The Hebrew Bible mentions two important objects. They are “kapin” and “tukim”. Clearly Kapim
is Kapi which is easily in Tamil Kavi i.e. Monkey and Tukim is the Tamil “togai”i.e. peacock.
2) Greece:
Tamil trade with Greece is amply borne out by the existence in Greek vocabulary of Tamil
names of many objects: the Greeeks ha ve Oruza for “rice” from the Tamil arisi. Tamil “Chiruttai”
become “cheetah” in English. “Corrundun” is clear transliteration of the Tamil “Kurundam”,
Sandalwood was derived straight from “sandana” or “sandu”.
The pearl of the Pandya kingdom was a great attraction to foreigners in those days. Pliny
mentions about cottonara as a centre of pepper trade. The place Cottanera is identified with
kuttanad
3) Light House

Perumpanatrupadai mentions about the light houses in order to direct the ships.The light
house was known as Kalangarai Illangusudar.
4) Harbour
Sangam literature and notes of foreigners refer to the harbours where foreign ships
anchored. Puhar (Chola kingdom) alias Kaveripoompattinam, Musiri (Chera Kingdom) and
Korkai (Pandya kingdom) were some of the noteworthy harbours of the sangam age.
5) Puhar (Kaveripoompattinam)
Puhar was a remarkable harbor of chola kingdom. Pattinappalai presents a vivid puicture
of the pukar port with the articles either imported or exported. Black pepper was brought by
carts. Sandal and fragrant incense obtained from the eagle wood came from the western
ranges. Pearl and red coral came from the southern and eastern seas respectively. Precious
things from Ceylon and rare manufactured things from Burma also arrived. .We learn from

Purananuru that Mavilankai, Puraiyaru or Purunthai and Pokar were the important chola ports
of those days.

47
6) Musiri
It was the gateway of western India on those days. Musiri was a busy harbor of chera
kingdom. Purananuru mentions that several ships of Tamil Nadu were anchored there. Paddy
(received in exchangeof fish), pepper, golden articles, ivory, silk and pearls etc. were found in
this harbor. Periplus states that these articles were exported.
7) Korkai
Korkai harbor was famous for its beautiful pearls. Periplus states that prisoners were
employed to collect pearls and korkai harbor belonged to the Pandya kingdom. Madurai Kanchi
was all in praise for korkai harbor. Korkai was also known for its Valamburi Sangu. Thus from
the above account it is very obvious that the foreign trade of Sangam Tamilaham was very
brisk and extensive.
The people of the Sangam age traded with Rome, Greece, Africa, Sri Lanka and South

East Asia. The Romans liked the pearls of the Pandya kingdom. Gemstones, ivory, sandalwood,
peacock, cotton and silks, textiles and spices were exported to Greece and Rome. Many gold
and silver coins that were issued by the Roman Emperors like Augustus, Tiberius and Nero
have been found in all parts of Tamil Nadu indicating flourishing trade. Major exports of the
Sangam age were cotton fabrics and spices like pepper, ginger, cardamom, cinnamon and
turmeric along with ivory products, pearls and precious stones .Major imports for the traders
were horses, gold, and sweet wine.
Thus Trade was a great source of income to the Government by way of duties and tolls
and hence it was the main source of country’s economy. Considering all these above mentioned
facts, it may be said that the economic condition of the country was sound
3.3.3 Tamilaham and Rome

We find large hoards of Roman Gold coins of the Augustan Age in many parts of South
India. This shows that the sangam people had brisk trade with Rome which resulted in the
inflow of considerable gold into Tamilaham. Periplus says that Tamilaham had a direct trade
route to Arabia, Egypt and Rome One of the most important articles which came from India
was cotton and perhaps silk,.

48
The eastern trade beyond Tamilaham with Burma, Malaya, Java, Sumatra and china
was mostly in the hands of the Tamils. Strabo says that 120 ships sailed to South India from
Harmuz and he saw a Pandiyan embassy at the Royal Court of Augustus. There was a brisk
trade in silk with China besides sugar. Greeks and Romans came to Tamilaham as traders but
soon arose many commercial colonies in Tamilaham. Greek merchants were called “Yavanas”
first, subsequently it was applied to Romans, still later to all foreignes including the Arabs The
foreign merchants moved about the bazaars freely and transacted business. There might have
been translators to help them in their transactions.
3.3.4. Coinage
Apart from the barter system coins were also used as medium of exchange in Trade.
The local coins were known as “punch mark coins” and were made out of silver, copper and

lead. They bear punch marks or symbols such as sun, moon, river, tree in railing, mountain etc.
Besides these gold coins, known as Kalanju and Pon were also used by the Sangam Tamils.
. In Puhar and in Madurai mints were situated
3.4 Summary
The Sangam people had brisk trade. The wholesalers, retailers and hawkers had indulged
themselves in brisk trade. Barter system prevailed in internal trade. The business people sold
their goods by openly announcing the profits that they were aiming at. Honest trade led to
increased trade and the increased trade led to the increased prosperity. Integrity in trade was
accepted as a general principle.

4.1 Introduction
Sangam literature can be considered as the more valuable and most reliable source for
the study of the Sangam Age. Sangam poets were not inhibited be excessively religious or any
other extraneous sentiments. The verses of Sangam poets belonged to a spontaneous and
natural type of poetry which is free from exaggeration and unnatural hyperbole, and by the
simplicity and directness, of smiles they serve as a useful and dependable source of history of
Tamil Nadu. The Tamil Sangam period has been truly called the “Augustan age” of Tamil
literature.
4.2. Literature
The Sangam literature consists of Tolkappiam, the Pattuppattu (the ten Idylls), the
Ettuttokai (the Eight Anthologies) and the Patintnkilkanakku (Eighteen minor works) and the
Twin epics namely Silappadikaram and Manimegalai.
The subject matter of Sangam literature is divided into two broad divisions namely Akam

and Puram and they are called as Akattinai and Purattinai. Akam speaks about love whereas
Puram deals witl other worldly affairs such as war, Government, society, etc.
4.2.1 Tolkappiam
Tolkappiam is the oldest Tamil Grammar. In fact it is the oldest extant Tamil Work .Its
author was Tolkappier. It is divided into three major parts called Eluttu Adikaram, Sol Adikaram,

52
and Porul Adikaram. Each Adikaram consists of 9 Iyals and in all 1612 Sutras. It is the traditional
method of expounding Tamil Grammar. Porul Adikaram reveals to us the Sangam Tamils concept
and practice of warfare in an elaborate manner.
4.2.2. Eight Anthologies
Of the eight Anthologies Narrinai, Kuruntogai, Ainkurunuru, Ahananuru and Kalitogai
belonged to the Aham group. Purananuru, Padirrupattu and Paripadal belonged to the Puram
group
(1) Narrinai
It consists of 400 stanzas: which explains about all the five Tinais. 275 poets wrote these
poems. The important name of the sea ports and other big towns are found in this work. Tondi,
Korkai, Kunrur etc. are some of them. This work was compiled by Pannadu Tanta Maran Valuti.
(2) Kurunthogai
205 poets composed all the 402 poems of this work. Purikko Patronised and Purikkudi

Kilar compiled these songs. The poems of Atimantiyar, Iraiyanar, and Velliivitiyar are found in
the Kuruntogai. The names of the rulers like Ori, Pari, Nalli etc., and Places like Srimallur,
Urantai, and Mantari are found. The social life of the Sangam Age is beautifully described in
this work.
(3) Ainkurunuru
The poets Orampogiyar, Ammuvanar, kapilar, Otalantaiyar and Peyanar composed 500
poems, in five divisions of 100 poems each, describing the five Tinais. These poems were
compiled by Pulatturai Murriya Kudalur Kilar. The characters of the three rulers were described
in these poems. The socio-economic lives of the people are narrated in this work.
(4) Ahananuru
It deals with all the five Tinais. It consists of 400 poems. Otherwise Ahananuru is known
as Neduntogai. This work was written by 145 poets and was compiled by Ukkirapperuvaluti.
Mauryan invasion of South India is referred in this work by Mamulanar.

53
(5) Kalithogai
It consists of 250 poems dealing with five Tinais. There are different views about the
author of the poem.. Some of the social customs and practices were depicted in this work.
References to the worship of Tirumal, Balaraman, Siva and Murugan are found in Kalithogai.
(6) Padirrupattu
It is a quasi-historical collection of Ten Ten of verses composed by the different poets.
Each poem depicts about a chera monarch. Karur, Musiri, Tondi are some of the important
places of Cheras, Utiyam Cheral, Imayavaramban, Nedunchelyan Cheran Senguttuvan etc.,
are some of the Chera Kings. Further it speaks about the rulers patronization of the Tamil
poets.
(7) Purunanuru
Each of 400 stanzas of Purananuru contains between 4 and 40 lines. 160 poets composed
these songs. These poems were composed in honour of 18 Chera rulers, 18 Chola rulers, 15

Pandiya rulers and a number of Chieftains of Tamilaham. This work serves as an important
source material to trace the History of Sangam rulers namely chera, chola and Pandiya
(8) Paripadal
It deals with both Aham and Puram. Though it consists of 70 poems we were able to get
only 22 poems. This literary work helps us to trace the socio-religious life of the Sangam Tamils.
The worship of Tirumal, Murugan, and Korravai were described in this work.
4.2.3 Pattupattu
Pathupattu is an anthology of ten mid-length books and one of the oldest surviving works
of Tamil poetry. They are Thirumurukarruppadai, Porunararruppadai, Sirupanarruppadai,
Perumpanarruppadai, Mullaippattu, Maduraikkanchi, Nedulvadai, Kurinjippattu, Pattinappalai
and Malaipadukadam.
These works are composed in aciriyam or akarvapa which has three lines as minimum
and thousand lines as maximum. Amomg the Ten Idyls, five belongs to Aatrupadai.

54
Aatrupadai means a literary device by which a bard or a minstrel who has received gifts
from some wealthy patron is supposed to direct another to the same patron. This gives the
occasion to the poet, among other topics, to describe in great detail the natural beauty, fertility,
and resources of the territory that has to be traversed to reach the palace of the patron
(1) Thirumurukarruppadai:
This work contains 317 lines, composed by Nakkirar, is a devotional song on Lord Murugan.
The author depicts the way to a devotee to attain the supreme bliss of Lord Murugan at the six
places called Arupadaividu. Six Abodes of Muruga are: Thirupparamkunram Thiruverakam
(Swamimalai), Thiruaavinankudi (Palani), Thirucheeralaivaai (Thiruchendur), Kundruthoraadal
(Tiruttani) and Pazhamudircholai.
(2) Porunararruppadai
Porunararruppadai, with 248 lines praising the famous chola king Karikal Valavan was

composed by Mutattamak kanniyar.
Porunaraatruppadai contains 250 lines of poems in the Achiriyappa meter. The poems
were written by the poet Mutathaamakkanniyaar in praise of
the Chola king KarikalaChola. Porunaraatruppadai belongs to the Ten Idyls collection and follows
the Arruppadtai style, a device used by most of the books in the Pattupattu collection
(3) Sirupanarruppadai
Sirupanarruppadai, with 269 lines praising Nalliyak Kotan, a chieftain under the chola
king was composed by Nallur Nattattanar. The poverty life of Paradavar, the virali and her
dance are given.
(4) Perumpanarruppadai
Perumpanarruppadai contains 500 lines of poetry in the Achiriyappa meter. The poems
were written by the poet Uruttirankannanar in praise of King Tondaiman Ilandiraiyan.
Perumpanarruppadai belongs to theTen Idyls collection and follows the Arrupadai style, a

device used by most of the books in the Pattupattu collection. The work mentions how a brother of
an ancient Chola king met with a Naga princess and had by him a son. The son was affectionately
called Ilam Tiraiyan or literally the Young Tiraiyan by the family. Tiraiyar was the name of the

55
naga tribe to which his mother belonged. Over the course of time he went on to rise to the
position of the Lord of Thondaimandalam and took on the title Tondaiman.
(5) Mullaippattu
Mullaippattu, with 103 lines, the shortest among the verses of Ten Idyls, is based on the
subjective element of Mullaittinai. The composer is Nappoothanaar. It speaks about the mental
condition of a separated wife from her husbandwho was away in the battlefield. Mullaippattu is
a pure love poem, and talks about the heroine longing for the hero who had left her to fight a
war. In the olden days, the soldiers use to come back to their home country during the rainy
season to look after their primary profession of agriculture. The heroine laments that although
the rainy season had already started, that her lover had not returned from battle. The description

of the country in the rainy season is particularly enjoyable in this book.
(6) Maduraikkanchi
Maduraikkanchi, with 782 lines, is the longest among the ten idylls based on the subjective
element of Kanchittinai, which belongs to Puram. Kanchittinai indicates the mortality of human
beings. The poems were written by the poet Mangudi Maruthanaar in praise of
the Pandya king Nedunjeliyan II on the occasion of his victory at the battle of
Talayanankanam.The author by way of praising the Pandyan king presents a detailed description
of his kingdom, his administration and his capital Madurai.
(7) Nedulvadai
Nedulvadai is a part of the Ten Idyls collection, which is the oldest available collection of
long poems in Sangam Tamils. Nedulvadai, with 188 lines, was composed by the poet Nakkirar
is based on the subject element of Mullaittinai, which belongs to Aham. But it contains an

indirect reference to Pandiyan king who was away in the war front and hence it is considered to
be of Vakaittinai, which is part of Purattinai.
(8) Kurincippattu
Kurinjippattu with 262 lines is based on the subjective element of Kurunchit tinai that is
pre-marital love or love at first sight. This contains a fine description of mountain scenery and

56
speaks about as many as ninety nine flowers including Kurinchi flower which will blossom once
in twelve years and they are found largely on the Western Ghats especially on the Nilgris. This
was composed by Kapilar in order to impart Tamil knowledge to Prakattan, an Aryan king.
(9) Pattinappalai
This love poem was composed by Uruthirankannanar. Pattinappalai with 301 lines, a
fairly long verse, has a fine picture of Kaveripumpattinam and its suburbs, which was then
Chola capital and the main sea-port: it also gives a detailed account of the destruction caused
by Tirumavalavan the pattutai talavan to his enemy’s countries. The splendor of river Kaveri,
the rich seaborns trade and he flags flying aloft over the city are vividly described.
(10) Malaipatukadam
It is also known as Kuttararruppadai. Malaipatukadam with 583 lines, the second longest

among the Ten Idylls is composed on the lines of Arruppadai style. It was sung by Perunkunur
Perunkausikar. In this poem a bard who received gifts from Nanan directs a dancer and his
group to the same patron for the purpose of receiving gifts. It also describes the lifestyle of the
folk dancers of the ancient Tamil country.
4.2.4 Patinenkilkanakku
Patinenkilkanakku is a collection of eighteen poetic works created during the Sangam
period.The poems are written in the Venba meter and are relatively short in length. Most of the
books deal with morals and ethics. Pathinenkilkanakku contains the following books: Nalatiyar,
Nanmanikkadigai, Inna Narpadu, Iniyavi Narpadu, Kar Narpadu, Kalavali Narpadu, Ainthinai
Aimpadu, Thinaimoli Aimpathu, Ainthinai Elupadu, Tinaimalai Nurrambadu, Tirukkural,
Tirukadigam, Achara kovai,Palamoli, Sirupanchamulam, Mutumolikanchi, Elathi and Kainnilai.

(1) Nalatiyar
It was composed by padumanar. It consists of 40 chapters. Each chapter contains ten
stanzas. It also deals with Aram, Porul and Inbam.Certain social customs of the people regarding
wedding, serving food to the poor in the backyard, disposal of the dead are described in this
work.

57
(2) Nanmanikkadigai
Nanmanikkadigai is a Tamil poetic work belonging to the Eighteen minor works anthology
of Tamil literature contains one hundred songs written by the poet Vilambi Naganaar. Since
this poem is famous and easy to understand, this work in included in the school Tamil Nadu
text books. Each poem of Nanmanikkadigai contains four different ideas. The
name Nanmanikkadigai denotes the fact that comparing of the four ideas to four well-chosen
gems adorning each poem.
(3) Inna Narpadu
This poem comes under eighteen minor works. It was authored by Kapilar. It is a collection
of 40 poems describing the most undesirable things one should avoid. One of the meanings of
the Tamil word Inna is one that brings displeasure. This poem indicates about four harmful
things one has to avoid in their life namely a beautiful and disloyal wife, the wealth of a miser,

a life under tyrant and a beauty of a flower without fragerance.
(4) Iniyavi Narpadu
Iniyavi Narpadu is a Tamil poetic work belonging to Patinenkilkanakku work. . This poem
belongs to sangam period. It is a collection of forty poems written by the poet Putham
Sernthanar. It describes the most desirable things in life. They have adopted the Venba meter
for their poems. This collection is very similar to Inna Narpadu. This work says that four
categories of things one should have in life for example: learning even at the time of begging,
to listen to the advice of learned persons, healthy children and strength to not covet other’s
spouse.
Thus both Iniyavi Narpadu, and Inna Narpadu explains in concise and simple manner
narrates about the moral codes essential for an individual as well as to the society. Further

these works insisting about the importance of education and individual responsibility in society.
(5) Kar Narpadu
This work comes under the eighteen minor works of the sangam age and it contains forty
poems written by the poet Kannankoothanaar .The poet belonged to Madurai region. The

58
poem deals with Ahattinnai and it narrates about the subjects like the intangibles of life such as
human emotions, love, separation, lover’s quarrels, etc. Many poems explain about how the
heroine was consoled by her friend by way of describing the beauties of the rainy season. Here
we should know the meaning of Kar namely rain in Tamil.
(6) Kalavazhi Narpathu
Kalavazhi Narpathu work belongs to Sangam age. This work contains forty poems and
the author of this work was the poet Poigayaar. The poem deals with Purattinnai. It deals with
the subjects like war, politics, wealth, etc.
(7) Ainthinai Aimpathu
Ainthinai Aimpathu contains fifty poems written by the poet Kannankoothanaar who was
from Madurai. The poems of, Ainthinai Aimpathu, deal with the agam (internal) subjects. Agam
denotes the subject matters that deal with the intangibles of life such as human emotions, love,

separation, lovers’ quarrels, etc. The poems of Ainthinai Aimpathu are divided into ten poems
for each of the five thinai, of Sangam poetry and describe in detail the situation and emotions
specific to each division of the land.
(8) Tinamalai Aimpathu
Tinamalai Aimpathu contains fifty poems. This work was written by the poet Kannan
Chenthanaar.The poem deals with Ahattinnai namely internal subjects of human beings. This
was divided into ten poems for each of five thinai of Sangam age namely Kurinji, Mullai,
Marudham, Neydal and Palai.
(9) Ainthinai Elupadu
This work contains seventy poems written by the poet Muvathiyaar.This work deals with
Ahattinnai of sangam age. Aham denotes the subject matters that deal with the intangibles of
life such as human emotions, love, separation, lovers’ quarrels, etc. The poems of Ainthinai

Elupatu are divided into fourteen poems for each of the five thinai, of Sangam poetry and
describe in detail the situation and emotions specific to each division of the land . They
are mullai, kurinji, marutham, paalai and neithal.

59
(10) Thinaimalai Nurru Aimpathu
This work contains 154 poems. This poem was authored by the poet Kanimeythaviyaar.
These poems dealt with Ahattinnai of sangam Tamils. TiIaimalai NurruAimpatu poems are
categorized into 30 poems for each of the five Tinnai. It explains in detail about the situation
and emotion specific to each thinnai.
(11) Tirukkural
Thirukkural poem consists of 1330 couplets divided into 133 chapters. This work was
divided into three broad divisions namely Aram, Porul and Inbam. . It deals with everyday
virtues of an individual. It is considered as one of the best Secular work in Tamil literature.
Thiruvalluvar was the author of this work. More than hundred scholars have written the summary
foe this work. It has been translated into nearly forty languages. The Kural has influenced

many scholars across the ethical, social, political, economical, religious, philosophical, and
spiritual spheres. In order to honour the author recently the Tamil Nadu Government erected
a 133 feet statue in the Kanyakumari sea shore.
(12) Tirukadugam
This poem contains 100 poems. The author of this work was Nallathanaar. The poems of
Tirukadugam are written in Venba meter. Tirukadugam uses the analogy of the traditional
herbal medicine, which uses the three herbs namely sukku, milaku, and thippili to cure diseases
of the stomach. Tirukadugam similarly uses three different varieties to explain the correct
behaviour.
(13) Acharakkovai
Acharakkovai contains 100 poems written by the poet Peruvaayin Mulliyaar. The poems
of Acharakkovai are written in the Venba meter. . Acharakkovai shows the influence of Sanskrit
literature and hence believed to be of a later period than the other poems in

the Pathinenkilkanakku works. The instructions in Acharakkovai are concerned with personal
ritual and the correct method to follow. Acharakkovai has 100 stanzas in venba meter

60
(14) Palamoli
It consists of 400 verses each of which embodies a proverb. The author of this work was
Munrurayanar. There are incidental references to the chera, chola and Pandya kings and some
of the important customs of the Sangam Tamils.
(15) Sirupanchamulam
Kaniyasan composed 97 stanzas which insist the codes of moral conduct, truth, honesty,
vegetarianism and non-injury to animals are some of the important virtues emphasized in this
work. The value of education, the qualities expected of an ideal teacher, the pupil of the housewife
are described in this poem.
(16) Mudumozhikkanchi
Mudumozhikkanchi belongs to the post sangam period. This work contains 100 poems.
The author of this work was the poet Mathuraikkoodalur Kilaar. From this title we infer that he
would have lived in Madurai. Mudumozhikkanchi was divided into ten groups of ten poems

each. Further this work followed a simple poetic style to enable the lay person to understand
the messages,
(17) Elathi
Elathi contains 80 poems. This poem was written by the poet Kani Methaviyar.
Elathi emphasizes the use of the traditional herbal medicine known as elathi which uses six
herbs such as elam ,ilavanka pattai , milagu , thippili , and sukku . It also instruct us about
six values of every aspects of life in every poem in four lines.The six values are fame,
wealth,integrity, courage, education and philanthropy.
(18) Kainnilai
Kainnilai is the last work in Pathinenkilkanakku. It contains 60 poems and the author of
this work was the poet Pullangkaathanaar. Unfortunately this work is available in a damaged
condition with many of its poems only partially available. This work deals with Ahattinnai. The

poems are divided into twelve poems for each of the five thinnai namely Kurinchi, Mullai,
Marudham, Neydal and Palai.

61
4.2.5 Post-Sangam works
Next important works in the sangam age are the twin epics. Silappathikaram and
Manimegalai are known as Twin epics.
Silappathikaram
The author of this work was Elango Adigal, brother of chera king Senguttuvan, The
reason for writing this epic is mentioned by the author in the following lines: The theme of the
epic is based on Silambu (anklet). It is woven around Kovalan a rich merchant of Puhar, Kannagi
his wife, and Madhavi, a dancing girl.
Silappathikaram as a literary work is held in high regard by the Tamil people. This work
was divided into three divisions namely Puharkantam, Maduraikantam and Vanchikantam and
has a total of 5270 lines of poetry. The story of this work involves the three Tamil kingdoms of
the sangam age which were ruled by the Chola, Pandiya and Chera dynasties.

This epic explains in detail about Tamil culture and their religion the town planning and
city types and the arts of dance and Music. Thus Silappathikaram serves us as a useful source
material to study about the socio-economic conditions and political conditions of the Sangam
age.
Manimegalai
Manimegalai is one of the Twin epics. Its author was Chithalai Chathanar. This epic
contains 30 cantons. Its story is a sequel of Silappathikaram. . This epic narrates the story of
Manimegalai. She was the daughter of Kovalan and Madhavi. She was a devotee of Buddhism
and hence naturally this work provides a vivid exposition of the Philosophical doctrines of
Buddhism. It also contains an exposition of logical fallacies.
4.3 Religion and Philosophy
Religion played a predominant role in the Sangam society. Sangam literature provides a

perfect conception of the various faiths followed in the Sangam age. It speaks about the rustic
form of Varunan worship by the fishemanfolk as well as the civilized form of Murugan worship

62
by the citizens of Puhar. Sangam classics present a vivid picture of the primitive form of kantu
worship of linga worship of the early Tamils. Beyond all these we see Pallis or the hermitages
of the Jains and Buddhists.
Tolkappiyar makes a reference to Kadavul means “He that transcends thought, word,
and deed” He makes a reference in another place about four Gods namely Mayon (Thirumal)
the God of the Mullai region, Seyon (Murugan) of Kurinji God, Vendan (Indra) the deity of
Marudham and Varunan (rain God) the deity of Neydal. Murugan was considered as the God
of Kurinji region, but at the same time, he was considered as a favourite God of Tiruchendur
located in Neydal region. Though Korravai the Goddess of Palai or the desert region has no
mention in Tolkaippiyam, she is accepted as the goddess of war and victory by literature.
(1) Murugan

Kurinji people worshipped Murugan or Seyon. The term Murugan means beauty, youth
and charm. He was worshipped as a war God. Nallantuvanar a Sangam poet says that Murukan
is the lord of the seven worlds. The “vel” (spear) is his favourite weapon, and from its name he
is called as “Velan”. Undoubtedly Murugan was the favourite God of the Tamils. The worship of
Murugan was done in the entire Sangam period Korravai is often mentioned as the mother of
Murugan. In Thirumurgarruppadai he has been referred as Muruku and explained as a God of
beauty and youth with phrases such as “the body glows like the sun rising from the emerald
sea”. Further this text explains him with six faces each with a function, twelve arms, his victory
over evil, and the temples dedicated to him in the hilly region. For example Thirumurgarruppadai

states that Murugan resides in the six sacred military camps of Tirupparankunram,
Tiruchchiralaivai, Tiruvavinankudi, Tiruveragam, Pazhamudirsolai and Kunrutordal Muruga’s
vehicle is pea-cock, which is associated with snake. Lord Murugan wears Kadamba garland.
According to Sangam classics, the Murukan worship was predominant in almost all the regions.
2) Mayon (Tirumal)
Mayon was known a Mal or Tirumal. There are six verses in Paripadal exclusively intended
for Tirumal. The term “mal” means great and hence Tirumal may mean the great God. He is
also known as Vishnu from which the term Vaishnavism was derived. This deity is referred to in

63
Sangam classics such as Purananuru, Paripadal, Kalittokai and Mullaippattu a well as
Silappatikaram. He was the prominence God of the Idaiyars of Mullai region. His vehicle is
Eagle.
Various incarnations of Vishnu were known to the Sangam Tamils. Varaha, Narasimha,
Vamana, Balarama, Krishna, Rama, Parasurama are mentioned in the Sangam literature. Rama
was the great hero who defeated Ravana. Parasurama was the one who had a battle axe in his
hand. Balarama was the elder brother of Krishna. Krishna saved the people from a severe
downpour. Krishna the incarnation of Vishnu is worshipped by all people who had accepted
Vaishnavism.
3) Indran
Indra was the deity of fertile soil. In some of the Sangam literary works, the name of Indra
is mentioned. Silapathikkaram describes indran as “Maalai venkudai mannavan, literally meaning

Indra with pearl garland and white umbrella. His vehicle was the elegant white elephant
(Airavadha). Puhar, the coastal city celebrated a festival for Indra. This festival is mentioned in
Silapadikkaram as Indhira vizha in detail. This festival was celebrated for want of rain.
4) Varunan
Neithal thinnai is known for its seashore place occupied by fishermen, with God of Sea
and rain known as Varunan or Kadalon. Pattinappalai narrates about the pen-picture of the
Varuna worship offered by the fishermen folk .The full moon day was an auspicious day to
worship Varuna, the sea God. On that day the fishermen neglected fishing in the dark wide
sea and erected a horn or sword of a gravid shark as a symbol of varuna and worshipped with
offerings of food (meat and Fish) and drink (toddy).
5) Sivan
Siva is one of the great Gods of Tamils and some uphold that he is the supreme among

them. The Tamils of the Sangam age considered Siva a one of the four supreme deities, others
being Murugan, Tirumal and Valiyon. It is said that Murukan is son of Siva, hence he is called
as Cey or Ceyon but he held primordial position among other deities. During the sangam age

64
no doubt Siva held a secondary position to Murukan. Nakkirar describes these four as the
props of universe. It is said that Siva has an eye on his forehead and hence he is known as
Nerrikkannan or Mukkannan- the God of three eyes. His favourite weapon is Trident. Siva is
also known as Nataraja on account of his dances which are called kotukotti, Kapali and
Pantarankan. Although these dances belong to the Tamil conception they flourished only after
the sangam age. Invariably no temple of Siva will be without a Linga at the sanctum sanctorum
of the temple and the Linga itself is called “Sivalingam”.
6) Korravai
Korravai was the Goddess of Palai regon. She was known as Palaivol {AncientGoddess).
She was the presiding deity of the Palai region and was worshipped by the hunters. She was
worshipped by the Tamils for achieving victory in battles and for fulfilling their wishes. She was

surrounded by ghosts which perform the Tunankai dance. She was also believed to be residing
in the weapons of war belonging tp the warriors. She is mentioned as the mother of Murukan.
Veriyadal was performed before her. Sacrifices were performed.
7) Thirumakal
Pattinappalai refers to Goddess Tirumakal. In sangam classics they refer the term “tiru’
means Tirumakal (Lakshmi), wealth and beauty. Manimekalai mentions about the Goddess as
Ilakkumi. She is said to be the wife of Mayon and goddess of wealth, prosperity, good fortunes
as well as beauty. Kapilar the sangam poet describes that Tirumakal seated on a lotus flower
had ben worshipped by elephants with water and flowers.
8) Brahman
Brahma is described as a four- headed God. He is also called Mamudu Mudiycvan and
so on. It is mentioned that Brahma himself emerged from the lotus which sprouted from the

navel Tirumal. Saraswathi, the consort of Brahma is not mentioned in any work.
9) Kaman
Kaman or Manmatha is the Hindu God of human love or desire, often portrayed along
with his female counterpart Rathi. His parents were Lord Vishnu and Goddess Lakshmi.
Sugarcane, bow and floral arrow are his weapons.

65
10) Yaman
Yamaraja is a God of death, the south direction is His place.According to Vishnu purana
Yama is the son of Sun God –Surya.
11) Balaraman
Balarama otherwise called Valiyon was the elder brother of lord Krishna.. Ploughshare is
mentioned as his weapon. . Silappadikaram refers to a temple for Valiyon.
12) Sun and Moon
Sun who was considered to be the greatest of the Devas, was also worshipped like all
other Gods. Worship of crescent moon was common. Sun was first worshipped before doing
any offering to God or Goddesses. Silappadikaram begins with a prayer to Sun God.
13) Ancestor Worship
Ancestor worship in some form or the other seems to be flourished in the early days and
this might have been emerged as the hero-worship that is the worship of “natukal” or the
memorial stone which is also known as “virakkal” or hero stone.
14) Sadukkabudam and Sattan

The early Tamils believed that Sadukkabudam resided on the cross roads in
Kaviripumpattinam. This deity is known from Silappadikaram and Muchukunda brought the
Sadukkabudam from heaven and installed in Manimegalai. The Sangam people believed that
this deity would kill bad people like an unchast woman, a liar and a disloyal minister. Maduraipatti
was the guardian of the city of Madurai. In Slappadikaram this deity appears and tells Kannagi
the events of her previous births. The Koillppavai was a very ferocious deity resided in the Kolli
hills.
Sattan was another local deity worshipped by the Sangam people. . He was also known
as Sasta, Aiyanar, Aiyappa or Hariharaputra, the sons of Siva and Vishnu. Sattan was one of
the names associated with the lord Buddha. It is known that the Vaishnavites treated the Lord
Buddha as one of the avatars of Vishnu himself.

66
15) Kandu and Linga
The early Tamils planted a big stump of wood and made offerings to that. This stump of
wood was known as Kandu and the Tamils believe that God resided in it. Some scholars are of
the opinion that Siva in the form of Linga was worshipped by the Tamils. Some other scholars
do not accept this phallic form of Siva as there is no reference in Sangam literature to Linga.
16) Nature Worship
Apart from sun and moon, Sangam Tamils worshipped Rivers, Mountains and Stars. It
was believed that the trees were the abodes of some deities. Banyan tree was associated with
Lord Siva and Vishnu. Kadamba tree was connected with Murugan and Korravai with Siva.
Elephants and bulls were animals of worship as they were the vahanas of Gods. They also
worshipped snake. They made offerings to the snake pits and these offerings by the Tamilians
are following even today.

4.3.1 Method of Worship
Lamps were lighted during the time of worship Flowers and Garlands were offered and
this was known as Puppali. Food was also offered to the deity.
Nadukal worship was common in the Sangam age. The Tamils bathed the deity, offered
peacock feathers and flowers. Toddy and rice balls sprinkled with blood of sacrificed animals
were also offered. The drum used in the battlefield was also worshipped. The devotees bowed
down in reverence before the deity.
People kept images of Gods in their houses and worshipped them. The images were
known as Paai. The deities were worshipped during sunset. Lamps were lit at dusk and prayers
were offered. Invocation to God at the beginning of all important ceremonies, praying for their
successful completion was the common practice of the time.
The Brahmins followed slightly a different practice. They chanted the Vedas and Mantras.

At the time of prayer, the adult Brahmins were found with their sacred thread. They performed
sacrifices to ensure prosperity to the people. The Tamil rulers were also performed many
yagas. For example Palyagasalai Mudukudumi Peruvalusi set up numerous sacrificial places.

67
. Animals were also offered for sacrifices. The construction of pillars in the yagasala and the
chanting of mantras by the Brahmins are explained in the sangam Tamil works.
4.3.2 Temples
Tamil literary works mentions temple as Kovil or Kottam From silappadikaram we come
to know that there were temples dedicated to Airavata, baladeva, Surya, Siva, Murukan,
Kaman, yaman, Sattan and so on. Manimekalai mentions about Durga temple. It also mentions
about Jaina Pallis and Buddhist Viharas. Both the epics Silappadikaram and Manimekalai
mentions about the temple for Indra. Senguttuvan is said to have constructed a temple for
Kannagi, the chaste Goddess.
For the construction of the temples they used perishable materials hence we are not able
to have these temples in Tamil Nadu. Reference to brick temple with gopuras is found in

Manimekalai. Flags were waving on temple tops. The place where the offerings were placed
was called Balipidhai.
4.3.3 Supernatural Elements
Animism is essentially the cult of spirits which are believed to exist in the shape of demons,
Ghosts and souls which are not visible to the human eye. The ancient Tamils believed that
ghosts with disheveled hair wandered about. They hunted the battle fields and reveled in playing
with the corpses of the dead soldiers. It is believed that ghosts were connected with the life
after death because ghosts were imagined to see the living spirits of dead persons.
The Sangam Tamils believed in the heaven and hell. They also believed that by performing
penance one could attain heaven. Siva, the God of destruction in the Hindu trinity was the God
of controlling death. The early Tamils believed that the infants could easily affected by the

ghosts. In order to safe guard from the ghosts the people used to worship village deities. They
also used white mustard in order to protect them against ghosts.
4.3.4 Superstitious Beliefs
The Tamils had many beliefs and like most ancients were to a great measure Superstitious.
They believed in the significance of dreams which they thought would always come true. They

68
felt that the exact time when a dream would be realized depended on the Jamam (the quarter
of the night) in which it occurred. A dream of the first quarter of the night was expected to be
effective in a year: that of the second quarter in eight months: that of the third quarter in three
months and that of the last quarter in ten days. For instance the dreams of Kannagi and
Kooperundevi become true very early. The following were considered as bad Omens by the
Sangam Tamilsand it was referred in Purananuru; i.e. the hooting of birds as bad omen, the
falling of burning logs in all directions, riding a pig, seeing one naked and oneself taking oilbath.
According to Ahananuru, the Tamils had profound faith in certain other omens also. The
lizard creeping along the steep wall was watched for the direction from which it hooted. It was

known as “Asariri. Kalithogai says that in those days journeys were undertaken on auspicious
days. The same literature mentions that it was considered lucky if the left eye of a girl or the
right one of a man quivered violently. According to Silappadikaram if the planet “Velli” (Venus)
appeared in the south it was a bad omen. The cawing of a crow was taken to portend the arrival
of guests,
The Sangam Tamils believed in ghosts and spirits and feared. Kuruntogai speaks that
Tamils believed that the nature of next birth of a man was decided by the thoughts of his last
moments in this birth. Untouchability prevailed during this time.
They believed in the efficacy of Margosa leaves and white mustard as protective against
the influence of ghosts-Pey: women applied ney and white mustard to the hair on heads of
children to protect them from evil influences

Left was inauspicious during this period. The bride after her marriage entered the motherin-law’s house placing her right foot on it. The dancer ascended the placing her right foot first
on it. The husband must not leave the company of his wife for fifteen days after the start of
menstrual flow for her: but is not to seek union with her during the menses period. Scientific
enquiry would show that this was not mere belief but the result of careful observation. It was
customary for the women, after the child-birth to go to the public tank for bathing. During the
period of “impurity”, they were “unapproachable” and must not touch the domestic utensils.

69
4.3.5 Jainism
It is well known fact that both Jainism and Buddhism sprang up simultaneously into
prominence and that while Buddhism received royal patronage while Jainism lacked these
advantages. According to K.A.N. Sastri “Jainism was the more persistent religion in its influence
on Tamil literature”. Jains had produced Jivaka Chinthamani, Chulamani, NilakesiNannul,
Yapparungala Virutti etc Thus they were intellectual giants who had made remarkable
contribution to Tamil literature. The tradition says that Badrabahu, the Jaina ascetic accompanied
by Chandra gupta maurya, led his followers to Sravanabelgola. From there they reached the
nearest place Kanchipuram. Hence it has been a strong hold of Jainism.
In the city of Puhar Jains were known as Samanas and their places of stay were called
Samanapalli or Amanapalli. The lay Jains were called “Ulaga Nonbigal”. At Uraiyur there was

an Aruhan temple called “Sri Kandappalli”.
The Amanappallis were retiring and resting places of the Jaina monastriesand these
places were surrounded by gardens full of flowering plants. Jainism became popular during
the time of Kalabharas.
4.3.6 Ajivikas
Ajivikas were another sect of Jains. Kannagi’s father Manaikkan was reported to have
joined this order and became a Jaina monk. The founder of this order was Mamballiputta
Markhali gosala. He established Ajivikism, which had a component of Jaina doctrine and his
own independent views. Kaundi Adigal was a Jaina ascetic who is said to have escorted Kovalan
and Kannagi.
4.3.7 Buddhism
Buddhism sprang up in Tamil Nadu during the SangamAge. Buddhism received royal
patronage, and their influence is clearly indicated in the Tamil Literature. The authors of
Manimekalai, Virasoliam, and the Kundalakesi were great Buddhists.

Buddhists learned Tamil like the Jains in order to spread their religion in Tamil Nadu.
Unlike Jainism Buddhism spread in various parts of ancient Tamilaham. Vjharas and Chaityas

70
were the Buddhist religious establishments. Manimekalai refers to a big Chaityas in
kavereipumpattinam. Manimekalai gives detailed account of the doctrines of Buddhism. The
important centers of Buddhism were Kaveripumpattinam, Karur, Uraiyur, Madurai and
Kanchipuram.. Maduraikanchi refers to a monastery in Madurai. The Buddhist monks preached
the virtues of self-control and non-violence. Women were also admitted with the Buddhist
order. Flower and incence were offered. The Kalabhara rulers were the followers of Buddhism.
From the available evidences we can say that to an certain extent Sangam society was
influenced both by Jainism and Buddhism. Some Tamils abstained from meat eating. The
Hindus adopted a few legends of the Buddhists.
4.4 Summary
In general there was a religious tolerance prevailed among the sangam rulers. People

worshipped according to their living thinnai but lord Murukan worship was famous among the
Tamils. Nature worship was also prevalent in the sangam age. Apart from Hinduism, Buddhism
and Jainism were also in existence. Sangam rulers donated liberally for the construction of
temples, monasteries, Pallis and Chaityas.

5.1 Introduction
The age of the great Pallavas of Simhavishnu line was perhaps the most formative period
of South Indian Culture. The administrative system of the Pallavas is considered as one of the
most important feature of society. The Pallavas had developed a very well organized and
efficient system of administration. The Pallava period witnessed excellent economic progress.
The revenue of the Government increased due to taxation and the economy of the country also
witnessed rapid progress.
They had introduced the beginnings of an elaborate local administration. Dry lands were
brought under cultivation. Lakes and canals were widened for irrigational purposes. Villages

were self-contained and enjoyed a semi-autonomous like status. Hence there was an industrial
freedom and economic progress in the villages. In short the villages played an important role in
developing the economy of the country and they are very often known in the contemporary
literature as the centers of socio-economic activities.

74
The history of any period can be reconstructed only on the basis of relevant source
material. Epigraphy assumes greater importance with the emergence of the Pallavas. The
economic life of the village during the Pallava period is derived from the different copper-plate
charters namely Pallankovil, Kurram, Kasakudi and Tandantottam as well as the glimpses
obtained in Tevaram and Nalayira divyaprabandam, hymns of Nayanmars and Alwars. We
infer from the inscriptions about land survey, land tenure, land tax etc. The villages and their
boundaries, private land, and Government land settlement in the villages, the different industries
or occupation followed are being mentioned. We are also able to form an idea about the size of
each village and the population. Thus these sources help us to learn about the economic
history of the Pallavas.
5.2 Kalabharas

Historians call the Kalabhara period as the Interregnum or interlude in the History of
Tamil Nadu. After the decline of the Sangam age they ruled over Tamil Nadu up to the Pallava
period. The Historians call this period as the Dark Age.
According to Dr N.Subramanian, there is a dark political pall descending over and
enshrouding the history of the Tamils for a period of three centuries namely 300 A.D to 600
A.D. Through this historical mist we get merely glimpses of the nature and activities of a people
called the Kalabhras who ruled the whole or considerable parts of the Tamil country having
captured power from the three traditional crowned monarchs of Tamilaham.
Who were the Kalabhras?
There is a mystery shrouded about the Kalabhara’s origin. According to Krishnaswamy
Iyengar, Kalabhras could be related to the Kalvar of the Venkatam origin. According to

Dr.T.V.Mahalingam the Kalabhras were oliyars. According to literary source Periyapuranam
Kalabhras were the Kannadians. According to Dr M.S.Govindaswamy Kalabhras ruled over
the Chola territory in the name of Muttaraiyar. Further he says that they patronized Jain poets
who composed Naladiyar. Thus there are various theories about them and we don’t have
reliable sources to study about them.

75
Religion of the Kalabhras
Kalabhras were Jains. Kalabhras suppressed other religions and promoted the religion
of Jainism. Jainism became a dominating force of the Pallava and Pandya rulers.
Decline of the Kalabhras
By the end of the Sixth century Kadungon of Pandya ruler defeated the kalabhras. Since
they are mentioned in the Kurram copper plate we assume that they would have lived up to 8th
Century A.D. without holding any political importance.
Thus after the Kalabhra period we have the Pallava rule in Tamil Nadu.
Agriculture
Agriculture is the cultivation of land and breeding of animals and plants to provide food,
medicinal plants and other products to sustain and enhance life. The land was classified as dry
and wet lands and taxes were collected accordingly. The entire lands of the kingdom were

measured. Every village was measured and sketch was drawn. There were two kinds of lands
viz., Puyal and Adai. The income of the former was shared by land owners and cultivators, and
the latter lands were crown lands.
The rulers took all possible steps to increase the area of cultivation as well as to increase
the yielding capacity of the lands. Dry lands and waste lands were brought under cultivation.
For these purpose lakes, canals and wells were used by the people. The lakes depended
mainly on rains. A large number of wells were constructed for drinking and irrigational purposes.
Agricultural lands were used for the cultivation of rice which was one of the staple food crops of
the country. Rice was one of the main items of barter. Apart from paddy, groundnut and cashew
nut were cultivated in large tracts of land. They used get wood from forest areas. In the coastal

belt cashew nut and coconut grooves were cultivated on a large scale. But unfortunately due to
the failure of monsoon (that is lack of rainfall) farmers were not able to get benefited out of the
yield from their lands. The region was not so fertile like cholamandalam.
Agriculture was the main occupation for the majority of the people. There were big and
small landlords as well as ordinary labourers who were paid wages either in cash or kind.

76
Through Forest and mines Government were able to get the good revenue. Lakes, tanks,
wells, rivers and even trees were counted and registered for purposes of tax assessment.
In the coastal areas salt was manufactured.
5.3 Industries
Apart from Agriculture there were other industries like weaving and dyeing, Stone cutting
and shell cutting, bead and bangle –making, pottery and terracotta works carried on throughout
the country.
(1) Weaving and Dyeing
Both cotton and silk clothes were produced. . Silk was an important item of export and
was very popular in countries like China. China imported silk clothes and saris in large quantity
from the pallava kingdom. Even today Kanchipuram was a flourishing trade centre of silk saris
and these saris are very popular in the international market. Majority of the people in this area
was engaged in this profession.
(2) Stone Cutting and Carving

Cottage industry was existed in the Pallava period. Semi-precious stones were used for
making beads of various size and shape. The art of cutting and polishing the stone were very
famous during this period. The excavations were conducted in places like Kanchipuram and
they founded numerous such beads. Stone studs were also made.
(3) Bangle Making
Shell and glass bangles were very popular during this period. People were able to get
employment through this industry.
(4) Pottery
Pottery or ceramic industries made rapid progress and the industry was spread all over
the kingdom. This industry provided vessels for domestic use to all sorts of people. The potters
organized themselves into guilds or corporations. They enjoyed a high status in the society.

77
Women folk were also engaged in this industry. Thus many people followed pottery as their
profession.
Besides the above, there were also other industries like sugarcane, oil pressing, carpentry,
ivory working, cattle breeding etc., which provided the village population to earn their livelihood.
The members of the village community maintained themselves by many of these organized
industries or industrial crafts. The village population included these industrial workers besides
Goldsmith, Traders, Merchants and Brahmins.
5.3.1 Land Revenue
We come to know that there were many kinds of lands from the copper plates from
Kuram, Kasakudi and Bahur. Land Revenue was the main source of income. Land was owned
both by the king and by the individuals. Land was classified into cultivable and non-cultivable

besides forests, pastures etc. The term Puravupon figuring in the Pallava records refers to the
tax in money on cultivable lands paid to the Government by the land owners. The kings owned
personal lands and hence they were able to donate tax free lands to the Brahmanas and
temples.
Lands donated to Brahmins were called Brahmadeya lands. These lands were exempted
from tax. More over these lands were not to be sold out. The Brahmins who mastered four
Vedas were lived in Chaturvedimangalam. Lands donated to the temples were known as
Devadhana. The revenue from the lands were spent for temples. The temples extended loans
to the people during the time of famine or drought. Lands given to Jain monasteries were
known as Pallichandam.
5.3.2 Land Tenure
The cultivable lands in the villages were held under different tenures. There were lands

whose produce was shared equally by the land owner and the tenant. There were also lands,
wherein 1/6 of the produce was to be given to the king. There were also instances where in the
tenants of the Government lands were changed periodically. Details were worked out to
compensate and reemploy the old tenants.

78
5.4 Trade and Commerce
The Pallava period witnessed a considerable development in the field of trade and
commerce.
5.4.1 Inland Trade
Regarding inland trade, every village had shops in those days. River transportation was
also restored under the pallava rule.
Each village had their shops and some inscriptions speak of the commercial activities of
these shops. Commodities like rice, salt, cotton, toddy, sugarcane, jiggery, pots, oil, coconut,
Palmyra and areca nuts, clothes, fish, milk and milk products .Ulagalantha Perumal temple of
Kanchi states that licenses were issued. Barter system was generally followed in the business
transactions.
5.4.2 Taxes
The main source of income to the Government was from taxes. The Inscriptions speak of
land revenue and the following professional taxes, namely IlamPutchi was levied who drew

toddy, Kussakkanam was levied on those who made pottery, Tatttukkanam was levied on
Goldsmith, Paraikkanam was levied on the Washer man, Padamkalai was levied on Spinners,
Tharikkurai was levied on Weavers, Ndumparai was paid to those who beat drums, Sungavari
was the excise duty, Manrupadu was levied in courts etc.
5.4.3 Foreign Trade
Mahabalipuram was an important port during the Pallava period. It is often mentioned
by Thirumangai Alwar and Chinese traveler Hiuen Tsang in their masterpieces. In addition to
Mahabalipuram, Nagapattinam was also a remarkable port. There was trade relationship
between Kanchipuram and China and South West Asia. Nandikalambagam gives an account
of the trade was going between Kanchipuram and China.

79
5.4.4 Trade Guilds
The various artisans and traders and craftsmen organized themselves into Guilds or
Corporations. They took care of the welfare of these people and at the same time made gifts to
religious institutions and public welfare activities.
5.5 Weights and Measures
As several of the Pallava inscriptions relate to gifts of land Gold and other articles of
produce, a scrutiny of these records reveals to us a number of weights and measures that
were current in the country. Most of these continued to be in use even during the post-Pallava
period. A few of them are still in vogue in southern Tamil districts.
5.5.1 Measures
The early Sanskrit inscriptions mention the extent of land measured by “plough”. There
were also other kinds of measures like Pattika, Nivartana, and Padagam etc. Veli and Kuli
were the most common land measures. There were other numerous measures with different

names and each denoted a different standard.
In the Pallava age rice and paddy were measured by the nali, marakkal, kuruni, and
Kalam. Ghee, oil, milk and curd were measured by the Alakku, Ulakku, Uri and nail. Padi was
also a measure and that is still in practice in our country.
5.5.2 Weights
Gold weights such as Kalanju and Manjadi were prevalent in the Pallava age.
5.5.3 Coinage
Coins were used as medium of exchange besides Barter system. Many coins of Pallava
rulers are available to us. Wheel, Swastik, Umbrella, Sangu, Arrow, Fish, Crab,lion, Horseetc.,
were found on the obverse of coins. Coins bearing the emblem of Nandhi and two ships are
also available to us. Coins were made out of Gold, silver and copper.

80
5.6 Social Conditions
The four fold division of society into Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, Vaisyas and Sudras continued
during the Pallava period in a modified form. They followed the principles of Hindu Dharma and
Varnashrmadharma. Kasakudi plates explains about the significance of observing the principles
of Varnashrmadharma. by all castes during this period . Besides there were artisans, goldsmiths,
carpenters, Idaiyars and farmer
5.6.1 Brahmins
Though numerically in a minority, they were at the head of the society. In general Brahmins
were educated people in the society. During the Pallava period many Brahmins were migrated
from the Andhra to Tamil Nadu. They were respected and honoured by the rulers by grant of
Brahmadeya land gifts. These Brahmins found employment in the temples for reciting Vedas

during services and also during the various royal sacrifices, such as Agni stoma, Vajapeya and
Asvamedha.
Brahmins were found employment as officers in the Pallava Royal court and Government
Departments. They were also serving as accountants in village assemblies. The Brahmans
were polygamous and married more than one wife. The Brahman girls married Kshatriya,
Vysia, and sudra men too This was called Pratiloma marriage while the members of non-
Brahman communities married Brahman girls under Anuloma marriage practice. This led to
numerous mixed castes.
5.6.2 Kshatriyas
The Talagunda inscription refers to the Pallava rulers as Kshatriyas. .The kings were
pious and God fearing. They were interested in the welfare of the people and promoting dharma.
They made liberal grants and gifts to the Brahmanas and scholars. .They performed Vedic

sacrifices. They were fond of war. The queens were also equally pious and took pride in making
gifts and endowments to temples and other religious and educational institutions

81
5.6.3. Vaisyas
Vaisyas were the business community during this period. There were also a few
Nayanmars who belonged to the community. The rich among them made grants of lands to
establish educational institutions, Hospitals, feeding houses and both construction and renovation
works of the temples. They provided large funds for these public welfare activities.
They organized themselves into a number of guilds and corporations. These guilds took
care of the welfare of the trading community and also for their business transactions. They
were able to influence the ruling family. They were associated with the administrative work
both at the centre and village levels.
5.6.4 Sudras
The lowest strata of society were the Sudras. They were followed different kinds of
professions apart from serving as agricultural labourers. The hymn of Alwars refers to a few of

them as Pulayas and Chandelas. as socially down caste people. There were great men like
Tiruppanalvar and Tandanar who belonged to this community. They were allowed to enter into
the temples and offer worship.
Besides there were Vellalas, Dhobis, shepherds, fishermen, hunters, Parayas, Panars
and Pulayars. They were identified by their professions.
5.7 Position of women
Women were highly respected in the society. They showed keen interest in religious and
temple affairs. Women enjoyed right to own property during this period and they have donated
liberally to the temples. Women had donated gold coins through Hiranyagarbha and Tulabhara
ceremonies.
Monogamy was in existence. Certain kings had two wives. Women were educated,
intelligent, beautiful and skilled in various arts and crafts. Besides serving in temples, women

indulged in spinning, weaving and selling of milk from door to door. The inscription of Mukteswara
temple state that there were many dancing girls. They enjoyed high reputation and influence in
kings’ court and in society.

82
During this period Queen enjoyed special concessions and privileges. They gave gifts
liberally to temples. The kings had matrimonial alliances with Rashtrakutas, Kadambars and
Gangas in order to gain political advantages. Queens like Charudevi and others patronized
religion. They donated lands to temples and they celebrated festivals. They had valuable jewels.
Women were fond of wearing numerous ornaments and garments. The Pallava sculpture
representing the queens and dancer bear testimony to this fact.
The Aryan culture had a great impact on Tamil culture. This we infer from the works of
Andal and Sundaramurthy Nayanar. Thiruppavai Nonbu i.e., fasting was observed by women
folk during the Pallava period.
There were no evidences either in literature or in the inscriptions about the practice of
Sati. Hence we come to the conclusion that Sati was not known to them.
5.7.1 Marriage

During this period marriage was conducted with the consent of the parents, However
love marriages were also permitted and received encouragement. Many rituals and ceremonies
were observed during the marriage. Homam was performed. The holy thread (Thali) was tied
to the neck of the bride with the instrumental music and in the presence of relatives and friends.
Inter-caste marriages were also existed. The Brahmana girls married the Kshatriya, Vaisya
and Sudra men. Similarly the non-Brahmin men married the Brahmana girls. From this we infer
that the caste was not a hindrance to enter into marriage at all levels of society.
5.7.2 Dress and Decorations
Both men and women wore costly dresses. Particularly members of the royal families
and ministers wore rich and beautiful dresses. The term Kalingam was used to indicate silk

clothing. Sirradai and Meladai (lower and upper garments) were used by the ladies. Jains wore
washed cloth during the pallava period. The ascetics wore yellow garments. Special types of
dresses were used by the Warrior class.

83
(1) Ornaments
Both the Pallava kings and the queens wore different types of ornaments. From the
inscriptions we come to know that they use the following ornaments: The crown-chains, Thodu,
Kundalam, Marakkuli, Anklets, Rings, padagam,Pathakkam,Valayal and Ottiyanam They also
adorned their shoulder with with pearl strings known as Veerachangili. . The ornaments were
made of either Gold, silver or copper. Palm- leaves were also used as ear-rings by some
ladies.
(2) Foot Wears
People wore chapel made out of leather, wood and skins. Umbrellas of different types
were common in those days.
(3) Head Dress
Royal family members both men and women wore crowns to adorn their heads. They
tied their hair into knots of different fashions: combing the hair was a common scene. Both
men and women decorated their body from head to foot. They took bath in scented waters and

applied sandal powder for their body. They wore flowers over the hair. It was also a customary
to wear flower on the right ear by young men. It was known as tonrippu
5.7.3 Food and Drinks
Inscriptions explains that the people of this age consumed red paddy (sennel) Cooked
rice was their staple food. Apart from this they cooked Appam, Sweet Pongal, curd-rice, gheerice, milk, dhall and butter. These food items were used by the royal family members also.
Special diets were provided for soldiers. They consumed non vegetarian food: grains like ragi,
cholam etc were also used for preparing food. Meat eating was very common. Betal and nuts
were served after the meals. Toddy was consumed by large sections of people. The rich people
drank wine and toddy of high quality.
Sports
Hunting, elephant riding, horse riding, Swimming, sword fighting and wrestling were the

favorite games for men. Dice was a favourite indoor game. The womenfolk spent their leisure
time in swimming, taming parrots in cages and Gardening.

84
5.8. Education
During the age of the Pallavas Hindu, Buddhist and Jaina educational institutions flourished
at Kanchipuram. Hindu educational institution received a patronage from the rulers and attracted
scholars from different parts of India. The language of the court and also the medium of
instruction was Sanskrit. The ruler MahendravarmanI was a very great scholar. Educational
institutions were patronized by the rulers. But there was no evidence regarding their educational
centers or their curriculum. One of these institutions must have been the Ghatika.
5.8.1 Ghatika
Ghatika was an educational institution. It consisted of a group of holy and learned
Brahmanas. There were many branches of study. The center of Ghatika was kailasanatha
temple at Kanchipuram. The study of Veda is angas. Mimamsa and the like were practiced in
the Ghatika.

The other centers of learning were Bahur, Bahur Palampathi and Sholingar. The Pallava
kings supported those educational institutions. The numerical strength of Ghatka varied from
place to place. It was a residential institution offering free boarding and lodging to the teachers
and taught.
(1) Agraharas
The Brahmadeya village and Agraharas undertook the teaching of the people. It provided
opportunities for the people to study Vedic literature and other subjects. The pallava rulers
founded numerous agraharas for the Brahmanas which helped in spreading literacy among
the people. They were named after the rulers or their queens.
(2) Temple as an Educational Institution
Temples served as centers of learning and provided free boarding and lodging to the
scholars. They provided courses for the architect, sculptor and the painter. They also employed

the musicians, dancers and actors. It is said that the Kailasanatha temple was fostering higher
studies in Vedic lures and philosophy. Provisions were also made for reciting Mahabharata and
Devaram hymns. Debates and discussions were held in the mandapas of the temples.

85
(3) Mathas
Both Saiva and Vaishnava Mathas encouraged the educational activities. The inmates
of the Mathas were all highly qualified persons and taught subjects of various interests to local
students. Secular subjects like astrology, medicine etc., was also taught to the students.
(4) Buddhist and Jain centers of Education
The viharas and Jaina Pallis functioned as centers of education for Buddhist and Jain
systems of philosophy. Hiuen-Tsang gives a graphic picture about the popular Buddhist University
at Kanchipuram, Many scholars came to this university both from other parts of India and
abroad similarly there were Jaina Pallis encouraged the study of Jaina philosophy. Jina Kanchi
was considered as the main center of learning for Jains.
5.9 Summary
The dark period of Kalabhara rule came to an end and the Greater Pallava dynasty

started to rule Tamilaham with Kanchi as their capital. Pallavas established their political stability
and supremacy in the Tamil Country. The economic condition of the country was stabilized and
the development of education was patronized by the rulers. Thus there was an all round
development in the Pallava territory. Though there were frequent wars, there was peace and
progress.
