6.1 Introduction
A unique feature of the Pallava period was that people belonging to different religious
followers lived together in the capital of the Pallava dynasty. The Pallava rulers followed religious
tolerance policy. The spread of Bhakti movement had provided stimulus to them. Both Sanskrit
and Tamil religious literary works came. We can see the decline of Jainism and Buddhism in
this period.
6.2 Hindu Religion
“The very soul of India, the very life blood of her civilization and culture is found not so
much in the palaces but in temples, not in politics but in philosophy” Religious philosophy is the
fundamental keynote in Indian History. It cannot be denied that the age of the Pallavas occupies
an immortal place in the religious history of India. The early Pallava rulers were the followers of

Vedic religion. The rulers performed many sacrifices like Aswamedha, vajapeya, Somayaga
and Agnishtoma. Simhavarman was creditied with the performance of 100 Yagas. .Simhavarman
and Paramesvaravarman have performed Aswamedha sacrifices. Almost all the early Pallava
rulers had a great faith in the Vedic sacrifices. Pallava rulers constructed many Hindu temples.
6.2.1 Vaishnavism
The devotees of Lord Vishnu were called Vaishnavites. Alwars preached Vaishnavism
during the Pallava period. There were twelve Alwars. Those who lived in the Pallava kingdom
were Poigai Alwar, Pey Alwar, Bhudhathalwar, and Tirumangai Alwar. Early pallava rulers were
stanuch followers of vaishnavism. From the inscriptions we come to know that rulers were
great worshippers of Vishnu feet. Sometimes the king and queen are compared to Vishnu and

Lakshmi respectively. Simhavarman was portrayed as the incarnation of lord Vishnu and the
queen of Dantivarman as an incarnation of Goddess Lakshmi.
Lord Vishnu was worshipped in three postures: i.e. Reclining, Standing and Seated. The
ten avatars of Lord Vishnu were worshipped. Among the ten Avatars, Varaha and Srivikrama
Avatars were the famous in the early pallava period. The advent of Narashima form was not
found prior to Narashimhavarman-I. Vishnu temples are found in Kanchipuram, Mamalapuram,

89
and Mahendravadi etc. Sacred f ood and flowers were off ered to the deities.
Vishnusarashranamam were chanted in the temples. Rulers donated lands to the temples and
they made as an endowment to the temples in order to do puja daily in the temples Festivals
were also celebrated in the temples.
6.2.2 Saivism
The followers of Lord Shiva were known as Saivites. During the Pallava period, Nayanmars
the Saiva saints had preached Saivism. There were sixty-three Nayanmars. Only in the later
pallava period Saivism flourished due to the patronage of the rulers like Narasimhavarman-II
Many Shiva temples were constructed at Kanchipuram, Panamalai, and Mamalapuram. In the
early part of the pallava period Shiva was not worshipped in the form of a Linga. The main
object of worship in a temple was panek of Somaskanda- Shiva with his son Kumara and his

consort Parvathi. This panel was either painted or sculptured on the rear wall of the central
shrine. It was during the time of Rajasimha-II that the worship of Linga became popular. Other
forms of Shiva were also worshipped. He was worshipped as Gangadharamurthy, Tirupuantaka,
and Kailasanatha.
In those days they have offered flowers and mantras were chanted for worship. The
ritual of abhisheka was not in vogue and the main ritual at the time of early pallavas was only
nivedhana. From the Kurram records we come to know that the ruler Paramesvaravarman
was the one who introduced the puja to Lord Shiva with a sacred bath, to be followed by
offering flowers, sandal and incense to the deity .Hence we can say that he was the one who
introduced the Abhisheka ritual in the temples.
(1) Saiva Sects
In the early centuries of Pallava rule there were certain religious sects like Kapalika,

Kalamuka and Pasupatha etc., as also the kaumaras, the Sastas etc,These were splinter
group of original Saivism. Their religious rituals included the offering of wine and Blood to
Bhairava and Kali, ferocious aspects of Shiva and his consort Parvathi. According to Chinese
pilgrim Hiuen Tsang “the kapalikas lived in the holes and crevices of the rocks, like Yaaksa who
haunt the place of Tombs”.

90
Bhairava and Kali worship
The chief centers of Kapalika, Kalamuka and Pasupata sects which flourished in the
Pallava Kingdom were Kanchipuram, Thirvorriyur, Mayilappur and Kodumbalur and certain
places in Tanjavour and Tiruchchirappalli districts. The prevalence of Kali, Durga and Mahisasuramardhini is clear from the sculptures in the shrines of Mamallapuram. The worship of Bhairava
can be seen from the sculptures of the terrible form of Siva Bhairavamurthi in the Kailasanatha
temple at kanchipuram.
Bhairava episode in Siruttondarpuranam
The Siruttondarpuranam explains in a detailed manner about how the Bhairava took the
form of a Kapalika and entered Saint Siruttondar’s house on invitation for a repast in his house
on condition that he was provided for food cooked flesh of a five year old boy. The request was

met in full by sacrificing his only son, five year old. The devotion of Saint Siruttondar having
been proved, the life of the boy was given back by the Bhairava, who then mysteriously
disappeared.
A Saiva math for the Kalamuka sect was located at Kodumbalur .They took to penance
and reciting of sacred hymns. The Pasupatas were also known as Maheswaras. They
considered Siva in the form of Pasupata as their chief deity and worshipped in the form of
Linga. They went about sparsely clad wearing the sacred ashes all over the body. They had
great faith in sacrifices. An offering of flesh to the deity was considered as an important form
of worship
The Kapalikas were worshippers of Siva in the form of Bhairava. They adorned themselves
with a garland of skulls. Animals and human sacrifices were given to Bhairava. The Kapalikas

took flesh, intoxicant drinks and worshipped their deity. They considered women a Sakthi. A
Kapalika Math was established at Kanchi. Kapalikas were also popular in Mayilappur. The
decline of the Kapalika sect in the Pallava Kingdom is brought out in Mattavilasaprahasana.
(2) Shanmatha
The Pallava period saw the rise of six creeds (Shanmatha) in the Hindu pantheon. There
is some evidence that the six creeds were introduced by Sankaracharya. The six creeds are

91
(a) Ganapatyam (worship of Ganapati), (b) Kumaran (Shanmuga), (c) Sauram (sun), (d) Saktam
(Sakthi), (e) Saivam (Siva), (f) Vaishnavam (Vishnu), Images of Ganapathi and Shanmuga
(Kumaran) are represented in the Pallava sculptures. Ganapathi worship was introduced during
the Pallava days. Temples of Ganapathi were construced. A Brahmana lady Devachchani set
up an impage of Ganapati in the Kailasanathar temple at Paramesvaramangalam and endowed
a perpetual lamp. In the later Pallava times Ganesa appears in the group of Saptamatri (seven
mothers).
The popularity of worship of Durga and Mahisasuramardini ferocious aspects of Sakthi is
clear from the sculptures found at Mahapalipuram. The cults of Saptamatri and Jyeshta were
famous during the Pallava times. The cult was popular from the reign of Dantivarma. Temples

of Saptamatri were constructed at Tiruttani, velacheri and Alampakkam during the period.
Jyashta, the eldest sister of Lakshmi, was another popular deity worshipped in this period.
Kailasanathar temple has the first representation of this goddess. She was considered as a
goddess of evil and was propitiated by devotees forwarding of evil. Brahma, Vishnu, Siva the
Trimurthis were also worshipped collectively Temples for Trinity are found at Mandagapattu
and MahabalipuramHari Hara (Siva-Vishnu synthesis) and Surya were also worshipped.
(3) Hero Stones
The ancient form of hero worship was also popular. For those heroes who fell in the
battlefield a memorial was erected and worshipped. Such memorial stones are sculptured
with the figure of the hero and the deed would be engraved. Such hero stones are available in
all parts of the Pallava kingdom.
6.2.3 Buddhism

Buddhism was patronized by the pallava kings from very early times. They were followers
of Mahayana form of Buddhism. Two of the early Pallava Kings-Buddhavarman and
Buddhyankura-were belived to be patrons of Buddhism. According to the Chinese Buddhist
scholar Hiuen Tsang who had visited India in the 7th century explains about the condition of
Buddhism. He says that Kanchipuram was a flourishing city and most of its population was
Buddhist. Further he mentions that there were over 100 Buddhist monasteries and over a

92
thousand monks. Mahendravarman’s work Mattavilasa prahasana mentions about the existence
of viharas. Raja Vihara was the chief vihara.
Among the notable scholars Dharmapala of the Nalanda university belonged to the resident
of the city Kanchipuram The material prosperity of the Vihara is explained in the words of
Devasoma. Uragapura (identified with Uraiyur) was the seat of the famous monk Buddhadatta,
who composed his Ahbidummavatara there. Kaviripumpaatinam was another Buddhist centre
having a big monastery. Bhutamangalam and Nagapattinam had also monasteries. In the
days of the Pallavas there existed different schools of Buddhist philosophy and logic. One of
the most popular schools of philosophy flourished was the Sthvira School. Another school of
philosophy was the Dhyna School. However there seems to be a decline in the morals. This

is indicated in the Matavilasaprhasana. To revive Buddhism steps were taken. Vajrabodhi, the
Buddhist monk visited the Pallava kingdom during rule of Narasimhavarman-II (A.D. 690) and
exhibited his miraculous power to relieve the people from the famine.
The religious condition of Tamil Nadu began to change after the 7th century due to the
advent of Saivism and Vaishnavism. Pallava rulers did not patronize Buddhism hence it led to
the decline gradually. We can conclude about Buddhism in the words of Pandit Hisselle
Dharmaratana Maha Thera “Although Buddhism declined in the Tamil country from the 7th
century onwards it was by no means eradicated”
6.2.4. Jainism
Jainism was another important religion that flourished in the Pallava kingdom from very
early times. Jainism seems to have more followers than Buddism. Unlike Buddhism, Jainism

received more royal patronage during the time of Mahendravarman I. A tradition over that
Mahendravarman was a Jain later converted to Saivism by the preaching’s of Appar. Jainism
became an important religion in the life of the people when Vajranandhi, founded the
DravidaSangha in A.D. 470. The famous Prakrit writer KundaKunda a Digrambara Jain is
related to Sivakumaramaharaja, identified with one of the Pallava kings of the Prakrit charters.
It is also during the time of Simhavaraman, Sarvanandhi, completed the copying of the Jaina
work Lokavibhaga in Prakrit. With the reconversion of Mahendravarman to the Saiva fold,
Jainism lost the royal support.
Kanchipuram was an important Jaina centre. Other Jaina centres are located at
Tiruppanmalai, Tirupparuttikkunram, Vallimalai and Ponvilaindapatti. It received royal patronage

93
of the Pallava king Simhavarman. The Pallankoil copper plates record the functioning of the
famous Nadisanga at the place Amanserkkai, and the patronage received from the Pallava
king Simhavarman. At Venkunram, Perumandur, Malaiyadippatti, Kilsatamangalam and
Pachapandavamalai, Jain Pallis functioned. At Vedal there was a nunnery with strength about
500 members. Jains were divided into monastic order and lay following with further subdivisions. The worship of prophets and celebration of great public festivals was the feature of
the normal religious life of the people. Trilokyanatha Temple in Kanchipuram and Chitharal
Jain temple were constructed during the Pallava time. Royal patronage played a vital role both
for the growth as well as for the decline of Jainism for example MahendravarmanI’s period
Trilokyanatha/Chandraprabha temple is a twin Jain temple that has inscriptions from

Pallava king, Narasimhavarman II and the Chola kings Rajendra Chola I, Kulothunga Chola I
and Vikrama Chola, and the Kanarese inscriptions of Krishnadevaraya. The temple is maintained
by Tamil Nadu archaeological department. This temple comes under the Archaeological Survey
of India.
Trilokyanatha Jain temple at Kanchipuram

94
6.3 Temples
Temples were known by the great name Devakula during Pallava times. The Vishnu
temple was name Vishnugraha or Vinnagaram. The temples of the Buddhist and Jain were
known by the term Palli. The Hindu temples were generally located near the village settlements
whereas the Pallis of the Buddhists and Jains were situated far away from the village settlements.
In the early days of the Pallavas temples were constructed out of bricks, wood or perishable
materials. From the days of Mahendravarman temple were carved into rocks. They are of
simple type with one Garbagriha preceded by a pillared Mandapa. Shrines for other deities
were also provided on the sides. In the cave temple Pradakshina was not provided. From the
time of Pramesvaravarman-I temples were constructed out of huge stone blocks. They were

big structures provided with a PradakshinaPatha and shrines for other smaller deities. Pallava
kings constructed many such temples. A temple for Trinity was scooped out at Mandagapattu
by Mahendravarman. At Vallam his chieftain Kandasena excavated a temple for Siva. A
temple for durga was carved at Mahabalipuram. Paramesvara-I and Rajasimha-II built temples
of Siva at Kuram and Kanchipuram respectively. Nadivarman-II built the famous
Vaikuntaperumal temple at Kanchipuram.
(1) Offerings
The deity was worshipped with the grunt of an endowment. Endowments of perpetual
lamps were popular form of worship provisions were made to freed the deity and Brahmanas in
the temple on various occasions. Flowers were also offered as a token of their love and
affection. In later Pallava times the deities were bathed first and flowers, sandal paste and

incense were offered. While puja is performed musical instruments were sounded. An offering
of the head to Durga was another kind of sacrifice popular during the Pallava times. Sculptures
in Mamallapuram portray a few instances of head offerings to Durga. Another kind of sacrifice,
Navakandam was also practiced. In this case the warrior would offer flesh taken from nine
parts of his body as a price for the victory vouchsafed by the goddess Durga. An instance of
offerings of Navakandam is known from Mallam epigraph.
(2) Philosophy

95
The religious Philosophy was shaped by Sankara and Kumarilbhatta. Kumariala elucidated
the philosophy of ritualism. Sankara preached by Adivaita Philosophy. The Nayanmars preached
Bhakti and it is only with Bhakti a man can become god. It was preached that no amount of
penance and self-torture or asceticism will be any use if it is not accompanied with Bhakti or
love. The rebirth was realised and cessation form rebirth could be achieved only by uttering
the name of god.
6.3.1. Religious Tolerance
It is generally believed that the various reglious group followed a safe path of tolerance.
Pallava kings have endowed to the heretical sects Jainism and Buddhism. A village was endowed
to JainaSangha at Pallava kingdom without any difficulty.
The devotional literature furnished any entirely different view. They provide some evidence

for the religious rivalry that took shape during this period. The quarrels with other religious
groups are known and to gain superiority with the other people they have viewed with each
other. The hymns of Gnanasambandar and Appar, invariably the tenth verse of every hymns
contains a through denunciation of the Buddhists and Jains. In pursuance of these aims to
wiped out Buddhism and Jainism they carried out a vigorous propaganda condemning the
Buddhist and Jains and upholding the Saiva faith. These saints engaged in religious disputations
with several sects and on numerous instances the saints emerged successful and established
the cause of their religion. Gnanasambandar came into conflict with Jains at Madurai and
proved the superiority of Saivism over Jainism to the Pandya king and converted him to Saiva

fold. By conducting some miracles the jains were defeated. At Podimangai and Tirvottur also,
the Buddhist and Jains were defeated. Tirunavukkarasar, experienced the healing power of
Siva, when he was relieved of the intense pain latter he was put to torture by the Jains, but he
established the supremacy of Saivism by performing some miracles.
Among the Vaishnava saints, TirumangaiAlwar exhibits his rivalry towards Buddhist and
Jains. At one instance he robbed the golden image of Buddha from the NagapattinamVihara,
and melted and used god for constructing the 4thprakara of the Siranganatha temple. Mahendra
destroyed Jains Pallis at Tiruppadirippuliyur and built a Saiva temple at Tiruvadigal. On the
basis of a representation of two men, being impaled sculptured in a panel in the historical

96
sculptures of Valikuntaperumal temple at Kanchipuram, it was suggested that members of the
heretical sects like Buddhists and Jains were impaled. However, in the panel there is no
evidence to suggest that the persons impaled were Buddhists and Jains. The confiscation of
the wealth in respect of few temples of the Buddhists and Jains could not be taken as an
uniform policy followed in the Pallava kingdom. In the Kanchipuram the capital city of Pallavas,
no damage was done to any of the temples of Buddhists and Jains. This could indicate that the
people largely practiced religious tolerance.

6.4 Bhakti Movement
-The Pallava period is considered as “The Age of Bhakti” par excellence in the Tamil

country. It is also considered as Hindu religious revival successfully led by the Alwars and
Nayanmars. The revivalist movement was started to stop the vigorous spread of the heterodox
religious-Jainism and Buddhism in the Tamil country. The revivalists visited innumerable
temple centers and gathered strength to their movement by their soul string devotional songs.
These songs were set to easy music tunes which attracted worshippers to this movement.

97
6.4.1. Saivism
Nayanmars played a significant role in the Bhakti movement. They were very pious and
orthodox men. The Periyapuranam of Sekkilar is a compilation of the biographies of the sixtythree Saiva saints. Appar, Tirugnanasambandar, Sundarar and Manikavasakar are prominent
among them. The Bhakti movement was stimulated initially by the 63 Nayanmars and it was
first started by KaraikkalAmmaiyar.
The episodes in the life of the Nayanmars created awareness among the people.
KaraikkalAmmaiyar was the wife a merchant at Karaikkal. When her husband understood
her bhakti towards God, he left her. She, denounced her young body and attained the form of
aged women to serve Lord Siva. There upon she stayed at Tiruvalangadu and sang hymns in
praise of the deity at Tiruvalangadu, Later she witnessed the dance of Siva at Tiruvalangadu.

She believed that there is only one God-Siva. Further she gave importance in her songs
about the uncertainty of life.
Among the 63 SaivaNayanmars the most important are Tirunavakkarasar,
Gananasambandar and Sundramurthy. They visited various temples in the country and sang
verses in praise of Siva. Their hymns were collected in the Saiva canonical work called Devaram
by Nambi Andar Nambi.. Their hymns portray a varied religious experience. Devaram hymnists
have visited a total of 429 shirnes.
(1) Appar
Appar (Thirunavukkarasar) was the holiest among the Saiva Saints. His original name
was Marulneekkiyar. . He was by birth a Vellala born at Tiruvamur (South Arcot district) and he

98
was a Jain at first and became a Jaina monk. At an early age he lost his parents. Sometime
later Thirunavukkarasar was infested with a severe fever. He could not be cured. Ultimately
he approached his sister Thilagavathi and was cured after offering prayers to Lord Siva. After
this incident Thirunavukkarasar became a Saivite. One hearing the conversion from Jainism
to Saivism the Pallava king Mahendravarman tortured Thirunavukkarasar. He was poisoned
and dropped into the sea with big stone, but he survived. These miracles convinced the Pallava
king Mahendravarman and he also converted to Saivism. Thirunavukkarasar toured many
places and began singing Sivan’s praise. Thiru GnaanaSambandar respectfully addressed
Navukkarasar as Appar (father) and he and Appar travelled together singing hymns. Appar is

said to have travelled to about a hundred and twenty-five temples in different cities or villages
in Tamil Nadu. He composed 3rd, 4th and 5th Tirumurais. His approach to God is known as
Chariya marga or Dasa Marga, where the relationship between God and devotee is that of a
master to slave. In his 81st year he attained the heavenly abode at Tiruppugalur.
(2) Tirugnanasambandar
Tirugnanasambandar was born in the family of Anthanar (Brahmana) in the first half of
the 7th century at Sirkali (Thanjavur District). At the age of 3 he was offered the divine milk from
Goddess Parvathi. . His parents took him to the shiva temple where Lord Shiva and his

99
consort Parvathi appeared before the child. His father saw drops of milk on the child’s mouth
and enquired who had fed him whereupon Tirugnanasambandar showed the sky and responded
with the song “Todudaya Seviyan” which happens to be the first verse of Devaram. Since
them he became a devoted servant of Siva. His hymns form the first three parts of Tirumurais.
He toured the Tamil country singing in praise of Siva from the very early age. With the attraction
of Jainism the pandyan king Koon Pandiyan became a Jaina’but this was not liked by
Tirugnanasambandar In the mean time the Pandiyan queen mangaikkarasiyar invited him
after the ruler fell ill. According to a Saiva legend Tirugnanasambandar performed music for
the king, which cured the king’s disease. Later with influence of Tirugnanasambandar the
pandiya ruler was reconverted to Saivism.

According to some Saiva legends he performed many miracles. He defeated Jains at
Madurai. He cured some persons of their diseases on his tour. The ancient text says that
Tirugnanasambandar brought two people back to life by singing hymns to them. One of those
resurrected was the daughter of a business man, who offered her to Sambandar in marriage.
He declined due to knowledge that he would soon die. He is said to have attained salvation
along with his bride during the marriage ceremony at the age of 16.
Tirugnanasambandar followed the kriya marga or sat-putra marga where the relationship
between the God and devotee is that of a father to a son.
(3) Sundramurthy Nayanar (Nambiyarurar)
Sundramurthy Nayanar was born at Navalur (South Arcot district) in a poor Brahmin
family He was brought up by the local chieftain NarasingaMunaiyadavriyar. When his marriage

was about to take place, it was stopped by the intervention of Siva, in the guise of a Brahmin,
who claimed him (Sundarar) as his slave. Sundramurthy Nayanar was taken to Tiruvennainallur
where the Brahmin disappeared into the temple. Thereupon Sundramurthy Nayanar became
a staunch devotee of Siva and praised him with his hymns. He was the author of the 7th
Thirumarai. Like the other Nayanmars, Sundramurthy Nayanar is also credited with many
miracles. Sundramurthy Nayanar became the friend of God and was known as Tambiran
Tholan(friend of God). Sundramurthy Nayanar’s approach to God is known as yoga marga or
sakha Marga, where the relationship between God and devotee is that of a friend to friend.

100
(4) Manickavasagar
Manikkavasagar was born at Vadhavoor in Madurai district.Manikkavasagar was a
minister to the Varagunavarman II of the Pandya king. He was sent to purchase horse for the
Pandiya army by the ruler. He spent the money in building temples of Siva. When the
Pandya king heard of this, Lord Siva sent horses to the Pandya court. However these horses
turned to be jackals. Thereupon the king realized his mistake and approved Manikkavasagar’s
devotion to god .His approach to God is a famous one in the Tiruvilayadal Puranam. His
approach to God is called Gnanamarga or Sanmarga. He has made an excellent contribution
Saivite literature. His masterpieces are Tiruvasagam and Tiruchirrambalakovai.
Manikkavasagar‘s work Tiruvembavai is a collection of 20 hymns and in that he has
praised the importance of Paavai Nonbu and praising Lord Shiva. These 20 songs and 10

songs of Tiruppalliezhuchi are sung all over Tamil Nadu in the month of Margazhi.
Manikkavasagar ‘s work Tiruvasagam was translated into English in the year 1921 by Francis
Kingsbury and C.E.Philips and Oxford University Press published this work
6.4.2 Vaishnavism
Vaishnavism is also known as Vishnuism and its followere are known as Vaishnavas.
They considered Vishnu as the supreme Lord. Alwars played a significant role in the Bhakti
movement. They were very pious and orthodox menthe Alwars are twelve in numbers.
(1) (a) Alwars
12 Alwars

101
Among the 12 Alwars the first three Alwars were contemporary to the early Pallava rulers.
The first three Alwars (Mudalawars) – Poyggaialwar, Puddattalwar and Peyalwar and
Tirumaisaialwar have spread the tenets of Bhakti movement in the Pallava country. The
DiyyasuriCharitam records the life history of these Alwars. All the Alwars were not normal
children born in the ordinary way and bear names commemorating some occurrence in the
lives. Tondinadu was their birth place. Poykkaialwar is said to have been born out of a lotus
in Kanchi, Pudattalwar, of the Madhavi flower in Mallapuram and Peyalwar of Kairava flower
at Mylapore. Tirumalisai, the fourth Alwar (7-8 A.D.) was a deformed child of a sage of the
village Tirumalisai, which took shape only after it was abandoned on the roadside and was
later brought by a Sudra.

The first three Alwars spent their early life in search of God. All the three wanderers met
accidentally in a Vishnu temple at Tirukkovalur on a rainy day. While sleeping they felt the
divine presence of Lord Vishnu on their mortal bodies who commanded them to sing His praise
.Hence they composed Nalayira Divyaprabandam.Their works are free from sectarian bias.
(b) ThirumalisaiAlwar was a follower of Vaishnavism. He visited important Vaishnava
shrines. He was a monotheist and preached that there is only one god Vishnu and that Brahma
and Siva were created by him.
(c) TirumangaiAlwar
TirumangaiAlwar was a kallar by birth. He restored to robbery to renovate Srirangam
temple. Lord Vishnu came in person in the guise of a bridegroom and uttered the eight syllable
mantra “Om Na Mo Na Ra Ya Na Ya” into the ears of the belligerent devotee and conveted him
into a benevolent one.
3. Other Saints

The Bhakti movement in the Pallava country was influenced by Nayanmars and Alwars
of the neighbouring areas, particularly from the Pandya country.
The contributions of Periyalwar and Andal to Vaishnava Bhakti movement are significant.
He was a Brahmin of Srivilliputtur in the Pandya country. He was the foster father of Andal. He
converted Srimara Srivallabha to Vaishnavism.

102
Sri Andal or Kothai was the greatest among the women mystics of India. Her Thiruppavai
contains 30 poems are very famous one. Even today in the Vishnu temples they recite
Thiruppavai in the morning time in the month of Margai. Tiruppan Alwar, a minstrel of low caste
was another important alwar, with his intense devotion acquired a place in the Bhakti movement.
Tondoraidippodi alias Vipranarayana Alwar, a Brahmin by birth was another great devotee of
Vishnu.Namalwar was a great mystic. His tiruvaymoli is supreme among the philosophical
literature of the world.
Thus the devotion and intense love of these saints have supported the Bhakti movement
from 6th to 10th centuries . Though these saints were born in Pandya country, they offered their
devotion, and love to the religious centers situated well within the rule of the Pallava territory.
4. Principles of Bhakti

Saivism: Bhakti is devotion to god. Devotion to God can be expressed in many ways.
Bhakti can be expressed in its full form in the temples. . Visiting to the temple, the abode of
Siva, was considered as one of the chief virtues of the Bhakti. Worshipping Siva or participating
in the pujas of Siva was considered as an important aspect of Bhakti. Reciting devotional
songs to the accompaniments of musical instruments was also favoured. Taking the deities on
processions and conducting regular festivals in the temples, were also recognized as a form of
worship. The Bhakti movement stressed the supremacy of God Siva, love to God was manifested
in the hymns of Nayanmars. The significance of five letters Panchakshara-Namasivya was

103
explained. Reciting the life stories of Nayanmars was considered as a way to attain moksha.
Temple construction, repairing the existing temples, and even cleaning the premises of a
temple were a means of showing Bhakti. These activities will ultimately lead to moksha. Similarly,
granting donations to temples for feeding Saiva devotees was also a way of showing one’s
devotion to god. Sincere devotion of the devotees to God was also treated as Bhakti.
Vaishnavism: One of the basic tenants of the teachings of Alwar is the social and spiritual
equality of the devotees, irrespective of their birth and economic status. Alwars laid emphasis
on the aspect of social equality among the worshippers of Vishnu. They preached that those
engaged in the service of Vishnu are all members of one society irrespective of their caste and

creed. The Bhakti in Vaishnavism is influenced by the spirit of service to Vishnu. The service
is explained in the Vaishnava phraseology as Kainkarya. It is an attitude in which the individual
considers himself as a servant (dasa) of god. The servant is longing always for doing service
to God. Another aspect of Vaishnava Bhakti is propounded in the attitude known as Nayaka
Nayakibhava. In this attitude, the Lord Vishnu is considered as the holiest of all beings
(Purushothaman) and the worshipper considering himself as a passionate woman entirely
dependent on Vishnu. Another important aspect of Bhakti was the total surrender to Vishnu,
great God. It is the prapattimarga, (complete surrender) an effective means of recurring
salvation. In worshipping the supreme God, the practice of severe austerities was discouraged.

More emphasis was laid on the repeated utterances of the thousand names of Vishnu than
performing elaborate sacrifices.
The movement
The Bhakti movement started in South India by spreading the life stories of 63 Nayanmars.
The life histories of these saints were summarized by Sundarar in his Tiruttodattogai. Together
with, the miracles of the Gananasambandar and Tirunavukarasar were also spread among the
people. These miracles induced some sort of confidence among the way worshippers in the
Hindu fold. The SaivaNayanmars expressed some sort of cosmopolitan outlook, in which,
devotion of god was considered as supreme virtue and all other caste differences were not
merited. In this the people of higher castes dining with the people of lower castes. The hunter
Kannappar and Pulaiya were taken into Saiva fold. On the Vaishnava side also caste distinctions

104
were not shown. Tirumalisai and Tirumangai were taken into Vaishnava fold. These instances
quickened the Bhakti movement in the Tamil country.
The conversions of Mahendravarman by Appar in the Hindu fold acted as an important
event which prepared a favourable ground for further conversions. These disputations between
the Hindus and Buddhists, as well as with Jains and the victory gained by the Hindu saints are
other reason for the success of the Bhakti movement. The Royal patronage to construct the
temples may be considered as another important reason for the spread of Bhakti cult in
Tamilnadu.

6.5 Literature
The Pallava rulers were great patrons of both Tamil and Sanskrit languages. Their capital

Kanchi had remained a great centre of Sanskrit learning. Most of the Tamil woks were religious
compositions. There are a few secular compositions also. Among the Sanskrit works mention
may be made to two works authored by the king poet Mahendravarman. They are of the force
style. Buddhists composed few religious works in Prakrit. The Tamils adopted a kind of literary
style known as andadi in this period. An andadi is a composition in which the last word or
phrase of the preceding verse is taken as the first word or phrase of the following verse. Such
andadi works are numerous in this period. Another style of works was popular in this period
was Prabhandam, Padigam, another style of poetry was also employed mostly in the devotional
literature. The use of Venba meter was popular in this period. Other methods followed in this
period are viruttam and Kattalaikkaliturai.

In the Tamil literary works Religious literary works are in prominent position. Let us analyse
their works. First we are dealing with Saiva works.

105
6.5.1. Saiva works
1. Devotional Literature:
According to A.L.Basham, “the hymns of the Nayanmars and Alwars are among the
greatest contribution to the world’s religious literature”. To prove to his words we have great
literary works of KaraikkalAmmaiyar
KaraikkalAmmaiyar
Works of KaraikkalAmmaiyar:
KaraikkalAmmaiyar’s original name was Punithavathy. She wrote many Tamil literary
works. Among the Tamil devotional literature works of KaraikkalAmmaiyar can be considered
as first work. She was a woman saint who sang two padigams of 22 verses on the Lord Shiva
of Tiruvalangadu (Tiruvalangadu Mutta-tirupptigam). In it she portrays in detail about the divine
dance of Siva in the cremation ground along with the ghost of that place. Two other works,
Thiruvirattainmanimalai and Arpudattiruvandadi were composed by her in the Andaldi style.

The first work consisted of 20 verses composed in Venba and Kattalaikkalitturai meters. The
later work consists of 100 verses and in this work she adores the God in various manifestations.
2.The Kshetrat-Tiruvenba of AiyyadigalKadavarkon was another work of 24 verses of
Venba meter written in Andadi style. In this work the author lists 22 Saiva shrines including
Ujjain (Makkalam) which were held in high esteem in his day. Though the author hailed from
Tondainadu, most of the shrines praised by him are located in the Chola country. The author

106
gave importance to a few religious centres and they are Kumbakonam, Chidambaram, Tiruvarur,
Tiruvanaikkal, Tirumalapadi, Mylapore and Tiruvotriyur.
3.Tirumular’sTirumandiram
The Tirumandiram is a Tamil poetic work written by Tirumular and is the 10th Tirumarai
which uses the texts of Saiva Siddhanta and this is first Tamil work to use this term In Tamil
the Tirumandiram is the earliest exposition of the Shiva Agamas. It consists of over 3000
verses dealing with various aspects of spirituality, ethics and praise of Lord Shiva This work is
more spiritual than religious and one can see the difference between Vedanta and Siddhanta
from his interpretation of “Mahavakavyas”.
This work is considered as a manual of Saiva mysticism. Tirumular was a Brahman
yogi from Kailasa, migrated to the south to meet the Agastyar. At Tiruvaduturai he entered the

dead body of a shepherded out of pity for the herd which had just lost him. He led the herd
back home in the evening and then abandoned the shepherd’s family. Then he meditated
upon God and wrote out the doctrines of Siva Philosophy in 3000 versus at the rate of one
verse in one year. All the 3000 verses of the tirumandiram are divided into 9 tantras (section)
and each trantra deals with one separate topic. Of the 9 tantras the second tantra, explains
about Sivapuranas, the third and fourth on yoga and the mantropasana, the fifth about the
different forms of Saivaism and the sixth on the Sivagurudarsavas. This work was written in a
simple language. He convinced that mortal body was not a hindrance for the attainment of
salvation. According to Venkataraman a historian Tirumular’s Tirumandiram covers the entire
feature of Siddhar cult of the Tamils
4. Thevaram:

Thevaram indicates the first seven volumes of Tirumurai. All seven volumes are dedicated
to the works of the three most prominent Tamil poets of the 7th century namely Saiva Saints
Gnanasambandar, Tiruavukkarasar and Sundarar. During the reign of Raja Raja Chola I
collection of these songs were found in Chidambaram temple and it was compiled by
NamiyandarNambi.

107
The songs were originally recited by these saints in the temples in praise of the presiding
deity, they have visited. All the three saints have collectively visited 429 temples in the entire
Tamil country and have sung more than hymns divided into 797 padigams, each padigam
containing approximately 10 verses and more. These 8000 hymns were divided into seven
books (Tirumurai). The first three books consisting 384 padigams were sung by
Gnanasambandar, the most celebrated Saiva hymnist. The next three books consisting of 313

108
padigams were sung by Appar and the rest was by Sundarar, which consistuted the 7th book of
the Saiva canon.
Devaram hymns contain many allusions to the saivasiddhantha philosophical system.
The hymns of Smabandar are well known for their youthful vigor and imagination. The
Spontaenous outpourings of devotion can also be witnessed in his hymns. In every one of his
padigams he condemns the Jains. In the hymns Appar condemns caste and conceit of learning.
He was preached equality of human beings and condemns orthodoxy and blind in the sastras.
The hymns of devaram are marked by an exceptional high literary quality. The practice of
singing Devaram is continuing in many Siva temples in Tamil Nadu even today.
6.5.2 Vaishnava Works
1. Nalayira Diva Prabhandam :
The contributions of the Alwars for the spread of religion are remarkable. The first three
Alwars belonged to the Tondianadu and have contributed to the devotional literature in a big

109
way. The other Vaishnava saints had also contributed to the enrichment of literature. The
hymns of the Alwars were compiled by NathamuniAcharya and it was known as Nalayira Divya
Prabhandam in the 10th century. The work contains 4000 hymns of the Alwars. It is divided into
four books and each book containing one thousand verses. The contribution of the first three
Alwars namely PoyagaiAlwar, PeyAlwar and Pudattalwar are known as ‘Tiruvandadi.” This
work is included in this fourth book ‘Iyarpa’. Each Tiruvandadi contains 100 pasurams (hymns)
composed in the Andadi style of Venba meter. The compositions are regarded as unequalled
for their simplicity and lyrical beauty. The main subject of the andadis narrates about the
Miracles and the Incarnations of Vishnu.
2. The TiruchchandaviruttamandNanmuganTiruvandadi

These two works were composed by TirumalisaiAlwar. The first work contains 120
pasurams and included in the first book (Mudalayiram) of the DivyaPrabhandam. It explains
about the Vaishnava philosophy which is beyond the comprehension of an ordinary person.
The latter work contains 96 pasurams in viva meter and included in the last book (Iyarpa) of the
DivyaPrabhandam. The theme of this work is give importance of the supremacy of Narayana
and Lakshmi. The greatness of devotees is also explained.
3. Periyathirumoli,
It is a work of TirumangaiAlwar consists of 1084 pasurams. The work is dedicated to
numerous Vaishnava shrines in the Tamil country as well as those in North India. It contains
valuable historical data on the different battles fought by Nandivarman-II against the Chalukya,
Pandya rulers. The flourishing condition of towns and temples and brisk overseas trade are

vividly portrayed in this work. Tirumangai Alwar’s other works are Tirukkuruntandagam,
Tirunedutandagam, Tiruvelukkurrikkai, Siriyirumedal and PeriyaTirumedal. The above
works consisted of 169 pasurams. They are included in the 2nd thousand (Periyathirumoli) of
the DiviyaPrabhandam collection. In the Vaishnav canon the contributions of Tirumangai (1253
pasurams) is one of the largest.
4. Other works
The saints of the Saiva and Vaishnava sect from the neighboring areas have also
contributed to the enrichment of the devotional literature. Though their works do not have any

110
direct bearing on the Pallava literature, they are referred here. Manikkavasagar’sTiruvasagam
form the 8th book of the Saiva canon. It contains 51 hymns. His Tiruttondartogai, sung at
Tiruvarur narrates the life stories of the 52 Nayanmars. The Tiruvasagam is the epitome of the
philosophic mysteries of Tamil Saivism. Tiruvarur Mummaikkovai and Ponvannattu Andadi are
the other works of importance.
Though a few Alwars come from outside the Pallava country they have praised the Lord
of Srirangam and Tiruvengadam, Kulasekhara has sung three decades in Periyatirumoli a
work consisting of 105 verses. Tiruppanalwar and TondaraidippodiAlwar have sung poems in
praise of Sriranganatha.
5. Prakrit and Sanskrit Works
Prakrit and Sanskrit literary works were flourished in the Pallava kingdom. The Pallava
royal family patronized Sanskrit poets. Prakrit language was encouraged by the Buddhists and

they authored few books. The Abhidammavatara of Buddhadhotta (5th A.D.) explains the
importance of dharma of Buddha. It further narrates about the flourishing status of trade in the
famous port city of Kaveripumpattinam. The life of the rich merchants and their political abodes
and five parts in the city are also explained. The other work, Vinayavinichchayam also written
at deverippumpattinam refers to the condition of Buddhism in the southern part of India. This
work serves us a useful source material to study about the social life of the people in the cities.
6. Works of Bharavi
The scholars praise the rule between Simhavishnu to Narashimavarman as the golden
age of the Sanskrit literature in the Pallava kingdom. Scholars from distinct regions have
enriched the Sanskrit literature. Bharavi’s Kiratarguniya, describes in 18 sections the penance

of Arjuna of obtain the Pasupatastra. Bharavi’s story is narrated in the
Dandin’sAvantisundarikatasara. Domodara, was the son of Narayansvamin, a Brahmin
migrated from Anandapura and settled at Achalpura (near Nasik). He secured the friendship
of Vishnuvardhana (King Eastern Chalukya) and in course of hunting expedition consumed
animal flesh. To expirate the sin he started on a pilgrimage to holy places in the courses of
which he stayed for sometime in the court of Durvinita. In order to patronize Sanskrit scholars

111
the pallava ruler Simhavishnu invited Bharavi to his court. Bharavi composed the literary work
in praise of the pallava ruler Simhavishnu.
7. Works of Mahendravarman
Mattavilasaprahasana was composed by Mahendra-I. It is a one act force in which the
play centres round the frolics of drunken kapalin, Sathysoma and his wife Devasoma. At one
state Satyasoma discovers that his skull bowl is missing and accuses a Buddhist monk. They
both find a Pasupata monk, as their mediator. Finally the problem was settled with the entry of
a lunatic with the skull bowl which he had taken from the dog of a chandela. They play is mixed
with fun, humor and wit. From this work we come to know about the social life and religious
conditions of the Pallava period.
Bhagavadgiugam
This is another work also written by Mahendravarman I. However the anonymous

commentator of the work assigned this work to Bodhayana. The name of the work is mentioned
in the Mamandur inscription along with Mattavilasa prahasana and hence the scholars have
come to a conclusion that this work was written by Mahendravarman I.
Avantisundarikatasara
Dandin was the court poet of the Pallava King Rajasimha-II.and he wrote
Avantisundarikatasara. The historical introduction of Avantisundarikatasara mentions that the
Chalukya king Vishnuvardhana and the western Ganga ruler Durnimita and Simhavishnu are
contemporaries. Kavyadarsha is the other work written by Dandin both the works are considered
as the most important Sanskrit Literary works.
6.5.3. Tamil Works
Though the Pallava rulers patronised Sanskrit scholars few Tamil literary works are also
available. Few works of the eighteen minor works (Padinenkikkanakku) are included in this
period. The Jains were patronised by the Muttaraiyars the feudatories of the Pallava rulers

112
Nandikkalambakkam
It is a secular work. It gives a clear picture of the history and achievements of
Nandivaraman-III. This was an important work composed during the days of Nandivaraman-
III. The author of this work is not known. It is a quasi-historical work of about 80 verses in
various meters. It describes the various events of the region of the Nandivarman-III. Traditionally
it is believed that the work was composed by the brother of Nandivarman-III, in order to kill
Nandivarman-III to get the throne. These poems were sung with the mystical vengeance and
finally Nandivarman-III was burnt alive when last verse was recited. The work refers to the
military victories of Nandivarman-III in several battle fields like Tellaru, Kadambar, Palaiyaru
and Kurukkotai. Few titles of the Nandivarman, like Avaninaranam, Todaivamdam, and

Desabhandari are mentioned in this literary work. Nandivarman-III is described as a great
lover of Tamil and Perundevanar (the author of Bhaatavemba) adorned his court.
Another important Tamil work was that of Bharatavemba of Perundevanar, described the
story of Mahabharata in Tamil Muthollayiram was written during this period. It deals with the
three great kings. The author of this work is not known. A Jaina work Sulamani was written by
Tolamoli Tevar also belonged to the Pallava period.
Among the works of grammar and lexicography are the Kalladam of Kalladanar, Pingalam
of Pingalanar, Purapporu Nenbamalai of Aiyam-artinae (editor) , Iraiyanar Ahapporul Urai etc.

Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism were the three major religious prospered in this period. The

generally suggested that there was religious tolerance in the Pallava Kingdom.

7.1 Introduction
The history and development of Pallava art and architecture constitutes a fascinating
chapter in the annals of Indian History says Dr C. Minakshi. The Pallavas began the great age
of temple building. Percy Brown says that if all the great powers that together made the history

of Southern India, none had a more marked effect on the architecture of the region than the
earliest of all, that of the Pallavas, “whose productions provided the foundations of the Dravidian
style”.

115
They were the pioneers in the history of the Dravidian architecture which constituted a
brilliant chapter in South Indian History.
The Pallava architecture shows the transition from the rock-cut temples to the stone built
temples. The earliest examples of the Pallava art are the rock –cut temples of the 7th century
A.D. The latest examples are of structural temples built in 8th and 9th century. The lasting
monolithic temples are known as Rathas and Mandapas. From this we can understand the skill
of the sculptors of the Pallava period. The shore temple in Mahabalipuram is the best example
for their excellence in the structural temples.
7.2 Art and Architecture
In the Pallava period there was a great encouragement to art and architecture. The
Pallava architecture is confined only to the religious architecture and not on secular buildings

like palaces which are not in existence today. In the Managapattu cave temple inscription
Mahendravarman I say that he completely avoided the use of bricks, lime and wood for the
construction of the temple for the first time. Nearly twenty cave temples were excavated during
the Mahendra period in different places. These temples dedicated to Vishnu, Siva and Tirmurthi
From Mahendravarman I to the end of the Pallava period we have two broad divisions of
architectural style. They are (1) rock cut temples and (2) structural temples

116
1. Rock-cut Temples
Mahendravarman I was the beginner of the rock-cut pattern. According to Dr.
T.V.Mahalingam, “it was Mahendravarman who handled hard rock’s perhaps for the first time
after Asoka and achieved a success that has earned for him a niche in the temple of Indian
art.” In the pre-pallavan period, only brick structures were built. Stone was not used for the
construction of temples. This is one of the reasons that we do not get any religious structure of
the Sangam Age. Therefore the introduction of stone masonry in the construction of temples
was considered to be a novel idea of the pallava ruler. The mandagapattu inscription says that
“This brick less timber less, metalless and amortaarless temple which is a mansion for Brahma,
Eswara and Vishnu was caused to be created by the king Vichitra- Chitta”.According to J.Dubrenil

“Mahendravarman imported the rock-cut pattern from the Vishnukundins.”
The Mandagapattu temple with three garbha grahas is dedicated to the Lords of Hindu
Trinity.The Pancha-Pandava temple at Mamandur, the Mahendra-vishngraham at Mahendravadi,
Malleswara temple at Dalavanur etc., are important specimen of this type. Most walls of these
temples are adorned with plastic arts of incomparable quality.
2. Rock-cut Architecture
The technique of scooping out a cave or a mandapa is very interesting. The work will
start from the top portion and gradually the middle and lower parts of the cave will be cut out.
Therefore the first portion scooped out will be the roof and its superstructure then comes the
body-walls and lastly the basement. This method is evidently seen, as there caves the Vimana
and the Garbhagraha scooped out and finished. But the basement is left untouched and stands
as rock portion. The same method was followed in the case of Ajanta and Ellora caves.

117
The caves of the pallavas seen in the Tondaimandalam are covering the modern districts
of Chingleput, North Arcot, Tiruchirapalli and parts of Andhra Pradesh. The cave is nothing but
a mandapa either square or rectangular in plan with one more cells on the interior of the back
wall. The mandapa bears one or two rows pillars – each row having morel the 4 pillars. It is
sometimes shown projecting with short pillars and looking like a shrine or niche. The caves
have flat roofs in most cases and there are a few with two are three storeys.
We may also notice some evolution or stages of progress in the cave architecture. There
are a number of caves which bear beautiful sculptures and carving on the interior walls and
pillars. The Mamallapuram caves can be suggested as best examples. They contain the figures

of Vishnu Sive, Brahma, Durga, Lakshmi, Sarasvati and numerous other forms of Siva and
avataras of Vishnu. There are Sculpturned panels depicting scenes from Ramayana.
Mahabharata and PuranasWe can see the pallava caves in the following places namely
Mamallapuram, Mandagapattu, Tiruchirapalli Rock for (foot of the fort) Mahendravadi etc.
3. Mamallapuram
Mamallapuram is a great centre of art and architecture of the pallavas and attracts tourists
and art lovers from all over the world. It has more than 14 cave -temples, 9 monolithic shrines,
3 structural stone temples and 4 relief sculptured rock panels. It has the earliest datable rockcut mandapas, rathas and structure temples of the Dravidian style. The monuments seem to
have been originally decorated with paintings, traces of which are noticed even today in the

Adi-varaha cave temple. These caves and rathas bear inscriptions in Pallava grantha characters
and from this we can assign their date.
4. Authorship
The authorship of the monuments at mamallapuram is controversial issue. There are two
theories (1) the monuments are dated according to their architectural styles; (2) according to
the palaeography of the inscriptions on the wall of the monuments. The first theory was put
forth by K.R. Srinivasan and according to him most of the monuments belong to Narasimha
Varman-1. He classified them as belonging to different styles such as Mahendra’s style,
Mamalla’s style etc. The Mahendra’s style was followed by Narasimhavarman-(Mamalla). The
style was continued under the successors of Mamalla like Mahendra-ll or Paramesvaram.

118
The structural temple was first introduced by Narasimhavarman-ll (Rajasimha). The second
theory was postulated on the basis of the study of the inscriptions. The inscriptions on the
rathas contain a number of titles borne by Rajasimha and therefore they were described to
him. Further he is believed to have excavated the mandapas also as the ruler has immense
interest to create varieties of monuments at the same place.
The Mamallapuram monuments may be studied under three categories namely (1) Cave
temple,(2) Monolithic rathas, (3) Structural temples.
7.2.1 Cave Temples
There has been difference of opinionabout the authorship of the group of cave temples,
penance panels and the Five Rathas. R.Nagaswamy expressed the view that Rajasimha
(NarasimhavarmanII) was the sole author of all the Mamallapuram monuments and inscriptions.

They are about a dozen cave temples. To name a few Dharamaraja Mandapa, Kotikal
Mandapa, Tirumurthi Cave, Varaha Cave, Adivaraha temple Ramanuja Mandapa,
Panchapandava mandapa and Mahishamardhani cave etc. There are few more caves but
they do not exhibit workmanship or sculptures. Among the above mentioned caves, the following
deserves detailed discussion.
1. Trimurthi cave
It is triple-called dedicated to the trinity namely Siva, Vishnu and Brahma. The three cells
are guarded by door keepers in bas-relies. The figure of the god is caved in bas-relief on the
back wall of the cells.
2. Varaha Mandapa
The cave is noted for its beautiful sculptures on the interior walls of the porch.. The
sculptures represent Vishnu in the vahara and Tiruvikrama avatars and also Goddess
Gajalakshmi and Durga.
3. Adivaraha Temple

It is one of the biggest caves with rich sculptures. Here again the Varaha avatara of
Vishnu is sculptured inside the shrine chamber. There are portrait sculptures representing the

119
rulers Narasimhavarman-l and his father Mahendravarman-l and their queens. This is an
interesting feature of this cave.
4. Mahishasuramardhani Cave
This is yet another triple-celled mandapa. The central shrine contains the figure of
Somaskanda in bas-relief. They are also sculptured panels depicting Durga fighting with the
demon and Vishnu as Sesgasatyin. These two panels are remarkable for their artistic merit
originally of treatment and skilful execution.
7.2.2 Monolithic Rathas
There are 9 rathas of which 6 are almost finished and the other 3 are unfinished and
incomplete at their bottom. Of these, 5 caves are found in one area and named after the
pancha pandavas in the later period. Each ratha is carved out of a single rock and it is cut
model of a structural temple of timber construction of the earliest period. They contain a
garbha and a verandah.
1. Five Rathas

They are named after Draupati, Arjuna, Bihama, Dharmaraja and Sahadeva
2. Draupati Ratha
It is but shaped and dedicated to Durga. It shares its platform with Arjuna ratha. There is
a huge sculpture of Durga on the inner wall of the shrine.
3. Arjuna Ratha
It is dedicated to Siva. It is square in share and single storied; and adorned at the top up
an octagonal dome. Chatiya motifs and string courses of miniature shrine motifs run around
the storeys.
4. Bhima Ratha
It is rectangular in plan with wagon topped or Sikhara having gable ends on either side.
The porch has rows of pillar with lion base. It is incomplete. This plan and shape served as
prototype for the Gopurams of South Indian temples in the subsequent periods.

120
5. Dharmaraja Ratha
It is dedicated to Siva and three storied and square in plan. The ground floor is unfinished
and the first floor houses the sanctum with pradakshina patha. The walls of the upper storey
contain small niches with sculptures representing various aspects of Siva and Vishnu. There
are inscriptions on the walls declaring its date of construction and author.
6. Sahadeva Ratha
It is unique in its ground plan because it has an apsidal ground plan and elephant back
top. It is known as Gajaprishta shrine in Sanskrit. This may be called a representative type of
the Vesara style of architecture prevalent in the Karnataka area.
7. Ganesa Ratha
It is also an apsidal shrine but with wagon top roof and gable ends. The above mentioned
rathas thus represent different shapes and style in the temples architecture of Tamil nadu. The

pallavas created these rathas to serve them as models for the future guidance. That is why
they present varieties. Further, they were no meant for offering worship as suggested by their
unfinished characters. It may be stressed here that these rathas with different ground plan and
Vimana served as prototypes for the storied temples and gopurams of the later period. Thus
this is an important contribution of the pallavas to Dravidian architecture.

7.2.3 Structural Temples
Importance of Shore Temple, Mahabalipuram
From Kuram records we get information about Structural temples. Shore Temple is granite
made temple at Mahabalipuram built during the period of Narsimhavarman. This group of
temples is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and is oldest structural temple in India.There is only

121
one temple i.e. the famous shore temple. It is one of the few earliest structural temples of the
pallavas. It is in a most dilapidated condition and its prakaras and frontal protions had been
ruined by Nature’s fury. However a conjectural restoration suggests that the temple had originally
two small concentric outer Prakaras with entrance at the western side. Now the temple is
rueing most, while its eastern wing abutting into the sea waters almost. The cell measures 12
square and 11 heights. There is circumambulatory passage around it. The vimana is three
storied. Inside the cell a Somaskanda panel is seen on the wall. On the western side, there is
third shrine of Vishnu in a recumbent position. This is later addition. As said earlier there was
originally one or two outer prakaras for the temples. But at present they are razed to the
ground.

The wall of the eastern shrine is decorated with rampant lion shaped pilasters at regular
intervals. It is an excellent temple, which is a combined complex of 3 shines, one dedicated to
Vishnu and the remaining two dedicated to Shiva. This temple indicates the culmination of the
architectural efforts that began with the cave temples and monolithic rathas. 7 Pagodas is a

122
term associated this temple. It is said that the 6 more temples were associated with it, all now
submerged in water.
TIGER CAVE AT SALUVANKUPPAM
1. Tiger Cave at Saluvankuppam
Besides the above monuments, there is yet another unique cave at Saluvankuppam
about 5 K.M. north of Mamallapuram. It is large mass of rock 60’ length and 2-‘height. A shine
is excavated at the central portion. The facade is shaped like the mark of a tiger with griffin
heads in relief and hence it is called tiger cave. It is said that the animal depicted is the
mythological Yali and hence it is also known as Yali Mandapam.
It is also said that the shrine was used as a stage to render musical concerts and excavated
according to the principles of acoustics of buildings. The mandapam is like an open air theatre
and even today some cultural events are held here. Small hillocks, big boulders set amidst

casuarinas’ trees and the sandy shores make this place as a great heaven for birds and a
picnic spot.

123
2. Pillars
The pillars show evolutionary stages. The pillars in the beginning are very simple. They
are very short, bulky and plain. They have a square base and bracket capital. In the next stage
they have became taller exhibiting more workmanship. The body is faced and fluted and the
capital is shaped like an inverted lotus flower and above it is placed a broad abacus (Palakai).
The base bears a squatting lion or yali. In the final stage, the lower portion of the pillar is
shaped like a rampant lion or yali. This type of pillar has become a permanent feature of the
later. Pallavan pillars and they may be considered as a criterion to identify Pallava monuments.
Plasters of this shape are being used as a decorative motif t adorn the outer walls of the
sanctum and prakaras as seen in the shore temples at Mamallapuram and Kailasanatha and
other temples at Kanchipuram.

They types of pillars were also adopted by the early Cholas in areas like Tondaimandalam
which marked the transitional stage from the pallavas to the early Cholas.
3. Kanchipuram
Kanchippuram was the capital of the Pallavas. It is one of the oldest and sacred cities in
India. In was flourishing as a centre of all the four major religions in India namely Saivism,
Vaishnavism, Buddhism and Jainism. It served as a meeting place for different religious sects
and cultures.Most of the pallava temples are located at kanchipuram and they are considered
to be earliest datable structural temples of the Dravida style. The following are the Pallava
temples which are inexistence today at kanchipurm (1) Kailasanatha Temple 2. Vaikunthaperumal
Temple 3. Muukteswara Temple 4. Matangesvara Temple 5. Amaresvara Temple 6. Airavarisvara
Temple 7. Piravatisvara temple and 8. Ravanatisvara Temple.

4. Kalisanatha Temple
It was built by Rajasimha. It is called Rajasimhesvara after him. This temple is the “greatest
architectural masterpiece”. It is an art gallery with innumerable minor shrines, considered to be
“apogee of the Pallava style”. It is famous to its architectural designs and sculptural wealth. It
is well proportioned, Substantial and rythmistic in its mass and elegant in its outlines.

124
The temple has three components 1. The main shrine with its vimana and the separate
pillar mandapa in front 2 Prakara and a separate shrine known as mahendravarmesvara in
front of the pillard mandapa and 3. Outer courtyard
5. Main shrine (Sanctum)
The main shrine is square sub-shrines attached at its three sides and corners. These
sub-shrines are projecting outside and thus give a star-shape outline of the sanctum.
The vimana has three storeys adorned at the top by an octagonal stone. The base of the
temple bears ornamental moulding and relief sculptures.
6. Prakara
The prakara wall bears as many as 58 inches with sculptures representing various aspects
of Siva etc. They were originally painted and traces of such paintings are visible even today.
They may be called replica of main shrine but in miniature forms. The prakara wall carries at its

centre on all the four sides a rectangular sala (wagon Topped roof) and this structural motif at
the top of the main entrance on the western side is imposing and suggests the Pallava’s
sincere attempt to design a pattern (rectangular as in the case of the gopuras) for the main
entrance to a Hindu temple. Further, the Mahendravarmesvara shrine has also a rectangular
ground plan and occupies the frontal portion near the entrance. This structure and its disposition
are marvellous and really a subsequent periods the Cholas and the Pandyas, picked up this
idea and also adopted this structural design while shaping the gopuras. The idea of providing
entrances in all the four directions is also evident from the distribution of the Salas at the top of
the midprakara walls of this temple.
7. Outer Courtyard
The entrance to the temple is provided in the outer courtyard on the western side and the

entry in to the prakara is provided by a narrow opening on both sides (southern and northern
sides)
8. Nandi Mandapa
In front of the temple at a distance, a huge monolithic Nandi is seen within a shelter. It
may be called as Nandi Mandapa.

125
9. Sculptures
The sub-shrines around the sanctum carry sculpture representing Siva, Vishnu, Brahma,
Somaskanda, Nandi etc. The well known aspects of Siva such as Bhikshatana Gangadhara
and Tripurantaka are also depicted. Similarly, as said earlier, the various cells on the inner
walls of the prakara bear beautiful sculputers in relief exhibition the Hindu gods and mythological
scenes. Since Kailasantha temple is the earliest of a series of pallava temple at Kanchipuram,
the sculptures there in represent the earliest phase of plastic art in Tamilnadu. They also exhibit
the scholarship of the master craftsmen in the execution of art specimens and sculptured
panels. They are narrative to some extent and informative to a large extent.
10. Inscriptions
There are a number of inscriptions noticed in the temple which help us to date the style

and the various temple complexes. The inscription belongs to both the Pallavas and Western
Chalukyas. The Chalukya king Vikramaditya-lV admired the architectural beauty of this temple
and made gold gifts to the temple. He was impressed with this style of architecture. Hence on
the same style he constructed the Virupaksha Temple at Pattadakkalis

126
11. Vaikunthaperumal Temple
This temple is famous for its historical sculptures. It is yet another wonderful product of
the pallavas times. It was built by parameswara alias Nandivarman Pallavamalla. It is a
Vaishnavite temple and is called paramessvara Vishnugriham in an inscription of the temple.
The plan of the sanctum is square and it has a pyramidal tower with three storeys and the
top is adorned by an octagon stone. The first two storeys are functional as they contain the
sitting and reclining form of Vishnu within the shrine chambers while the ground floor has the
standing figure of Vishnu. All the three chambers are alike in plan ad size with a circumbulatory
passage around the sansctum. The Vimana bears the various forms of Vishnu including a few
of his avataras such as trivikkrama, Narasimha etc. There are scenes from Bhagavata and

pranas. The walls of the sanctum in the ground floor also contains the avarataras of Vishnu
and Krishna as goverdhana.
In front of the shrine champer is a pillared mandapa and a cloister (pillard verandah)
running round the inner prakara. There is also an outer prakara with a ruined gopura of the
period.
These panels are narrative in character and tell us the history of the pallava dynasty from
beginning. The events that lead to the election of Nandivaraman to the pallava throne are
clearly portrayed in successive panel in a Chronological order. Further as many as 14 panals
bear labels with description of the scenes. These historical panels are unique in the annals of
South Indian sculpture and are considered to be an important source for writing the history of
the pallavas upto the time of Nandivarman. These sculptured panels hide may be important

historical and political events of the contemporary period and they are yet to be properly identified
and interpreted. It remains to be done.
12. Other Temples
The Kesava Perumal temple at Kurram is the master piece of the Pallava art. The other
temple at kancheepuram namely is Muktesvarar temple. This temple is the “Zenith of Pallava
Art”. Are very small ones with a sanctum and a pillared porch. The sanctum is located on a
high plinth of about 10 feet high. Steep steps lead to the porch. An enclosure is also noticed in

127
a few temples. They are belonged to the later pallava period, i.e., after Naddivarman’s time.
The dimensions of these structures suggest that the pallava resources were drained on account
of frequent wars with the chalukyas and consequently they did not have sufficient funds to be
diverted to the construction of temples on large dimensions.

13.JainKanchi

128
Jain kanchi forms part of kanchipuram but it is familiar with this term mainly on account
of its association with jainsm and jain temples. A regular colony of jains was in existence in
those days at this place. It is also known as Tiruparuttikunram. There are two jain temples at
this place – one is dedicated to Vardhamana the 24th Tirthankara and Chandra Prabha, the 8th
Tirthankara. According to local traditions, these temples were built by a pallava king at the
instance of 2 jain teachers who were residing at this place. Both the temples are located very
near to one another. These temples have been renovated during the Chola and later periods
and at a time of renovation work the temples lost their original architecture features
14. Panamalai Temple (Near Villupuram, S.A. District)
The temple is known as Talagirisvara temple. It is built by Rajasimha. In plan and design

it resembles the kailasanatha temple. It has a square sanctum preceded by a vaestibule (narrow
passage) and an ardhamandapa. The sanctum has projecting miniature cells at the centre
cells of its three sides and this arrangement give star shaped outer design for temple. The
northern cell contains painted figures of a dancing Siva and Parvathi. The traces of paintings
are still visible.
15. Tiruvatikal Temple
It is situated at about 45 miles South East of Villupuram. It is a famous Siva temple
known as Tiruvirattanesvara temple and it is sung by Appar. It was built by Parmesvaravarmanll. But during the time of Nirapatunga and Nandivarman, the temple received additional changes.
The Vimana has 5 storeys and much of its original structural portions are hidden under
the thick coat colouring material recently applied during renovation.

7.3 Sculpture
The sculptus of this period are the earliest in Tamil Nadu and hence they constitute the
earliest art in the history of the Tamils. Though there are references to making stone images
and sculptures in the Sangam works, we do not have any specimens on hand for study.

129
The materials used in making sculpture are (1) granite and (2) sand stone. The latter
variety was used more frequently as it was easy to chisel and carve on the stone. But the
granite is a hard stone and it may crack while chiselling and the Pallava sculptors voluntarily
picked up this stone to exhibit their skill in the art of sculpting.
The sculptures are found scattered over the entire Thondaimandala area, adoring the
walls, pillars, storeys, basement and balustrades of the caves, rathas and the structural temples.
The sculptures in the temples at Kailasanatha and Vaikunthaperumal are covered with thick
coating of plasters (stucco) this is a special feature of sculptural art of the later pallavas.
Though there the different types of sculptures and panels it is very difficult to trace any
stages of evolution. However, the lengthy panels and massive sculptures and figures of this

period may represent the initial stage and later gradually they were reduced in size and
proportions suggesting improvement and advancement in the subject.
The following are the salient features of the pallava art and sculpture.
Namely the theme in most cases is religious but secular and social scenes are also
portrayed and the contemporary society is vividly depicted. The flora and fauna are also
represented. The fauna is represented by both wild and domestic animals. Birds are also
included in the panels.The everyday life has also been chiselled. For instance, marriage scene,
milking the cow, processions, festivals, selling, markets etc deserve special menting. The stories
from ancient puranas even from Mahabharata and Ramayana are shown in narrative panels.
War scenes are not known to the Pallava artisans. Buddhist and Jaina sculptures are also
seen.

There are sculptured panels depicting the contemporary political events. For instance,
the sculptured panels of the vaikunthaperumal temple are considered to be master pieces in
the whole history of South Indian art. The election of Nandivarman Pallavamala, to the throne
and his carnation was attended by the nobles and ministers.
The various figures like men and women, gods and goddess, different garments numerous
ornaments from head to foot and present varieties of hair dressing and crowns, however,
garments and ornaments are fewer in number they are not lavishly executed.

130
The figures are represented in a related position but in different places to suggest depth
and perspectiveness. Light and shade are effectively exhibited. Dynamism and naturalism are
explicitly noticed. But sometimes, anatomical details of human figures are not faithfully brought
to surface. However attempts have been made to represent life size figures in a natural way.
Prominence is being given to human figures as well as animal’s kingdom.
7.3.1 Sculptures at Mamallapuram
Among the sculptures at Mamallapuram, the following deserve special mention.
1. Krishna as Govardhana
The Panchapandava Mandapa, contains very lengthy panel, measuring about 50’ x 8
running over the entire back wall of the mandapa. This is one of the biggest sculptured panels
(bas-relief) seems in South India. Here Krishna’s youthful exploits and adventures among

cowherds and in Brindavan are being narrated. The panel shows Krishna holding up the
Govardhana hill in his left arm in order to shelter a group of men, women and children of the
cowherd community.
2. Arjuna’s Penance
This is the biggest bas-relief sculpture in the history of the Indian art and as you all know,
it provides a rare and unique feat to the eyes of the visitors – particularly the foreigners. This
sculptured panel is said to represent the “Arjuna’s Penane”. The story is that Siva appeared
before Arjuna in the Guise of a wild kirata (hunter) Arjuna was doing penance to invoke the
blessings of Siva and accordingly, this scene is represented on the rock surface. But apart
from Arjuna and Siva, there are some other features which suggest that the scent may be
interpreted as depicting the Bhagiratha’s penance and descent of the river Gangas. This

explanation is offered on the rock which is supposed to represent the descent of the river
Gangas and a Naga and Nagini are offering worship to the goddess with their folded hands
from the banks of the river. It is well known fact that the Nagas are water spirits.
There are figures of other deities like the sun and the moon and Devas and Gandharva.
Siva represented with four arms attended by his little ganas or attendants. A small shrine is

131
shown and in front of it is seen Arjuna or Bhagiratha doing Penance. The entire rock which
measures about 60’ x 30’m stands for the mount Himalayas. It is interesting to note that the
scent exhibits a variety of animals like lion, elephant, and monkey etc. are moving towards the
river. A monkey family is also vividly chiselled. Further it is amusing that cat is also doing
penance on the other bank of the river opposite to Arjuna surroundered by mouses looking at
the cat with awe and wonder.
Therefore this panel represents and only the religious scene from the ancient literature,
but also the wild animal life and the forestry in the contemporary period. The technique and
style and superb and the animal representations are realistic and conform to the norms of
anatomy. The various figures have been arranged and displayed in a fantastic way that the

story hidden is readable and brought to surface. The above mentioned pieces of sculptures
and panals speak the high scholarship of the sculptors of the pallava period and the plastic art
has reached a high water mark during the period.
7.3.2 Paintings
Great impetus was given to paintings during the pallava period. It is amply seen in the
inscriptions of Mamandur. Mahendravarman took steps for the compilation of a commentary
called Dakshina Chitra (South Indian Painting). He followed the rules and regulations suggested
for this work.
Sittanavasal Painting

132
Sittanavasal is an important centre of the paintings of the age. The walls were first coated
with lime paste to cause even surface. Then paints of natural herbs were used to colour the
sketches. The south Indian School of painting seem to have flourished re4aching its apoage
under the pallavas
Mahendravarnman was called “Chitrakarapuli” due to his contributions to the paintings.
The paintings on the roof of Kudimiyanmalai, on the walls of Kailasanatha temple,
Adivaraha and Mamandur cave have clearly shows their interest in the field of paintings.
Music:
Under the pallavas music seems to have developed well. The Mamandur inscription
contains a note on the notation of vocal music. The Sanskrit inscription of Kudimiyan maalai is
famous for its reference to musical sounds and instruments. Mahendravarman himself was an

expert in Music. The Alwars and Nayanmars composed their hymns in various musical notes.
Dancing:
Dancing was developed during this period to a greater extent. The various poses of the
Nataraja at Kailasanatha temple indicate their interest over dance. There were dancing girls in
the temples during in this period.
Drama:
The Pallava rulers showed great interest in the field of drama. Mahendravarman wrote a
beautiful social drama Mattavilasaprahasanam in Sanskrit. From Penenkattai we know the
importance of drama. There is reference about dance group in the Vaikundasperumal temple.
From these references we get a fair idea about the Pallava’s interest towards Drama.

7.4. Summary
The Dravidian style of architecture started with the Pallava rule. It was a gradual evolution
starting from the rockcut-cave temples to monolithic rathas which finally concluded with the
structural temples Architecture reached its zenith under the Pallava rule. . The period is also
called as the age of “poetry in stone”. The magnificent Kailashnatha temple is carved out in
stone, bears the testimony of the period. The monolithic seven Pagodas or rathas named after
Pandavas are architectural wonders, though sea-erosion has taken its toll.
Therefore, it may be said that pallava period witnessed the emergence of stone masonry,
the introduction of rock cut techniques, the construction of structural buildings for the first time
in Tamil Nadu. Further, they were responsible for the introduction of Dravidian style of architecture

in South India. This style gained momentum in the subsequent periods and reached its zenith
of power during the later Chola and Vijayanagar periods.
