8.1 Introduction
The Chola dynasty was one of the longest ruling dynasties in the History of South India.
From the various sources we get a detailed description about the administration, society and
economic conditions of the Imperial Cholas. The Cholas had a fertile valley of the Kaveri River
and they also ruled a larger area from half of the 9th century till the beginning of the 13th century.
The Chola period was a well-advanced period in all spheres. Caste system was prevalent
during the chola period. Brahmanas and Kshatriyas enjoyed special privileges. The inscriptions
of the later period of the Chola rule mentions about two major divisions namely Valangai and
Idangai castes. The cholas had a good economic condition. Reclamation of forest lands and
the construction and the maintenance of irrigation tanks led to agricultural prosperity. They

have issued Gold, Silver and copper coins. Reclamation of forest lands and the construction
and maintenance of irrigation tanks led to agricultural prosperity.
8.2 Population
The exact numbers of the population during this period is not known, periodical survey
was not conducted. The ports, important cities and towns were thickly populated because of
busy activities. There cannot be the slightest doubt that under the cholas of the Vijalaya line,
Southern India was vastly more populous and that social life had become far more complex
than in the Sangam Age.
8.2.1 Caste System
Caste was the basis of social organisation. Each caste was more or less a hereditary
occupational group with an active organization for the regulation and protection of its economic
and social interests. Though there were various sections in the society, it is interesting to note

that there was practically no evidence of ugly social conflicts or jealousies. The general
impression derived is one of social harmony in the chola period. The upper classes enjoyed
high privileges in the society. Heredity was not always a bar to a person changing his occupation
and his group- relations with it.

138
8.2.2 Communities
Brahmanas
Though learning and teaching the Vedic literature, performing rituals and officiating
ceremonies were considered as the main duties of the Brahmins, the inscriptions of the Chola
period throw light on the other occupations in which the Brahmanas engaged themselves.
They played the part of chief priests of the temple, Gurunatha of the emperors, ministers, royal
officials, general, poets, arbitrators, administrators etc. They occupied high positions during
this period. A large number of Brahmins were invited from North India and were given
Brahmadeya for their comfortable life. Higher education was in the hands of the Brahmin
teachers. The vedapatasalas were under their control.
The Brahmanas had knowledge in Vedas, Puranas, Upanishads and other spiritual and
religious matters. They helped the common people to understand the great principles underlying

the epic stories. The Brahmanas acted as Rajagurus to the chola kings. They served in the
temples. Some served as ministers and commander-in-chief .They were given many grants
like Veda vritti, Bharatha vritti and Bhata vritti for such services.
The administration of Brahmadeyas and Chaturvedimangalams were left under the control
of the Brahmins. The assembly was known as Sabha. The qualification required to become a
member of the Sabhas were prescribed. They assisted the local court in deciding cases as
they were well versed in Nitisastras.
The administration wheeled around the king during the time of the Cholas, very little is
known about the ministers who assisted the king. But some were very powerful and treated
well by the monarch. Anirudda Brahmarayan was the Brahmin minister of Sundara Chola,
father of Rajaraja-I. The king granted him a village as Ekabuga, Brahmadeya. Anirudda’s

father was a teacher and grandfather was a priest. Krishnan Raman a general of Rajaraja-I
served as Olainayakam in the reign of Rajaraja-I. He built compound wall of the Brahadesvara
temple. His son also served as general under Rajendra-I. A Brahmin served as a revenue
official under Rajadhiraja-I.
Though the administration of the area was left under the control of the government officials
and local authorities, in importing justice they used to consult the Brahmins of the locality as
they were the masters of Nitisastras. When the Kammala’s claims the rights of performing

139
Vedic sacrifices the Brahmins made it very clear to the kind that Kammalas should not be given
such rights as it was the privilege of the Brahmins.
The Brahmins were engaged in trade also The Brahmins were very much devoted to
their spiritual ideals and culture and simple living and commanded the respect of the other
classes. Many grants were made in their favour in almost all parts of the Chola country by all
classes of people without any distinction.Both Siva brahmanas and Vaishnava brahmanas
lived during this period. Both were patronized equally. Thus the Brahmins enjoyed special
privileges in all spheres.
Vellalas
The vellalas were a powerful community of people. They owned lands and they were in
position to donate lands to the temples. The vellalas had their own flag. They had separate

army for their safety and security. The vellala ladies had high respect in the society. This we
infer from the Kaveripakkam inscriptions. Certain inscriptions of Rajaraja I refer to the
appointment of Vellalas in the Siva temples to recite Tiruppadiyam.
Kammalas
They enjoyed special privileges which were given by a chola monarch. The privileges
were: the blowing of two conches, the beating drums and so on at domestic occurrences, good
or bad: the use of sandals when they went out of their houses: and the plastering of the walls
of their residences with lime plaster. The construction of houses with two storeys and with
double doors is also mentioned together with the right to decorate the front of their housed
with garlands of water- lilies.
Other Communities
There were other group of people lived in the chola dynasty .One among them was

Kaikolar community. They were weavers and merchants but they also maintained armies. Their
main roles were trading and military. Another section of the society was Rathakaras. It means
chariot maker. There were also Shepherds, Paraiyas and Puliyas.

140
Right and Left hand classes:
No picture of social divisions in South India under the cholas will be complete without a
reference to the broad division of the industrial population of the country into Right-Hand and
Left-Hand, Valangai and Idangai divisions. These two divisions were never friendly and there
were various instances to prove their enmity between each other. During the time of Kulonthunga
Chola-I a clash between the right and left hand castes resulted in the burning of the village and
the destruction of its sacred places.there were many divisions on each side. It is said that there
were 98 sub-divisions in the left hand classes. Their primary occupation was agriculture. Both
Idangai and Valangai sects had separate temples for their worship. They used separate pavilion
for religious purposes.
Thus in the chola period we can come across the importance of the Brahmins in the

society. They followed the Arya fourfold divisions in the society. There were other communities
also lived without any quarrels.
8.2.3 Slavery
From the literary evidence we come to know that a considerable number of the population
especially among the agricultural labourers lived in a condition of slavery. Like any other property,
the rich had the right to buy human beings also. Free men and women were made slaves for
various reasons, and it would appear that there were several grades among the slaves. Most
of the sales are recorded in the inscriptions are sales of persons to temples. Sometimes they
were voluntary: two ladies sold themselves and their dependants and relatives to a temple in
the Tanjore district: in these instances, the religious motive must have been more dominant
than economic. But in another case when six persons were sold to the same temple in the

same year for 13 kasus by another person, neither the voluntary nor the religious character of
the transaction is so apparent. Similarly many were sold to the temples. It is interesting to note
that women were presented to a temple to sing Tirupadiyam and to serve as chauri bearers to
God.
Though they were presented they had to be under the custody of the temple authorities
and they had to serve in the temples as slaves. It was also a practice that some facilities were

141
dedicated for temple service by officials. The dedicated families were not ill-treated by the local
authorities. Instead they were enjoyed some privileges on the festival days though they had to
work hard. Anyhow as they were compelled to discharge their duties assigned by the officials
and the local assembly they were identified with slaves. Devaradiyar were dedicated to the
temple and they were assigned to work of singing and dancing in the temple. Some women
were also appropriated to the place service.. As sridhana or dowry, wives brought slaves to
their husbands. If he wanted so sell the slaves, he had to get the consent of his wife. Sometimes
that temple after having purchased the slave employed them as slave’s mutt. They were marked
with the trident mark and assigned specific duties to them. If they failed to do their duty, they
were punished.

Slavery was also due to poverty. In times of famine, destitute persons escaped death by
selling themselves and sometimes their unborn descendants for their keep. When the husband
died the wife became the legal owner of his slaves and property. The labourers were not
permitted to own slaves.
Though the basic necessaries of life were enjoyed by the slaves of the Chola time, the
owners were very strict about the slaves. It is clear from various records that the slaves were
owned by the temples and mutts, sole to them voluntarily, or compulsorily. There is no direct
evidence to show that the rich people owned slaves. But as the rich had sold the slaves to the
mutt and the temples, it could be presumed that the wealthy people also owned slaves during
the Chola time.
Thus during the Chola period there were two kinds of slaves viz., temple slaves and

household slaves. Some slaves were purchases: some were given as presentation to temples:
some were sold during the time of famine and drought. Slaves in the temples considered
themselves as slaves to God but not to human beings. This fact is greatly accepted even
today. .

8.2.4 Women
During the Chola period it was generally felt that the women were well treated and they
were not placed under any restraints in their social life activities though modesty was considered
the highest among their graces.. It is clear from various records that the women of the royal
family and upper classes owned property and had the right to dispose of at as they wanted.
Members of the royal family like sembiyanmadevi, Vannavin Maadevi and kundavi were the
great patrons of religion and temple building. Many Chola queens and princesses donated
freely to the temples, schools and hospitals. They were instrumental to build several temples
also. Polygamy was prevalent amongst kings and the rich people had more than one wife.
Women were interested in music and dance and instruments of various kinds were known

to them. Some women attached themselves to the temples and the palaces. They served the
kings and the royal ladies. Though women were respected they did not have equal right. Wife
was expected to look after the household affairs. Chaste women were respected. The
employment of female labour in the less skilled occupations was perhaps quite as common as
at present.
1. Marriage
Marriage is considered as an important stage in a woman’s life in society. It binds together
two individuals as husband and wife. Marriage leads to life, which is considered to be the basic
unit of society. .Kings and rich men married more than one wife. Common men had only one
wife. Marriage was celebrated according to Vedic rites. Apart from ornaments and jewels, rich
women were given slaves also when they left for their husband’s house. Married women have

high status in the society. The bridegroom had to pay a certain amount to the girl’s parents
before marriage. Dowry system was unknown to the people of the. Girls were named at the
age of twelve. The tying of tali was in vogue in the Chola period.
2. Sati
Sati or self-immolation of a woman on the funeral pyre of her husband is occasionally
mentioned in the inscriptions, but the reference is so few that it can be hardly regarded as a
common practice in the Tamil country under the cholas. Gangamadeviyar, the wife of Vira-sola

143
Ilangovelar, is said to have endowed a lamp before she entered the fire: this was perhaps early
in the reign of Parantaka I. The Tiruvalngadu plates mentions about the Vanavan-mahadevi,
the queen of sundara Chola. Viramadevi, the queen of Rajendra-1 who committed sati; some
of the wives of chieftains also committed sati.. A man who killed a relative of the Chola king in
a wrestling match was sentenced to death. His wife followed him in spite of opposition from the
parents. In most of the cases, women lived after the death of her husband and did service for
the promotion of Saivism. Sembiyan Mahadevi’s services are remarkable. Endowments were
made by descendants for the spiritual benefit of the deceased. Some women took to sati to
escape cruel treatment of the hands of the relatives especially the other wives of their husbands.
3. Widows

The condition of the widows from time immemorial was very pathetic. They were symbols
of misfortune and their presence was inauspicious. They lost their identity as the light of the
homes. They had to lead simple life renouncing the joys of life, only very few widows followed
sati. Others were at the mercy of the male members of the house. The condition of the king’s
wife and noble’s wife were slightly better. So they owned property, they had their own entity and
they had the right to lead life of their own. But there also they seemed to dedicate their life in
religious activities. Rich women endowed grants to temples and schools. Sembiyanmadevi,
the widow of gandaraditya engaged herself in builing many Siva temples and granted lands.
4. Courtesans
The class of courtesans has always held a considerable place in Indian society. The

courtesans had their own place in history from very early times. They were known as kanikaiyar
or parathiyar in the sangam society. They had separate streets for themselves. There were
different varieties in them.Similarly the Chola society also witnessed a separate community of
people known as courtesans. Usually they were attached to temples participating in religious
festivals. They were experts in music and dance. She mixed freely with men and was under
no obligation to observe the restraints imposed on matrons in their social intercourse. Her
private company was given to select friends, and her choice was guided by sentimental and
aesthetic as by mercenary motives. The courtesan led a life of cultured ease and pleasure
provided amusement and intellectual companionship to those who could afford the luxury.

144
During the reign of Rajaraja-1 there were several dancing girls attached to the
Brahadeesvara temple. They were known as talicheripendir. They were housed near the temple
and grants were made by king for their maintenance. They had to participate in the festivals
and daily activities of the temple. They were well versed in music and dancing. Some were
good actresses enacting dramas. As this group of women dedicated themselves to temple
activities and festivals and lived near the temples, they were known as Devaradiyar or
Talicheripendir and natakakaiyar. Usually these women never married. But there were a few
exceptions that were married. Most of courtesans were rich and pious women. They also made
many endowments for various public benefactions.
The dancing girls were given all facilities during the cho;la period. The title of ‘Talaikkol”

was given to a girl who excelled in dance and Music. The courtesans who were very well
versed in music and dance were given the title as talaikadi by the Chola rulers. The way in
which they were treated by the monarchs and chieftains gave them a good status.
This system of Devaradiyar was abolished in British times but its rudiments are still found
in isolated areas.
8.3 Buildings
During the Chola period many palaces, big houses and public buildings were constructed.
The people had a good knowledge and technique of building big and small houses. The rulers
lived in big palaces. The Cholas had palaces in Tanjore, Kumbakonam, Palayarai,
Gangaikondacholapuram and Madurai. Recently excavated palace at Gangaikondacholapuram
indicates the maganificent craftsmanship in temple construction. The important cities were

well planned. There were multi storied buildings with all facilities. Burnt bricks were used for
the construction of the building. Stones were used for foundation.. Separate areas were allotted
to various occupational groups. Streets or areas were named after them. Market places were
well planned. The soldiers lived in areas allotted to them in the capital. Royal women were
living in separate palaces. Around the fort moats were dug to safeguard the same. Chola
emblems were kept in the front. Beautiful gardens were found in the palaces. Painting was
lavishly used in temples and houses. The decoration was fantastic in many buildings.

145
8.3.1 Dress
The people of Chola period used both cotton and silk dresses. From the existing sculptures
we know the various types of dresses of the people. Women covered their breast by a piece of
cloth called “kachchai”. They also used blouses. Women folded the sari and inserted the frills
on the left side of the hip. The people used bed sheets. Special type of dress was used by the
soliders. Tailoring was known to them. Every temple had its own tailor. The tailor stitched
clothes for Gods and Goddesses. Comb was used by the ladies .Cosmetics was used by them.
The ladies applied turmeric powder: they also used flower: kumkum. Kings and queens wore
silk dresses. Costly stones and pearls were also used in making the royal dresses.
8.3.2 Food
Rice was the staple food of the people. Various kinds of rice were used like Tuvellarasi,

Hilly rice etc. Tamarind, pepper and salt were added in preparing various dishes. Milk, curd,
buttermilk, and ghee were also used. Vegetables formed a part of the food. Meat and fish were
eaten by the non-vegetarians. Mango, plantain, jackfruits, etc., were available. Root crops and
honey were also taken by them. Guests were treated very well. Toddy and wine were taken by
the poor and rich respectively.
Many inscriptions give a detailed picture of the food given to the Brahmins in temples and
mutts, of they were not given prepared food, they were eligible to get rice, vegetables, salt,
pepper, ghee, curd, earthenware pots, fuel, areca nuts and betel leaves. Though the poor were
not in a position to have rice and vegetables they consumed rice mixed with water. Rice flakes
were also eaten. Oil was used to prepare food.
8.3.3 Ornaments

Various kinds of jewellery were known to the people of the chola period. Queens and
royal women wore ornaments from head to foot. Ornaments were made of gold and silver.
Precious stones, pearl and coral were used in making jewels. Ring, bangles, chains, necklaces,
armlets, girdles etc., were some of the common ornaments. Tali was worn by the women.
Grants were made to the goddesses in various temples for ornaments especially tali. Chola
inscriptions give a list of ornaments donated to temples, and poor people wore jewellery
according to their status.

146
People were fond of perfumes. Women used delicate perfumes on their dresses. Ahil
smoke was spread on the hair. Women painted their hands and feet with reddish paste. Sweet
smelling ointments were used by women to their bodies. Betel leaves were used to colour the
lips of women.

8.3.4 Funeral practices
The people of the Chola times disposed of the dead in two important ways. They either
buried or cremated the dead. Weeping and wailing were the common actions when the rituals
followed. Drums were beaten and conch was blown. When the husband died, very few wives
followed the system of Sati and most of them remained as widows. The relatives carried the
dead body to the burial ground.

Cremation was done by placing the dead body on the funeral pyre. There are references
to hero stones in the Chola inscriptions. Nadukal or hero stone was erected for the warrior who
had fallen in the battle. The hero stones were worshipped by the relatives of the dead warrior.
8.3.5 Customs and Manners
The people believed in starting a new work on an auspicious day. For marriages and
other ceremonies also they choose good day and good time. They believed in the significance
of dreams and thoughts they would came true. It was considered lucky if the left eye lash of a
girl or the right one of the man quivered. If the right eye lash of a girl quivered, it was unlucky
for her.
The karthigai day in the month of Karthigai was celebrated. By beating the drums the
arrival of flood was announced to the people. The child birth was followed by certain ceremonies.

Casting of horoscope was practiced. Naming ceremony and thread economy were conducted.
The male child was permitted to go to the teacher after performing some rituals.

147
The guests were respected and given good feast. Betal leaves were given to them.
During ceremonies and feasts drinks were served. Chappals made of wood were used by the
people. Rich people used golden screws in the sandals. The practice of setting apart some
food to crows before one began eating was in practice. They had their own significance for the
cry of the crow and the noise of the lizard. They believed in the existence of spirits and ghosts.
They believed in undoing their crimes by donating money or land to the temples.
8.3.6 Pastimes
People of the Chola time had enough pastime and entertainments, in towns and villages
the people spent their leisure hours in various activities. In villages cock fighting was popular.
Hunting, chess playing, wrestling, bull fighting, etc., were also practiced. They showed keen

interest in music and dance drama, Rajarajanatakam, sakkikuthu, Aryakuttu and many other
kutus, were enacted by them. Women were keeping pet animals and birds. They also played
balls, ammanai and kalang.

8.4 Income
A sound system of finance is the back bone of any Government. The Cholas had a very
good system of economy. Land Revenue and trade Tax were the main source of income to the
cholas. The king needed income to protect his people, to establish his status and power of
wage war with his enemies and to give many facilities to his subjects. Hence the Government
levied taxes on land, trade etc.
8.4.1 Land Tax
Land tax was collected according to the produce of the land. It was given in cash or kind.

The Panchavaravariyam and the Sabha of the village were entrusted with the duty of collection
of land tax. They collected money and grains were sent to the central treasury. As 1/6 of the

148
produce was given to the Government, the rest went to the peasants who owned the lands.
The land tax was known Puravuvari, Puruvu denoting the cultivable land. The
puravuvarithinaikkalam was the committee, which was in charge of collection the land tax in
each reign. Granaries were kept in each village to store the grains collected from the peasants.
1. Other taxes
Apart from the land tax, many other taxes were levied. Angadippattam was levied on the
shop keepers. Idaippattm was a levy collected from the shepherd who owned sheep and cattle.
Kannalakknnam was a small levy on the couple during their marriage. Odakkuli was collected
from boatmen. The tax given by the local people for their safety was known as Nadukaval.
Maraviral was a tax on those who enjoy the produce of the trees in public places. Ilaikkulam

was a small tax levied in betel leaf cultivators. Ulgu was the customs duty levied on objects of
internal and external trade. There was prosperous trade with the eastern countries. Chola
kulottunga-1 abolished the customs duty and was called as Sungam Thavirtha Chola, the
Chola who abolished the customs duty. The Chola inscriptions give a vivid account of the tax
levied on each occupation. Though many taxes were mentioned, the people never felt the
burden of taxation.
8.4.2 Collection of tax
The Sabhas of the village assembly was entrusted with the work of collecting the tax
from the land owners. Though they were prompt in paying the tax, there were defaulters. When
the tax was not paid regularly, the Government gave full right to the Sabha to confiscate the tad
was also confiscated. Some such lands were sold to the local temples. Though the Brahmins

enjoyed many privileges, if they failed to pay the tax, they were also treated in the similar way.
When the Chola power deteriorated, there were confusion and some of the village
assemblies misappropriated the funds. When such cases were found, the defaulters were
punished. Similarly, when the Government officials misused the collected tax, the village officials
were strict with them and they regulated the entire system.

149
8.4.3 Expenditure
The income they get from the people should be well spent for their welfare. The king and
royal members had their own properties. Special officers were appointed to administer the
income and expenditure of the state. The state had to spend on various issues. Defence,
agriculture, irrigation, police, foreign relationship, law and order, justice, education etc., were
some of the heads on which the Government had to spend. As the village assemblies were
looking after the administration of the villages, the central Government was free from shouldering
big burdens. When the public money was misused by the Government officials or local bodies,
the Central Government interfered and set right the entire matters.
8.5 Agriculture
Agriculture was the backbone of economy. The heart of the chola country lay in the

kaveri delta. Kaveri delta was highly responsible for the progress of the people. The vast
majority of the people lived a rustic life in the villages and agriculture was their main occupation.
Possessing a strip of land was considered to be prestigious. The village was mainly a settlement
of peasants :and the village assembly was an association of landlords. Individual ownership
and common ownership were known to the people of Chola times. Inheritance of land from
father to son and selling and donating the land to others were common features. There were
great and small land owners. Many landless labourers cultivated their lord’s land and share the
proceeds of agriculture according to the labour they had put forth. The distinction between
persons paying the land- tax (irai-Kudigal)and those who did not was clearly established, and

the former had usually a larger share in the tasks of local government..
From the inscriptions we come to know that, apart from the regular agriculture labourers,
there was a class of hired day labourers who worked in the fields for daily wages. The
remuneration was given in grain. Those who worked in the flower gardens attached to the
temples were also paid in grain. Sometimes when land were donated to temples certain portions
of the land was set apart for the residences of the families of the labourers engaged in cultivation.
Those labourers were not owned of lands. But they were entitled to the use of a house -site
near enough to the place of their work and to get wages fixed in advance, the proceeds of their
labour on land being altogether the property of the institution that owned the soil on which
they worked.

150
1) Tenancy
Tenancy cultivation was also common, both on private estates and on quasi-public land
such as that of a temple: after paying a fixed amount to the land lord in advance the tenant
usually kept for himself as his share what remained after payment of the direct expenses of
cultivation and any minor dues assessed on the land held by him. He employed labourers to
cultivate his land and pay them accordingly.
2) Tenures
All cultivable land was held in one of the three broad classes of tenure.which may be
classified as: peasant proprietorship called vellan-vagai in the inscriptions: service tenure
,comprising all the holdings described such as jivita, bhoga, kani, vritti and so on: and
eleemosynary tenure such as Brahmadeya, devadana and salabhaoga resulting from charitable
gifts and governed by the special terms laid down in each case in a separate document drawn

up in set terms and engraved on copper plates or stone .
8.5.1 Survey of Lands
During the Chola period lands were surveyed and boundaries of lands were properly
marked. Classification of land into different grades, as twelve grades and unclasped lands
being alluded to make it clear that the rate of assessment differed with the fertility of the soil.
But it is not clearly stated in any of the record about the proportion of the produce that formed
the normal share of the state. The revenue from agricultural lands was periodically reassessed.
The classification of the lands was revised from time to time in accordance with the changes in
cropping, fertility and so on.
If in each village there were some lands which were exempted from all taxes, they were
used for residential purposes, the temples, tanks, the channels passing through the village,

the area occupied by the pariahs, the quarters of the artisans and the cremation ground.
8.5.2 Peasant Proprietors
The ordinary ryotwari village as we now call it was the Vellan- Vagai, having direct relations
with the Government and paying a land-tax liable to revision from time to time. . If a man

151
owned long stretch of land he could employ peasants and pay them their wages and after
paying the tax to the Government own the rest of the produce.
The conversion of Vellan Vagai into Brahmadeya and Brahmadeya into Vellan Vagai was
common. The Vellan Vagai into at least two broad classes – one directly remitting a variable
annual revenue, to the state and the other paying dues of a more or less fixed and standarzied
character to the public institutions like temples to which they were assigned.
8.5.3 Service Tenure
Service-tenures were of various types. The assignments in favour of public servants as
remuneration for their official work under the Government have already been noticed: these
assignments were, however only of certain rights to taxes and dues from land .Some servants
paid the tax to the Government. But if the lands were given to the servants as tax free, they

enjoyed the whole produce. Lands of such kinds were referred to as Irai Nelngal and Irai
Irangal in the Government record books. The temples often parcelled out their lands and
assigned them as Jivita Bhoga, Kani, all terms are used indifferently, for persons who fetched
water for bathing the deity, kept watch over the temple premises and so on.
Individual donors often earmarked their gifts of land to temples for particular purposes.
Lands were given for maintaining rest hoses, lakes, maintenance of teachers in schools and
for the village physician etc.
The charitable lands could be divided into three main divisions. They were Brahmadeya,
Devadana and salabhoga. When the lands were donated to the Brahmins, those lands are
known as Brahmadeva. Sometimes such lands were made tax free too. Devadana was the

land donated to the temples. Sometimes both Brahmadaya and devadana were combined in a
village (i.e) Devadana Brahmadeya. A devadana was different from Tiruvidaiyattam and
Tirunamattukani which were lands held in absolute ownership by the temples like any other
land owner.
When land already owned and cultivated formed the subject of gift after purchases, the
question was to deal with the occupancy right of the actual cultivators of the land. They had to
decide the rights of the cultivator and the landlord. Often these lands were made tax free either

152
by total remission by the taxing authorities, central or local or both or by the tax being secured
by a lump sum payment made in advance as Irai -Kaval. In the absence of clear statement to
such effect, the lands were liable to the usual taxes.
The Anbil plates of Sundara Chola mentions about ekabhoga brahmadeya .If a village
donated to single Brahmin, it was known as ekabhoga brahmadeya. To maintain the homogeneity
of the Brahmadeya villages by excluding, all other classes from owning land in them. In large
villages where such homogeneity could not be attained, two types of village assemblies (i.e)
Sabha and Ur were administrating the villages.
In case of unsettlement of the boundaries between the lands held by two temples due to
erosion by the river, king officials fixed the new boundaries in consultation with representatives
of both the temples of the Sabha of both the villages.

Land register was maintained by the village assemblies. When the register was lost the
village authorities, with the sanction of the central Government took steps prepare a fresh
register.
The Devadana lands were marked off by means of boundary stones bearing the emblems
of the diety. Devadana lands were managed by the authorities of the temples subject to
supervision and control of the village assembly on the one side and the Central Government
on the other. The authorities of the temple acted in accordance with the local assemblies in
paying the remuneration to the servants for the performance of services or supply of articles
required for use in the temple. The local people willingly worked even in the unfertile land
owned by the temple than before. When lands were donated to the temples, the donor wanted

to secure the maximum benefit to the temple of its tenants from his gift. The tenants also
readily helped to attain that object. The officers of the Central Government audited the temple
accounts periodically. Prior sanction of the king was necessary to change the tenants of the
Devadana lands. In some villages, a portion was donated to Brahmins and the rest to the
temple. Similarly a village was divided into devadana and vellan-vagai lands.
The lands donated to the Vishnu temple were known as Tiruvudaiyattam. Pathandam
was name given to the lands gifted to jain and Buddhist temples. Madappuram were the lands

153
given to the mutts. The lands given to feed the Brahmins, Sivayogis etc., were known as
salabhoga.
Most of these lands were exempted from taxation. But still these donees had to pay a
small amount known as lraiyilikkanam to the Government.
8.5.4 Irrigation
The prosperity of an agricultural country depends to a large extent on the facilities provided
for irrigation and the importance of securing an adequate water supply was recognised in
South India from the Sangam age. As agriculture was the main occupation of the people,
facilities were provided for irrigation, rivers, streams and dependable channels leading off from
them were the main source of water supply. The areas in which there were no rivers and
streams, the people resorted to use water from tanks and lakes. The Chola-varidhi of Sholingur

the Kaliyaneri near Anaimalai in Madurai, Kallinangaikulam at Solapuram, the Vairameghatataka of Uttiramerur dating from pallava times, the “big tank” of Bahur, Madurantakaperieri in
Madurantakkam, Sembiyam Madevipperi near Tirumalapadi, Gandaradittappereri in
Ulagapuram, Sundaracholappereri and Kundavaipereri in Brahmadesam and the
Rahjendrasolap-periya-eri at Punganur were some of the tanks mentioned in chola records.
Rajendra-1 founded the new city of Gangaikondacholapuram and dug a very big lake and
named it as cholagankam. This action of Rajendra was very helpful to the people of that area
in irrigating their lands. These tanks were used for irrigational purposes.
The village assemblies maintained the lakes in their area every year before the rains set
in, they got the sit removed from the tanks to secure the proper depth needed to store the full

supply for the next year. Endowments were also made to safeguard this important work from
the neglect of the penury of village authorities. Donations were made for annual repairs, in
some villages’ eriayam. A special cess was collected for the purpose from the peasants in the
village.
The water rights attaching to particular plots of land were often enumerated on the
occasion when they changed hands by sale or goat. The water in the tank was to be distributed
between the villagers and temple in that area in the ratio of their holdings. Some follow common

154
land of the village was converted into a bund and a channel was dug for irrigation to the
cultivable land of the village.
Another aspect of agriculture that deserves special mention is the steady progress of
reclamation of forest and waste land that was being brought under the plough. No direct
statement on the gross yield of land can be traced. On fertile paddy lands the number of crops
raised each year was two or three. Nothing definite is known about the share of the landlord. It
differed from land to land according to the fertility of the soil similarly the value of land also
differed from place to place.

8.6 Industry
During the chola rule, the Tamil society showed improvement in the field of industry.

Though there were no large scale industries as in the modern times, there was a good sign of
all round activity that resulted in industrial growth too. In most of the industries, the rule was
production for the local market. There was brisk internal trade in many articles. The merchant
had highly organized mercantile corporations in various parts of the country.
The Chola society was based on caste cum occupational groups. Various occupation
lists concentrated on producing various products needed for the people. Descriptions of various
kinds of occupations were given in the social conditions under the cholas. Here mention could
be made about metal industries.
Metal Industry
The metal industries and the Jewellers’ art had reached a high state of perfection.
Household utensils made of metal were confined to the rich, especially they used vessels

made of costly metals like gold and silver. The temples were the store houses of treasure
during Chola period. Various types of vessels were in use in temples for many purposes. They

155
were donated by the king and the rich people. Similary images of gods and goddesses were
made of costly metals. The Tanjore inscriptions give a detailed account of the vessels and
images donated to the Tanjore temple by various people. The Chola bronzes are good proofs
of the mastery attained by the braziers of the time in the art of manipulating alloys of metals
and casting them into very graceful and beautiful forms. Copper, bronze and brass were used
in such work besides gold and silver.
Jewellery
The chola inscriptions are rich with information regarding the jewellery used by people of
that period. Gold, pearls and precious stones were used in making jewels and ornaments. The
records give the names of the ornaments used by the people to beautify them from top to
bottom. Some of the ornaments of the chola time have gone out of use. The jewellery mentioned

in Tanjore inscriptions alone give us an ideas of the amount of the wealth held in the form of
jewels and of the flourishing state of goldsmith’s trade.
Salt
The manufacture of sea -salt was carried on under Government supervision and control
and subject to considerable imposts in kind and money, local and central. The salt- pans of
Marakanam, Kanyakumari, Vaiyur and Ayturai were important centres of salt manufacture,
which was a widespread industry all along the sea coast.
Building
The cholas were great builders. Many places, buildings and temples were constructed
by them on a grand scale. Brahadeeswara temple in Tanjore is a living example of the engineering
skill of the cholas. The materials used for the construction were manufactured in large quantity
providing job opportunities, to many people.
Weaving industry

Weaving industry was given special attention during the chola period. The weavees of
Kanchipuram were well recognised by the kings and the rich people. Some were appointed as

156
weavers of royal Government. Some were given the management of the financial affairs of the
temples. The temple accounts were periodically audited by the weavers who managed the
temples.
8.6.1 Transport
There were big and small roads connecting important cities, towns and villages. The
local authorities and the Government maintained the roads. The villagers gave free labour
required for it. The vali was slightly better than footpaths and not suited to wheeled traffic. The
big and better class of road was known as Peruvali, the great road. There were truck roads
leading from one part of the country to another. Such roads were Tanjavurperuvali,
Vdugapperuvali, and Kongappervali. There were choultries on the way so that the travellers
and traders proceeded after taking some rest. Though waterways were not much used in

South India, water transport was not unknown to the people of the chola times. Boats were
used to carry men and foods from one side to the other. Beasts of burden and cardts were
made use of to transport the goods from one part to the other.
8.7 Trade
The chief articles of merchandise that entered into long distance trade were goods of
great value. The important goods imported were wood, amber, camphor, precious gems,
bamboos, ivory, ebony, paper sandalwood, perfumes, drugs and condiments. Important things
exported were spices, drugs, fine variety of textile, jewels, semi-precious stones, ivory, ebony,
amber, coral, perfumes etc.
There was a great demand for horses and the Arabs involved themselves in horse trade.
The cholas had a good cavalry. The kudirai chehettis mentioned in chola inscription were the

dealers of horses who imported horses from Arabia and sold them to many monarchs and
chieftains.
8.7.1 Merchant guilds
The Chola society saw powerful trade guilds and corporations. They were Manigramam,
Valanjiyar, Chithrameli, Periyanattar, Tisalayirattu Ainurruvar, Anjuvannathar and many others.

157
Nadadesa Tisaiayinattu Ainurruvar formed the most important of all these guilds. They
got the name as they were five hundred traders who went to thousand directions in all countries.
This guild was very popular and powerful.
They conducted extensive overseas trade. Because of their trade contacts and prosperity
they were well respected by the monarchs and the rich people. They formed their administrative
body and passed resolutions. By a resolution of their body, the Nanadesis and their followers
resolved to convert the village of Siravalli into nanadesivadasamadi Erivirappattinam and confer
certain privileges on its residents. The nanadesis were served by regiments of foot soldiers
and swords men. The nanadesis visited all countries in the course of their trade. The Central
Government and the village sabhas respected the Nanadesis. They had their own mercenary

army for the protection of the goods in their storehouses and in transit. They were involved in
local administration. Their success and prosperity were to sdme extent independent of the
changes of war and peace among the status in which they carried on trade. They built a Vishnu
temple at Pagan in Burma. They donated gifts also for the maintenance of the same.
Manugramam was another guild which carried about inland trade. They granted devadana
villages to temples. Temple walls were also built by them. They dominated in mportant towns.
There were Uraiyur manigarramam, Kodumbalur manigramam, llangopattinattu manigramam
etc. The Manigramattar were mentioned in the records of Nandivarman-III himself. They had
commercial contacts with foreign countries also.
Similarly, the valanjiyars were also a guild of merchants who were considered to be

powerful in some important towns like tirupurambiyam and Tinnevelli. They donated lands to
local temples and Brahmins. They maintained some mutts also. The Brahmins of Ennayiram
also joined with the valanjiyar in south Bazaar of Ennayiram. The valanjiyars were considered
to be merchants from Ceylon who traded in many towns in Tamilnadu. A Ceylonese inscription
mentions them as Ceylonese and followed Buddhism. Though they were Buddhists, they donated
to other religious institution and temples also.
The Anjuvabbathar had extensive overseas trade of the time. They are said to have
belonged to the race of vasudeva kandali and Mulabhadra. There were many sub-divisions
among them. They visited many countries in north India and South India and the foreign countries

158
also. . They penetrated into many countries by land and water routes. They trade in elephants,
horses, precious stones spices, perfumes and drugs. They carried the merchandise on the
backs of asses and buffaloes. They were referred to in some copper plates and inscriptions.
Palchandamalai, an old literary work is quoted Kalaviyarkarigal. In that there is a mention
of Anjuvannathar who were supposed to be the Muslim traders in tamilnadu having good internal
and external commercial contacts. An inscription in Thittandathanapuram in Pandya country
mentions about Anjuvannathar. Similarly they were popular in Nagapattinam also.
Sugam was levied on the good imported in ships and carts from across the seas or the
interior. This formed an important part of the income to the government. But Kulottunga-1
abolished sungam and was celebrated as Sungam Tavirtha Chola (the chola who abolished

customs). This practice was continued by his successors also. Tough a portion of income was
reduced, the introduction of free trade allowed the flow of foreign goods into the country.
The merchants had full freedom and scope for initiative and capacity for voluntary
organizations. The guilds carried on trade when the conditions were favourable and they paved
the way for the economic prosperity of the country.
There was local organization of merchants called Nagaram in big trading centres like
Kanchipuram and Mamallapuram. The members were known as Nagaratter. The Nagarams
raised voluntary contribution from their members for specific purposes such as for maintaing
perpetual lamps and temples, maintaing temple servants, feeding the Brahmins, celebrated
temple festivals etc. The donation was made either in cash or in kind.

Borrowing on promissory note was known as Kaiyeluttolai was in practice in chola period.
Sometimes the local administrative bodies also borrowed money from individuals on promissory
notes. Temples which were very rich also lent money in the same way.
8.7.2 Foreign Contacts
Even from the sangam age the Tamils carried on good trade with the foreign countries.
During the reign of the Imperial cholas, these contacts were strengthened. The Chinese had
trade relations with many countries of the east and west. The Chinese Government itself was

159
interested in expanding the foreign trade. They sent their missions to various countries
expressing their eagerness to have commercial contacts. These missionaries went with
government seal and contracts carrying with them gold and rice quality of cloth. Similarly the
Chinese Sung Government promised certain rights and safety to the foreign merchants in their
land. These developments gave such encouragement to the foreigners to trade with china.
Rajaraja-1 also sent his envoys to china with pearls and precious articles. They
started in 1002 A.D. and reached china in 1015 A.D. The Chinese emperor received them with
full honour and kept them in a big palace and gave them rice presents. Similarly in the time of
ranjendra-1 the contacts continued. He sent a mission to china in 1033 A.D. The trade thus
started with China appears to have been carried for a long time The Chinese record also

confirms this by stating that during the time of kulottunga-1 around 1077 A.D. an embassy of
seventy-two men were sent to china. Further the Chinese record states that the chola ruler
sent presents to the Chinese emperor for a long time.
A Tamil inscription in Sumatra dated corresponding to 1088 A.D. which mentions about
the Tisai - Ayirattinnurruvar shows that the merchants of South India had settlements outside
India especially in Persian Gulf and the China Sea. .. The cholas exported pearls, elephant’s
tusks, coral , transparent glass, betel nuts, cardamoms, cotton stiffs with coloured silk threads
and cotton stuffs.
During the reign of rajendra-1 there was contract between the Tamils and kadaram.
Rajendra-1 is said to have undertaken an expedition to kadaram and defeated the ruler and
assumed the title as kadaram Kondan. He defeated obstacles were thrown on chola trade with

the East, the merchants complained to the chola ruler and hence he undertook a campaign
and the chola merchants renewed their trade contracts with the East. Similarly in 1068A.D.
Virarajendra invaded kadaram at the request of its ruler and safeguard his position there. This
brought in more concessions to the Tamil traders srivijaya.
8.7.3 Coins
The gold, silver and copper coins of the chola monarchs help us to a certain extent to
trace the economic history of the time. This is further proved from their inscriptions. . The

160
earliest chola coin known to us belongs to the period of Uttama Chola. It is a good piece, a
unique specimen, once in the possession of Sir Walter Elliot. Its observe and revere are identical,
the centre occupied by a seated tiger facing a fish to the proper right and separated from it by
a line, the legend Uttama Chola in grantha letters along the circular margin and ring of beads
at the perimeter. The weight of the coin was between 50 to 60 grains. Though that coin was
lost, it gives an idea of the coins of the imperial Cholas.
Kalanju was used in recording payments by weight. There are some mention the Pon
and equate it tothe Kalanju, implying thereby that the Pon was coined gold of the full weight of
one Kalanju. The coin was also called Madurantaka devan- madai and was served as the
standard of fitness for testing gold any yielded the same interest as one Kalanju of the fine

gold. Maduantaka was the name of Uttama Chola and it could be summarised that this coin
must have come into use in his time.
Rajarajan Kasu issued by Rajaraja-I was exactly half of this madai. Twenty kasus were
equal to ten Kalanjus. Some of the coins were named as anradunar kasu (good current kasu)
and palangasu (old kasu)
The Madurantakan madai was used in the reign of Kulottunga-I: and it is sssssaid to
have been equivalent to the kalanju of the fineness of 9and a half mari or two kasus. But this
high standard was not maintained at all times. The inscriptions state the change in standard at
different times and places.
Some of the gold coins of Rajendra-I bear his regnal years and the title
Gangaikondacholan. Similarly his son Rajadhiraja-I issued coins with his regnal year and the
title Malainadukonda cholan.

Several other types of madais were in use from the time kulothunga-I. They were
Jayamadai, Uttamagandamadai, Chamaramadai, Birudamadi, Bhujabalamadai,
Palampullimadai and Gandagopalamadai. The fineness of Madurantakanmadai of 91/2 mattu
was the same as that of sembon. One madai was equal to a kalanju of gold. Two kunrimanis
made a manjadi; 20 manjadis made a kalanju. Hence it could be summarised that madai, tha
gold coin-was equal to fourt kunrimains.

161
The llakkusu, Ceylon kasu, which was also half a kalnju of the fineness of mdai, was
used in Ceylon even from the 7th century A.D. The Ceylon type was with a rude human figure
standing in the obverse and seated on the reverse. These type of coins were in gold llakarunkasu
the black kasu of Ceylon was also in use. It is not known whether it was made of silver or
copper. As inscription of Parantaka-l states that the ilakkasu was the equivalent of akkams. It
is not clearly known what sort of a coin the akkam was perhaps a twelfth of the kasu and
therefore a twentyfouth of the kalanju. It is also presumed from inscription that the llakkasu of
Parantaka-l’s time and kasu of Rajaraja’s time were of the some value and fineness. It is also
surmised that akkam was equaivalent to a gold coin weighing 1213 kunrimani.

From the time of kulottunga, the term kasu was applied to copper coin of very low value
and its content varied greatly from place to place with each issue. These copper coins also had
the same design as the coins of Rajaraja-1 but the human figure was more degraded and the
legend was roughly executed.
8.7.4 Weights and Measures
Videlvidugukal was used for weighing gold in the time of Aditiya-1. During Rajaraja-1’s
time the weight adavalan was for weighing gold and dakshinamervitganan for jewels. Other
measures mentioned in inscriptions were viayakattarkal, kemponagarasunirai, etc. Though
the absolute weight of these different units could not be determined, they all used the same
denominations of kalanju divided into 20manjadis, each manjadi being the equivalent of two
kunris. The fineness of the gold is explained in terms of touch such s nine mattu by the
kasunirakal.

Nilam or veli vatika was the unit measure of land. Lengthy rods were used to measure
the lands. They were called the sixteen spans 9kol, the maligaikkot and so on. Ma or seru was
one twentieth of the veli though it could not be definitely stated how many kulis made of a ma
or seru, it was generally accepted in some places that a ma contained 250 kulis by the 16 span
rod and in some other places one hundred kulis by the maligai-kol made up ma. But in some
other place 300 kulis by the sixteen span rods were reckoned to the ma. In land measures, as
in currency, the same tendency to standardization of the part of the Central government could
be traced by the side of the persistence of local usage. Attempts were made to impose a

162
uniform system on the provinces outside the chola country proper. But those efforts and
standardization were not very successful as known from the chola inscriptions.
For measuring liquids and grains, various kinds of nails and marakkals were used.
Adavallan, rajakesari, vidividangan komalam, Kanchchippeduninran were some of measures
used during chola period.Another standardised unit of value was, strangely was the adu (Sheep)
Thus from the chola inscriptions we come to know about the weights and measures used
during the Chola period.

8.8 Summary
However, there was cooperation among various castes and sub-castes in social and
religious life. The position of women did not improve. The practice of ‘sati’ was prevalent among

the royal families. The devadasi system or dancing girls’ attached to temples emerged during
this period.
The period of Cholas witnessed economic prosperity and extensive trade and commercial
contracts. Agriculture was well taken care of by the digging canals and big lakes. The weaving
industry, particularly the silk-weaving at Kanchi flourished. The metal works developed owing
to great demand of images for temples and utensils. Commerce and trade were brisk with
trunk roads or peruvazhis and merchant guilds. Gold, silver and copper coins were issued in
plenty at various denominations. The people of the Chola time were highly civilized. In the
fields of art and architecture also they showed their merit. The women were highly esteemed.
The Brahmins enjoyed high privileges and favours. People belonging to other castes were

respected according to their occupation and financial status. They also contributed to all round
developments in their times.

9.1 Introduction
The Cholas were staunch Saivites. But while following Saivism as their parental religion
they were not hostile to other religion. Rajaraja I and some of his successors endowed liberally
to a Budha vihara at Nagapattinam and even kulottunga II could endow the Srirangam temple
liberally. Nambiandar Nambi and Nathamuni compiled the Siva and Vaishnava literature in the
Chola period. Prof.K.A.N.Sastri says that the chola period has been called as “the silver age
of South Indian Saivism and Vaishnavism”.
9.2 Saivism
Saivism is considered as the oldest religion in Tamil Nadu. Saivas adored Siva as the
supreme God. . Siva was worshipped both in the human and Linga form .Siva was considered
as the God of fertility. Parantaka -1 was a devotee of Siva. The Tiruvalangadu copper plates
describe about him as the bee at the lotus feet of Siva and the Larger Leyden grant states that

he covered with gold the Siva temple of Chidambaram. Hence he was known as Ponveynda
peruman. Gandaraditya and his wife Sembiyanmadevi were staunch Saivities. Gandaraditya
was the author of the single hymn called Tiruvisaippa and this is included in the ninth Tirumarai
of Saiva Canon. Sembiyanmadevi after the death of her husband devoted all her attention to
religious activities. She built many Siva temples in the Chola region and the brick temples were
reconstructed with stones. She gave many grants to various temples in the Chola territory. The
magnificent Siva temple at Tanjore is the finest monument of a splendid period of south Indian
history. Rajaraja-1 built it. Karuvur Devar a contemporary hymnist, celebrated the new temple
in his sacred hymn. Rajendra-1 was also a great Siva devotee. He built a big Siva temple in his

new capital Gaingaikondascholapuram. Though not in this grand scale, make other Chola
rulers also built Siva temples in their realm.
Rajaraja-1 constructed a stone temple of Siva in Polonnaruwa after the annexation of a
part of Ceylon. It is one of the important Hindu monuments of Ceylon. The earliest inscription
found in this temple is dated early in Rajendra’s reign. A Chola officer named tali Kumaran built
another temple called Rajarajawara at Mantota which was also named Rajarajapura and
endowed the new temple.

166
The Tanjore temple built by Rajaraja-1 is the finest monument of splendid period of south
Indian history and the most beautiful specimen, of Tamil architecture at its best. It has long
compound walls beautiful Vimana and numerous inscriptions. The chola ruler was very much
interested in painting. They painted the walls and ceiling pradakshina passage round the sanctum
of the temple. The theme of the Tanjore chola paintings is religious, drawn mostly from
periapuranam. The episode of the title of Sundaramutthi forms the subject of some of the best
panels.
The Gangaikondacholapuram temple built by Rajendra-1 described as the femine counter
part of Tanjore lacking the virile qualities mason line vigour of its predecessor, but possessing
a rich and voluptuous beauty of its own.
Nambiandar nambi compiled the Devaram songs which were sung in all Siva temples.

Many festivals were celebrated in the temples. They celebrated the birthdays of the emperors.
Masimaham was grandly celebrated. In the month of Ani, Ani Tirumanjana Vizha was an
important festival. The Mahamagam festival at Kumbakonam is known from an inscription.
Thaipusam, Sivarathri, Chithirai Vishu, Aipasi Vishu, Karthigai etc. were important days and
special grants were made for these celebrations, Parantaka celebrated Indra Vizha at Kalahasti.
Saivism spread all over the Chola County. The great officials, generals of the chola
emperors also contributed to the establishment of Siva temples. Lands, jewels, vessels etc.,
were donated.. Concessions were given to the temple employees, singers, dancers, and servants
of the temples were well looked after.
9.3 Vaishnavism
The history of Vaishnavism in this period was quite similar. Tradition confers upon

nathamuni the honour of having done for Vaishnava lyrics what Nambi Andar Nambi achieved
for the Saivism. Worship of Vishnu was also in practice during the chola period.The chola
rulers built Vishnu temples and donated for various purposes. Tiruvoymoli was sung in all
Vishnu temples. Singing of Tiruvoymoli during Tiruppalieluchi was a common practice. During
various festival times also Tiruvoymoli was sung in temples. Endowments were made for
maintenance of the singers of Tiruvoymoli was Tirunedundandagam in Vishnu temples.

167
Grants were made for singing Tiruppadiyam in Vishnu temples. Food offered to the deity was
distributed among the Sri Vaishnavas who recited Tiruppadiyam during worship. The hymn of
Kulasekara Alwar beginning Tettarudiral was recited before the deity during worship. The hymn
of Kulasekara Alwar beginning tettarudiral was recited before the deity during three nights in
the course of a festival in Srirangam.
The record of kulottunga-lll mentions the creation at kanchipuram of Bashyavritti for the
Ramanuja Bhaya as being regularly expounded by a competent person. Divyachuri charita
and yathiraja Vaibhavam state that Saint Ramanuja was persecuted by chola rulers and some
scholars identified the chola ruler with Virarajendra or Adhirajendra the predecessor of
kulottunga-1.
Nathamuni popularised the poems of Alwar by having sung them in temples during this

period. The collection of the work is called Nalayira Divya Prabhandam. His grandson Alavandan
further elaborated the Visistadvaida philosophy. His grand son was the famous Saint Ramanuja.
He has earned a very good name and fame in the history of Vaishnavism.
A chola inscription states the immigration of Bhattas from North Indian to important religious
centres in the south. The mutts which maintained these external contacts belonged to the
various schools of pasupatas, kapalikas and so on.
In some mutts provision was made for the convenience of pilgrims. The pilgrims were
supplied with salt, castor oil and medical aid was to be given for those among the disciples who
fell ill and had no one to look after them.
There was a rare incident mentioned in the record or Rajaraja-ll as Gukai-idikalaham, a
revolt in which monasteries were demolished. The cause for the same is not mentioned in the

record.

9.3.1 Temples
The great living chola temples in Tamil Nadu stand testimony to the achievements of the
Chola dynasty. .Splendid in architecture, sculpture, painting and bronze casting, the magnificent
temples are UNESCO World Heritage sites .Temple was the pivot of all activities in the ancient
period. The early temples were structure of brick and mortar. The cholas followed the art of
erecting structure temples of stone from the 10th century onwards. The Anbil copper plates of
Sundara chola state that Aditiya-1 covered the banks of kaveri along its whole course from the
mountain to the sea, with a number of impregnable temples built of stone and dedicated to
Siva. The king’s relative and officials played a dominant role in temple building activities. Either
as renovation old structures or new ones, or more rarely as commemorative monuments of a

sculptural, the construction of stone temples continued throughout the chola period.
The chola rulers were not only mighty conquerors and great administrators, but also
great builders. They were great patrons of art: during their reign the most magnificent temples
and bronze icons were created in the South India. The Great living chola temples comprises of
three temples namely the Brihadisvara temple at Tanjore, the temple at Gangaikonda cholapuram
and the Airavatesvara temple at Darasuram.The patrons of Lord Siva dedicated magnificient
architectural splendours to their beloved God.
Gifts were offered to all temples and administered with great care. Land was a common
gift and the lands donated to the temples were made tax free. Each generation handled with
caution what was handed down it, and by means of fresh additions, managed to leave a richer

heritage to its successor. The vast and growing wealth of the temples brought them into more
intimate business relations with the neighbourhood.
Big Temples
The Brahadeesvara temple in Tanjore was built by the chola king RajarajaI, the king
received divine command to build in his dreams. The grand design and magnificience added to
architectural splendour of the chola capital. The great temples of Tanjore known as
Brahadeesvara temple was the richest temple of the Rajaraja-1. He himself donated to it a vast
amount of gold and treasure in the form of ornaments, jewels and vessels. Much of it was

169
booty that fell to him as a result of his wars. He set apart lands in several villages through his
domination including Ceylon yielding good income. 400 dancing girls were there in the big
temple.
The singers of Tiruppadiyam with the accompaniment of musical instruments were also
gifted. The queens, elder sister and high officials of Rajaraja-1 also donated for various purposes.
All the cash endowments amounting to several thousands of kasus were loaned out to numerous
village assemblies at rates of interest fixed in kind or money. Camphor, cardamom deeds,
champak buds etc., were also provided for the means of each endowments.
The Tanjore temple had played very important role in the country’s economy. Employment
of many architects and sculptors was made possible because its construction was extended

for many years skilled artisans were employed in casting numerous icons. The chola inscriptions
state about the minute skill of the goldsmiths in making beautiful ornaments and jewels. The
numerous icons of the Big Temple Were decked with varieties of jewellery.
Many men and women were employed for the services of the temples. Hence the temples
of chola period proved to be centre of all activities (i.e.) as land holder, employer and consumer
of goods and services, as bank, school, museum, hospital and theatre, in short, as a nucleus
which gathered round itself all that was best in the arts of civilised existence and regulated
them with the humaneness born of the spirit of Dharma. When there were serious problems,
the kings officials and king himself interfered and settled the matters.
9.3.2 Jainism
Though the chola rulers were Saivities, they were tolerant towards other religions also.

Jainism had a good patronage of the kings and the people. They donated to Siva and Vishnu
temples and in the same way gifted to the jain temples also. Such gifts were known as
pallichchandam and they were made tax-free. There was a big monastery at vedal. Temples
for parsavantha were also found in the chola region. Other important Jaina centres were
Rajendrapuram, Sendalai, Tiruppanmalai, Tirunarungonadai, Tirumalai, Tirumalavadi,
Tirupparuttikundram and Kuhur.

170
Kundavai the elder sister of Rajaraja-1 built jain temples at Tirumalai and Tirumalavadi
and donated lands for the maintenance. Tirupparuttikunram near Kanchipuram is famous for
the Jain shrine and that place was known as jain kanchi.
9.3.3 Buddhism
Buddhism was not as popular as jainsm in the chola region. But still a few rulers like
Rajaraja-1 were very generous in making grants to the Buddha Viharas. The celebrated Leyden
copper plates state the way in which he encouraged the erection of chudamani vihara in
Nagapattinam by the sailendra king Sri Mara Vijayottungavarman. The lord of Sri Vijaya Rajaraja
donated the village of Anaimangalam to the Choodamani vihara at Nagapattinam.
Rajendra -1 confirmed this grant after his father’s death and caused it to be engraved on
copper plates.Kulottunga-1 also supplemented this grant on a representation made by the

king of kadaram through his envoys. kulottungs-1’s copper plates mentions about the existence
of two viharas namely Rajaraja perumpalli and Rajendra solapperumpalli at chola
kulavallipattinam otherwise known as Nagapattinam. The embassy from kadaram comprised
the king for the issue of the grant while he was kanchipuram was a stronghold of Buddhism
too,
9.3.4 Education through Religious Institutions

171
The village school was imparting knowledge to the pupils. If the pupils assembled in the
temples and mutts, popular education was provided by the recitation and exposition in temples
and other public places of the epics like Ramayana, Mahabharata, and puranas. Sometimes
the elements of philosophy from the standpoint of particular sects were also similarly expounded,
for Sivadhama Somasiddhanta and Ramanujabhasya.
Higher education was pursued in schools and colleges attached to mutts and temples.
The mutts, and the pallis, the viharas are centres of learning which often owned large libraries
and transmitted by successive copying a vast mass of manuscript literature on a variety of
topic which increased in volumes and diversity from generation to generation.. The teacher
were also donated with grain etc., for teaching Vedas, grammer, mimamsam, Vedanta etc.

similarly to Tribhuvan the students who were learning Manusastra, Bharatam, Ramayanam,
were given daily allowance. So also were the teachers. In the Tirumukkudal temple, endowments
were made for the teaching of Rig and Yajur Vedas and Vyakarma.
The students who were learning grammer and medicine were provided accommodation
in local mutt at Tiruvaduturai. Bhattas and Siva charyas were also granted lands. A thirteenth
century inscription mentions the foundation of library (saraswathi Bhandaram) in the srirangam
temple. Several endowments were made for rewarding the students who attained merit and
distinction in various scholastic pursuits. The numerous mutts the chola period served as more
or less important centres for the promotion of learning, religious or secular in Tamil. An important
work task of the mutts was to train the hands of choristers who sang the Tiruppadiyamin the
temples.
