9.4 Literature
In literature the age of the imperial cholas constitutes the most creative epoch of south
Indian history. During this period, Tamil and Sanskrit literatures were extensively cultivated:
there was also some writing in Pali undertaken mainly by the Buddhist divines of the period.
Compared to Sanskrit literature, Tamil literature reached its zenith maily because the Tamil is
the language of the people and language of learning. .The Prasastis or Meykkirts of the chola
rulers from the time of Rajaraja-1 are best examples of the literary growth of the age. The
stately diction, the easy flow of the verse and animated narration of historical incidents mark
them out as a class by themselves in the literature of tamil.
In the composition of the prasastis, the various metres are handled with great skill. The

complex laws of tamil prosody are observed with an easy grace which saves the author from
the use of obscure words or the adoption of forced constructions. As narrative poetry, these
inscriptions share some of the qualities of imperial prasastis.
Some literary works of the cholas period are lost. But their names are mentioned
casually in the inscriptions. Rajarajeswara n atakam, a drama and Rajarajavijayam, a kavya
belonging to the reign of Rajaraja-1 are not available. The former was to be enacted in the treat
Tanjore temple during festivals and the latter was to be read in the temple at Tiruppundurutti.
Rajaraja-1 created endowments for both the purposes. Tirunarayana Bhatta wrote kulottunga
chola Charitai, a work on kulottunga-1 the poet was granted some land, for the same. Kamalaya
Bhatta wrote kannivanpuram and Pumpuliyur Natakam in tamil. The first one was a sthalapurana

and the second one was a drama. The author was given tax free land. Aranilaivaiskan
Trialokyamallan Vatsarajan of Arunbakkam rendered Bharata in elegant tamil. Varadayappulavar
of kuratti composed vallaiantadi a poem in praise of the local deity. The tiles of the above
mentioned works are known only from the records.
9.4.1 Important works
In the beginning of the chola period perungadai or udayanan kadai the tamil version of
Brahatagatha was written by a poet named knongu velir. Tirutakkadevar wrote
Jivakasinthamani. The author is said to have born of the race of the cholas. His work was one
of Mahakavuyas in Tamil. This was known as Mana nul, book of marriages. In its present form,
the poem contains 3145 stanzas, of four lines each.

173
Valayapathi and kundalakesi, two other Mahakavyas in tamil were composed more or
less about the same time as sivakasinthamani. They are known by fragments cited in other
works. Kundalakesi is a Buddhist work whereas sivakasinthamani is a Jaina work.
Kalladanar wrote kalladam which comprises a hundred pieces each purporting to depict
a particular mood of life. Kaladanar refers to the miracles wrought by Siva on account of
Manickavasagar, Darumi, Idaikkadur and others.
The kalingattupparani composed by the poet laureate Jayangondar during the reign of
kullotunga-1 the parani is the war poem which depicts not only the pomp and circumstance of
war, but all the gruesome details of the battle-field.
Ottakuttar a famous poet of the chola time wrote Nalayirakkovai in praise of his patron
Gangeya. . He was patronised by successive chola rulers.begining with vikramachola: on

each of them he composed Ula, besides a parani celebrating Vikrama cola’s Kalinga war, and
a pillaittamil on kulottunga-ll. The last poem is easily among the best among the known
compositions of the poet. The stories of the circumstances leading to Kuttan’s composition of
the Takkayagapparani, Eluppelupadu and the ltti-elupadu being more to Anthropology than
History. Ltti-elupadu was the poem consisted of seventy verses calculated to bring back to life
the 1008 youths whose lives had been sacrificed for the goddess to inspire Ottakkuttar to sing
in praise of Sengundar community to which he belonged. Saraswathi Andhai was composed
by kuttan in praise of the goddess of learning. Another composition was Arumbaittollayiram.
He is said to have set up an image of saraswathi in a temple in his native kuttanur he had the

title kavipperumal inscribed in inscription. The village of Kuttanur on the banks of Arsil river in
the Tanjore districtkeeps alive the memory of the poet and the patronage of his talents by the
chola rules who gave him the village as a fief.
A greater poet than Ottakkuttan was his junior contemporary Kamban the celebrated
author of the Ramayanam. This poem is the greatest epic in Tamil literature. His patron was
Sadaiyan of Vennai..He was patronized by the contemporary chola monarch also granted him
a field called kambanadu and the title kavichichakravarthi. Besides the Ramayanam, Kamban
wrote Erelupadu, sadagoparandhadi and Mummanik-kovai. The Erelupadu, together with

174
Tirukkai -valakkam is a eulogium on agriculture and the cultivator class, the vellalas. The
Venbas composed by kamban are said to have brought back the life of cedirayan,the son of
sadaiyan the patron of kamber, kamber composed andhadi to please the god of srirangam
before whom approval was sought by the poet for his Ramayanam and who made it a condition
that kamban should praise his beloved devotee sadagopan in a centum of verses.
Pugalendi, a contemporary of ottakuttan was renowned poet. He composed a
kalambakam on korrandai the chief of Jinji (senjiyarkon). His masterpiece is nalavenba, a
poem narrating the story of Nala in about four hundred stanzas in the venba metre.
The kulottunga kovai is a kovai on kumara kultottunga who is identified with kulottungalll. The kovai like the ula is a peace poem. It purports to deal with the stages in the development

of love between a lover and his love from the moment them are thrown together by accident. In
portraying each situation, details relating to the birth and achievements of the hero are worked
in by the poet. The Tanjaivanan kovai is another secular work of the period was compile by
poyyamolipulavar. Vanan of thanjai, the hero of the kovai was the reputed minister of the
pandya king Kulasekhara.
9.4.2 Religious literature
Periyapuranam was written by sekkilar. It is also known as Tiruttondapuranam. This
work inspite of its being a purana is unique for its historical and biographical interests.He was
born in Kunrattur in a vellala family. He built a temple of Siva in his native town of kunrattur. The
chola king requested him to expound the life-stories of the saints,the ruler desired Sekkilarto
write down the lives in a great poem , and gave him much wealth to enable him to undertake

the task Sekkilar then retired to Chidambaram, and with his mind filled with divine grace-.there
was a voice commanding sekkilar to start the work with the words Ulagelam and he began to
compose Tiruttondar-Puanam in the 1000 pillared mandapam in the temple, and the work
reached its completion with a total of 4253 stazes. Then the king himself came to Chidambaram
and listened to his work. Periyapuranam was hailed as a veritable fifth Veda in Tamil and took
its place as the twelfth book in the Saiva canon. Sekkilar was honoured with the title Tondar
Sirparavuvar the singer of the glories of saints. The periyapuranam influenced the lives and
thoughts of the saivities. It is one of the masterpieces of Tamil literature. Kulonttunga-ll. was
the chola contemporary king of Sekkilar.

175
TheTiruvilaiyadal puranam of Perubarrappulyur Nambiperubarrappulyur nambi
compiled the Saiva cannon in the form of ten books, the first three comprisiong padigams of
Tirugnansambandar books four to six made up of 307 padigams of Tirunavukkarasu, 100
padigams of Sundarar forming the seventh book Tiruvasagam, of Mannikavasagar being the
eighth and number ofTtiruvsaippa by nine different authors and the Tirumandiram of Tirumular
forming the last two books. Nambi arranged the eleventh book of canon at the request of the
chola king. It included the padigams left over and the pasuram uttered by siva himself and the
compositions of nambi himself. The periyapuranam is counted as the twelfth book. Among the
authors of the ninth book of the canon, Gandaraditya father of uttamachola finds a place.
Karuvur devar who has sung hymns on three chola temples the adityesvara at kalandia

the Rajarajaeswara at Tanjore and the Gangaikonda Cholavara at Gangaikondacholapuram
was native of karuvura and the legends centring round his name has found a place in the
karuvurpuranam, Sivagnanabhodam was written by Meykkandar in the first half of the
thirteenth century A.D. This is short treatise of dozen sutras which seem to have been translated
from a Sanskrit original. Meykkandar explains and illustrates the arguments of each of the
sutras and fix their meanings.
Tiruvundiyar and tirukkalirruppandiyu are written by two authors, teachers, and disciple
according to tradition and both known by the name or rather title uyyavandadevar, they are
both works meant to present in an easy style the main aspects of Saiva doctrine and practise.
Arunandi wrote Sivagnanasittiyar.It is a comprehensive statement of the true doctrine

introduced by a critical discussion of rival system of which no fewer than fourteen, including
four schools of Buddhism and two Jainism are passed under review. Arunandi also wrote
Irupavirupadhu which expounds the doctrine in the form of a dialogue between teacher and
pupil.
Umapathi sivacharya was the author of eight works on the doctrine which complete the
tale of the saivasiddhanta sastras in Tamil. They are sivaprakasam, Thiruvarutppa, vinavenba,
porrip pahrodai kodikkavi, Nejuvidu Dudu, Unmaineri Villakkam and sankarppanikkam.

176
Very few Tamil works of vaishnavism were written during the chola period. Great Vaishnava
Acharyas composed many devotional poems and philophical works in the Sanskrit languages
in this period yamunacharya. Yadavaprakasa and Ramanjua have contributed to the growth of
vaishnavite literature during the period.
Ramanujanurrandhadhi was written by Thiruvarangattu Amudanar, the disciple of
Ramanuja. It is a poem of hundred verses in the kalitturai metre in praise of Ramanuja. The
central idea of the poem is that without the grace of the Guru there is no way to salvation.
Striking contributions were made in the fields of grammar, rhetoric and lexicography. The
Yapparungalam and Yapparungalakkarigai of Amitasagara, a Jaina ascetic composed towards
the close of the tenth century. The text and commentary of Virasoliyam belonged to the reign of

Virarajendra. The text was written by Buddamitra and its commentary was by Perundevanar.
Virarajendra is mentioned as a great scholar in that work. Virasoliyam is written in kaliturai
metre and planned on the basis of a synthesis between Tamil and Sanskrit systems of grammar
and rhetoric and comprises of five sections sandhi, sol, porul, yappu and Alankara.
The Dandiyalankaram is the only work devoted entirely to a discussion of Alankara or
Ant as it is called in Tamil. The name of the author and his age are not known. But scholars
have assigned him as the grandson of kamban who was the author of Dandiyalankaram. This
is composed in sutra style and it treats of the nature of poetry and of figures of speech fewer
than two generic head (i.e) Arthalankara (porulani) and Subdhalankara (Sollani).
The Neminadam of Gunavirapandita is a short work comprising of less than hundred

verses in the venba metre and treating of the orthography and parts of speech (eluttu and sol)
of the Tamil language. The Nannul (god book) written by pavanandi belonged to the
reign of kulottunga-lll. It treats of elluttu and sol in a simple way. The Nambiyahapporul was
written by Narakavirajanambi, Lexicography. The pingalandai and chudamani are two lexicons
written during the chola period. Mandala purusha wrote chudamani also known as Nigantu
chudamani. The payirm of pingalandai states that it was composed by the author of the earliest
Tamil nigandu (i.e.) sendan divakaram.

177
9.4.3 Commentaries
Though it is difficult to point out the exact age of the early commentators, some of them
must have flourished in the centuries of chola role. Elampuranar was an important commentator.
It is commentary on Tolkappiyam is a model of verse and critical elucidation of a difficult text.
Senavarayar composed a commentary on the solladhigaram of tolkappiyam. Perasiniar wrote
commentary for parts of the poruadhigaram. He also wrote on Tirruchirram-balakkovaiyar,
adiayrkkunallar wrote a good commentary on silappadhigaram parimelegar wrote beautiful
comments on thirukkural and paripadal.
9.4.4 Sanskrit Literature
Sanskrit learning and Sanskrit literature flourished during the chola rule. Various
endowments were made for colleges where different branches of Vedic and Philosophic study
were pursued and to the popularity of the prabhayakhara Mimamsa and of the Rupavatara

introductory verses in Sanskrit lexicon Nanarthanava samksepa state that a village of Saiva
Bhamins learned in Sanskrit lore was established in the chola country by kulottunga-1 and
from that village of certain kesavaswamin of the Vasta gothra, a member of a family of hereditary
grammarians, was in the service of Rajaraja-ll and he was commissioned by the king to prepare
for the use of young scholars, this Sanskrit lexicon in which the words are arranged in alphabetical
order and their various meaning set forth, as directed by the king himself.
Haradatta, a well known commentator on sutra literature, lived in the ninth or tenth century
A.D. Bharataswamin commented on the samaeda; sadgurusishya composed the commentary
on Aitreya Brahamana and aranyanka. He also commended on kaytayan’s saranukramani
and on the Asvatayana srauta sutra.

Bhagavata prana which synthesises Bhakti and Adavaita Vedanta is said to have been
composed in south India in the tenth century A.D. Vishnu chitta composed commentary on the
Vishnu purana in the thirteenth century.
Kulasekhara Alvar wrote Mukuntamala, a devotional poem. Saktibhadra composed
Ascharyachidamani which deals with an episode in the rama saga. It is believed to have been
the first full blown drama to be produced in the south. Unmadavasavadatta written by Sakitbhadra
is not available.

178
Kulasekara, a kerala ruler in the 10th century dramatised incidents from the Mahabharata
in stage worthy manner in the Topatisamarana and subhadra Dhanamjaya. He patronised
Vasudeva who wrote Nalodaya and Bilomangalaswamin who composed Krishna karnamrita a
devotioanal poem. In the thirteenth century saradatanaya wrote a great work on rhetoric
Bhaaprakasa and also a treatise on music called saradiya.
A commentary on the ksumanjali was written by udayana. Varadaraja wrote
Tarkikaraksha. He was identified as the author of vyavaharanirnaya on work on low and
nayavivekadipika; an expose on mimamsa of the prabhakara school.
Saiva philosophy is represented in saskrit by Haradatta charya author of Srutisuktimala
also called chaturedatatparya sangraha and hariharataratamya a sectarian polemic. Srikanta’s
bramamimsabashya expounds th sutras of badarayana form the saivas standpoint. Many

agorasivacharya and umapatisivacharya wrote many works on Saiva system in Sanskrit.
Ganasicacharaya commented on the sivaganaboda section of the rautava ahama.
In lexicography the vaijayathai of yadavaprakasa deserves special menion. In grammer
Haradatta wrote Padamanjari a commentary on kadika vaman and jayaditya. A commentary
called purushakar on the Deiva of Deva was written in thirteenth century by krishnalaisuka.

9.5 Summary
These temples of Southern India represent an outstanding creative achievement in the
architectural conception of the pure form of the Dravida type of temple which is known as the
“Great Living Cholas Temples”. The Chola style involves use of granite to create design consisting

of deities, warriors, kings and dancers. The Dravidian structures reflect the prosperity of the
Chola Empire. The glories still live in the wonderful temples.
Devaranayakam was a temple official in charge of singing Devaram songs in temples.
Tiruvembavai of Manikkavasakar was also sung in Siva temple. The devaradiyar were also

179
entrusted with the singing of Tiruvembavai in temples. In literature cholas constitutes the most
creative epoch of south Indian history. Thus the Cholas constituted the most creative epoch of
South Indian History in the literary period

10.1 Introduction
Under the Cholas “art reached and passed its meridian”. According to the historian J.
Dubrenil, “the pallavas were excelled in sculpture. The cholas were above all architects. Their
style is distinguished by simplicity and grandeur” The temples were the principle nursery of art
and architecture. The temples and paintings of the early Cholas are found in larger numbers, in
the former Pudukottai state (present Tiruchirappalli district). They are also in good state of
preservation. They present us fairly a good idea, how later pallava architecture grew into the
chola style proper. As far as the architectural history of Tamil Nadu is concerned it may be said
that the early Chola period is the transition period-from the late pallava style into the chola
style. There are several stages in the process of evolution, which are well represented by a few

early chola temples in the Tiruchirapalli and tanjavur district. The architecture of the cholas can
be divided into the early chola temples, and the later chola period.
10.2 Early Chola Architecture
The early Chola period may start from the reign of Vijayalaya down to the beginning of
the reign of Rajaraja, the Great, and the author of the magnificent Tanjavur temple. Among the
early Chola temples, the following deserves mention:
 Vijayalaya Cholesvaram at Narttamalai (Pudukkottai).
 Balasubramanya temple at Kannanur (Pudukkottai).
 Koranganatha temple at Sinivasanallur (Tiruchirappalli).
 Nagesvaraswami temple at Kumbakonam.and
 Muvarkoil at Kodumbalur (Pudukkottai).
The main features of the architectural style of the above temples are as follows: Namely
abundant stones were used for the construction of the temples. The temples are not large in

dimension. They are small ones which implied limited resources and local developments. The
temple complex includes: a pillared mandapa or portico, open courtyard around the temple.
Small sub-shrines are seen in the courtyard lacing inwards resembling the main shrine.
They are scattered over the courtyard unlike in the Kailasanatha temple at Kanchipuram where

182
they are attached to the main shrine. Vimana consisting of 1 to 5 storey in dimensioning order
the plan of the Vimana is either square or circular or combining both patterns.Dome shaped
sikhara, Round kalasa, The pillared mandapa is often closed and open as seen in modern
days.The external walls of the sanctum and mandapa are decorated with ornamental plasters.
“Niches are not seen in the earliest examples while in later ones; there is one on each side of
the sanctum. These niches bear sculptures of Brahma, Dakshinamurthi and Vishnu or
Lingodbhava or Ardhanari.
Below the cornice at the top of the sancturm wall a frieze of bhutas is seen. The corner
of the cornice is shaped into scroll work. Above the cornice is another frieze of lions. The
parapet over the ceilings carries miniature shrines (panjarams).The Vimana contains one or

more storeys. Each storey is terminated by a roll cornice with kudu motifs. The lower storey
carry miniature shrines at intervals .Pillars in the earliest examples are of the pallava order. In
the later ones, two changes have been introduced one relating to the capital and the other to
the abacus. In the capital a neck moulding has been introduced where it joins on to shaft. To
the lower part of the capital is added another member in the form of a vase or pot. The abacus
is much expanded.
Let us now see how these features are present in the temples complex of the above
mentioned temples.
10.2.1 Vijayalaya Cholesvara
It was built in the time of Vijayalaya as the very name suggests. He is the founder of the
early Cholas. It is one of the best preserved examples. The cello is circular and located within
a square prakara. This is not usual feature seen in tamilian architecture.

There is a closed pillared mandapa in front of the cella. The vimana has four streys- the
three lower ones are sqare, while the fourth and the upper most is a circular. The vimana is
surmounted by a dome-shaped sikhara and a round kalasa at its top. There are no niches on
the external side of the walls. The pillars are of Pallava order. There are two Dwarapalakas,
measuring about 5’ seen inside niches. They are half-turned towards the entrance and crosslegged. They have only two arms as in the Pallava temples, There are about 7 small shrines in
the open around main shine.

183
10.2.2 Balasubramanya Temple
This temple is also very similar to the former. Aditya-I constructed many Siva temples.
Balasubramanya temple is one among them. There are elephant figures introduced in the
corners just below the sikhara as also in the four corners of the roof of the shrine.
10.2.3 Korangantha Temple
This temple is situated in the town of Srinivasanallur about 59 kilometres from
Tiruchirappali. This temple was built in the reign of Parantaka and is dedicated to the God
Ranganatha. It consists of a square cella vestibule and rectangular pillared madapa. The
height of the vimana is about 50’. This temple represents some development with regard to the
pillars. The temple is protected by the Archaeologocal survey of India
10.2.4 Muvarkoyil
Muvarkoyil
Moovar Kovil or “The three temples” is situated in Kodumbalur , 36 kilometers from

Pudukottai. These temples were constructed by the Chola feudatory and Irukkvel Chieftain of
Boothi Vikramakesari as per the inscriptions. The temple is very important as it is living example
of early to medieval chola architecture. The inscription in the temple also gives us a glimpse of

184
the political climate of South India between 8th to 10th centuries as well as the relation between
the royal houses of Chola and Irukkuvel.
The temple consists of three shrines separated from one another. They stand on a
north-south line and face west. Each of these has an ardhamandapa in front. Proceeding to
ardhamandapa is a bigger mandapa common to all three shrines. It measures 91’X41’ (northsouth & east-west). In front there is a Nandi pavilion. In between the Nandai mandapaand main
central shrine is the dhwajasthamba. Around the whole group is a pillared cloister with as many
as 15 sub-shrines of varying proportions. They all resemble the main shrines. There is an outer
enclosure with a thick massive wall with a gopura entrance at the west. The basement of main
shines contains horizontal mouldings and the lower most moulding consist of lotus petals

(padmakosa). There are large number of sculptures on the walls of the sanctum representing
Siva as Ardhanari, Vinadhara-Dakshinamurthi, gajari, Samharamurthi, kiratamurthi, Ganadhara,
Harihara, Chandrasekhara, Chandra, Surya, Uma, Jeystha and Saptamatrikas. It is one of the
best examples of early Chola temples containing elegantly carved sculptures.
10.3 Later Chola Architecture
Temple architecture received great impetus from the genius of Rajarja-I and his son
Rajendra, Rararaja built many temples, and they are bigger than those described above. These
temples are noted for their sculptures and ornamental work. The plinth portion, the cornice as
well as the portion below the same, the different storeys in the vimana and the external wall
surface-all have received greater attention and studded with beautiful sculptures, minute carvings

and ornamental motifs. The yali frieze was introduced into one of the horizontal mouldings of
the plinth-the Ganas in the portion below the cornice are shown in various poses like dancing,
they are also shown with pot bellies or with lions or monkey faces. They are very humorously
portrayed. The cornice is decorated with creepers in the space between kudus. The kudus are
surmounted by lion faces. The lower most storeys of the vimana bear sculptures reprsenting
Siva, Brahama, Vishnu and other minor deities. The top most storeys carry elegant bull figures
at the corners. The sikkara is ribbed with 8 sides. These are some of the features of the
temples architecture during the early years of Rajaraja’s reign. Among the temples of the
period mention must be made of the following:

185
Tiruvalisvaram temple at Brahamades (Tiruchirapalli).
Uttarakailasa at Thiruvadi (Tanjavur district).
Vaidyanatha temple at Tirumalavadi (Tiruchirapalli).
2 temples at Dadapuram (North Arcot).and
Sivadevale (Ceylon).
Gopuras
The cholas had also paid some attention to the development of gopuras. The gopura
was considered as an essential adjunct in the sam exil line. We hear of the early Chola gopuras
in their inscriptions also. There are also some stray examples surviving still. The temples at
Tirukkattalai and Melappaluvur, we find the existence of the gopuras. There seems to have
existed a gopura in the temple at Kadambavanesvara at Erumbur (South arcot District) as also
other places as evidenced from inscriptions.
The beginning of the eleventh century synchronized with many developments in temple

architecture. They are: Elaboration of the vimana-its height was raised to about 200, Elaboration
of the gopuras.Greater attention was paid to the embellishment of the internal and external
wall surfaces of the mandapas.
Numerous sculptures and carvings were introduced to represent a variety of iconographic
forms and sports of many deities.
There are four important temples of the later Cholas which exhibit the maturity of Chola
architecture. They are:
 Thanjavur temple built by Rajaraja.
 Temple at Gangaikondacholapuram built by his son Rajendra-I.
 Darasuram temple at Kumbakonam and
 The temple at Tribhuvanam.

186
10.3.1 Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur
The Brihadisvara Temple houses a 3.7 meter tall linga of Lord Shiva and the tallest
vimanam in the world. The wonderful designs of the gopurams in the temple are decorated
with sculptural depictions of various Gods and Goddesses. The massive proportions and
simplicity of design of the temple is believed to have provided inspiration for other buildings.
Constructions not only in South India but also were in South-east Asia has been modified from
the grand designs.
This temple was completed in 1009 A.D is a fitting memorial to the achievement of
RajarajaI. It is the largest and tallest of all Indian temples. It is a masterpiece reflecting the high
water mark of Tamilian architecture. It consists of a ardhamandapa, mahamandapa and a
Nadimandapa. They are arranged in the centre of a spacious walled enclosure, with a gopura

entrance in the east. There is also the second enclosure with another gopura. Ther is a pillared
corridor running round the temple at the interior of the first enclosed wall. There are a number
of sub-shrines built at the cardinal points and at internals in the corridor.
The main item of attraction in the temple is the Vimana. It is dominating the entire
surrounding. The measurements of the Vimana portion are: Base-82' side, Height of the base-
50', Vimana total height-200' from the ground and 13-Tiers.
The storeys in the vimana contain beautiful sculptures, miniature shrines, pavilions, aches
with sculptures etc. The walls of the base of the vimana contain a number of aches with images,
pilasters etc. It is also interesting to note that the monolithic Nandi of this temple is one of the
largest monolithic bulls in South India. There are also traces of Chola paintings left on the

callings and wall of the inner circumambulatory passage found.
10.3.2 Gangaikondacholapuram Temple
The Gangaikonda Choleswara temple was constructed by Rajendra I in memory of his
victory over northern kingdoms. The city of Gangaikonda cholapuram was erected as the
capital of the cholas by Rajendra chola I.
The temple houses a four meter height of Shiva lingam. This lingam is the tallest among
the other chola temples. Other attractions of the temple are the colossal representation of

187
Navagrahas. These auspicious nine deities are placed in a circle. The structure shaped as a
Chariot and the sculpturesof Chandeswarar and Gnanasaraswathi are other attractions.
It was built about 1030 A.D.-two decades after the erection of Thanjavur temple. It exhibits
the same style. It is larger in its plan, but not so tall, the vimana is about 180' height. But its
base is about 100' square. Hence the width of the vimana was increased. The vimana contains
only 8 tires. Though the vimana has the same construction as that of the Thanjavur temple,
there are some novel features introduced into the elevation of the vimana. For instance, the
strong lines in the elevation of the Thanjavur vimana are replaced by elegant curves. The
pyramidal body is slightly concave and its angles and the sides slightly cuirved to effect a sort

of convex outline. These curves enhance the shape of the vimana. While comparing the two
vimanas, Brown observes: “Each is the final and absolute vision of its creator made manifest
through the medium of structural form, the one symbolizing conscious might, the other subconscious grace but both dedicated by that divinity which has seized the same”.
Besides the main temple, there are also separate shrines for Chandikesvarar and the
Goddess. This is one of the largest pillared mandapas that we come across during the Chola
period. Pillared mandapa of longer dimensions are the special features of the later period i.e.
Vijayanagar. There are also transepts between the sanctum and mahamandapa on the north
and south, as in Thanjavur temple. Lastly mention must be made of the embellishment done
on the outside of the walls.

The chola style continued to flourish for a century longer. A large number of temples
were constructed; it is not possible to mention them here. But temple at Darasuam and
Tribhuvanam deserve mention. Darasuram temple was built by Rajaraja-II while Tribhuvanam
temple, by Kulottunga-III. The front portion of the Darasuram temple is shaped into a chariot
with wheels drawn by mythical animals. The temple contain beautiful sculptures and images
besides sculptured panels representing some Nayanmars.. Both these two temples have many
features in common with those of two great temples.

188
10.3.3 Darasuram Temple
Darasuram Airavateshwarar temple gopuram
The Airavateswara temple at Darasuram is smaller than the other great living chola
temples. This temple is in Darasuram is the third in the list of the great living chola temples.
Darasuram is a panchayat town located 3 kilometers from Kumbakonam in Thanjavur District.
The town is known for this temple constructed by Rajaraja Chola II in the 12th century A.D. This
temple is recognised as the UNESCO World Heritage monument along with the Brihadisvara
Temple and the Gangaikonda Choleswara temple
This temple is a storehouse of art and architecture. The vimana is 85 feet high. The front
mandapam itself is in the form of a huge chariot drawn by horses. The temple has some
exquisite stone carvings.
Origionally it has a number of enclosures with gopura entrance to each, but only one is in

extinct. The temple has the same plan and parts as the Tanjore temple, but there is a
mahamandapa in front of a pillared agramandapa with porch on the south. This is called
“Rajakambirantirumandapam”. It is built like a chariot on wheels drawn by elephants.
This temple bears numerous sculptures and carvings. One of the most fascinating is the
series depicting scenes from Periyapuranam on the base of the grabhagriha wall. The scenes
depict the lives of the Saiva Saints with labels beneath.
Anther interesting features of the sculptural art of this temple is the occurrence of Kumbha
panjara motif, on the exterior walls of the sanctum and manadapas at redular intervals.The

189
vimana has five storeys and the sikhara is of circular shape. There is a shrine for Parvathi to
the north of main shrine.
In front of garbhagriha there is a Nandi shrine and balipitha. There is Amman shrine also
on the northern side. It is a replica of the main temple but miniature in size. The outer gopura
is in ruins. The inner gopura is external and has two storeys.
10.3.4 Tribhuvanam Temple
Tribhuvanam Kambaheswarartemple
The kambaheswarar temple is dedicated to Siva. It is situated in the town of Tribhuvanam
near Kumbakonam. Siva is worshipped as kambaheswarar as he removed the quaking
(skt.kampa) of a king who was being haunted by a Brahmarakshasa. According to this temple
wall inscription we infer that this temple was constructed by Kulothunga chola III in memory of
his victory over North Indian rulers.

The temple follows the Dravidian style of architecture. An unusual feature of the temple
is that the vimana is extremely high. The architecture of this temple is similar to other three
temples. There is a separate shrine for Sarabeswarar in this temple.
There are shrines for Devi, Somaskanda, chandikesvara etc. The temple as a whole is a
vertical sculpture gallery of varied iconography. There are not only scenes depicting stories

190
from Ramayana, Mahabharata and Puranas but also secular scenes. There are numerous
natya poses depicted

10.4 Impact of Chola Art and Architecture
The influence of Chola art on other countries, particularly on Indo-China and the Far East
is so great. A few temples of 12th and 13th century A.D in Suth East Asian countries bear the
traits of the Chola architecture. Further, the famous Nataraja figures have also been found in
those countries.
The Chola period has witnessed a tremendous progress in the realm of sculpture and

iconography. The art of this period may be studied under three different heads: namely Sculpture,
Icon and Portraits.
10.4.1 Sculpture
Sculpture was generally a subsidiary to architecture. It was employed as decoration on
the walls, pillars, plinths, roofs and other spots in temples. Sculptures appreciated the value of
plan spaces on the walls and did not crowd them with too many figures. The worked on hard
stones like granite, “Large frescoes in stone” were not produced unlike the Pallava period. The
sculptured figures paid more attention on the rich iconography of Siva and Vishnu.

191
Narrative sculpture in stone are in small panels, sometimes as small as 6 inches by 4
inches as at Nagesvaraswamy temple at Kumbakonam and rarely more than 2 feet by 1 foot.
Naturalism was the cream of Chola plastic art. Then spiritualism and dynamism comes.
Decorative sculptures are seen in many forms like architectural motifs, floral and vegetable
patterns, friezes of animals, birds, dancing figures with musical attendants and of legendary
and puranic stories. Men and women are gracefully chiseled as seen in the Nagesvaraswamy
temple at Kumbakonam. They are shown in profile wearing costly jewelers and drapery. They
are shown in various actions and poses with different head dress. The effects like light and
shade and perceptiveness are vividly portrayed on these figures.
Scenes from Ramayana, Mahabharata and Puranas are vividly chiseled. For example,

the lives of the 64 Nayanmars are sculptured in narrative panels on the basement wall of the
Darasuram temple. They are subsequently removed to Thanjavur Art Galley. They bear labels
also.
One of the Ramayana panels from Tribhuvanam show Ravana with many arms and
heads carrying off Sita in his chariot and the bird Jatayu which fought Ravana. There are also
small panels-the Agni presenting payusam to Dasaratha, the king distributing the same to his
queens, birth of Rama, the fight of Tataka, Hanuman’s meet with Ravana are some of the best
examples of Chola sculptural art.
Similarly one can notice friezes of alternating elephants, lion and yalis, ganas and birds
on the mouldings of the plinth or walls. Yet another piece of Chola art is the dyarapalaka figure.
These figures are considered to be door keepers of the abodes of the gods. They are shown

on the side of gateways, entrances to temples and shrines. They are shown with either 2 or 4
or 8 arms with different objects and weapons held in the arms. Female’s dvarakapalakas
(dvarapalikas) are shown in the shrine of goddesses. Their facial features and anatomical
details serve as criteria to identify Chola style.
10.4.2 Portraits
The Cholas excelled the Pallavas even in portraiture. The best specimens are seen
adorning walls of Koranganatha temple and Nagesvaraswami temple. They were well preserved

192
and nearly life size. This art is so unconventional, but original in conception and spirit. Particularly
the Chola ladies are gracefully shown. They are realistic human figures, full of feminine grace
and the joy of life. This humanism is the principal contribution of the Cholas to South Indian Art.
In their free and easy poses, in the divergence of their features and forms, with a pronounced
individuality to each figure, in the excellence of their modeling and in the successful treatment
of facial expression, particularly of the eyes and lips, these sculptures have no parallel in any
other phase of South Indian art. They are not modeled in the round but carved on jewellery of
the both men and women reveal much of life the stone and are undetached.
The examples of early portraits have been noticed at Tiruvaduturai. A beautiful bronze of

women is now preserved in the Free Art Gallery, Washington, who is identified as Lakshmi or
Parvathi. The portraits of Cholamadevi and Kulottunga-III are also noticed at Kalahasti temple.
10.4.3 Icons
Icons of Siva, Vishnu, Nataraj, Lakshmi, Parathi, Subramania were made both in stone
and metal (bronze).
(1) Icons in stone
Siva and his various other forms such as Tripurantaka, Dakshinamurthy, Nataraja
Lingodbhava, Gangadhara, were very popular, eight armed Durga is an icon noted for its
artistic merit. Icons of Vishnu were less in number than those of Siva. Various Devi’s like
Lakshmi, Parvathi, Tripurasundari etc., deserve mention.
These figures throw a flood of light on the development of hindu iconography during the
period. Sometimes these gods are shown along with their months like Bull, peacock, Garuda

etc. These icons exhibit the high workmanship as well as the scholarship of the chola sculptors
in making these images.
(2) Metal Icons
Bronze images were cast in large numbers. They were made by the Cire Perdu process.
The images were made solid, hollow or semi-hollow with sides. Again there are various forms
of bronze icons representing men, women, animal, gods, goddesses etc.

193
The Nataraja image holds the first place among the Chola bronzes of this type are spread
all over the Museums of the world. Some of them are still under worship in temples. The
Nataraja figure has been cast in various forms and size. He is shown as a dancing Siva and
hence he is known as king of dance. He has four arms with flocks of flying hair and he flown
scarf. He holds objects like damaru, fire etc. One of his feet is shown crushing a demon
(ignorance). It is described very often as “this dancer is danced upon the bodies of the dead”.
The Natarja icons from Nageswarasamy, Tirvallangadu,Gngaikondacholapuram and
Chidambaram are masterpieces of Chola art. Besides, the other forms of Siva, Vishnu, Lakshi,
Parvathi and other minor deities are represented in bronze.
Besides icons, there are also copper seals issued which speak of the progress of metal

casting during this period. The Karandai copper plates deserved special mention in this
connection.
10.5 Paintings
Painting is delicate products of art. The art painting has had a continuous history and
made steady progress right through the ages. The Cholas continued the tradition of Pallava
paintings. There are few good specimens still preserved in temples like Thanjavur.
The technique of Chola paintings is quite different from that of Ajanta. Here the ground
plaster is of course lime mortar below, with a fine coat of lime-wash above it and on which the
colour pigment were laid on accordance with the “fresco” or “lime medium” technique, no
adhesive was used as gum or glue and it is the important feature that distinguishes the chola
paintings from these in Ajanta. The areas of panels vary from 24 squares to 60 squares.
10.5.1 Tanjore paintings

The paintings are found in the walls and ceiling of the pradakshina passage around the
sanctum in the Tanjore temple. The theme of the paintings is religious drawn mostly from
religious texts. The episode of the life of sundaramurthi forms the theme of a few panels. The
Kailasa scene with Siva, rishis and apsara maidens is yet another fascinating panel. Siva is
painted red and one of the rishis blue. There are other panels depicting Siva is painted man

194
and sundaramurthy Nayanar, Nataraja, Tripurantaka and Brahma are also vividly painted. On
the western wall of the shrine is depicted Nataraja worshipped by a royal devotee by his queens.
The royal figure of Rajaraja-I.and his teacher Kanuvardevar is also portrayed.
There is second circumambulatory over the one in which the paintings have been noticed.
The inner wall of this passage also contains traces of chola paintings. There numerous dance
poses are painted. The lives are drawn in light red or brown and deepened by black or reddish
brown. The other colours used for flesh and drapery are defined by black or reddish brown.
The other colours used for flesh and drapery are defined by delicate brush work. The dancing
forms are fill of action and expression. The hair is done to elaborate coiffures of different styles

and decked with high in celestial beings. The eye lids are not pronounced flowers. The eye
brows are set low in human forms and but highly expressive. The noses are long, straight and
sensitive very rarely cured. The women’s dress consists of a sari of muslin tied round the wait
covering down to the ankles and thrown into folds decorated by floral geometrical designs. The
men are show with strong body, beard, moustache and knots of hair on the head. Thus the art
of painting developed in the chola period.

11.1 Introduction
The 13th century was a period of Pandyan revival. Their power reached its zenith with the
celebrated reign of Jatavarrman Sundara pandaya and Maravarman Kulasekhara Pandyaa
which cover the second part of the 13th century. Till 1218, the Pandyas were obliged to take
subordinate position and pay tribute to the Cholas. They reasserted their independence to
such an extent that the latter half of the 13th century has come to be called as”The Age of the
Second Pandyan Empire”.

For the study of social and economic life of the Pandyas of the Second Empire, we have
sources like epigraphy and foreign accounts. Some of the earlier inscriptions are purely historical.
Foreign accounts particularly those of Marco Polo are extremely valuable for recapturing the
social life of the people.

198
11.2 Economic life
Agriculture
People settled in the fertile plains of Vaigai and Tamarabarani rivers. These rivers made
the land fertile hence most of the people lived on agriculture. They made use of the rivers for
their agriculture. Thus the fertile lands of the country were immensely important for the growth
of economy. During this period lands were measured properly. After proper measurement
boundary stone was laid and regular fencing work was undertaken by the Government. It is
mentioned in many copper plates. Moreover the periodic land surveys are indicated by reference
to scales like Sundara Pandyanarkoil and Vira Pandyankoil. The yard which was used to
measure the land during the time of Maravarman Sundara Pandya-I called “Kuditangi”.
Boundaries were marked by stones. Kuli, ma and veli were four kinds of lands Viz.,
Vellan Vagai

In this kind the land-owners were called Vellan Vagai. They were brought under the
control of the state. They paid the taxes regularly. It is stated that they had to pay an annual tax
of 642Kalams of paddy and 40 Kalanju to the Government.
Brahmadeyam
Brahmadeyam lands were given to the learned Brahmins as an honour by the kings and
queens. Rich people also donated this kind of lands to the Brahmins. Parantaka Viranarayanan
gave a village called Dinachutar Mangalam in the Sinnamannur Copper plates.
Devadanam
The lands offered free of tax were devadana. For Shiva temples, Tiruvidaiyattam to
Vishnu temples, Pallichandam to Jains and Buddhist temples.
Service Tenures
This kind of lands was given to the villagers for their meritorious service. Besides the
villagers, soldiers were also given such lands for their heroic deeds in battles.

199
The gifts were written in the documents If any future boundary disputes arised that should
be settled easily by these documents. When the documents had been lost new documents
were given. Dalavoypuram copper plates referred to these issues of new document. In Shiva
temples the boundary stones were laid with Trisulas engraved, in Vaishnava temples
Thiruvazikkal was laid and in Jain temple boundary stones with Mukkudal was laid. The
exemptions were noted in the name of the contemporary king and recorded on copper plates.
Lands were classified as Nansey (wet). Punsey (dry) and tottam (garden). All cultivable
land was held in one of the 3 broad classes of tenure, which may be distinguished as peasant
proprietorship called, “Vellan Vagai” in the inscriptions. The assessment of revenue was fixed

with reference to the fertility of the soil and the nature of the crops rose. The revenue was paid
in cash or in land.
Broadly stated, only the cultivable land was assessed. The villages sites the quarters
occupied by the lower classes and artisans, the courtyard and flower gardens attached to the
temples, the threshing floor, the village grazing ground, the saline earth, the land just on the
bed of river, the land where breaches had occurred and marshy places excluded. Those that
had referred damage or had failed altogether were excluded.
11.2.1 Land Tenure and Cultivation
The tenant and the land-holder were related by the usual terms of tenure and the landholder was obliged to pay taxes like land task, water cess, tank duty etc. The status of the
cultivator or the farm labourer was deplorable. The unequal distribution of wealth was a significant

feature. Transfers of property were common. The legal acts were recorded on copper or stone,
under royal orders if it was of public interest. We have enough information to speak authoritatively
about service tenure, military grants etc. The military tenure to solders called “Veera Boga”.
There is an interesting record belonging to the times of Jatavarman Sundara Pandya which
gives considerable information about a village called “Vikrama Pandya Chathurvedi Mangalam”.
Here service-tenure was given to teachers of Sutras, teachers of Vedas, village
accountant,Goldsmith, village doctor, carpenter, potters, washer man, barbar, village watchman,
(Padikappar) and village servant (Vettiyan). The residents of this village were 108 Brahmins.
The temples also specialized in service tenure. The charity tenures related to the Brahmins,
the temples and the schools. Temples land were given to lessees or tenant for cultivation.

200
We get enough information in regard to the forms of land tenure to enable us to see that
the conditions of tenancy cultivation varied in accordance with the locality. An inscription from
Alangudi (Tanjore) gives an unusually detailed account of the rights and duties of landlords
and cultivators. Tenancy cultivation particularly in the case of land owned by Brahmins was
quite common.
11.2.2 Irrigation and Method of Irrigation
The main sources of irrigation were Vaigai and Tamaraparani rivers. The secondary
sources were Vellaru and other canals. River irrigation was in vogue to a greater extent. Several
canals were dug in Vaigai River for the purpose of irrigation. Many tanks and canals were
constructed by Parantaka Viranarayanan. Among the canals the following were very
important:Parakarma Pandyan ground canal, Vasudeva grand canal, Veerapandyan canal and

Sri Vallabha ground canal. A dam was constructed during this period. It was called Parakarma
Pandya kallanai. Apart from these irrigation works, a canal was dug in River Pennai for the
irrigation of the farmers at Tiruvanmalai.
The kings maintained Eri Variyam to look after the lakes. Tanks and lakes were peoperly
maintained by the variyam.
Facilities were made available by the rulers and the aristocracy of the land. The
maintenance of their amenity was facilitated by suitable taxes. A very interesting record from
Sarkar Periyapalayam (Coimbatore), of a certain Sundara Pandya contains details as to the
duties of the person who was appointed a fisherman “Pillaiyan” who had to look after the anai
(anicut) and the channel. He had to be given certain income and privileges. He had to see that
the water, did not flow above the dam, but was properly directed into the tank. If there are any

defects in the tank and dam, then he had to report the villagers and temple authorities. The
appointed village servant called “vettiyan” and he would repair the dam. And for this he was
given pieces of rent-free land and some payment in grain. Pillaiyan was also to collect the
taxes Vayakalpattam (canal tax) and passipattam (fishing tax) from the temple tenants at Suralur.
Reclamation of Waste lands:
Barren lands and uncultivable lands were brought under cultivation in those days. Series
of successful steps were undertaken by the Government to remove the sands from the fields

201
affected by heavy floods. No wonder the Government authorities paid great attention to increase
the yield of these lands.
11.2.3 State Help
A record at “Pon Amaravathi” throws light on forbidding the temple authorities to take
water from “Idengalikaman” evidently for the purpose of irrigation. Village assemblies maintained
the excavation of canals and other facilities. Reclamation of spoil of land and fresh cultivation
of virgin soil were both encouraged. Two records of Jatavarman Sundara Pandya mention
some lands as having been sold by the village for a certain sum of money, with the exemption
of water taxes in compensation for the labour involved in reclaiming them from their waste
condition.
During the reign of Jatavarman Sundara Pandya (1251 A.D.) a new flood embarkment
substantially built on the side of the Coleroon was raised with the aid of funds collected in the

form of a special cess from the inhabitants in the neighborhood.
Reference to arid as well as fertile lands is available in the sources indicating variation in
the natural fertility of the soil which could be aggravated by failure of the monsoon and or by
the practically continuous warfare which raged all ground.
11.2.4 Agricultural Products
Some of the important products were Thinai, Varagu, Ellu, Payaru, Kuruvai, Karumbu,
Kolundu, Karunai, Manjal, Inji, Senkaluneer, Valai, Valuthalai, Poosani, etc. Non-agricultural
products were Maa, Pala, Narthai ,Elumichchai, Kulaviralli,Nelli, Iluppai etc,. Among the nonagricultural products, which were valuable as cash crops are cotton, arecanut, coconut, Palmyra
etc The Vadakkadamai tax ½ panam on every ma levied on gardenland, growing plantain,
ginger, turmeric, or betel. Some of these were paid in cash, but most of them in kind.

11.3 Industry and Trade
In the Pandya period, trade played an important role both in the economy and polity of
the country. The highways were made use for the development of trade. Many trade guilds

202
emerged in the Pandyan region. The wide use of coins, weights and measurements by the
merchants shows the flourishing trading activities emerged in the Pandyan territory.
General Industry was ancillary to agriculture and largely confirmed to the manufacture
of the iron-wheel, wooden vehicles. Ships and simple carpentry, building construction, spinning,
weaving, manufacture of salt and making of religious structures like temples, processions cars
and images, were other major industrial efforts. Naturally industries were only domestic based
Simple workshops, where the blacksmith made the wheel, or the carpenter his wooden wares
could be called factories of a sort.
Weaving was the most important industry. We hear the tax on weavers for their profession
called “Tariyiral” levied on looms Cotton textiles manufactured in Madurai were quite famous.The

needs of the people being simple the industry could not have been complicated. Rope making
manufacture of leather sheaths, making of ornaments, manufacture of baskets and above all
the pottery were well known industries from the beginning.
11.3.1 Foreign Trade
The Pandyas being a sea farming people developed the overseas trade to a great
extent.From Periplus and Ptolemy,we got information regarding their trade and ports. Foreign
trade was one of the planks on which the economic prosperity of the country depended .From
the earliest times the Pandya country has been famous for its pearl. There was a group of ports
lay in the Pandya Kingdom;Kayal, Vadalai, Devipattinam, Tondi and Passipattinam. Their
importance arose in general from their exports of pearls and import of horses. The articles of
imports were other kinds of luxuries like pepper, pearls, ivory, textiles and gold ornaments.

Trade with Ceylon was continuous and considerable.
11.3.2 Foreigners’ Account
The Venicean traveler Marco Polo mentions in particular the profitability of the pearl
fisheries at Kayal, the chief emporium of Pandya Kingdom. The horse of Kayal had considerable
political important and a good part of the revenue of the kingdom was spent on the purchase of
horses for the king and the army. Macro Polo was also criticizing on horse trade that the
country’s wealth was wasted as the climate was unsuited to Arab horses’ .According to him,

203
king was extremely rich. The king possessed many other treasure of great value besides the
best of the pearls that were found in the kingdom. The king was also wearing a fine silk thread
strung with 104 large pearls and rubies on his neck. Both Marco Polo and Wassof, the Muslim
historian agree in saying that the Pandya king had 1200 crores of gold dinars in his treasury.
They have also not failed to mention the personal attendants of the king. Who protected the
king, and die with him, when the king died. They were king’s “Trusty Lieges” or body gusrds
known to epigraphy as “Tennavan Apattuthavigai”.
11.3.3 Inland Trade
It was a self-sufficient economy, since the basic requirements of the people were all met
by local products. Inland trade was managed by hawkers and the merchants collecting in the

periodical or daily markets. Certain commodities like salt had to be transported over long
distances i.e. from sea-coast to the interior villages. The few main roads which connected
distant parts of the country were important as much for the traders as for the army. These
roads were called “Raja Peruvali”. Barter was the usual mode of exchange of commodities,
while currency was used in capital cities and for foreign trade The currency of the realm seems
to have comprised different varieties of Coins and people had to take care to specify the type
of coins to which each transaction had reference like Palam-Soliyar kanu,Vira Pandya Kasu.This
confusion was because the traditions of a number of rulers simultaneously ruling in different
parts of the country.Macro Polo, also mentions this; for these rulers not only did they causes

inscriptions to the engraved and endowments to be made each in his own name, but they
seem to have even exercised the Right of Coinage.
11.3.4 Merchant Guilds
The merchants organized themselves into groups or guilds. They were Ainnurruvar, the
Nanadesis, (foreign trade), Mani-graman, Valangiyar, Nagarattar, Anjuvanam etc.Manigramam
means Vanigrammam or association of merchants. We have evidence of many of these
merchant associations acting in union in their public activities .The people of 18 provinces
Visayam attend (Epigraph of Ramnad district) and came to an agreement that on all articles of
merchandise that were measured, spreads and folded and on some other specified goods
access of one Kasu per achehu should be collected. The corporations that attended the meeting
were self-regulating corporations of different classes of merchants.

204
These merchants guilds were greatly autonomous, which meant that they enjoyed the
advantages of freedom from state interference, but also suffered from the disadvantages of
lacking state backing. the mercantile community had no elementary banking operations. Lending
through houses specializing in monetary transaction and fixation of rates of interest were quite
common .But the agency for the horses supplied to the Pandyan kings enjoyed the patronage
of the kings. Macro Polo distinctly tells us that the king extended great favour to merchants and
foreigners so that they were glad to visit his city.

11.4 State Economy
It seems that the ‘Pandyan kings maintained carefully revenue and administrative records
on Palm leaves, which were later recopied and preserved”(copper plates and stone
inscriptions).The kings issued oral orders to their immediate servants and these orders were
called “Kelvi”. In the case of revenue order the oral “Kelvi” was written in orders or grants by
officers called “Variyilar”: From inscriptions we come to know about their sources of Taxes.
They are namely Land Taxes, Duties on Articles of trade, Excise tax, Professional taxes and
miscellaneous item.
11.4.1 Taxes on Land
Land revenue was the main source of income to the government. The taxes on land fall
into four main groups:(a)Land revenue proper, (b) Taxes for maintenance of irrigation works,

(c)Taxes for the maintenance of village officers,(d)Taxes for the maintenance of temples and
Brahmins.Tamil inscriptions mention,”Kadamai, antaraya, viniyogam and vadakkadamai”.
Antaraya and Viniyogam are grouped under one item viz.,”Kudimai”.

205
The assessment of revenue was fixed with reference to the fertility of the soil, and the
nature of crops rose. The village assemblies helped in collecting the revenue from the assesses
in the village .Lands which became useless due to loss of fertility by the soil procedure that
appears to have been usually followed in making gifts to temples of lands freed from all taxes
and other assessments. The large number of remission recorded owing to a variety of causes,
shows us that such representatives were not without value. Some such cases were scarcity of
water, flood, plunder, the ruined condition of the village, desertion of land by peasants, being
filled up with sand owing to the vicinity of the sea, and ceremonial occasions like the king’s
coronation.
Taxes were collected ,so that the village police could be remunerated .The administrator

,however, was in a sorry state. The assessee had to bribe the tax collectors so that there
could be no excess levy. It was possible in the state of affairs prevailed them for a chief to
hold a part of the country around the village and demand a ransom of 4,000 gold pieces, and
the affected villagers had to sell at their properties to meet their savage demand. There is no
record to show that such high handedness was suitably punished by the king. The state, levied
heavy taxes. Two inscriptions of ‘Maravarman Sundara Pandya’, from Ramanad district, seem
to contain more direct evidence of heavy and oppressive taxation and thus the village people
preferred “Woodland life than village life”. But Brahmadeya and Devadena lands were exempted
from tax. But sometimes, the Devadana lands and Brahmadeya lands had to pay a nominal
tax.
11.4.2 Duties on Articles of Trade and Excise

The export of special local manufacturing like textiles, pearls etc., earned a lot of foreign
exchange for the country and for the royal treasury also. The king took 1/10th of the total
earnings from pear -driving and sale of pearls as his royalty. Besides this, there was duty
known as, ‘Sungam’ which raised the revenue of the state.
11.4.3 Professional Tax
One inscription states that a tax of six panams per anum was levied on each Shop-
Keeper (a sort of consolidated sales tax) on each weavers ,i.e. Kaikolars, and on each oil

206
monger, the ‘saliyar’. Tax on industries was levied; the artisans also had to pay the tax to the
state. The tax was often changed on the instruments used by the professional- the washing
stone of the washer man, the loom of the weaver, etc. Professional taxes were generally annual,
remissions were occasionally granted, ,specially for the benefit of the artisan classes, in new
settlements .The idangai and valangal groups were also taxed as idangai vari and valangai
vari. . The potters paid Kusakkanam oil press, the Sekkiraiu, goldsmiths ‘tattar-pattam’ and the
tax of ‘virpidi ’levied of barbers, carpenters, metal dealers and dyers
11.4.4 The Pandyan Coins
One of the early coins of the Pandyans showing their emblem of the two fishes.
A good number of Pandyan coins have been discovered and are found mentioned in

inscriptions. .A few gold coins throw light on the pandya rulers of this period.On these coins a
fish appears sometimes singly, sometimes in pair, along with symbols like a bow, a conch, a
discuss etc. The copper coins of the pandyas besides having a fish emblem also have the
chola standing figure or the chalukyam devices associated with fish. The intermingling of the
symbols of various dynasties on the pandya coins, perhaps indicate their conquests and defeats.
On a few of these coins the name Sundara Pandya, Sundra or merely the letter “Su” is found
and to whichof the sundara pandya they refer, is difficult to say .Some coins bear a boar with
legend “Vira-pandya’,read doubtfully on one side ,the figure of Venugopala on the other side.
.They are assumed to have been issued by the pandyas but cannot be attributed to any particular

king. Then there are some coins which show the title of the rulers’ .But only a few of them may
be attributed to any particular ruler with the help of the epigraphs. The coins bearing fish
symbols are known having tha tittle ‘Kondandarman’,Kanchivalangam Perumal,Buvanaka

207
Veeran, Nenmani kail Yugaraman, Sonadu Kondan (Sundara Pandya-1),Ellamthalaiyanan
(Jatavarman Sundara Pandya-1.)
Difficulties regarding genealogy are peculiar and special to pandya history. This is largely
because unlike inscriptions elsewhere, the pandya’s epigraphs do not openly or clearly help us
to formulate the order of successions. The astronomical data occasionally obtained are so
confused that as K.A Nilakanta Sastri says, “ignorance at least of astronomy is bliss”. This is
another difficulty which again is found mostly among the pandyas. The traditions of a number
of rulers simultaneously ruling in different parts of the country and many rulers bearing the
same names add to the difficulties already enumerated.
11.5 Social Life
The society under the Pandyas was based on the traditional fourfold division, namely the

Brahmins, Kshatryas, Vaisyas and sutras. There were other communities like Vellalar, Ayar
and Idaiyar etc. However the caste system was not rigid. Generally people were respected not
on the basis of the caste but on the basis of their profession. Despite caste divisions and
political chaos during the Pandyan rule there was a sense of unity among the people. We
come to know that the village assemblies carried on many public activities smoothly.
11.5.1 Brahmins
Brahmins were given first preference in the society. They were highly educated and led a
simple life. They were respected for scholarship and character. The pandya king gave donation
and gifts to them and charity lands for their settlements. They accommodated them in comfortable
and separate quarters, settled them exclusively. Brahmin village called Brahmadeyas later it

was known as chathurvedi mahgalams, etc., and kings endowed tax –free lands for their benefit.
During the time of sundara pandya -1(1261-A.D )many villages were put together and called
“Sundara pandya chathurvedi Mangalam “after the name of the king 200 vlis bof lands were
given to the 121 vedic Brahmins of the village.Besides this,there were physicians, village
accountant, carpenter, blacksmith, potter, barner, vettiyan(village servant), washerman, who
were patronized by the state with service tenure lands.

208
The Brahmins served as priests in the temples, spread vedic knowledge and performed
the vedic rites or yajnas. Apart from these traditional and tribal religious functions they were
employed in the king’s court as Magistrates and ministers. They earned the titles called
“Brahmarayan Enade and Veeramangala Perarayan”. But in the reign period of Jatavarman-
Sundara Pandya we come across the doings of some Brahmins whose profession seems to
have been highway robbery; but they were severely punished.
11.5.2 Communities other than Brahmins
Most of them were distinguished from each other by the profession what they pursued.
Agriculture was the main profession of the people. Next to agriculture Trade and industry
accounted for the second place in the society. The Pariah, beat the Parai, a drum, the Minavan

was the fisherman, the Umarar traded in salt and so forth the peasants were the largest rural
community. Vaisyas were traders. The artisans like the goldsmith, the cobbler, the blacksmith,
the weaver, were all classified as communities. When a new art or craft was developed a new
community also came up. Thus the number of communities tended to grow and some of them
split into sub-communities In the middle ages we hear of two communities, the ‘Idangai and
Valagai’.Their origins are unknown. It is possible that they were particular martial communities.
These communities however continued even long after their functions had ceases. We hear of
the Idangai and Valagai in the records of the early19th century also
Next to the Brahmins, the community of cultivators were most important. They were
known as “Vellalars”-men of high esteem considered to be the backbone of the State; they

took part in the administration of the state as ministers and commanders of the army. The
Vellalars, as landlords, quite rich, extended charities to the temples .But the poor gentry of the
same group worked in the fields as labourers or tenants.
We see the other and most important section of society was merchants and their
occupation was trade. These-merchants made Pandya country extremely rich through their
inland and foreign trade. Substantial qualities of pearls was Traded by them. They also submitted
precious stones, rubies, sapphires, emeralds, to the King and thus in the words of Marco Polo,
“what this king wears between gold and gems and pearls is worth more than a city’s ransom”.
Marco Polo’s view was also supported by the historian Wasaf also.

209
Thus without this merchant class, the prosperity of the state was impossible. These
merchants were called “Vaishyas”, but in Pandya country they were also known as “Nagarattar
and Chettis”. They were extremely rich, also did social services, and earned name and fame
among the subjects. Pillayarpatti inscription of 13th century, speaks about tjese merchants.
These Nagarattar were also members of “Thisai Iyarirathu Innurruvar”. They protected the
temples, and managed the temple festivals. A record of the late13th century narrates dispute
between the Chettis and Oil-Mongers (Vaniya-Nagarattar) of Aragalur (Salem district) with
regard to the management of temple festivals, and apparently the Chetti’s succeeded in the
end.
These communities formed merchants guilds for easy and swift trade (we have already

mentioned in economic condition, the various guilds that were formed under them) they stayed
in cities and towns and the streets, where they lived were called after their names “Nanadesi
perun theru, Innurruvar peru theru”.etc. We also have many epigraphical’s evidences for their
temple patronage. Apart from the communities mentioned above we have fisherman or
“paradavas” community which lived along the sea coast of Pandya kingdom. They alos looked
after the pearl fisheries of kaayal.
11.5.3 Women
In the Pandyan kingdom, women were generally treated on par with men. They took part
in public functions along with man. They were allowed to possess property. The women from
royal families got more opportunity to educate themselves. The famous Vaishnavite Alwar
Andal had lived in the Pandyan territory and attained glory during this period. Generally the

married women had concentrated more on the up-keep of their house and their children. They
also followed vocations like spinning, pot making, painting,etc. and raised their family income.
They had also extended help to men folk in agricultural activities. Women spent their leisure in
playing in-door games like dice, chess, etc.
Dress and Ornaments
The people wore clothes made of silk and cotton. The rich were fond of silk garments.
Ordinary people wore cotton clothes. The rich people were also fond of decorating themselves

210
with various jewels and ornaments. The kings and nobles wore costly ornaments studded with
pearls, corals and precious stones.
11.5.4 Slavery
Slavery was not unknown though it was perhaps not very harsh. People often sold
themselves into slavery to clear debts. They commuted their debts into slave labour. There
was no slave market. Some of the rich people donated slaves to the temples for service.
11.5.5 Devadasis
In Pandya country, the institution of Devadasis literally mean “Servants of the Lord” and
they were dedicated their services to the temple. They were experts in dance and music. Some
of them were belonged to aristocratic families, but out of love to Lord, they surrendered
themselves to Lord. But some of them were sold to temples. They were honoured by the
society: the kings also patronized them. Besides their services in temples, they became

exponents of dance and music. Temple trustees had given them charities, besides the rulers.
There were men slaves in the temples. They were sold themselves and some of them
were sold by their masters to service in the temples.
