11.6 Education and learning
The village school assembling under the shade of a tree or in the verandahs of temples
and mathas was a common institution, and its teachers were among the staff of the employees
remunerated from the common land held by the village. Stone masons and copper smiths
were to be found everywhere to engrave inscriptions on stone and copper, and the work done
often with remarkable accuracy and art. The maintenance of the complex records of the

211
Government, local and central and the employment for this purpose of considerable staff of
officers and clerks might have stimulated them as now to resort to scholastic education as an
avenue to public employment.
Popular education in a wide sense was amply provided for by the recitation and exposition
in temples and other public places of the national epics like Ramayana and Mahabharatha and
the Puranas. Higher education was generally pursued in schools and colleges attached to
mathas and temples. The mathas, the palli and vihara were centres of learning which often
owned libraries and transmitted on a variety of topics which increased in volume and diversity
from generation to generation. The colleges were called “Ghaikai Vidya Sthanam or Salai”we have many references to Pandya country colleges. We have records for “Sri Vallabha

Perunsalai of Kanyakumari”, “Parthiba Sekara Puram Salai”. State patronized Ghatikas by
giving lands known as “Salabhoga”.
The purposes of education consisted of
(a) The Brahmin who did their Vedic studies, perhaps other studies as well.
(b) The students who equipped themselves exclusively in Tamil studies and the allied
subjects
(c) The mechanics and the craftsman learnt their trade hereditary at home.
(d) The merchants concentrated on arithmetic and book-keeping and calculation of interest
rates. Apart from these there was a vast multitude which had no need for any kind of
education-formal or informal.
Public discourses on religion and morals and musical recounting for mythological stories
for the benefit of the common men provided a popular course of education which was collected
through the ear by the illiterate. The rules were very strict in colleges for the maintenance of

discipline.
11.6.1 Services of Mutts
During the 13th century the mutts increased in number due to the patronage from the
rulers and scholars. Mutts’ service did education next to temples. At “Thiruppathur” many

212
Saiva Siddhantha scholars lived. There were Saiva mutts at in Sermadevi, Tirunelvel, Aruviyur
and courtalem. The Vaishnavas also maintained mutts at Alagarkovil, Thirukkurungudu and
Vanama-malai. They taught here Vedas, Ithihas, Puranas and “Nalayira Divya Prabhandam”.
Grammar and composition were taught both in Tamil and Sanskrit.
There were libraries attached with temples and mutts, were known as “Saraswathi
Bhandaram”. There was one library at Chidambaram which was started by one “Sami Thevar”
and maintained by “Pallavaarayar” an important officer of that period. Here they collected
manuscripts and copied them to preservefor future, again an inscription from Sermadevi,
mentions about a grant of lands to a library “Saraswathi Bhandaram” in a temple in the locality
and records containing endowments for the recitation and study of the vedas and Puranas in

temples are frequently met with. Thus we see that the mutts and temples encouraged enriching
education and religion in the Pandya country.
11.6.2 Temple, the Important Social Institution
From inscriptional evidence we come to know that the temple played a vital role in the
villages. We have seen enough to realize that the most fruitful sources of our knowledge of the
history of the country are stone inscriptions preserved in temples and copper plate grants. Of
these the stone records in temples are more numerous and varied in their interest. In addition
to throwing light on matters like land-tenure and revenue administration those records enable
us to reconstruct with some confidence the part of the temple in the general social economy of
the time. It is clear that in the middle ages, in South India, the temple was much more than a

place of common worship. Sir Charles Eliot says, “Temple Worship is not so important for the
Hindus and Church service for the Christians. They set more store on home ceremonies and
on contemplation”. And yet, every village had its temple, and in every temple was the object of
universal attention at the hands of the princes and the people of the land. The temple is
historically more important as a “social and economic” entity than as a religious institution. The
history of Hinduism, even in South India, is much more than the history of her temples. But the
story of the social life of the country, of the common people, centers round the temple in a
manner that is perhaps equaled only in Medieval Europe, although with this vital difference that
in South India the Villagers held the temple, while in Europe the Church of the Monastery held
the village.

213
The temple was the centre of universe culture. The best architecture and sculpture as
such painting, as there was, were lavished on it. Fine arts like music, dancing and jewelmaking flourished in the temples and primarily on their account. Several temples contained
libraries and were centers of religious and secular learning. The drama, closely allied, to the
dance, was promoted by some temples; Above all, the temple was for the village, the most
powerful economic support.
A few facts, gleaned from a mass of similar data, anyhow be set down to confirm these
statements about the temple and its part in the life of Medieval South India, An inscription of
about A.D 1260 from Madambakkam (Chingleput) dated in the 10th year of Jatavarman Sundara
Pandyas, states that the assembly of the village seeing that it was not possible to maintain the

lamps, offering and festivals in the temple from the income available for that purpose, assigned
the North division. “Vadakuru” with its wet land, garden lands; houses and house sites to the
temples, but retained there in 3000 kuli o land with houses, and housesites for their own use.
They also decided to pay the dues on them such as “Ponvari” and “Nattuvari” from their own
pockets and agreed that “If ever owing to unfortunate circumstances, we are induced to sell
this land; we shall do so, for the price at which it then sells, to the sacred treasury of the
temple”.
An inscription from “Kamarasavalli” (Trichy) of the 10th year of Jatavarman Vira Pandya.,
gives an idea of the manner in which funds were raised by the inhabitants of the “Valanadu” for
affecting certain repair to the temple. They agreed to pay to the temple, a small cess on all

merchandise sold by the :e.g.1/2 panam on each bundle of clothes for women, on each “podi”
of pepper, and one kasu on each “podi” of paddy. Maravarman Kulasekhara Pandyan records
mentions about the local resident’s provided provision of the lamps in the temple
Another record from “Mannar kovil” in the 19th year of Kulasekhara deva mentions about
the acuisition by the king’s order (Niyiga) of private houses for a second prakara to the temple
being built according to “Sastra”.
The villages of Vayaiur (Chengalput) came to an agreement in the 8th year of Jatavarman
Sundara Pandya (1258 A.D.) by which they released all the lands which belonged to four
temples which were probably all situated in Vayalur, and relinquished their previous hold on

214
them , whether that was by mortgage or by purchase. The king Kulasekhara made certain
temple lands rent-free on receipt of a specified sum for the expenses of the journey. An
inscription from Sermadevi mentions a great of a land to a library “Saraswathi Bhandara in a
temple in the locality, and record containing endowments for the recitation study of the Vedas
and Puranas in the temples. A record from Pattamadai (near Sermadevi) is of more than
ordinary intersecting as it registers a grant to a dancing girls for enacting a drama, on certain
festival days.
We see that the temples are furnished numerous occasions for disputes on various
matters. A record in the 16th year of Maravaraman Sundara pandya state that the authorities of
temple of Devanayaka Permal in Tiruvendipuram decided to follow the system of worship

practiced in all other temples. But we have no means of knowing the nature of the innovation
the necessitated this, rather conservative affirmation regarding the manner of worship.
A record of the late 13th century, narrates a dispute between the chetties and oil-mongers
“Vaniyanagarattar” of Aragalur (Salem District) with regard to the management of temple festivals
and apparently the Chetties Succeeded in the end. There were also disputes as to the order of
procedure in which the scared ashes in Siva temples and the prasadams in the Vishnu temples
were to be received or the rope of the God’s car “The Ratha” had to be held in drawing it such
other matters. A Case of dispute between two Bhattars as to the right of conducting worship in
the temples which was settled by the intercession of the village assembly has been mentioned.
11.7 Marco Polo’s Accounts

Marco Polo was the prince among the medieval travelles. He presents a spot study of the
Pandyan society.
According to Marco Polo new araharas were created in the Pandya kingdom. During the
rule of Maravarman Kulasekhara Pandya many agraharas were established and 18 Brahmins
were invited to occupy the place. It was renamed as Chaturvedimangalm.According to Marco
Polo Vellalas was called Bhumiputtirar and Nattumakkal. The vaisyas were called as Chettiars
or Nagarattar.

215
Marco Polo has something to say about the common people of the country. The manner
of dress seems to have amazed him. He said roundly that there were no tailors at all in the
country, nor was there any need for them. “Seeing that everybody goes naked only the decency
to wear a scrap of cloth; that the king goes as bare as the rest” The life of common people was
very strange to polo, they worshipped as sacred animal and people, “would not eat beef anything
in the world”.
He also mentions the custom ‘sati’ as a common practice and the practice of allowing a
condemned criminal who was sentenced to death to sacrifice himself to some God or other of
his choice.
The following observations of Marco polo deserve quotation:
“Let me tell you the people of this country have a custom of rubbing their houses all over

with cow-dug, moreover, all of them great and small, king and baron included to sit upon the
ground only… The people of the country go to battle all naked with only a lance and a shield;
and they are most wrecked soldiers…. They will kill neither beast nor bird, nor anything that
hath life. In their practice that every male and female do wash the whole body twice a day.
In eating get use the right hand only and no account touch their food with the left hand. ... And
whenthey drink they do not put the vessel to the lips, but hold it aloft and let the drink spout into
the mouth. So also they drink only from drinking vessel and every man has his own.
A reference to Devadasis is also by Marco Polo. “Certain abbeys in which are god and
Goddesses to whom many young girls are consecrated”-the nature of the institution of the

temple girls, seems, however, tohave been hardly understood by the traveler.
Marco Polo refers to the use of the betel leaves, “All the people of the city Kayal have a
custom of perpetually keeping in the mouth a certain leaf called, “Tambul”. The Lords and
gentle folks and the king have these leaves prepared with camphor and other aromatic spices
also mix with quicklime. And this practice was said to be very good for the health”
Marco Polo concludes! “The men of this country have their beds made of very light can
work, so arranged that, when they have got in and are going to sleep. They are drawn up by

216
cords nearly to the ceiling and fixed there for the night. Not that everybody does this, but only
the nobles and greatfolks, for the other sleep on the streets
Marco Polo has given a cear picture about the trade that was going on during the Pandya
period.
There are certain defects in his account. But for such isolated defects (people went
naked. There were no tailors) Marco Polo is an authority on medieval social history.

Through Marco polo’s account we come to know about the social life of the people of the
Pandyan country during the 13th century. To conclude we can say that the people in the Pandya
kingdom lived in a prosperous manner. Through the temple’s services people were educated

12.1 Introduction
The Pandya kings generally followed religious tolerance. They had made liberal donations
and gifts to the Jain monks and to their educational institutions The Pandya rulers patronized
Tamil scholars. They gave importance for the development of Art and architecture.
12.2 Religion under the Pandyas
ThePallavas and Pandyas cherished and nourished the Hindu religion during the 6th
century A.D. It was continued by the later Pandyas in an exemplary manner. The pandyas
patronized Saivism, Vaishnavism and Jainism. The Nayanmars had preached Saivism while

the Alwars preached Vaishnavism .They had spread the spirit of Bhakti among the people.
The spread of Bhakti cult inculcated religious feelings and service mildness’ among the people.
These qualities had taken deep roots in the Tamil society.
12.2.1. Saivism
The Saivaite saints namely Thirugnana Sambander and Manickavasagar had lived in the
Pandya country and propagated Saivism. Ninrasir Nedumaran was a Jain at first. He patronizes
Jainism. His wife Mangaiyarrkkarasi and his minister Kulachirai were staunch saivites. Both
invited Thirugnana Sambander to Pandianadu. It was at the request of Mangaiyarrkkarasi that
Thirugnana Sambander went to Madurai and tried to convert the king to Saivism. There was a
terrible debate between Thirugnana Sambander and the Jains. His songs firmly withstood
against water and fire i.e. he got glorious victory both in Punavatham and Analvatham were
completely burnt and were taken away by the river water. Thus they were completely defeated.

220
Nearly 800 Jains were impaled. Later on the Pandyan ruler became an ordent Saivite. He took
keen interest in patronising Saivism with great vigour and rigour.
Manickavasagar was a great mystic, author of Tiruvasakam. He lived during the reign of
Varaguna II. Later on he became his minister. He lived his entire life for Saivism. He composed
his songs in praise of Lord Shiva. Besides Tiruvasakam, he also composed Tirukkovaiyar.
Kun Pandya is said to have persecuted thousands of Jains.
Kings and Queens Contribution to Saivism
Many Siva temples were constructed by the Pandya rulers. For the purpose of renovation
and maintenance Pandya rulers provided endowments. Varaguna II gave 1400 gold coins to
Subramanya Swamy temple at Tiruchendur. The coins were utilized for daily pujas. He also
gave 290 gold coins to the temple at Ambasamudram.

Sadayavarman Sundara Pandyan provided gold plates foe Chidambara Nataraja temple.
The western tower of the temple was constructed by him. The eastern tower of Meenakshi
Amman temple at Madurai was also constructed by him.
Kulasekhara Pandyan erected the sanctum sanctorum, Arthamandapam, Manimandapam
and Sannadhi Gopuram during his reign.
In addition to this, the Pandya Queens did a lot for the promotion of Saivism and Siva
temples. The queen of VikramaPandya constructed Ulagamudayal Sannadhi at Tiruvannamalai.
The queen of Veera Pandya gave gold ornaments and other valuable gifts libeally to the
Siva temple of Tiruvorriyur.
12.2.2 Vaishnavism
During the Pandya period Vaishnavism was greatly revived like Saivism in the country.
Alwars were highly responsible for such rejuvenation of Vaishnavism. Among the Alwars
Madurakavi, Nammalvar, Periyalvar and Andal belonged to Pandya kingdom.

221
The contest against the heretical sects is carried on the Vaishnava Alvars as much as by
Saiva Nayanmars. But the history of the Alvars is even more obscure than that of the Nayanmars
and it is not possible to say much of any of them with confidence. We have the intention to fix
the age of ‘Madurakavi’ and his Guru ‘Nammalvar’ by identifying Madurakavi Alvar, with the
minister ‘Marangari’ who is also called ‘Madurakavi’ in the Anamalai inscription. Nammalvar
was born of a Vellala family at Alwartirunagar (earlier called Kurugur) in Tirunelveli district. His
personal name was Maran and he seems to have gained the name ‘Sadagopa’ on the occasion
of his initiation. He renounced the world in his thirty fifth year to practice Yoga. His hymns are
rightly regarded as embodying the deepest religious experience and philosophic thought of
one of greatest seers of the world.

The same suggestion as in the case of nammalvar, has been made that another Vaishnava
saint Periyalvar, who live about the close of eighth century and the beginning of ninth century
was the contemporary of ‘Jatila Parantaka-I’, most probably. Periyalvar does refer to a Pandya
king ‘Nedumaran’ in the lines. All that we can refer is that if this Nedumaran is the same as the
contemporary of Gnanasambandar; this Alvar may also be assigned to their age and likewise
his daughter Sri Andal. It seems more likely however, that the reference is to ‘Sri Mara Srivallabha’
(815-2). But this reference can only be tentative and in any case there is no reason to assign
periyalvar to the items of Jatila Parantaka-I. But the reference in Periyalvar to the Pandyas and
the instance we have already noticed of the creation of two temples to Vishnu in the time of

‘Paranataka Nedunjadyan’, furnish sufficient evidence of the influence of Vaishnavism in the
Pandya country in this period.
The only woman Alvar, Andal or Kodhai, was the real or adopted daughter of Periyalvar.
In her intense devotion to Vishnu she dreamt of her marriage with that god and described her
experience in her hymns. To about the same period belonged Tiruppanalvar, a minstrel of low
caste, who was not permitted to enter the temple of srirangam and tondaradippodialvar, a
Brahmin from Thanjavur district whose real name was vipranarayana; and whose intolerance
of Buddhism and Jainism was nearly as great as that of Tirumangai Alvar. Kulasekhara, the
ruler of Kerala, was the next Alwar who among other shrines of Vishnu, sang of those at
Chidambaram and Tiruvali; and lastly came the celebrated Nammalavar and his pupil Madurakavi

Alvar, as we have mentioned above. All these Alvars were belonging to Pandya country and
enriched the shrines of south by their devotional hymns.

222
The Pandya country had 17 Tiruppathikal or ‘Alvar Mangala Sasana Sthalas’. They were
also called ‘Divya Desams. Among them ‘Nava Tirupathigal’ or the nine most important were
‘Alvartirunagar, Srivaikunam, Vanamamalai, Tirukkoilur, Alagarkoil, Srivilliputhur, Tirukotiyur,
Darbasayanam and tirukkurungudi’.
12.2.3 Hymns by the alvars
The Alvars have praised the Gods presiding over the various shrines. But all these have
taken up in their works only the temple of Ranganathar at Srirangam and no other places out
of the ‘Nurrettu tiruppathigai’ i.e., 108 the holy Vaishnava shrines have been praised by all.
This accounts for the special importance and sacredness of the shrine at this place. The praise
of those Alvars about the various shrines are contained in the Tamil work ‘Nalayira Divya
Prabandam’.
In the middle of the 12th century, Nathamuni gave a definite shape to the ‘Vaishnava

canon. ‘Nalayir Divya Prabhandam’ and his grandson Alavandar also called “Yamunacharya’,
was the great acharya of that period. The greatest of the Vaishnava achariyas was undoubtedly
Ramanuja.
The thirteenth and fourteenth centuries witnessed the rise of a schism among the
followers of Ramanuja; due to a difference in their interpretation of Prapatti (surrender). So
there established two schools as a result of schism called ‘Vadagalai and Tengalai’. Tengalai
School looks upon Pillai Lokachariya (1213) as its founder. The next great teacher and writer in
Tengalai school was Manavala Manunigai (1370). The leader of the Northern School or
Vedagalai was Vedanta Desika (1268), the poet philosopher and man of affairs
12.2.4 Jainism
By the side of Saivism and vaishnavism and the other forms taken by Hinduism to which

attention has been drawn, Jainism had a fair following and enjoyed the patronage of the princes,
and people though not to the same extent as the orthodox creeds. The ;land of the Jaina Pallis
(pallichandham) was a recognized category of tax free land known to the revenue accounts of
that time. Tamil literature was greatly enriched by the writings of the Jaina authors.

223
The Central feature of the development that followed in the succeeding centuries was
the determined efforts made by the exponents of Brahmanism in its various forms to suppressed
the heretical sects of Buddhism and Jainism an effort which was apparently marked by greater
success against the Buddhism than against the Jains. In Hiue Tsang’s account mentions
about the decade of Buddhism in the south and the envies the prosperity of the Jains.
Hence we can trace the survival of Jainism even at a later age. The Jaina teacher referred
in the work ‘Jivaka-Chivadamani’ about the Jains conditions in the eight century another
inscription in the same period records a grant of land to the Jaina temple. Rajasimha II the last
pandia ruler of this age his said to her endored among others, several Jaina temples. A record

from mangadu of Jadavarma sundarapandia (1251 A.D) contains a gift of land Pallichandham
a jain temple to certain Jain temple. From the above facts we come to know that Jainism was
able to survive unlike Buddhism inspite of the raise of Saivism and vaishnavism
12.2.5. Buddhism
In the epigraphical sources we are not able to find reference like Jainism about Buddhism.
Buddhist writers also contributed for the development of the Tamil literature though not to the
same extent as the Jains. Tiruccopuram (South Arcot) records of Jadavarma Sundarapandia
mentions about a certain ‘sariputra pandita’ figures as a donor and there is a reference about
‘Sangathar” most probably members of Buddhist Snagha. With the inference of epigraphy
and literature we come to know that Jainism as lost his importance than Jainism in the 12th and
13th Centurries
12.3. The Role of the Temples

The Temple has been described as a social institution besides being a religious one. The
role played by the temples in general life of the people every village has been discussed in the
pandian inscriptions. Temple becomes a center for social activities in the village schools were
established and religious discourse were conducted. In its multi-pillared mandapas kings were
crowned the temple was a banker. It owned property but it was exempted from the taxes. It
employed a large bureaucracy of servants highly officialised in the case of temples like
Srirangam. A center of economic activities involved In stone masonry, carpentry jewellery ,

224
gold smith and so on iron making i.e., sculpture in stone and metal, garland making special
textiles and other ancillary industrial activities center around the temple providing employment
to variety of people in the village. Every segment of society officials warriors priest merchants
and peasants were all involved with the temple activities endowments were made for the temple
by both pious people and current and prospective sinners
The religious endowments of the kings and the epigraph of the temples:
The elaborate arrangements made for the management of the affairs of the temple and
endowments were carefully recorded in the inscriptions on its walls
The epigraphs of the age furnish numerous instances to private benefactions to temples
for the burning of lamps, the maintenance of gardens, etc., and one of these records from

Tirupputtur mentions the gift of ten dinars (kasu) by a Brahmin lady for the burning of a lamp.
As inscription from Tiruchendur tells, as the king Varaguna Maharaja distributed among
16 villages, a large endowment he made to the local temple for meeting the cost of service in
the temple; throughout the 12 months of the year. The total endowment consisted of 1,400
gold kasus and these kasus were to be a permanent endowment, only the interest being spent
fo9r the purpose specified. Again a sum of 290 gold kasus was in the 16th year of same king,
placed in the hands of the assembly of ‘Ambasamudram’ be utilized likewise as a permanent
endowment. The 580 kalams of paddy per anum, to be given by the assembly were to be
devoted to meet the cost of offerings ‘ TiruAmudu’ to be made for four times a day in the temple

of Tiruppottudaiya Bhatarar at IIIangokkudi according to a detailed scheduled of offerings given
in the inscription.
There are few inscriptions, Which provide for the distribution of the food offered to the
daily among Sri Vaishnavas reciting ‘Tirupadiyam’ during worship, and create the endowment
of land for the maintenance for three persons who were to recite ‘Tiruvoymoli’regularly in the
temple.
Jatavarman Parantaka Pandya dedicated to the Goddess Kumari and called the
A’Tennavar Tham Kula Deivam’,a whole Nadu as an endowment for the distribution of liberal
gifts to all who attended the ‘Taipusam’ festival on the day succeeding it.

225
A Suchindrum inscription of ‘Maravarman Srivallabha’, dated in his 10th year, refers to
‘Andapillai Bhatte Ariaprayaji’ at whose instance the king made a great of land to Suchindrum
temple.
The minister of Maravarman Sundara Pandya, namely,’Solan Uyya-ninraduvan’, built
the garbhagraha, the ardha mantapa and mahamantapa of Perumal temple at ‘Tiruttangal’ and
conducted ‘Sundara Pandya Sandhi’ in the tenmple, in honour of Maravrma Sundara Pandtan
(1216). He also constructed a stone temple for Tangal Isar and his consort Gowri.
Besides a long Sanskrit stone inscription in the Srirangam temple, there are several
stanzas in Sanskrit, celebrating the king, Jatavarma Simdara Pandya’s (1251 A.D.) martial
prowness and political power and recording his splendid gifts to various temples in Tirunelveli,
Chidambaram, Tirupputkuli, Kanchipuram and other places.

12.3.1 Epigraphical Importance of Srirangam Temple
The kings of this dynasty mentioned in the Srirangam inscriptions are ‘Maravarman
Sundara Pandya-I’ and ‘Jatavarman Sundara Pandya-‘. The former is the contemporary of the
Hoysala narasimha-II. His accession has been fixed as 1216 A.D. from his Srirangam record
which dated in his ninth year.
Jatavarman alias Sundara Pandya-I was the other king mentioned in the inscription. His
date of accession has been fixed as 1250a.ad.from his Jambukeswaram inscription. His
Srirangam inscription is two in numbers; the first one describes in Sanskrit verses a large
number of gifts he made to the temple.
The other inscription of this king also celebrates his victories over the Cholas, Keralas
and Hoysalas from whom he carried a large booty and from which he performed the Tulabhara
ceremony and presented the gold to the temple.

Sundara Pandya also gave Tulabhara Dana to Chidambaram temple and offered golden
roof to the temple. The western tower of Chidambaram was constructed by him. He also gave
three villages as endowments to Tiruvaanaikkal temple on his birth day ‘Chitirai Tingal’. At
Madurai, he constructed the eastern tower of Meenakshi Amman temple.

226
Maravarman Kulasekhara (1168-1347) constructed the Swami Sannadhi, the Mandapam,
Mani Mandapam and Sannidhi Gopuram of Meenakshi temple. It seems that Maravarman
Sundara Pandya (1216-1238) has also been constructed the Amman Koil Mandapam and
Tirumadil. Parakrama Pandya (1315-1347) constructed the western power of this great temple
of Meenakshi. Vikrama Pandya’s wife (1283) gave endowments to Tiruvannamalai temple;
and “Ulaga Mulududaiyal Sannadhi” was arranged on her name; In North Arcot Tiruvattiyar
temple; she offered precious stones to Lord Nataraja of Chidambaram.
(1) The Mathas and Ascetisim
Besides temples, there were mathas representing different sects of Hinduism which were
also recepients of several gifts from the king and the people of the country, some of which have
been incidentally touched upon.
(2) Saiva Mathas

Some inscription refers to the important Saiva mathas of the Pandyan country in the
thirteenth country, which were patronised by Maravarman Sundara Pandya-II
(3)Viashnava Mathas
The two important mathas were vanamamalai,Tirunalveli District and ahobila matha.
Ahobila matha had its branches throughout pandya country.from inscriptions we came to known
the following mathas namely.
1. Thiruvadudaiyar Matha, Alagarkoil. 2. Kulasekhara matham, Alagarkoil. 3. Tirumangai
matha, Tirukkurungudi and4. Arulalathan Matha, Alwar Tirunagar.
An inscription of maravarman sundara pandya of thirteenth century, says that the arulathan
matha of alvar tirunagar was established by Tirukkurungudi Mamunigal.

12.4 Literature under pandyas
Post-Sangam or pandya –pallava period
After giving the oldest body of works now known in tamil language the literature of sangam
age , the next great epoch in the annals of Tamil literature extends over a period of there and
a half centuries (500-850). This period is known for Tamil literature as Pandya –pallava age,
under which it grew rapidly.
In this age ,the inflow of northen Sanskrit influence became even more and marked than
before, numerous words and concepts in the domain of ethics, religion and philosophy were
freely borrowed band incorporated nin tamil.There was a preponderance of jaina writers to
start with Jainism and Buddhism were then waxing strong. But the rising tide of Hindu reaction
soon produced a great volume of popular devotional literature, which was set to music and

ravished the hearts of common folk. Notable developments occurred in Grammar and
lexicography, but here the jains and Buddhists continued to hold the palm. Almost all writing
was in verse, and there was little prose worth mentioning.
Most of the important didactical works composed in the period have been grouped together
under the title. The Eighteen Kilkan-Nakku; (from about the thirteen century, because of their
being composed in various short meters, generally types of the venba). Certainly the best
known of them all, possibly also among earliest is the kural of Tiruvalluvaar, acomprehensive
manuval of ethics, polity and love.K.A. Nilkanta Sastri, suggests the early centuries of Christian
era; 450-550 A.D. May be the best date for the kural .To the same period must assigned the
‘kalavali’ of Poygaiyar ,and the ‘Mudumolikkanji’a short work of 100 stanzas on mutability by

kudlurkilar of Madurai.
The age of the remaining works in the collection may be given tentatively and with in
broad limits ,as follows ,between 550and 650 A.D ‘ Karnapadu’Inno-Narpadu, Aindinai-Aimbadu;
Naladi, Nanmanikkadigai and Palamoli; between 650 and 750 A.D. ‘Tirukadugam’ Aindinai
Yelubathu, Tinaimalai Aimbadu, Kainnilai, Eladhi, Tinaimalai-Nurraimbadu, Sirupanchamulam,
Iniyavainarpadu and Asarakkovai.

228
The Kanarpadu is a love poem; as well as Kainilai are also on the theme of love and love
belonged to the class of Aham works. Naladi is a Jaina anthology (400) put together by
Padumanar, and arranged in forty chapters; the names of the poets whose songs are collected
are unknown but the reference to Muttairyar in two of the stanzas give the clue to the date of
the collection. Nanmanikkadigai (100 stanzas) by a Vaishanva poet, Vilambi Naganar and
Palamoli is a Jaina work of 400 venbas, each citing a proverb and mention some incident or
story to illustrate it. The author of Thikadugam was a worshipper of Vishnu, the other works
were by Jains. The Asarakkovai is a veritable Tamil Smrithi by a Saiva author based avowedly
on Sanskrit originals.
12.4.1. Bhakti Literature
The wide spread Hindu religion revival for which many Savia Nayanmars and Vaishanava

Alvar worked together, furnished a powerful stimulus to the growth of a popular devotional
literature. Basides the work of Nayanmars, the ‘Tirumandiram of Trimular ‘ is a manual of Saiva
mysticism im 3,000 verses.
Among the Saiva saint of this period, who earned themselves an abiding place in the
literature and herats of the Tamils was “Manikkavasagar” who’s ‘Thirvasagam’ forms the eighth
book of the Saiva Canon. He was the Minister of Varaguna Pandya-II and renounced the world
and become a saint. The transparent sincerity of the passionate outpouring of the saint in the
‘Tirunasagam’ makes a deep, impassion on the reader’s mind. The ‘Tirukkovai’ is among the
earlist of the full-fledge ‘Kovais’ which treat of love in a schematic poem of 400 stanzas, each
depicting a particular situation. His other work ‘Tirvempavai’ is also noted of merit.

‘Manikavasagar’ poem has a double meaning throughout, the main theme being the love of the
soul of God. The ‘Karikovai’ of ‘Kari Nayanmar’ and the Muttarajan –Kovai mentioned in the
commentary to be Yapparungalam(tenth century) may be earlier than Triukkovai and the
‘Pandikkovai’ also perhaps an earlier poem is available only in numerous citation. It mentions
several battles fought by the successors of Pandya kingdom (590-620). Side by Side with the
Saiva nyanmars, the Vaishnava Alvars also labored along the same lines for the revivals of
Hinduism and their devotional songs constitute in their final reduction the four thousand sacred
hymns,Nalariya Divya Prabandam’.

229
The celebrated ‘Periyalvar’ and his daughter Andal, belonged to Pandya country
contributed nearly 650 verses to the collection between them. Sri Andal claimed that the Lord
of Srirangam was her lover, and her poems are suffused by her passionate longing for
companionship with the Lord, her works ‘Tiruppavai’ (30 songs) and ‘Nachiyar Titmozhi’ (143
songs), with her father’s are placed first in the canon. The hyman of Andal which starts with the
words ‘Varana Mayiram’ telling of her dream-marriage with Vishnu is sung at all vaishnava
Brahmin marriage even today.
The notable work for periyalvar is ‘Periyalvar Tirumozhi’ and Tirupallandu”. The next
Tondarippotri Alvar has two hymns, ‘Tirumalai’ and ‘tirupallieaucchi’. ‘Tirumangai Alvar, Tondaradi
Podi Alvar and kulasekara Alvar, were contemporaries. Kulasekara wasa author of devotional

poem in Sanskrit mukundhamala’ beside the 105 Tamil verses forming the ‘Perumal Tirumozhi’
in the Tamil canon of the ‘Vaishnavas’.
Nammalvar’s work is held in the highest respect as it is believed to embody the deepest
philosophical truths taught by the Upanishads. The 1,101 shanzas comprising the ‘Tiruvoymozhi’
hold the place of honor and have been most elaborately commented on by later exposition of
the vishistadyaitha system of philosophy. Madurakavi himself was an Alwar wrote one hymn in

12.4.2 Pandya Chola Period
The later period has Muttolayiram’, it must have been a work of 900 venbas, made up of
300 verses in praise of the three monarchs of the Tamil Country.
The impulse to produce devotional religious literature with was so active in the last periods,
500-850 A.D. continued with some fore far into his 850-1200 i.e., the work of poet-saints of

Pandya-Pallava period was continued in the age of Cholas by a succession a poets and

The Vaishnava religious literature during the thirteenth and the beginning of fourteenth
century was mostly compressed in Sanskrit. Nathamuni’s grandson ‘Alvanoar’ or Yamunacharya

and the great ramanuja himself wrote almost all their works in Sanskrit. Even the commentators
onTiruvoymozh, Nanjiyar, Nambillai, Periyavacchan and vadakku Tiruveedipillai all others of

‘Tiruvarangattu Amudanar’, the disciple of Ramanuja, wrote, ‘The Ramanujanurrandadhi’ in

12.4.3 Imperial Pandiya Period
The Philosophical literature of Saiva siddhanda had its beginning towards the end of this
period ‘Tiruvundiyar’ by Tirukkadavur Uyyavanda Devar and ‘Tirukkalirruppadiyar by

In the first half of the thirteenth century meikandar who formulated the tenets of saiva

12.4.4. Later Pandya Period
At the end of the fourteenth and beginning of fifteenth century ‘Svarupananda Desikar’
and his student ‘Thathuvarayar authors to anthologies on the philosophy of advaitha. The

The philosophical and religious literature of vaishnavism durig this period were in Sanskrit.
The commentaries adapted the ‘Manipravala style’

Vedantha Desika, an eminent wrier in Sanskrit was also the author of a number of tamil

Taruvoymozhi Pillai (1307 A.D.) wrote commentries on the hymns of Priyazhwar

Many of the later Pandyan monarchs and those of some other dynasties were gifted

12.5 Art and Architecture under the Pandyas
Aerial view of the Madurai Meenakshi Amman temple
The Pandyas contributed more for the development of architecture. Gopuras, Prakaras,
Vimanas and Garbagrahas are the salient features of the Pandya temple architecture. The
pandyas were great patrons of art and architecture. According to A.LBasham, “Architecture
reached its culmination under the Pandyas and marks the transition from the chola to the
exquisite and extravagant products of Vijayanagar”. Dr K.V. Raman says that “not only in the
quality of outpost but also in the intrinsic qualities of beauty and magnificience, the Pandyan
moments stand out as grand land marks recalling to our minds the long and arduous vicissitudes
through which the art tradition and art impulses of the Tamils passed from age to age and
reached the fame of glory during the middle of the 13th century”.

Madurai, Chidambaram. Kumbakonam, Tiruvannamalai, Srirangam temples are good
examples for the development of Pandya architecture. The images of horses and other animals
are carved on pillars. According to A.L.Basham, “the zeniths of Pandyan architecture are
Meenakshi templeat Madurai and Aranganathar temple at Srirangam.
12.5.1 Early Rock-cut Caves
The Pandyan period is marked as Renaissance period in the field of rock-cut temple.
The early structural monuments in the Pandya country are in sense lineal descendants of

233
“earlier rock-cut caves”. These caves are distributed throughout the Pandya countryand easily
to mind similar excavations of the Pallavas, notwithstanding a few varieties in detail. Possibly
the earliest of these caves is the one at “Pillayarpatti” containing an archaic inscription in what
appears to be Protovatteluttu More than 50 rockcut temples were excavated from the Pandyan
kingdom. More rock cut temples are found in Thirupparankundram, Anaimalai, Karaikudi,
Kalugumalai, Malaiyadikurichi and Trichy. These temples were constructed for Lord Shiva and
Vishnu.
The cave at Anaimalai contains a foundation inscription in early grantha and vatteluttu,
characters citing the kali year 3871 equivalent to 770 A.D .The inscription is that of Maran
Jadayan states that the rock-cut temple of Narashima was started by Marankari, a minister of

the king, but as he died before the completion hence the work was completed by his brother
Maran-Eyinan. who performed the consecration ceremony.
Another cave with an inscription of the lintel of the door way is the one at
Thirupparankundram, containing an epigraph mentioning the excavation of a temple for Siva
in the kali year 3874 corresponding to 773 A.D. Cave temples are also found at Kalugumalai
and Trichy. Unfortunately there is no definite clue to find out the precise date of the excellent
monolithic at Vettuvankoil in kalugumalai, which is a precursor to all the later temples in the
Pandya region: but its architectural style would suggest that it may be dated somewhere at the
beginning of the ninth century.
12.4.2 The Structural Temples
Structural temples were built on stones. They were simple in style. Each temple consists

of Garbhagraha, Arthamandapa and Mahamandapa. Such structural stone temples are found
in Kovilpatti, Thirupattur and Madurai. The Pandya kings constructed structural temples at
Ukkirankottai, Ambasamudhram, Thiruppattur, Mannarkudi, Madurai, Alagarkoil, Enaadi,
Srivilliputtur and Sinnamannur, Internal structure of these temples were constructed un a planned
manner.
Few famous structural temples of the Second pandyas were at the Vadapadrasayi temple
at Srivilliputthur, Siva temple at Ambasamudram, Vijayanarayana temple at Nanguneri and

234
Lakshmi Narayana temple at Athur. Pandya rulers built big gopurams at the temple entrance.
Pandya rulers renovated Alagar kovil and Jambukeswara temples.
12.5.3 The Pandya Style of Architecture
From the above mentioned temples we come to know about the superstructure of the
temples had both octagonal and square types of Sihara. . The octagonal Sikharas remind us
about some of the Pallava monolithic and structural temples. The Pandya monolithic are seen
at Kalugumalai. The square Sihara style belongs to the Pandyas.
From the paleography of the inscriptions found in the few Pandya temples we can say
that the earliest Pandya temple was at Tirukkurungudi. And the temple must be belonged to
the ruler Varaguna I. This temple has an octagonal Sikhara.
Ukkirankkottai temple is in Tirunelveli district.It has two shrines and both the shrines

have inscriptions of Sadayvarman. The main shrine of the first temple is a simple sanctum the
second has a vestibule ove which the superstructure of the sanctum extends
Sri Sowmya Narayana Perumal Temple – Tirukkoshtiyur is a village located near Tirupathur
on the way to Sivaganga. This place is very important to Vaishnavites because Sri Sowmya
Narayana Perumal temple is one of the 108 Divya desams, the holy shrines for them. It was
constructed by the Pandyas. This temple is surrounded by high walls on its four sides; with a
Rajagopuram at the entrance is a spectacular one.
Unlike the other temples the inner infrastructure is palnned in a such a manner i.e.
inside the temle cpmplex the shrine for Vishnu is constructed in 3 stages similar to that of three
floors in the building. These stages represent Boologam (earth), Thiruaprkadal and Vaikundam;

Narayana appears in three stages in three forms. On the ground floor Narayana appears as
Krishna in the dancing posture. In the next floor he is seen as Sayana thirukolam (Sayanareclinng, thirukolam- posture) a posture resting on Adisesha. And at the top level Narayana is
seen standing as Sri Sowmya Narayana Perumal. These forms of Narayana has been described
by Alwars as Nindran (means standing posture) Kidanthan (means sleeping posture) and
Aadinan (Means dancing posture). While the uppermost tala in this square, the first and the
second are rectangular. The sikhara is of the octagonal type.

235
12.5.4 Art and Architecture of the Pandyas
The pandyas of the imperial period added the gateway towers and reduced the central
tower over the sanctum to a mere vimana. The prakara lying between the outer towers and the
sanctum received greater attention. Outer Mandapas came in. The simplicity of the pallava
style developed into a matured beauty subject to detailed decorative atte4ntion and an
enlargement of the temple complex at the hands of the Pandyas.
The pillar also underwent a further evolution under the Pandyas the “idol”became more
pronounced with a scalloped edge, the corbal was moulded into a pendant or drop, and the
palagai increased in width. Some of the architectural pillars of the temple of Nellaiyappar temple
at Tiruneleli, when struck, produce a musical sound.
Sculpture:
Pandyan sculptures are beautiful and ornamental. Some sculptures are engaved on

single stone. Pandya period is considered as the renaissance period in the art of sculpture.
Sculptures od Somaskanda r, Durgai, Ganapathy, Narashima and Nataraja are very good
specimens. Sculptures at Kalugumalai, thiruparankundram and Narthamalai are very famous.
Paintings
The beauty of the Pandya mural painting can be seen in the Chittannavasal cave temples
constructed during the time of Srimara Srivallabha .Pandya, The ceilings and the pillars at
Chittannavasal bear the paintings ofdancing girls, the kings, the queens, plants and animals.
The picture of Lotus, bathing elephants and playing fishes were good at Chittannavasal. Oil
painting was also there. They are outstanding examples of Pandya paintings.

13.1 Introductin
The rule of Madurai Sultanate was one of mere wars and expeditions, victories and

defeats. Malik Kafur was the important military commander of Alauddin Khilji who invaded
Madurai and paved the way for the establishment of the Muslim rule in Tamil Nadu. Their rule

238
lasted roughly for half a century but they were able to leave a permanent impact in the history
of Tamil Nadu. The rule of Madurai Sultanate came to an end with the rise of Vijayanagara
rulers.
It was the enmity and dispute over the throne of Madurai Kingdom among the royal
family members that brought Malik Kafur to the Pandya kingdom. The Chronicles of Ibn Bhattutta
and Madhuravijayam of Gangadevi are the best available sources for the study of the Madurai
Sultanate apart from the coins issued by the Madurai Sultanate rulers themselves.
13.2 Causes for the Malik Kafur’s Invasion
The Pandiya king Maravarman Kulasekhara Pandyan had two sons namely Jatavarman
Sundara Pandyan and Jatavarman Veera Pandyan. The elder son, was by the king’s wife and
the younger, was by a mistress. The king announced Veera Pandyan as his successor contrary

to the tradition. As a result Sundara Pandyan killed his father and became the ruler in 1310.
With the help of the local chieftains Veera Pandiyan started the civil war. In that war Sundra
Pandya was defeated and he fled the country. Sundara Pandya sought the help from Delhi
sultan Ala-ud-din Khilji. The sultan agreed to his request and sent an army under the leadership
of his General Malik Kafur. With his help, Muslim army from the north entered Tamil Nadu in
1311. The army engaged in murder, rape and looting as it passed through Tamil Nadu. Thus
the result of the internal quarrel in the Pandyan royal family led to the first invasion of Tamil
Nadu from Delhi Sultan. The result of this invasion was devastating to Tamil Nadu.
Malik Kafur fought against Sundara Pandyan also. He fled to southern Tamil Nadu. His

main aim was to plunder the wealth of Tamil Nadu after achieving this he went back to Delhi.
Only for a brief period of few months his army stayed in Tamil Nadu. During this period he
gathered gold, precious stones, horses and elephants. It is said that he had taken over 90,000
sovereigns of Gold, and famed pearls, 612 Elephants and 23,000 horses.
Thus the first invasion of Tamil Nadu from Delhi was a direct result of the internal quarrel
in the Pandyan royal family. This was the very first time Tamil Nadu was plundered by a ruler
from Delhi. Even though Malik Kafur left Tamil Nadu with the looted wealth in 1311, the Tamil
nation laid devastated and demoralized. Tamil Nadu would never recover from it fully and

239
achieve its past glory. The lost sovereignty was yet to be recovered. Thus he set the stage for
the consequent arrival of the Madurai Sultanate.
13.3 Brief Rule of the Delhi Sultans
There were few more invasions after Malik Kafur left Tamil Nadu. Roughly from 1327 to
1335 and it was headed by Khusrav Khan and by Ulugh Khan. These invasions shattered the
Pandyan Empire beyond revival. While the previous invasion was content with plunder, Ulugh
Khan annexed the Pandyan dominions to the Delhi Sultanate. Thus Tamil Nadu became a part
of Sultan Mohammad bin Tughlug’s Empire of the Delhi sultanate. Then the commanders of
the Delhi Sultanate revolted against the sultan and established an independent rule under the
name of Madurai Sultanate. Thus the Delhi Sultan rule over Tamil Nadu ended within eight
years.
13.4 Origin of the Madurai Sultanate

In Tamil Nadu from Madurai they ruled as an independent kingdom for a short period and
they were known as Madurai Sultanate. In 1335 then viceroy of Madurai, Jalaluddin Ahsan
Khan announced his independence from the Delhi sultanate. Thus he founded the Madurai
Sultanate rule in Tamil Nadu. Jalaluddin Ahsan Khan and his descendants ruled Madurai till
1378. The last sultan, Ala-ud-Din Sikandhar Shah was defeated in a battle with the Vijayanagara
Empire led by Kumara Kampana. Thus the Madurai Sultanate ruled only for a short period of
43 years, with eight different rulers. This short lived Muslim dynasty at Madurai came into
existence following the decline of the Second Pandyan Empire.
13.4.1 Jalaluddin Ahsan Khan
Coin of Jalaluddin Ahsan Khan

240
Jalaluddin Ahsan Khan, the Tughlug Governor of Madurai declared his independence
and established the independent Sultanate of Madurai. Thus he was the first Sultan of the
Madurai Sultanate and father-in- law of the Historian Ibn Batutah. Immediately Delhi Sultan
Mohammad bin Tughlug sent an army to reassert his supremacy. But his army was defeated
by Jalaluddin Ahsan Khan. Tughlug took his revenge by killing Jalaluddin Ahsan Khan’s son
Ibrahim who was the purse-bearer of the Emperor. Jalaluddin Ahsan Khan was killed in 1340
by one of his nobles. Thus he ruled only for a brief period of five years.
13.4.2 Ala-ud-Din Udauji and Qutb-ud-Din Firuz
After Jalaluddin Ahsan Khan’s murder, Ala-ud-Din Udauji Shah came to power in 1340

A.D. In a battle he too was killed soon by the Hindu armies. He was succeeded by his son –inlaw Qutb-ud-Din Firuz Shah. After assuming power within 40 days he was also murdered by
Ghiyas-Ud-din Dhamagani. He took over as Sultan in 1340.
13.4.3 Ghiyas –Ud- Din Muhammed Damaghani
Ghiyas–ud-Din Muhammed Damaghani, was defeated by the Hoyosala king Veera Ballala
III in the beginning of the battle but later he was able to capture the Hoyosala ruler and murdered
him in 1343. He robbed him of his wealth, had him killed and in the walls of Madurai his stuffed
body was displayed .In 1334 Ghiyas –ud-Din Muhammed Damaghani died.
Ibn Battuta Chronicles
During Ghiyas–ud-Din Muhammed Damaghani’s rule the Muslim Moroccan explorer
famous for his extensive travels through Africa and Asia, visited his court. He married the
daughter of Jalaluddin Ahsan Khan. His travel account narrates about Ghiyas–ud-Din

Muhammed Damaghani’s atrocious behavior towards the local population.
13.4.4 Nasir-Ud-Din Muhammed Damghan Shah
Ghiyas –ud- Din Muhammed Damaghani was succeeded by his nephew Nasir-ud-Din
Muhammed Damghan Shah. He was a solider from Delhi. After he became the Sultan he
realized the threat from the officers and nobles and also from his various political enemies.

241
Hence he dismissed many and killed them. As a result the decline started in his period and
within a short span of time he also was murdered.
13.5 Decline of the Madurai Sultanate
Due to the struggle for power the Madurai sultanate’s rule in Madurai declined rapidly.
There are no references about the sultanate for some period. There was a lack of any coinage
issued during this period. However we are able to get the coins from 1358 to 1378 indicating
the ruler’s names. They were Shams-ud-Din Adil Shah, Fakhr-Ud-Dim Mubarak Shah and Alaud –Din Sikkander Shah. From this we infer that they ruled till 1378.
From Madhuravijayam of Gangadevi we come to know about the defeat of the sultans at
the hands of Kumara Kampana, the son of Bukka the Vijayanagar Emperor. The army of
Kampana defeated the Sultan’s forces at Samayavaram and captured Kannanur- Koppam, a

stronghold of the Sultans. In another battle the Sultan was defeated, that took place in between
Trichy and Madurai, in which the Sultan was killed. Thus the tyrannical rule of the Sultans at
Madura came to an end by the invasion of Kumara Kampana. The southern part of Tamil Nadu
came under the rule of Vijayanagar. This tremendous victory made Kumara Kampana as the
Viceroy of the Tamil country under Vijayanagar.
Kampana’s invasion has been narrated in the Sanskrit poem Madura Vijayam written by
Kampana’s wife Gangadevi. After this victory they were able to restore Srirangam’s temple old
glory. During Harihara II’s rule in Vijayanagar formally declared in 1378 their possession of
Madurai.
13.6 Summary
The struggle among the brothers of the Royal family in the Pandya country led to Malik
Kafur’s invasion. With this defeat permanently Tamil Country has gone to the foreign rulers

namely the Sultans, Vijayanagar, Nayaks, Maharashtrans and Nawabs till our independence.
From contemporary historical accounts, we come to know of the rulers of Madurai Sultanate,
as tyrants and persecutors of Hindus. Both Ibn Battutta’s and Gangadevi’s accounts contain
graphic descriptions of atrocities committed by the Muslim Sultans on the Hindu population.
