14.1 Introduction
The Vijayanagar Empire was established to save Hindus from the Muslim onslaught and
Aggressions. They safeguarded the varnashrama Dharma of Hinduism. The Society during
theVijayanagar-Nayak times was divided into several sections. The Brahamanas and Vellalas

245
were the two dominant groups in their period. There were other communities like Chettis,
Vanniyar and Srigopala’s. One of the important features of the Vijayanagar-Nayak society was
the adoption of alien communities from the Telugu and Karnataka regions. The Saurahtras and
later the Muslims and the Christians formed themselves as separate social groups. The
Vijayanagar and Nayak economy was based on land. Many new areas were brought under the
plough and agricultural production increased considerably. The king followed a policy of liberal
industrialization
14.2 Social Conditions
There were many divisions in the society during this period. The establishment of
Vijayanagar rule in tamilakam added a new element to the population.
1. Brahamanas
A large number of Telugu Brahmins were settled in Tamil Nadu during this period. The

Brahmins enjoyed high status in the society. They participated in all the activities of the society.
The Brahamanas were learned and functioned as priests in the temple. They also served as
ministers and generals in the empire. They have led contingents of army to the battle fields. A
few of them owned estates. There were a few traders also among the Bahamians. They led a
simple life and spent their time in reading Vedas and shastras. Their dress was a simple two
piece cloth, the first worn around loin and the second a long one worn round the shoulder. All
Bahamans wore a sacred thread. They were given lands by the rulers for their livelihood.

246
2. Vellalars
The Vellalas occupied a good position in the society next to that of the Brahmins. They
were found in large numbers in Tirunelveli, Coimbatore, Salem and North Arcot. They were the
owners of land. Cultivation was dependent on them. They formed the biggest section of the
population in the country. In this period they organised themselves into a corporate body called
Chitra-melipperi-yanadu. They worshipped the meli (the plough share). The corporate body
also looked after the marketing of agricultural products. The srigopalas and manradis lived by
rearing cattle. Srigopala tended cows and traded in milk and milk products. The manradis
reared sheep. They had close relationship with temples. It was with the manradis the temple
sheep were entrusted with. The manradis are to supply a particular amount of ghee for

maintaining perpetual lamps in the temple The Vellalas did not take wineand meat in those
days. Widow Remarriage was not allowed in this community.
3. Martials communities and Others
Among the martial comunities, the Vanniyar, Tandirmar, Agampadiyar and Marvar may
be mentioned. These communities have now settled as land owners and cultivators. The
primary occupations of the chettis are komattis was business during the period. They were
interested in trade and commerce. The Devaradiyar was another important community attached
to the temple. They were the Servants of the temple and performed dances in front of the deity
at appointed hours. Their position was degraded into devadasis later. The betel growers and
cultivators of oil seeds formed another dominant sub-group. These two communities functioned

as traders also. The cultivators of oil seeds were one of the affluent communities in the Tamil
country. They extracted oil from the various oil seeds. The betel growers also had a promising
trade.
4. Artisan Communities
The artisan communities formed another distinct group. There are five artisan groups
namely (1) goldsmith (2) brass-smith (3) black-smiths(4) carpenters and (5) idol makers. The
first four communities supplied the household utensils and furniture. Each one of these
communities lived in a village and offered their services to the society. Craftsmanship was

247
usually hereditary. They were collectively named as Panchalar. There seems to have subsects among the Panchalas. The inscriptions to Devaraya-1 mention 74 sects among the
Pandyachalas. There was a quarrel among themselves for their privileges. Many instance are
known from epigraphs. In one instance Attur, the gold-smith and black-smiths quarreled and
finally agreed on a settlement in 1526 A.D. The Panchalas is Kallidaikkurichi disputed among
themselves for certain privileges which was later Conferred upon by Virappa Nayak of Madurai.
The Panchalas lived with other communities for securing certain privileges at public
festivals in temples. In 1632 the nature of Tiruvamattur agreed that they will not-ill-treat the
artisan communities or deprive of their privileges. They further agreed that the rights and

privileges enjoyed by the artisans in other areas like Tiruvannamalai, Padaividu Senji and
Kanchipuram would be accorded to them. The ptivileges to Kanmalar were withdrawn in certain
other areas like Tirunavalur sirmai, since they were not entitled.
5. Kaikolas
Weaving was the main occupation of the kaikolas of this period, The weavers formed a
sizable group in the Tamil country. The Saliya, Niyayattar, Seniyar and Kaikkolars are the
different weaving communities. Among them the Kaikkolars occupied a supreme position. They
generally lived in separate streets close to the temple in the 16th and 17th centuries separate
settlements of weavers were also established with the advent of European traders. The kaikkola
weaving settlements were also established near the port cities. The Kaikkolas also fought for

certain social privileges. The Kaikkolas of Kanchipuram and Virinchipuram enjoyed the privilege
of using dandu (palanquin) and Sangu (conch). In 1485 the same privileges were extended to
the kaikkolas of Valudalampattu rajya. The Kaikkolas of Kanchi were also given some privileges.
In 1503 the privileges were extended to the Kaikkolas of Tirubhuvanamdevipparru and
Nenmalaipparu the kaikolas had the title of: Mudaliar” in those days. The Government collected
taxes for their “Taris”.
6. Paravas
The Paravas were a fishing folk lived along the east coast. The paravas on the south
pandya region took to pearl fishing also. Some of them were weavers. There are merchants

248
who traded in the painted cloth known as calico. When the Jesuit missionaries visited the east
coast many paravas were converted to Christianity. Their food consisted of meat, fish and rice.
7. Other Communities
The paraiyan and Pallan were untouchables. They were the low-caste people. They
lived in separate place called as “Cheris”.
. They were the agricultural labourers. They also performed the menial services in the
village. They led a miserable life. In many cases the labourers were slaves (adimai) and they
were just the property of their masters.. Non-Brahmin and Brahmana land lords owned such
slavesThe barbers, potters and washer men were the other communities lived in Villages.
From Srivilliputhur inscriptions we come to know that there was a struggle between Devendra
Kudumbas and Parayas. After this struggle Parayas were given certain privileges.
8. Telugu communities

The establishment of Vijayanagar rule in Tamilakam added a new element to the
population. Most of them seem to have migrated along with the viceroys.The important telugu
speaking communities in Tamilakam are the Kammavar, Balijas, (Bangle merchant), Uppuliya,
Saniya etc,. This rule also witnessed the large scale settlement of the Reddis, an agricultural
community from the Telegu area. The reddis were divided into two groups: (1) Pangala Reddis
and (2) Panta Reddis. With the Telugu speaking communities the Telugu Brahmanas also
came. The Nayaka the militant Telugu community was another influential community that survived
in the Tamil country. The Telugu speaking Uppilians (Salt merchants) spinners and dyers,
senians (weavers), barbers leather workers, oddans (house buldes) and Dombans (basket
plaiters) were the other communities who have settled in parts of Tamil country.

The above Telugu speaking people were distinguished by their own characteristic manners,
customs and forms of worship.
9. Saurashtras
The saurashtras (Pattunlkarar) were another group who hailed from Saurashtras and
settled in parts of Tamil country. They migrated during the Vijayanagar times. They settled in

249
the Tamil country under royal patronage. An important settlement flourished in Madurai. They
assumed Brahmans caste names and spread certain legends that they were originally Brahmans.
They had some disputes with Brahmins over certain social rights. During the regency of
Mangammal, she established the right to conduct upakarma ceremony by the Saurashtra
community by issuing a copper plate to them.
14.2.1 Valangai and Idangai Groups
The different communities in the Tamil country aligned themselves into two main groups
as the Valangai (right hand) and Idangai (left hand) groups. About the origin of these two
groups many traditions are available. T.W. Ellis mentioned that the agriculturists were Valangai
sect and the non-agriculturists like merchants also accepted the theory. However there is no

positive and artisans formed into Idangai. M. Srinivasan Iyengar evidences in support of this
history. The origin could be traced to the military classifications of the Imperial Cholas. Those
who took up arms on the right side of the military formation were the right hand group. Those
who formed the left side of the formation were left hand groups. According to tradition each
group consisted of 98 sub-sects.
The two groups had frequent conflicts among themselves. The disputes were sometimes
on trivial matters like which group the right to wear white or red colour flower has. On some
occasions they quarreled for participation in festivals. A similar agreement was also made
between the two groups in 1440. These two groups organised themselves into a body at times
of distress. Sometimes this proved threat to the government also. The two groups joined together

in opposing the introduction of a new measuring rod. They agreed that they shall not submit to
any outsider even if the local vijayanagar Governor with Brahman and Vellala land holders
oppress them in collusion with government officials. It was an open revolt against the government
officials. It was an open revolt against the government that took place in 1429. This peasant
revolt was not confined to a small area. Its repercussions can be seen in the whole of the Tamil
country.
The occupation of Telugu and Kannada speaking people led to the rise of certain social
problems. Since these two groups followed their masters and settled down in the Tamil country
with that they commanded a high social status as conquerors of the Tamil people. Probably

250
this led the earlier inhabitants giving up their original occupation and taking up menial works.
The Tamil Semmans, who on the advent of the Madigas (Telugu) and Chakkiliyans (Kannada)
had taken up menial service in the village, tailoring lime quarrying and selling. Further these
groups undertook some temple services jointly.
14.2.2 Foreigners
There was a considerable foreign population in the Tamil country, The Portuguese, the
French and the Danish contributed to the foreign, population. They generally lived in separate
quarters. Most of their settlements were created by them. These foreign populations had their
own churches and mosques in their settlements. Some Christian missionaries mingled with
the Hindu population and attempted conversion to their religion. They had a mixed reception
among the native population. The Muslims also made some conversions.
14.3 Education

Only a few communities were able to get education in this period.. The Brahamanas, the
Kshatriyas and the Vaisyas were in need of education. Each village had a small educational
institution often paid by the local population. The teacher taught the students according to his
own Syllabus. The school was normally held in the house of the teacher. Education was generally
of gurukula type. Mutts also played an important role in the spread of education. They specialized
in the religious philosophy. Much of the Vijayanagar-Nayak educational system was inter-woven
with religion. So part of their education was centered round religion and religious philosophies.
The Brahmanas had an educational system of their own. They learnt Vedas and allied
literature. Temple premises were utilised for conducting classes. At Adayapalam, Appaya

Dikshitar established a school in the Kalakanteswara temple and made provision for the teaching
of about 500 students in the Srikantabhasya. In the Arulalaperumal temple at Kanchipuram a
school was held to teach Vedas. The teacher appears to have remunerated by assignments of
lands. Lands were granted as adhyayana vrutti. King Achutaraya made a grant of village for
promoting Vedanta studies. In 1535 a piece of land was granted at Virinchipuram for the teaching
of a few sections in the Rig and Yajur Vedas. Madurai was a great centre of learning. According
to Robert de nobili. There were about 10,000 students and the Nayaks of Madurai supplied

251
food and cloth to them. Encouragement was given for the recitation of religious literature in the
temples also. In 1523 a gift of land was made for the recitation of Sanskrit Vedas, Dravida
Vedas and the exposition of Vedanta.
According to Robert de Nobili four methods of study were followed in schools and they
were: The course was divided into four parts the first dealing with evidence, the second with
knowledge and the third with authority. Each of these parts was divided into smaller divisions.
Sciences like astrology, astronomy and medicine were also taught. There seems to be
no special schools to teach these subjects. Experts in the fields trained the students. They
were generally selected among their own communities. The Vaisyas learned the science of
mathematics and the art of trade. The kshatriyas learnt the art of administration and warfare.

Temples maintained libraries. They were known as Saraswati Bhamdara. One library is
mentioned in the Arulalaperumal temple at Kanchipuram. In 1579 the first Tamil Book was
printed with the advent of the Europeans, This book was a summary of Christian doctrines.
14.4 Family
The prosperity of a society rests with the proper running of the family. The family was the
smallest unit, and many such units constituted into a society. In the Vijayanagar Empire that
basic unit was well organized. The heads of the family unit was undoubtedly the father. Mother
was respected as the second important person in the family. There were joint family units as
well as individual households. In the joint family unit the property was held by all the eligible
members of the family. The property ordinarily descended on the male members. Where male

members are absent, the right of property passed on to the female.
14.4.1 Women
The women normally stayed indoors and attended to their household duties. In some
communities women went outside and earned their livelihood. Among the cultivators the women
helped men in their agricultural pursuits. The women in some communities possessed enormous
wealth of jewels. They also inherited property is certain occasions. Many women were reputed
authors. The authoress of Raghunathabyudayan mentions that there were in the court of

252
Rahunatha of Thanjavur many accomplished women proficient in composing four kinds of
poetry, some women were capable of explaining works written in various languages. They
were able to sing very sweetly and play on the Veena and other musical instruments.
Temple dancers form a separate group. They were entrusted with the duty of performing
dance in front of the deity on specified hours of a day. They are also singers who sang devotional
songs in front of the deity on festival occasions. They lived near the temple quarters and
received remuneration from the temple. Their services were hereditary. These dancers also
danced in the car procession also. A performance of about 30 dancers in the car festival at
Thiruvaiyaru was witnessed by a Jesuit missionary.
14.4.2 Marriage
An important institution in the social life was marriage. Marriages were generally arranged

by elders. Love marriages were also known. Normally a marriage was arranged between parties
who have attained majority. Child marriage was popular in certain communities. Polygamy was
a popular system in this day. The king’s nobles and the public married more than one wife. The
system of giving dowry was prevalent in the period. Land and gold were granted as dowry.
Bride money or giving sradhana to bride was also popular. However it was opposed by the
people. The Brahmanas of various subsets in the padaividu rajya during the times of Devarayall they signed an agreement that they shall not perform marriage after receiving gold from the
bride’s party. The marriage shall be in the form of kanyandan and those who conclude the
marriage after receiving gold shall be liable for punishment by the king and shall be

excommunicated. The agreement was also binding on all the communities like kannadgas,
Tamilars and Telugus.
14.4.3 Sati
The customs of sati was practied. The foreign travelers Barbosa, Caesar Frederic, Nuniz,
Baradas, Pietra Della Valle and Linschoten give evidence for the prevalence of sati in South
India. There seems to be some preference with regard to the following of sati among various
communities. The customs also differ from place to place. The women seem to have either
burnt along with her husband. The foreign travelers give graphic descriptions of the ceremonies

253
attached with sati. The performance of sati, could not be considered universal. It was probably
popular among the nobility. Sati was not compelled but voluntarily performed. The performance
of sati was commemorated by the erection of sati stones. One these stones were sculptured
the representations of the widow who committed sati on the death of her husband. They are
generally sculptured with a pointed pillar or pose from which projects a woman’s right arm bent
upwards at the elbow. The hand is raised with fingers stretched and a lime fruit is usually
shown placed between the thumb and four fingers. Such sati stones are very few in Tamil
country but in Karnataka they are numerous. One of the famous performers of sati was the
queen of Vijayanagar chokkanatha. Another famous performance was by the wives of Tirumalai
Nayak.
14.5 Housing

The people lived in different types of houses. They nobility lived in fully palaces. These
palaces had many big rooms enclosed with spacious yards. The Nayak chiefs also lived in big
palaces. These residences of Nayaks were ordinarily situated on plains. Palaces were also
constructed at the hill tops and places of strategic importance. These palaces were surrounded
by a big fort. Madurai and Thanjavur had Nayk Palaces. At Shehji the palace was situated on
the top of hill. At vellore was a palace situated within a fort which served as the residence of
Bommi Nayaks. These palaces are self contained big houses. They contained provisions for
keeping a big army contingent.
The rich people also lived in big houses. These houses were built of burnt bricks and the
walls coated with lime plaster and polished. Big pillars and massive walls are the characteristics

of these buildings. Sometimes painting was executed. Wood, coconut, and Palmyra tree rafters
were employed in the constructions. Doors and windows were out of wood. The middle class
lived in small houses. Some of these houses had upper storey with balconies. The floor of
these houses were normally made of the floor consisted of fine lime mortar laid over a rammed
rubble mixer. The poorer sections lived in small doors. Up to a certain height mud walls were
used in small thatched houses. They had small doors. Up to a certain height mud walls were
raised and over which the roof was laid out. The floor was laid up with rammed earth.

254
Houses in the villages were arranged on the two sides of a long street. The villages
ordinary consisted of more than one street. Each street was assigned to particular community.
The communities who were in charge of the temple lived adjacent to the temple.
14.5.1 Food
Rice was the staple food of the people. With rice the people took a good amount of
cereals. Kambu was a common food among the common folk. Vegetables supplemented the
food. Meat and fish were consumed by a section of people. The Brahmanas, Vaisyas and
Jains took vegetarian food. Food was eaten in plantain leaves also. There seem to have regular
feeding houses for travelers also. These choultries were established on highways by kings and
philanthropists. Proper grants were given for the maintenance of these choultries. In many
temples, Brahmanas were fed with different items of food.

Chewing of betel leaf was an important custom followed in this period. The king and
nobles chewed a good amount of betel. The Vijayanagar and Nayak court accorded certain
special privileges to the betel page. The poorer sections also followed this custom. Women
also chewed betel leaves. Chewing betel leaf after the food was the common custom adopted
among the different communities. Betel was also offered to gold and in many temples provisions
were made to the offer of betel to the deity after the sacred food offerings. Provisions were also
made for the supply of betel to the persons who were fed in the temples and choultries.
14.5.2 Dress
The people wore different types of dress. Cotton was the common material used by the
masses for making their dress. The kings and nobility used silk for their dress. Satin was also

in use. Wool and linen were also used for making costume. The dresses of the nobles were
embroidered with many designs. The designers were executed with gold threads, the nobles
and rich wore a cap of gold brocade covered a piece of fine silk stuff. A long silk cloth was used
as a turban. People wore different types of turbans. The well to do people wore the lower
garment with many folds, which are gathered in between their thighs. The common people
went quite naked excepting a piece of cloth in their middle. The courtesans wore white garments
of very thin cloth or silk or bright colours. One part of their dress was tucked on to the girdle and

255
the other end was thrown over the shoulders. The common folk used one of cloth worn around
the girdle and used another piece of cloth to cover their upper parts of the body.
Rich people wore foot wear. There are a few types of chapels usually worn by wealthy
persons. However the majority walked barefooted.
Women wore a head dress. Caps embroided with flower designs were used by them.
Women decked their head with flowers. On festival occasions men also wore flowers.
14.5.3 Ornaments
Ornaments were worn by all sections of the society. Gold ornaments of various sizes and
shapes were worn Necklaces, ear rings and armlets were commonly used. The gold ornaments
were sometimes inlaid with precious stones and pearls. Strings of pearls formed a kind of
necklace. Finger rings and girdles, bracelets, and head ornaments of different sizes were also

worn by them. Diamonds, neck rings, double neck rings and nose ornaments are the other
ornaments worn in this period.
The people use perfumes also. They smeared the paste made up of with musk, sandal
wood, saffron and rose water. The women used to apply saffron musk to their body.
Games
One of the largely participated games by all sections of the society was wrestling, these
matches were periodically hold in the headquarters of the Nayaks, kings and nobles also
witnessed the animal hunt as a pastime. Sometimes they enjoyed the fight between man and
animal. Cock fights and bull fights were also witnessed by nobles and kings.
Raghunathabyudayam mentions the existence of a Gymnasium to witness these matches.
Hunting elephants or witnessing elephants hunts. Horse riding was another pastime. Among
other pastimes chess may be mentioned.
14.5.4 Fine Arts

Dance and Music provided great relief to the people. Dramas were also performed. These
entertainments relieved the people from their stress. Puppet shows were also popular in this

256
period. Dance was greatly encouraged by the people. The Devaradiyals of temple dancers
performed dances in public places also. They danced in front of the deity on festival occasions.
Ragunatha Nayak, the Thanjavur Nayak king designed a new type of dance in this period.
Kolattam another play performed dance in small circles striking the sticks in their hands of the
beat of music. Music reached new heights in the Tamil country. The instruments Vina, Mattala,
Kottu and Nadaswaram were used to produce melodious music.
14.5.5 Festivals
Maharasankaranithi, Sri Rama Navami, Ugadi, Deepavali, karthigai and Holi were some
of the festivals they celebrated. These festivals in a way refreshed the minds of people. There
were public and religious festivals. One of the important public festivals celebrated was

Deepavali. The harvest in the villages could have celebrated by cultivators. There were many
religious festivals. The Makara Sankaranthi and Ugadi were other important festivals. In
temples also they celebrated festivals. For example the marriage of the deities called for a
festival in some big temples. Other festivals are Festival of Floats, Hunting festivals, spring
festival and Masi Makam festival. Apart from all these they have celebrated the king’s birthday
with the usual splendor in the temple.
14.6. Economic Condition -Agriculture
Agriculture was the backbone of economy. The centre of agricultural economy was the
village. There were three major groups of villages. They are Donative Villages, Royal villages
and Villages of Cultivaton.
A village donated to a temple, mutt or a Brahmana may be included in the first category.

The devadana, Brahmadeya, Thiruvidaiyattam and Madapura are the village donated to temples
and Brahmanas. In the second category the Pandaramadai and Amaram villages may be
included. These villages were fully owned by the state. The Military chiefs granted to the officers
of the army and Nayaks are also to be included in this category. The amaram villages also
come under this group. The lands in the last category of villages were owned by individual
cultivators separately.

257
14.6.1 Villages
Villages were not planned properly and constructed. A village consisted of a living quarter,
cultivable lands, streets and waste lands. Different sections of the village population lived in
different quarters. The landlords lived in big houses and occupied the village’s prestigious
place. The agricultural labourers and merchants occupied other parts of the village generally
located adjacent to the main settlement. Other members of the communities occupied different
places within a village. The untouchables have a separate quarter. The houses were mostly
built of mud walls supporting a thatched roof. The wealthy people lived in big houses built with
burnt bricks. Roofs-tiles were also been used. The walls of big houses were plastered with lime
mortar and sometimes decorated with paintings. The floor was made up of rammed earth

plastered with cow dung. The wealthy people had used a fine variety of lime mortar for their
floors. Wood was also used in the construction of houses. There was poor sanitary condition in
those villages.
14.6.2 Land
The village lands were divided into three categories. These 3 categories were divided
on the basis of the crop cultivated in the field. The land cultivating paddy was identified as
nancey (wetland) while the land produced non-paddy crops was categorized puncey (drt land).
Land which produced crops like plantain, coconut, jack fruit, palms and flower-bearing plants
was classified as thottailam (garden land). The lands were further sub-divided into different
categories on the basis of their fertility. There were various types of waste lands. Wooden
ploughs were used by the farmers to plough the lands.
14.6.3 Ownership

The king was theoretically the lord of all land but he was not the actual proprietor of the
soil. The king also recognized the right of the people for the proprietor of the soil. Apart from
the royal villages the absolute enjoyment of land was vested with the owner of the land. The
property of the father was usually inherited by the son. The ownership of the land contained
the following eight-fold rights of possession. Nidhi, Nkisepa, Jala, Pasana, Aksini, Agami, Siddha
and Sadhya.(deposits, buried treasure, water, stones, akshini future income, past income and
probable income.)

258
Land granted to officers’ form a separate group. The service tenures were given to officers
to remunerate their services to the village communities or state or agencies like temple or mutt.
They will hold right of enjoyment till they are in service. The right of enjoyment is normally
hereditary since the service is inherited. Such service tenures were granted in the villages to
goldsmiths, potters, barbers, physicians, village watchman and other village servants. A few
pieces of lands were held by village assembly as common lands. The royal estates formed a
separate group. The state had absolute right over these lands.
14.6.4 Irrigation
Irrigation system was very excellent in those days. Agriculture was given encouragement
by the rulers. Rivers Wells and canals were utilized for irrigation. The kings dug new canals. In

using the river water for cultivation the individual land owners paid a small amount as water
cess. Where there were no rivers, lands were cultivated with tank water. In drawing water from
tanks turn-system was adapted. This system envisaged a fair use of available water by all the
cultivators. Lands were irrigated by private wells also.
(a) Maintenance of sources of irrigation
The people, public bodies and the state undertook the construction and maintenance of
tanks and irrigation canals. The local temple at Tiruvamattur purchased a piece of lands in
1486 A.D, for digging a canal from the river leading to the irrigation tank of the village. The
public bodies also made provisions for the maintenance of village tanks.
(b) Maintenance by State
The state helped in the repair and maintenance of tanks. In 1402 the silted up channel in

the village valuvur led to the abandonment of lands by cultivators. The state soon repaired the
tank. The state encouraged individual;ls by making certain grants to undertook the maintenance
work of sources for irrigation. In another instance, the Dalavy set apart the income from the
lease of fishery from the tank at Kodungalur for deepening it. The state also encouraged the
people to maintain tanks by remitting certain taxes since the cultivators could not cultivate their
lands owing to the silted condition of the tank.

259
Distribution of water to the lands from the village times settled amicabbbly among villagers.
In certain other tanks often created problems. One instance of dispute over the distribution of
water from the local tank among the villages of Alattur and Attipattu is reported in 1406 A.D.
Government solved the irrigational conflicts in a smooth manner.
14.6.5. Methods of Agriculture
Lands were ploughed with wooden ploughshares. To strengthen the wooden tip a piece
of iron plate was attached at the point. The ploughshare was held by the cultivator. It was
drawn by Buffaloes. The crops were cultivated in two seasons. They are Kar and Pasanam. A
third crop (Kadaippu ) was cultivated in some fertile areas. Cultivation was also carried out in
the parts of lands in the river and tank-beds on certain periods of the year. On the dry lands one
crop was harvested for the year.
Crops

Rice was an important production. It was the main crop cultivated on a large scale. The
inscriptions refer to the Kuruvai variety of rice. Among the cerals , Varagu and Tinai were
cultivated in great quantities. Among pulses, the green gram, black gram, horse gram and
beans were cultivated. Sugarcane and oil seeds were grown. Pepper was cultivated among
the spices. Chinamon cloves and ginger were the other important items of spices produced in
the Tamil country, Cardamom and mustard were also produced.
The Vijayanagar and Nayak age produced garden crops like Mango, jack-fruit, orange,
lime, grape, plantain, tamarinf and coconut. Apart from the above garden crops brinjal, garlic,
onion, pumpkin and turmeric were produced in some places. Cotton and sugarcane cultivators
were restricted to certain areas in the Tamil country.

The condition of farmers was not satisfactory. They lived on debts. The debtors were
treated as slaves. Most of the agriculturists were very poor. They had to pay heavy taxes to the
Government.
14.7 Industries
During the rule of Vijayanagar and nayak many industries were started. Small scale
industries were well developed but it was restricted to a limited area due to raw materials

260
availability. However there were few industries existed like oil pressing, sugar industry and
textile industry.
14.7.1 Village Industries
There were Augar factories in the country. Jaggery, palm-jaggery, sugar were produced
in those factories. Coconut trees were cultivated largely during this period. The byproducts like
rope, mat and toddy were obtained from these trees. .These products received a good market
in both rural and urban areas though these products were manufactured in the country side.
Oil Pressing was another important industry. The oil pressers are famous in South Arcot,
Chengalpattu and Trichy. More oil seeds were cultivated in these areas hence it was easy for
them to sell their products in these places. The sekku vaniyar (oil monger) paid comparatively
a high percentage of tax to the state than other communities.

Pottery was another important rural industry. It was mostly a local industry catering to the
needs of the locality. People used fine variety of pottery in their houses. The temple also
utilized the services of potter. Fishing industry was also in existence near the village tank and
other water reservoirs. They sold fish in the nearby markets. Fishing boats and nets were
employed.
14.7.2 Textile
Generally Textile Industry plays an important role in the country. In Coimbatore and
Ramanathapuram cotton was produced. Cotton was manufactured in kan-pa-mei and it was a
famous place in Coimbatore. Apart from Coimbatore, Madurai also manufactured cotton in
some areas. Raw silk was manufactured in the western parts of the Tamil country. However
they used to import raw silk from Karnataka.
First raw silk was processed, dyed and woven into fine pieces of 4 to 5 feet in width and

12 to 13 feet in length. Kaikkolars, Saliyars and occasionally the Paruaiah were engaged in
this industry. The Padmasalis and Saurashtrians later occupied parts of the Tamil country
under the royal patronage and monopolized silk weaving.
The state encouraged the weaveres on many occasions. Sometimes the state used to
reduce or exempt their taxes when they were burdened with tax. Due to the Government

261
support at the correct time the industry is able to survive. During the Nayak rule Saurashtrians
were given concessions and they were able to settle in many parts of the country. Finally
Madurai became one of the chief centre of their activity.
Dyeing
Dyeing was another important industry. In Kanchipuram and in Madurai Dyeing of yarn
by weavers were performed. Indigo was abundantly available and hence they used for dyeing
textiles. Myrabolan was also used as a dye stuff in Tamil country.
14.7.3 Mining and Metallurgy
Mining was another important industry which fetched good revenue to the state. Main
centers of mineral collection were North Arcot and Coimbatore districts. From different parts of
the Tamil country semi- precious stones were collected. Diamonds were obtained from the
mines of Kurnool (Vajrakarur ). Skill workers were done the cutting and polishing of precious
stones.

The main revenue to the Government came from the Gold and Silver mining industry. In
Tamil Nadu from Dharamapuri and North Arcot districts they have collected Gold from gold
mines. Iron and copper mines were also located in parts of Tamil country. Iron and copper
mines were also located in parts of tamil country. The manufacture of metals i were entrusted
to small units. In remote areas these units functioned.
14.7.4 Jewelry and Weapons
Manufacturing jewelry was a subsidiary industry of gold mining. For minting coins gold
was used. Various types of gold ornaments were manufactured by craftsman. Temples were
also supplied with Gold jewelry. With the iron , weapons of war were manufactured. Household
articles were also manufactured and were in use. Every village possessed a goldsmith, a
blacksmith and coppersmith.
14.7.5 Carpentry and Fishing

Carpentry was another profession of utility value, found an important place in the country.
Besides manufacturing chariots, palanquins, carriages by guilds of carpenters many household

262
objects were manufactured. The skilled workers constructed ships and boats. In the construction
of houses also the services of a carpenter were utilized. The cart, wheel and a few related
object were manufactured by some specialized craftsman. From foreign traveler’s accounts
we come to know that they manufactured leather goods like shoes.
Pearl fishing
Pearl fishing was another important industry which yielded good revenue to the state.
Fishing was the monopoly of the state. Through pearl fishing the state received huge money.
The fishermen with special training were employed as dives and pearl catches were sold to
highest bidders. Kayal was the centre of pearl-fishing in Tamil Nadu. Portuguese showed keen
interest in purchasing the pearls Manufacture of salt was under the control of the state.
Labour

The chettis, Senaikkadaiyar, Kaikkolar and Vaniyar were considered industrial group.
They were given a common name Pattadai. The industrial class seems to have occupied a
position og greatness among other classes. This impact produced some changes in the
economic condition of the country.
The craftsmen produced articles in their place and brought them to the market centers
for sale. The output of articles was limited since each craftsman was entrusted with the work
of completing one product from raw materials. The women folk helped in the manufacture of
certain articles. The state patronage played a vital role for their development.
14.8 Trade and commerce-inland trade
Trade and commerce both inland and foreign were carried by Chettis or Komatis, Brisk
trade was going on between Tamilaham and neighbouring countries. The articles of Trade

were many Rice, Millets, Wheat, Vegetables, Salt and spices were brought to market centres
or weekly markets (sandai) and were sold. The coconut, oil jiggery, betel, areca nut and fruit
were also brought to the marketing centres. Cows, oxen and horses were sold in fairs. Fairs
were organized weekly in those days. For example the Friday shandy (Fair) of Senji was a
popular one. Raw cotton, cotton thread and raw silk were included in the trade articles.

263
14.8.1 Exports and Imports
The Tamil country traded with foreign countries. Rice, Kandala’s sugar etc., were exported
to Aden, Ormuz and Ceylon. It exported a good deal of articles it seems rice was the most
important food item exported to foreign countries. Another important item exported from Tamil
country was powered sugar (yellow sugar). Wheat and millets were also exported. Coconut
was another chief item of export. The Indian pepper was in great demand in the foreign market.
The Black pepper was exported in large quantities. Green and dried varieties of ginger were
exported to foreign countries. Besides these food articles, dye stuffs were also in great demand.
The indigo, myrabolan, two important dye stuffs were imported in large quantities. Cinnabar
and henna were also exported. Among the metals exported into western countries iron had a

lion’s share. Some of the precious stones were exported. They include some varieties of
diamonds, rubies, sapphires, amethysts and topazes. Most of these precious goods were
shipped to Arabia. The cotton and silk clothes were other items of goods that had a great
demand in the western markets. Many varieties of cotton cloth were shipped to foreign markets.
The calico and painted cloths were also exported from the country.
Imports
The Vijayanagar Kingdom imported many articles. Gold, silver, Tin, Lead, Copper and
Opium were imported from Aden and china. Some precious stones were imported from Ceylon.
Akil, camphor, Spices etc., were imported from Sumatra, java and Malaccas islands. The imports,
included pearls from Ceylon and Ormuz,. Ceylon supplied rubies, sapphires, garnets and cat’s
eyes. Among other imports may be included spices like Cloves, Cardamom and cinnamon,

which came from Sumatra, Malaccas Islands and Ceylon. One of the pried articles of trade
was Camphor was imported sandalwood were also imported from Java. From China opium
was imported, saffron, rose water and musk was also imported. Elephants and horses were
also imported from Ceylon and Arabia respectively.
14.8.2 Transport
Trunk Roads were constructed for the purpose of trade and commerce. For inland trade,
highways were used. River and channels were used for the movement of goals. Bullock-carts

264
were utilized for transporting goods from one place to another. The cart was the dependent
system of road transport. For transporting big bundles to a long distance cart was employed.
Pack horses were also employed for transporting goods on a limited scale. Sometimes articles
were carried on head-loaded. Gunny bags and baskets were used in the transporting of goods.
For crossing rivers and carrying heavier objects over waterways ferry boats were employed.
Boats, Catamarans, ships and small boats were utilized for transporting goods through
water. Small boats and rafts were sometimes used. Parisal was kind of basket boat used in the
Tamil country. The Parisal was built of wicker rafts. Catamarans were also employed for
transporting at times. For going into seas ship were employed.
14.8.3 Ports
The overseas trade was controlled by a good amount of ports situated on the east coast

of the Tamil Country. Nagapattinam was an important port. The other ports on the Tamil coast
were Tirumalairayanpattinam, Tharangambadi (Tranqubar), Parangipettai (Porto Novo),
Thevanampattinam, Sadurangapattinam (Sadras) pazhaverkkadu (pulicat) and Mylapore. Many
ships sailed from Malabar anchored at this ancient port to take rice. At Devanampattinam all
kinds of cotton cloth, printed and woven, were ex[ported Some of the articles imported into this
port included pepper, nutmeg, cloves, sandalwood, alum and raw silk, kunimedu was another
important port city. Chaturangapattinam and Mylapore ports were also important. Palaverkadu
(Pulicat) was another port city situated on northern end of the Tamil country. Ships anchored at
these ports sailed to Pegu, Malccca and Sumatra. Cloth was an important item exported in this
port.
Trade routes

Owing to a brisk inland trade, it can be expected that there were a good number of well
guarded trade routes in the country. These trade routes were maintained by to have connected.
Vijayanagara amd Mylapore, running the state between merchantile centres. A road appears
through Chandragiri, Tirupati and Pulicat. Another road connected Kalahasti, Tirupati and Kanchi
and Tiruttani was considered as resting place. Another road connected Tiruvannamalai,
Chidambaram, Madurai, Rameswaram and Dhanuskodi, Another trade route connected
Vijayanagara with Pulicat the port city.

265
14.8.4 Guilds- Craft guilds
Guilds were organised locally but functioned as extra territorial organisation. There were
two types of guilds (a) the craft guilds and (b) merchant guilds. The craft guild was a territorial
association organised to supervise the production of goods. They followed hereditary
occupations. Barbosa also remarks about the hereditary nature of their progressives inscriptions
speaks about different functions of 18 craft guilds in which were included the smiths, potters,
oil pressers, weavers, washer men and barbers. The most important and the best organised
seems to be the guild of the panchalas or smiths (five chases). They formed themselves into a
corporate body. They claimed their descent from visvakarma, the son of Brahma, as their
progenitor. The members of the guild lived in specified localities in the urban areas. The guilds

acquired some privileges from the king from time to time. The kammalar of kanchipuram received
some social recognition from the king. The weavers of Kanchipuram and Virinchipuram enjoyed
certain rights. The agricultural community formed themselves into a corporate body called
Chitrameli-Periyanadu. It seems that this body had control over the production and distribution
of the produce from the land.
(a) Merchants guilds
Merchant’s guilds formed a separate group, which is primarily a corporation of merchants.
The merchant guilds were many. Some of the guilds were named banajigas, nanadesis,
Vaniyanagarathar, Vaisyas, Mummuridandas, Chettis, Ayyavole and Manigramam. There were
Brahmana and muslim merchants also. The horse traders (kudirai chettis) constituted themselves
into a guild. They are said to have come from the north of the Tamil country. Another important

guild was that of the saliva weavers. Manigramam, an old corporate body also existed in this
period. This body consisted of merchants of this guild had certain privileges.
14.9 Trade Communities - Chettis
Trade was carried out by various communities. The chettis were enterprising businessmen.
They traded with foreigners also. They sold pepper for precious stones and costly wares. One
cinnama chetti was an influential merchant who helped the Dutch to carry over trade with
Indian traders and weavers. One of his dependants was Sesadri Chetti at Porto Novo who rose

266
to the position of a chief Indian merchant at Madraspatnam. The Chettis settled in the eastern
countries also
The Malabars were another enterprising community that carried on a part of the trade in
the country. They traded mostly in spices, coconut, palm sugar, in return for coarse rice and
iron.
(a) Muslims
The Muslims dominated the trade between the fourteenth and seventeenth centuries.
Then was a substantial Muslim population even as early as the 13th century. They brought
goods from China, Malacca and Bengal. The coastal trade was largely controlled by them.
However on the west coast, the Muslims were humbled by the Portuguese.
(b) Portuguese
The 16th Century witnessed the arrival of the Portuguese in the Tamil country. The first
settled on the west coast and from there, they traded with the Tamil merchants frequently they

established their settlements in the Tamil Country. One such settler they located at Santhome,
Mylapore. It continued to be a flourishing trade centre.. For the cloth manufactured in the Tamil
Country and Coromandal coast there was a great demand in Portugal after the debacle at
Talikota of the Vijayanagar Kingdom, the Portuguese trade received a setback in the whole of
south India However, in the beginning of the 17th century they established several settlements
in the Tamil country. A settlement at Nagapattinam was a flourishing trade centre they lost
some of the centres like Vellore and Chandragiri to the other western merchants.
(c) The Dutch
In the sixteenth century, the Dutch, the Danes and the English made their appearance
on the east coast. The Dutch in 1608 established a factory at Devanampattinam near, Cuddalore

with the permission of the Nayak of Gingee. The rivalry of the dutch worked havoc to the
Portuguese ships in the sea. The Portuguese obstructed the Dutch in getting a hold in South
India. The Portuguese, through the Vijayanagara king stopped the establishment of a factory
at Devanampattinam. Later the Dutch were expelled completely. The Dutch established a fort

267
at Pulicat but was razed to the ground by the Portuguese Later the Dutch, with the English
jointly established a factory there, which however, failed to function due to mutual mistrust.
(d) The Danes
The Nayaks of Thanjavur encouraged the establishment of factories by the Danes at
Tranquebar a small fort was built and soon their trade prospered. They established some
factories in the inland centers also.
(e) The English
In the beginning of the 17th Century, the English tried to settle in Pulicat with the help of
the Dutch. However, this attempt was failed by the mutual mistrust. In 1622 on the invitation of
the Nayaks of Thanjavur, the British sought permission from him. However the Danes
manipulated the events and the king refused permission. The British returned to their factory at
Masulipattinam. In 1637 another attempt was made by the British. This time Francis Day was

able to secure a factory site at Madarasapatnam near Santhome (Mylapore) from the local
Nayak. Venkatadri Nayak. A Fort was built at this place and gradually the settlement became a
strong one. They manufactured long cloth, painted cloth and many kinds of stuff. Laterthe
Vijayanagar ruler also confirmed the Nayak’s permission. The English received some privileges
from the king and their trade prospered.
14.10 State Economy – Sources of Income and Expenditure
Since No Government can be run without finance and since Government finance is got
mostly through taxation Tamil Governments from very early times levied many kinds of Taxes.
The Vijayanagar rule in Tamil nadu was not an exception to this. Many kinds of Taxes were
imposed and collected during this period.
The most important item of state source was land tax. Tax was believed on all types of

cultivated land tax was assessed on the basis of a systematically and survey. Wet and dry
lands were assessed. On the dry lands the assessment was received much was than the wet
land assessment. The land tax included some cases are assessment valakkai and nikuli (water
case). On wetland the tax was collected in Paddy and on dry land it was, collected in panam.

268
On garden crops like banana and coconut the tax was collectedin the respected crops. On
some categories of land. tax was exempted. When the crops failed, tax exemption was granted.
There were state-owned villages in the kingdom. They were Bhandharavadai villages. The
lands in these villages were leased out to the highest bidder in this way the state received a
lump sum from the leaseholder.
Income was derived from other resources. The weavers, the fishermen, shipherents and
oil mongers paid tax to the state. The Barbers, potters and washer men also paid their share of
tax to the state. From the merchants the State collected tax. The tolls and customs collected at
various points on the highway amounted to a good part of the state income at the port the
goods were paid a duty. Excise duty was levied on the manufacture of salt and on drawing

toddy. The shops in the market centers also paid a duty. The income from the fairs contributed
a good share in the state income. Taxes were also levied on various articles of trade.
Military contributions supplemented the revenue of the state. The Nayaks and the Military
chiefs paid a lump sum every year. Contributions from the conquered territories also increased
the income of the state. Customary payments were also demanded from the subjects.
Benevolences formed another important feature of the state income. The judicial fines were
also considered as a form of the Royal income. Confiscated property also contributed to the
state’s revenue.
Expenditure
The state spent large sums of money on various development activities. The state took
active part in the construction of temples. Large sums of money were spent on the construction

and repairs of temples. Endowments were instituted by kings and queens in several temples
and portion of the state revenue were set apart for this purpose. A good portion of the state
income was spent on military organisation numerous military expeditions undertaken both by
the Vijayanagara and Nayak rulers sliced a part of the state income. A percentage of the state’s
resources were spent on excavations of irrigation tanks and canals. Another portion of the
income was spent on maintenance of roads and construction of rest houses. Though the officers
were remunerated with a grant of land, one portion was set apart to the salaries and expenses
of the royal officers. Another good portion was spent on the royal household.

269
(a) Currency
In the early years of the Vijayanagara rule the use of a standard currency was limited to
certain transactions. A good part of the commercial transaction was carried by barter system in
some areas of then Tamil country. The use of the currency was increased gradually in both the
state and commercial transactions. A well regulated currency system of the Vijayanagara Empire
was adopted in Tamil country and the Nayaks followed it. A uniform weight standard was also
followed. The currency system was based on a unit of gold weighing about 50 or 52 grains. In
the Vijayanagara Empire this gold coin was called by various names as follows: Pon, Varaha,
Pagoda and Gadyana. In the Tamil country all the above names were used but the Tamil from
Pon was popular. In the Nayak period Varaha and Pagoda became popular terms. The Pagoda

appears to be a half of a varaha. The Katti was one-fourth of a Varaha Panam, another
popular currency was one-tenth of a Pon. The tar was the only silver coin. Kasu was the copper
coin popular in the Tamil country. Irefai, guligai, cakkaram and madai were the other names
applied to coin in the Tamil country.
The coins
The medium of exchange in all commercial transactions was gold. Gold coins called
“Ramadunga” are available in plenty. The people used “pagoda” as medium of exchange (one
Pagoda is equal to three rupees). Panam and Kasu were in use during this period. Frier has
mentioned that one pagoda is equal to eight Shilling.
Figures were inscribed on both sides of the coin. Figuerslike Uma Maheswari,Hanuman,
Lakshmi and Narayanan were inscribed on one side of the coins. Figures of Ox, pig and elephant

were inscribed on the other side of the coins. In the Ramadanga kasu figures of rama and Sita
were inscribed on one side and thefiguers ofHanuman on the other side. Generally the coins
were round (circular) in shape. The name of the king who issued the coin was also inscribed on
the face of the coin. The coin system of the Nayaks was similar to that of the Vijayanagara
kings.
(b) Mints
There was a central mint at the capital for minting coins. The provincial governors were
permitted to issue their own coins. The Tamil provinces also issued coins from their own mints.

270
During the Nayak rule mints were established at gingee, Thanjavur, Tiruchirapalli and Vellore.
There were some smaller mints also in the country in these mints moulded metal was poured
into the terracotta moulds and coins were extracted by the process of cooling.
(c) Weights and Measures
For conducting trade various units of measures are needed in the Vijayanagara days,
various units were popular. The regional units of measurements then in current were also
adopted. However a few broad units were common to the whole country.
The popular unit of weight was a maund. Twenty maunds consisted of baram, which was
the heaviest. The maund was sub-divided into lesser units of visa, paam, seer and talas. The
capacity measures adopted in the country were units. pilavu, kanam, ulakku etc. thepopular
unit of capacity measures was kalam, One-twelth of a kalam, was a marakkal another popular

capacity measure.
The land was measured by ancient units of measure like veli, ma and kuli, veli, was the
popular unit of measurement. Twenty ma consisted of a veli and a ma consisted of 100 kulis.
The Kuli-ma ratio varied from area to area was no uniformity among the land measures of the
Tamil country. Land was measured by different lengths of measuring rods. The most important
measuring rod which was used in the Tamil country was Rajavibhadan kol equivalent to about
9.5feet. There are other measuring rods, whose lengths are equal to 19 and 21.5 feet.
(d) Famines and flood relief
The economy of the state was distributed on many occasions by famines. The state
undertook famine relief measures. Failure of monsoon was one of the most important reasons
for the famine. Unprecedented floods resulted in the spreading of epidemics and loss of precious

property and grains. One famine is referred to in 1381.A.D. in an inscription at kuttalam. At
another time in 1402 the thanjavur area experienced a famine. In 1412 another famine occurred.
The state took various other measures and helped the affected by providing shelter and food.

271
14.11 Summary
There were different communities lived in this period. For the first Christians and Muslims
were able to convert the Hindus to their faith. Printing press entered into the country mainly to
print their religious works.
Their rule witnessed the rapid urbanizations in the country. Commercial activity increased
and merchants from distant places thronged the cities of Tamil country. It is in this period
Europeans took a keen interested in the South Indian trade. All these factors induced a
remarkable change in the economy of the Tamil country in this period. This period paved the
way for the east India Company to govern our country later.
