15.1 Introduction
The Vijaya nagar rulers encouraged all religious faiths. Hinduism was their favourable
religion Hindu temples were repaired and rebuilt in their period; some of the temples were
enlarged with additional gopurams and praharas. New temples were built Vellore, Kanchipuram
and Kumbakonam. They have also patronized Tamil scholars.
15.2 Hinduism – Saivism
The saivites constituted a lare majority among the Hindu religious group in the Vijayanagar
Empire. Siva’s various forms were also worshipped. Gangadhara, Dhakshinamurthi and
Umamhesvara forms of Siva were popular. Siva’s consort parvati was also worshipped in her
benign form. Ferocious forms like Kali, Durga and Mahisasuramardhini were also popular.
Separate shrine was constructed for the consort of Siva near the central shrine in the temple
complex.

The Saivites were classified into three small groups, namely Advaitins, Pasupathas and
Vira Saivaism. The Vijayanagar rulers, from the sangama brothers up to the commencement
of Virupaksha’s rule followed Pasupatha Saivism and patronized Advaitham.
The Advaitins were the followers of the philosophy of Sri Sankara who advocated the
theory of non-dualism. Sri Sankara established two monasteries, one at Sringeri and the other
at Kanchipuram. In 1546, the Sangama brothers of Vijayanagar made grants to monasteries.
The Pasupathas paid great attention to the Saiva Agamas and the famous saint of the
sect of Saivism was Kaivilas Kriyasakthi. Harihara I and Bukka I were the dixciples of Kriya
sakti. Under this sect, Lord Virupaksha was the royal family deity.
The Vira Sauvas constituted the influential religious sect in Vijayanagar Empire. It was

made popular by Basava, a minister. The Virasaivas were the staunch saivas and they carried
Lingam always with them. They rejected the authority of the Vedas: disbelieved in the doctrine
of rebirth, objecteto child marriage, approved the marriage of widows and cherished an
intenseaversion to Brahmins.

275
Temples for Siva were built many parts of the Tamil Country. In some big temple centres
the existing temples complexes were enlarged by the addition of mandapas and prakars. Big
and tall gopuras were built in a few other temple complexes. Tiruvannamalai, Madurai,
Kanchipuram, Thanjavur, Tiruchirapalli, Srivilliputtur became big religious centres.
15.2.1 Vaishnavism
The Vijayanagar days were very favourable for the spread of Vaishnavism in South
India.The Vijayanagara king’s patronised Vaishnavism. Vaishnavism had a large following in
the Tamil country. Vishnu was worshipped in his various forms. The avatars of Vishnu were
worshipped. Sridevi and Bhudevi were also worshipped. Separate shrines were now established
for the concords of Vishnu within the temple complex. The Alvars and Archariyars were now
elevated to godhood and were worshipped.

Since the days of Ramanuja the great Vaishnava philosopher, the Vaishnava creed was
gaining a large number of followers. After the death of Ramanuja the followers of Vishnu were
divided into two sections. Namely Vadakalai and Tenkalai. The origins of these sections may
be traced to the 14th century. They were divided on various aspects from their caste marks to
the doctrines.
Vadakalais preferred Vedas as their basic scriptures while the followers of tenkalai adopted
Tamil scriptures as basic to their religion. The Vadakalai wore a cast mark (nanam) resembling
‘U’ on their forehead, different from the Tankalais who were with a stem attached at the bottom
of ’U’ the caste mark.
The Vadakalais thought that salvation could be achieved by one’s own self effort even
without surrender. They held that Lakshmi is one with the Lord Vishnu. The Vadakalai followed
strict caste system.

The tenkalais on the other hand believed in Saranagadhi (self surrender to God) and
awarded a lower position to Lakshmi than Vishnu. They were liberal enough to admit other
members of lower caste into Vaishnavism.

276
15.2.2 Kings’ Patronage to Religion
The early Vijayanagar kings were Saivites. The later kings changed their faith to
Vaishnavism. So both Saivism and Vaishnavism flourished during this period. The Saluvas
were Vaishnavas, devoted to Narashima of Ahobalm and Venkatesa of Tirupathi. They patronised
saivism also.
Under Krishnadevaraya, and Sadasivaraya, Vaishnavism gained a large number of
followers . Krishnadevaraya built a temple for Lord Krishna which he carried to his capital with
great renovation from the fort of Udayagiri.He encouraged the vaishnava literary scholars namely
Venkata Tatarya and Vysa Tirtha .Coins issued by them proclaim their conviction towards
Vaishnavism.
Krishnadevaraya remitted 10,000 varahans in favour of Saiva and Vaishnava temples in
the Cholamandalam. The Northern gopura of Chidambaram temple was built by him. He made

substantial additions to Siva temple at Tiruvannamalai. He also made substantial improvements
to the Varadarajaperumal temple at Kanchipuram
The Nayaks had their individual preferences, some wee followers of Siva and others
patronised vaishnavism. However the king practised religious toleration.
Achyutaraya granted a village to the temple of Varadaraja, and Ekambaramatha at
kanchipuram. He built the image of Lord Thillai Govindaraja in the temple of Nataraja at
Chidambaram. Achyutaraya also made a grant of 82 villages to the temple of Nataraja at
Chidambaram.
The Nayaks built many new temples and provided additions to old temples. The Madurai
temple (Meenakshisundareswarrar) temple complex was enlarged by the construction of
mandapas. The pudumandapam was constructed by the Nayaks of Madurai. The Subramanya

shrine in this temple of Brihadisvara at Thanjavur was built by a Nayak King. The Nartanmandapa
of the Perur temple was constructed by a Nayaka. A few Mandapas were built by the Nayals in
the Ranganatha temple at Srirangam and Jambukesvara temple at Thiruvanaikkavasl.
Vaishnavism received still greater support at the hands of the rulers of the Araindu dynasty.
At every stage the saivas opposed the spread of Vaishnavism.

277
15.2.3 Mutts
During the Vijayanagara period the Mutts assumed greater importance. Their main aim
was to propagate religion and philosophy. They were many Mutts in the Tamil country. One of
the famous Mutt existed in Kanchipuram was the kamakottipeda. It is believed that the Mutt
was founded by Adi Sankaracharya in honour of Goddess Kamakshi. The Mutt was patronised
by Krishnadevaraya who made a gift of two villages to the Mutt.
A branch of kamakotipitha was established at Tiruvanaikovil. The Nayaks of Madhura
made a gift of land for feeding Brahmanas in the Mutt. Another Mutt which had substantial
following was the Golaki Mutt’. This mutt had centres in Andhrapradesh, Karnataka and Tamil
country. In the Tamil Country the centres were located in Devikapuram. Tirupparankunram,
Tiruppattur and Piranmalai..
The Dharmapuram Mutt appears to have been founded in the 16th century by Kumara

Gurupara. The Tiruvavaduthrai Mutt was established by Namasivaya Desikar in the sixteenth
century. Another Mutt that deserves mention is the Tiruppanandal Mutt. Among the other Mutts
located in Tamil country mention may be made to the Triuvenkatanatha Mutt (Puliyankulam),
Jnanaprakasawamigal Mutt (Kanchipuram), Angaravan Mutt (Tiruvorriyur) and Periyadeva
Nayinar Mutt (Chidanbaram).
The Mutt was administered by a head (pontiff) o f Mutt.The head of a Mutt was also the
administrator of temples attached to the Mutt. Many of the heads of Mutt were great scholars.
Sadasiva Brahmendra and Chansrasekara Saraswati are two pontiffs who have established
their philosophical lore in the Tamil country during the 16th century. Isana sivacharya,
KumaraGuruparar, Ambalavanaswami and Namasivaya Desikar were the other heads who
have extensive knowledge in the Saiva Siddhanta Philosophy.
15.2.4 Philosophy

The Saiva Siddhanta Philosophy received great impetus during the Vijayanagara period.
The earlier doctrines of Adi Sankara were also being followed. Generally the followers of the
advaita philosophy of Adi Sankara were known as Smartas. Meykandadeva, another philosopher
made Saivism a popular religion among the masses. The Saiva Siddhanta philosophy is largely

278
based on the Agamas. It seeks to determine the relation between God, Matter and Soul. The
philosophy advocated Bhakti in preference to rituals and ceremonies. The other great exponents
of Saiva Philosophy were Arulnadi Sivacharya and Umapati Sivacharya.
The 16th and 17th century Tamil country saw the rise of mystics (Siddhars) who propagated
Saivism in their own way. These Siddhars were a kind of distinguished philosophers who raised
above all religious and communal barriers. There were eighteen Siddhars in the ‘Tamil country’.
Among them about a half could belonged to the Vijayanagar period. Mention may be to the
Siddhars, Sivavakkiyar, Sivaprakasar and Tathuvarayar. The Siddhar Sivavakkiyar ridiculed
the worship of idols without sincere devotion. He emphatically expressed that there is no use
decking idols with flowers and performing ceremonies. Another Siddhar Sivaprakasa, had

disputations with Christians. Thathyvarayar was another Siddhar who was against the idol
worship.
On the Vaishnava side, the Ramanuja’s Visistadvaita philosophy was favoured. There is
a slight variation in the Vaishnava philosophy since there appeared Vadagalai and tengalai
groups. However to attain salvation bhakthi and surrender (saranagati) were considered
important. Vedanta Desika, (14th century) followed some of the doctrines of Ramanuja. However
he emphasised varnashrama dharma system. The followers were the vadakalai sect. Pillai
Lodacharya and Manavala Mamuni headed the tenkalai sect who opposed the conservative
ideas and fought for equality among the followers of Vishnu.
The philosophy of Vittoba, Vallabhacharya and Madhava were followed in philosophies
during the Vijayanagar period. During the Nayaks rule these philosophies could have gained
some more support among the masses.

15.2.5 Jainism
Jainism also received patronage in the Vijayanagar period. The Jains were minority in
Number. The kings patronized Jain Pallis. There was a Jain Palli at Thirunanurgondai in those
days. A large number of Jains lived at Tirupparuttikkunaram, Salukkai and Vijayamangalam.
The Minister of Harivhara-ll built a mandapa in the Jain Palli. Krishnadevaraya gave liberal
donations to the Jain Palli at Tirupparuttikkunaram. Even the Jain Pallis at Kavanthai and
Nagarkovil also received gifts from Krishnadevaraya.

279
15.2.6 Buddhism
During the Vijayanagar period.Kanchi and Nagapattinam were the centres of Buddhism
Buddhism flourished in Tiruvalarkoil, Kumbakonam and Tiruvalanjuli. In those places Buddhist
Viharas were established to spread Buddhism . Budhism followere were limited during this
period.
15.2.7 Islam
Islam reached India before the establishment of the Vijayanagar Empire. The Muslims
traded with the Tamil country in a small group. After the invasion of the Malik Kafur the Muslims
established a Sultanate in Tamil country. Conversions were made in large numbers. In the
initial stages the Muslims destroyed temples and plundered the wealth. . They spread havoc in
many villages. But Devaraya II entertained Muslims in his court, allotted them lands and
erected a mosque. He placed a copy of Koran before his throne to command the loyalty of the

Muslims. Krishnadevaraya and Ramaraya also followed the same policy.
On the eastern coast many settlements were established to house the followers of Islam. The
Nayak queen Mangammal made a gift of villages to the Durga. The Durga at Nagur gained
importance from the vijayanagar period. Conversions to Islam were forced. Some of the Hindu
temples were also modified as Durgas. However, these conversions were more during the 18th
century in the Tamil country.
15.2.8 Christianity
Christianity began to spread in South India with the coming of the Portuguese. In 1533
the Paravas of the coastal region in the land were the first to convert to Christianity. The
paravas had monopoly over the fisheries. According to father Heras, at least 20,000 were
converted to Christianity. In the Nayak court of Madurai Jesuit missionary, Robrt-de-Nobili

began a campaign of conversion of the Hindus of the Tamil country. He has learnt the vernacular
languages to attract the masses. But he failed in his attempt. The Vijayanagar rulers followed
the policy of tolerance towards Christianity. They permitted them to construct churches in many
places like Chandragiri, Santhome etc., But Ramaraya did not approve his earlier ruler’s
permission. However with the rise of commercial establishments, the westerners were allowed
to build churches. These churches were constructed within their commercial establishments.

280
15.3 Literature
The Vijayanagar kings appointed regional governors to rule over various territories
of their territory in Tamil Nadu and was subsequently ruled by the Madurai Nayaks, Thanjavur
Nayaks and Gingee Nayaks. Hence this period was referred as the “Vijayanagar and Nayak
age” in Tamil literature.This period witnessed an enormous output of philosophical works,
commentaries, epics and devotional verses.
The Vijayanagar and Nayak rule in the Tamil Country saw a great deal of literary activity.
Tamil, Sanskrit and Telugu works contributed to the richness of the literary movement in this
period. Many of the Vijayanagar and Nayak kings patronised scholars. They have also composed
several works and contributed to the flowering of the literature in this period.
15.3.1 Tamil
The Puranas, Ulas, Andhadi and Kovai literature flourished during this period There

were religious and secular works also. A good number of works were devoted to the philosophy
of the age.. Many commentaries were written in this period. A few translations into Tamil were
made. One of the important contributions of this age was the prose writing initiated by the
foreigners. Another important change in the style of writing was the adoption of Manipravala
from of prose by some authors in their works.
1. General works
One of the scholarly contributions of the age was Bharatam by villuputturar. It renders
the story of Mahabharata in tamil in 4350 versus. Adiviarama pandya’s Naidadam was another
great work of this age. It portrays the life of Nala,t he ruler of Nishada country. The poems of
kalamegam fall into a separate group as ‘Taniapdai’. They were composed in simple style. He
is famous for his instant compositions (asu kavi) on any subject. Murkkudarp-pallu (17th century

A.D) was one of the greatest pally works by an anonymous author from Thirunelveli region.
The peasant life of that reign is vividly portrayed in this work. Another important work of this
period was Kudralak Kuravanji by Tirikudarasappa Kavirayar. It was written in simple and
appealing language. The work was in praise of kudralanthar, the presiding deity at Kudralam.
Supradipakkavirayar, composed Virali-vidu-thudhu and kulapanayakanthal. The first work was

281
written in the form of a message sent by the dancer musician Virali. The second work is a love
story of a Nayaka and a courtesan. A historical balled ‘Ramappayan Ammanai’ was composed
in this age. It deals with the wars of a general of Tirumalai Nayak.
2. Puranas
The Jains also contributed to the enrichment of Tamil literature in this period. The work
Merumandirapuranam by Vamana Muni narrates the story relating to Meru and mahendra, two
Gandharvas of the tirthankara of jaina kanchi. Mandalapurada’s sripuranam was an adaptation
of the Sanskrit Adipuranam. Maraijnasambandar’s work. Ongugoyil puranam is in praise of the
presiding deity of Ongukoyil in Tirupattur. He also wrote kamalalaya puranam and Arunagiri
puranam. The Chidambara puranam, aTamil translation from the Sanskrit work, was by
Tirumalainatha of Chidambaram. The Bhagavatta Puranam by Sevvaichchuduvar and Achandir

puranam by virakavirayar may be mentioned. The last mentioned work was written in 12 sections.
Tirumaluvadi puranam, kamalai Jnnanaprakasa Panditar, Linga puranam and kurmapuranam
of Ativirarama Pandiya, may be mentioned as important contributions of the age. The
Tiruvilaiyadal puranam by Paranjodi Munivar and Kanda puranam by kachiyapa sivachariyar
are an excellent work. The Tiruvilaiyadal puranams have taken their themes from Saiva traditions.
The 64 sports (Tiruvilaiyadal) of Siva at Madurai are narrated in these works. The Kandha
puranam is a great work on the birth and achievements of kanda (Muruga) written 10,000
verses.
3. Sthala Puranas
In this period many sthala puranams were composed. They speak in elaborate details
the traditional history of a temple and their neighbourhood. These temple histories were written

in simple style devoid of any literary excellence. Among the many sthala puranams, the following
may be mentioned: Tiruvorriyur puranams by Gnanaprakasar Thiruppattisvarapuranam and
Thiruvalanjulipuranam by Revana, Siddhar, and Viruddhachala puranams by Gnanakkuttar.
4. Minor works
The Ula literature received a patronage in the hands of many poets. The irattaippulavar
(Mudusuri and IIamsuriyar) wrote an Ula, Ekambaranatha-ula in praise of the deity

282
Ekambaranatha at Kanchipuram. The great poet Kalamegam wrote the Tiruvanaikkaval ula in
praise of the deity at Tiruvanaikkaval Madurai-chokkanathar ula was composed in praise of the
presiding deity at Madurai by Tirumalainatha. Seria Kavirajapillai wrote a ula on Tirukkalainatha.
His other ulas are cheyyur Muragan ula and Ratnagiri ula.
The Andadi was another form of literary composition popular in this period. Among the
many andadhis mention may be made to Ramanujanurrandadi by Manavalamamuni and
Tirukkaruvai padirruppattu and adadi by Varatungarama pandya. Among the other literary pieces
composed in this period mention may be made to Mummanikkovai, Naaratnamalai (by Vedanta
Desika), Sukulagamasarum (by Maraijina sambandari), Annamalaikkovai (by Jnanaprakasa

Panditar), Kandarkavlivenba, Maduraik-Kalambakam, Muthukumarasamy pillaittamil and sakalakala-vallimalai (all by Kumara Guruparar)
5. Devotional Literature
Works in praise of deities were also composed in this age. The most important contribution
in this period is undoubtedly that of Arunagirinathar’s Tirupugal. It consists of 1360 verses on
Muruga. Jhanaprakasa Desikar’s Kachikkalambakam praise the greatness of the deities in
Kanchipuram. In praise of god at Alvar Tirunagiri two works were composed by perumal
Kavirayar. They are Tirukkurukamanmiyan and Marankilavimuninalai. Kumara Guruparar’s works
Sakala-kalavalli-malai at was in praise of saraswathi Muthukumaraswamy pillaitamil by the
same author was in praises of the deity Muthukumaraswamy at Vaidhisvaran Kovil.
6. Works on Philosophy
A good portion of the works produced in this age was devoted to religious philosophy.

Swarupananda Desikar’s Sivaprakasa Peruntirattu was a work of 2,824 verses in the Saiva
Siddhanta. Another small Kuruntirattu was an anthology by Tattuvarayar. It deals with the
Advaita philosophy. Another work on Saiva philosophy was Tattuvaprakasam by Tattuvarayar
or Tiruvarur. The Advaita Siddhanta is explained elaborately in the Kaivlyanavanitam by
Tandavarayaswamigal. It consists of two parts. The first part entitled Tattuvavilakkappadalam
deals with the advait Siddhanta. The second part entitled Sandekam-telidapadalam is devoted
to the explanation of certain philosophical ideas. Irusamaya Vilakkam by the Vaishnavite
Harudasar was another good work which explains the merits and demerits of the two religions
Saivism and Vaishnavism.

283
However the superiority of Vaishnavism is established. Maraijanasambandar of
Chidambaram wrote pari- pasupasap-panuval, Sankarpa- nira- karanam paramopadesam Saiva
Samayaneri. All these works explain the philosophy of Saivism..Siva Gnanandabodam was
another good work on Saiva Philosophy written by Kamalai Jnanaprakasa panditar.
Gurujnasambandar’s Sivalogasagram was another work also explains Saiva philosophy.
Pramodachandrodaya
7. Works on Grammar
Works on poetics and grammar also contributed to the richness of the Tamil literature in
this period, Paranjoti’s Chidam-barappatiiyal is a work on poetics. Another. work on poetic
composed in this period was Navanitappattiyal llakkanavikkam was a work on Tamil Grammer
by Vaidyanatha Desikar of Tiruvarur. Maranalankaram was a work on rhetoric composed by
pillaipperumal Kavirayar Kumara-gurupara’s Chidambaracheyyutkkovai was a work on Tamil

prosody.
One of the greatest nigandus produced during the Vijayanagar rule was by
Mandalapurudar. His early work on Tamil lexicography entitled Chodamani-nigandu explains
the meanings of words in 10 sections. Sivapprakasar’s Tarukkapari-bhasu was a work on tarka
(debta).
8. Commentaries
This period witnessed a large number of commentaries were written. Adiyarkunallar had
written a commentary on Silappadikkaram. Senavaraiyar wrote a commentary for Tolkappiyam.
Then arrived the legend Parimelalagar, whose commentary on Tirukural is still considered as
the best one . Other celebrated commentators such as Perasiriyar and Naccinarikiniyar who
had composed commentaries in the various works of sangam Tamil literature.
9. Translations
Tamil translations to various Sanskrit works appear in this age. The Bhagavatham was

translated into Tamil by Arulaldasar. It deals with the ten incarnations or Vishnu. Another Tamil
version on Bhagavatam was made by Vadiraja Aiyangar. Another important work translated

284
into Tamil was Soundaryalahri by Kaviraja Panditar. Varatunga rama pandya translated
kokkokam, a work on erotices.
15.4 Contribution of Foreigners
The Christian missionaries also enriched the Tamil literature by their contributions. Robert
de Nobili wrote many works in Tamil. On them mention may be made to the following works:
Nanaopadesam. Mandiramalai, Athumanirnayam, Sattiya-veda-lakshnam, Kadavul-nirunayam,
he prepared a Tamil-Portuguese dictionary. Another missionary who made significant
contributions to the Tamil literature was Beshi (Viramamunivar). He wrote the famous epic
Tembavani, which narrates the life story of Christ. His other works are Tirukkovalurkalambakkaam and kitteri-anumanal. He wrote a few prose works namely, Vediyar Olukkam.
Vedavilakkam and Parmarrttaguru-kadai may be mentioned. He started the art of lexicography

in Tamil country by preparing Sadurakardhi. He has translated a part of Tirukkural into Latin.
15.5 Sanskrit
Many Sanskrit works were produced in the Tamil country during their period and they
patronized the Sanskrit poets. Several kings of the Vijayanagar and Nayak dynasties were
great authors. Raghunatha Nayaka of Thanjavur, himself a great poet, also patronised poets.
Ramabhadramba lived in his court. In the court of Sevappa Nayak of Thanjavur flourished the
illustrious author Govinda Dikshita. Srinivas Dikshita was patronised by Sevappa Nayak of
Ginijee.
1. Madhuravijayam
Madhuravijam by Gangadevi, wife of kumarakampana, the second son of Bukka-1, was
an important work of this period. Though this work written in the court of Vijanagar, it can be
considered here since it speaks about the conquest of Madurai in the Tamil country. This work
describes in excellent literary style.

2. Works of Vedanta Desika
The contributions of Vedanta Desika, to the Sanskrit literature in this period are noteworthy.
He was a prolific writer both in Sanskrit and Tamil and has written about 90 works of which very

285
few are available works, the Yadavabyudaya was an important work. It is a long mahakavya
describing the life of lord Krishna in 21 canots. The padukashasara is a poem of 1,000 verses
on the paduka of Rama. In the Sankalpa-suryodhya he presents a drama in 10 acts. The work
was written to explain the system of Visitadvaida. In it he personified evil and good dispositions
of men. Taking the model from kalidasa’s from kalidasa’s Meguhata, he wrote Hamsa-sanaesa.
He wrote a didacatic work the subasita-nivi in 144 stanzes. He was the author of a commentary
on Sirbhasya of Rmanuja. He has composed many stotras like Hayagrivastotra, Astabhviastotra, Tudarasana stotra and a few prabhandas.
3. Works of Appaya Dikshita
Yet another contribution to the Sanskrit literature was made by papaya dikshita who lived

in the 16th century. He is credit with the authorship of 1.4 works. The kuvalayandha is a work on
figures of speech and the Vrittivartika was a trantise on the significance of words in their poetic
use. His works chitramimansa and LAkshanavali were on literature criticism and the appreciation
of poetry. In his Anandhalahari he attempted to sybthesis all the four philosophies (Advaita,
Visishtadvita, Sivadvaita and Dvaita) and bringing the on to a progressive line of thought
culminating in Advaita. He wrote a commentary on culminating in Advaita. He works a
commentary on Yadavabhyudayam of Vedanta Desika and another commentary on srikanta’s
Shaiva-bhasyas. In the commentary on saiva-bhasya he has tried to establish Sivadvaita in
preference to advaita.
4. Others
Raghunatha Nayaka, the Nayak king of Thanjavur also contributed to the enrichment of

the Sanskrit literature. He works on music entitled sangita-sudha and harata-sudha. These two
works incorporate the newly discovered rahas and talas by him. His other contributions are
Nalacartia Partijatapaharana, Valmikicarita, Gajendramoksha. These works are based on
Tradition and Religion. His Archyntarayabhudayam was a work on the life of his father achyuta.
On the life and achievements of Raghunatha, the work Raghunanda ahabyudayam was written
by Ramabhadhrambha, who live in his court.
Nilakanta Dikshita (great-nephew of appaya Dikshita) wrote to Mahakavyam: The
Sivalilarnava in 22 canons and the Gangavvatarange. He also wrote Nilakantavijaya-campu,

286
Vairagyasataka, Anyapadosasataka, anandasagarastava and Sivo-ka-rasamanjari. The last
two works were of brilliant devotionally lyrics addressed respectively to the beloved Mother and
Father of the Universe. He wrote a drama Nalacarita-nataka and a commentary on kaiyata’s
Mahashashyarpradipa Ragavendra tirtha contributed about 42 works. Among then his
commentaries on four Vedas may be considered significiant. Parimala Nyayamuktavali-bahva-
Sangraha and Tattva-Manjari are his other works. He wrote Sathiya-sudha and commented on
Jaimini’s Sutra and Kaumarila’s Darsana.
Srinivasa Dikshita of Satyamangalam was patronised by the Gingee Nayak. He wrote 18
plays and about 60 poetical works, most of which are now lost. The poetical work
Bhavanapurushotama composed at the instance of the Ginee king, was an allegorical poem.

Bhaishmiparinaya-champu was a small work on the marriage of Krishna and Rukmani.
5. Telugu
The Nayaks of Madura and Thanjaur patronised telugu in the 16-17 centuries. The
Prabhandha and Desi type of literature became popular. In Thanjaur court Yagshagana,
Kuravanjis Kuravanji and Jakkinis were the literary styles adopted. These works contain
dialogues and songs resembling dramas. The Yakshagana, is a king of literary piece, borrowed
probably from the kannada and telugu country. Music formed an important piece in this. The
Jakkini is also a king of drama Ragunatha Nayaka wrote a few telugu works. The
Parijatapaharangam deals with the life of Krishna. The Valmiki caritam, Ramayana-
Yakshangana, Rukmani-Parinaya-yakshagana, were the other works.
Cemakuri venkatakavi patronised by Viyarabhava Nayak wrote two works. The

Sarangadhara-caritan and the vijayavilasa. Krishnadhvari’s sleskavya called Naisadha-parijatiya
as another important work. Vijayaraghava Nayaka wrote many dreams like the kaliyamardhana,
putanaharna, prahaladanataka and the Rajagopalavilasa Rangarajamma (queen of
vijayaraghava) was a great poet. She wrote a biographical work mannarudasivilsa inthe
Yakshagana, style, Kadiriipati’s Sukasupati was another good work composed in this age.

287
15.6 Summary
The early Vijayanagar rulers were saivites while the later rulers were Vaishnavites. Hence
both Saivism and Vaishmavism flourished during this period.. On the other side, new religious
started to have a food-hold in parts of the country. Islam and Christianity became recognised
and started spreading vigorously. Mosques and churches were built and large conversions to
new religious were made. In the midst of these religious Buddhism and Jainism also thrived..
There was a tremendous growth in both tamil and Sanskrit literature during this period.

16.1 Introduction
Under the patronage of Vijayanagar rulers’ temple architecture received a new impetus
and reached to new heights According to Professor S.K.Saraswathy “The most frequent design
is one which the shaft becomes either a central core or background for a group of statuary, of
substantial proportion and carved practically on the ground”. Important features of Vijayanagar
style were Monolithic pillars, ornate brackets, decoration on exterior side of the walls, etc.
During the period of Vijayanagar Rulers, Temples became very elaborate both structure
and organisation. Old temples were amplified, modified and altered. Pillared mandapas were
added to the existing temples are the most important fact to be noted. The most important of all
the mandapas, is the one called kalyanamandapa. It is generally located on the southern side

of the entrance to the temple i.e. to south of the mahamandapa of front mandapa. This is very
ornate pillared mandpa with a raised platform at its entire. It was meant to conduct the annual
celebration of the marriage of the deity and hos consort. Second thing is that the Amman
shrine was becomes a common feature the beginning of which has been noticed in the later
Chola period. Third factor is the construction of 1,000 pillared mandapas of which give access
to the temple proper.

290
16. 2 Secular and Civil architecture
The secular architecture may further be divided into civil and defence architecture. Under
civil architecture may be included town planning, palaces, houses ettc. The defence architecture
includes structures like fortress etc.The vijayanagara rulers had to fight against the Muslims
and the Bhamini Sultanas who has a powerful army and ammunition. Thereofore their first and
foremost duty was to protect their capital and other centres of political authority and cultural
importance by way of construction strong and durable, palaces, moats around them, long and
whole roads and highways etc. Further, the emperors were leading a luxurious life for which
they had to raise palatial buildings with proper town planning. The accounts of the foreign
travellers who visited the Vijayanagara country contain vivid descriptions about the town planning

and buildings activities of the period. Further, there are a new structural remains still extent in
places like Hampi which once served the great capital of the dynasty. Unfortunately most of
the Vijayanagar is now in ruins, represented by the well known site Hampi which is dotted with
little hills of granite.
16.2.1 Hampi Ruins
The palace was the most impressive building in Vijayanagar. There were halls of public
and private audience. The halls were decorated with beautiful painted pictures. Usually the
walls and pillars were ornamented with sculptures made of stone or wood. Among the civil
buildings that still exist at Hampi/ two of the impressive basements stand out above many
others. They are (1) the king’s Audience Hall (2) the Throne platform.

291
16.2.2 Audience Hall
The basement is nothing but a terraced platform. It seems to have been originally
surmounted by pillared pavillons with pyramicial roof, with several storeys. The audience Hall
is a hall of hundred pillars, arranged in ten rows. The pillars have square bases cylindrical
shafts and bracket capitals. The basement is divided into three spacious diminishing stages
one above the other with fights of stumps and sides. It is decorated by broad hold mouldings
and string sources. On the whole the Hall presents magnificent appearances and exhibits the
architectural grandeur of the age.
16.2.3 Throne platform
The base of this platform is also divided into three spacious diminishing stages. It is
square in plan. The lowest storey has sides measuring 132 feet and the highest tier 78 feet.

The top most tiers are lavishly embellished by means of beautiful mouldings. The lower two
tiers left plain. However they bear a series of figures and animals in low relief. These carvings
enhance the beauty of the monuments.
16.2.4 Town Planning
Town planning of this period drew attention of the contemporary writers and travellers.
Numerous cities with palatial buildings were created. Lengthy highways and cross roads were
laid in order to facilitate smooth flow of inland trade activities. Coastal areas were linked with
inland routes by a chain of roads and cross roads.
The palace was the seat of royal activities. It had numerous apartments like durbar hall,
bed rooms, kitchen, store rooms, guest houses within a massive defence wall. It was surrounded
by a deep moat. Beautiful gardens were also provided. The houses of the ministers, Army

chiefs, and other high officials and wealthy people had many storeys and apartments with
playgrounds and gardens for purposes of outdoor games and entertainment. The walls of the
palaces and buildings were whitewashed and painted pictures were hung on the walls. Wooden
figures of animals and birds were hung in the walls.
Bridges were constructed across the rivers and canals. Tha remnants of such bridges
have been recently brought to surface.
Dams were built at important places to store water for purposes of irrigation.

292
16.3 Defence Architecture
Massive fortresses were built with stone, clay and bricks. They were built around the
important cities and the residential quarters of the royal families. This fortress understood the
onslaughts of the Muslim invaders. They gave protection not only to the rulers but also to the
public at times of wars and natural calamities like inundation. There fortress tell us the fall of
the wards between the Vijayanagars and the Bahminis.
16.3.1 Gopuras
The Vijayanagara rulers paid special attention to the construction of gopuras. The
rectangular basement of the gopura was enlarged and divided into two zones- upper and
lower. It was built of granite stones. These zones bear numerous niches with several of Siva
and Vishnu besides flora and fauna of the times. The super structure of the gopura was generally

built of bricks and was adorned with numerous stucco figures of both religious and secular
scenes. Contemporary socio-economic life has been vividly portrayed in the various storeys of
the tapering gopura. The scenes like bazaars, shopping, procession, marriages etc. deserve
special mention.
On account of increase in the number of outer enclosures, the gopuras also grew in
large numbers to adorn gateway. The ruined or incomplete super structure of the gopura of the
earlier period was also build of bricks during their period. This is evident from the extent of
gopuras in a few temples of the Chola and Pandya period in Tamil country.
The gopura constructions received greater attention during this period and it is one of the
major contributions of the Vijayanagar dynasty to South Indian temple complex.
16.3.2 Mandapas

More pillared mandapas were built in front of the sanctum in the same axial line. Further,
the front mandapa deserves special mention as it has a peculiar arrangement of pillars i.e., 12
pillars in 3 or 4 rows so as to have 9 equal squares. This type of mandapa is known as Navarang
mandapa. The construction of this has become a permanent feature in the Vijayanagara temple
complex. Wherever they made additions to the old temple, this mandapa was added. 100

293
pillared and 1,000 pillared mandapas were also built. They were built either in front of the
Navranga Mandapa or in the southern or northem corner of the outer prakaras. Particularly,
the 100 pillared mandapas were built in the south east corner of the outer prakara of the main
temple. The mandapa has omate pillars and a raised platform at the centre. It is known as
Kalyanamandapa or Natyamandapa. The annual celebrations of the marriage of the main
deity are being conducted in this mandapa.
The pillars are of different varieties. Most of them bear horses or mythical animals with
riders or soldiers in fighting mood. These figures suggest that the age of the Vijayanagar is one
of the chivalry. The riders and even the galloping animals are highly dressed. The roof of the
architrave and other party of the mandapa are stamped with minute and delicate carving. The

best examples of Kalyanamandapa may be seen in the Vardaraja Perumal temple at
Kanchipuram, Vellore Temple and the horse mandapa at Srirangam. This mandapa is another
noteworthy contribution of the Vijayanagar Rulers.
16.3.3 Tanks and Gardens
The outer prakaras were often provided with sacred tanks and gardens. The tanks were
dug to bathe the deity on certain festive occasions and the abhiseka water from the sanctum
will be let out into this tank to sanctify it.
The garden was cultivated to grow flora for the deity. Sometimes medicinal herbs were
cultivated in such gardens. Besides, kitchen, store room, staircase to the upper storeys in the
prakara wall was also built in the outer prakara complex. Thus the temple complex drew both
horizontally and vertically not only to cater to the needs of the devotees but also to the public

general. Therefore the temple became a centre of not only religious activities but also served
as an institution of public welfare. This is the major contribution of the Vijayanagar rulers to
South Indian culture and History.
16.4 Vijayanagar Temples in Tamil Nadu
When Tamil country was brought under the Vijayanagar rule a few temple cities received
special attention and patronage under the vijayanagara rulers. These centres are; Kanchipuram
Vellore Chidambaram Kumbakonam .Srirangam Madurai and Viruchipuram.

294
1. Kanchipuram
The Ekamabara natha temple at kanchi possesses one of the largest towers in South
India, measuring 188 feet and it has ten storeys. It was built by Krishnadevaraya. The
Rajagopura of the temple contains a large number of sculptures with beautiful decorations.
There are many mandapas in the temple.
2. Vellore
The Jalakandesvara temple within the fort of Vellore received additions and alterations
during this period. The Kalyana mandapa of this temple is celebrated for its sculptural wealth
and elegant carvings. The horsemen on the pillars present varieties of dress and jewellery. It is
one of the best specimens of the Dravidian architecture.
3. Chidambaram
Krishnadevaraya built a good part of the modern tower (north Gopuram) of Chidambaram
temple. The height of the tower is 140 feet. Stones were used in the temple up to first floor: but

bricks were used in the later portions. The noteworthy feature of the temple is the “Thousand
Pillared Halls”. Each pillar is remarkable forits monolithic construction and perfection.
There are also shrines for Sivakamasundari and Subrahmania within the temple prakara.
The square pillars in these shrines are remarkable for their carvings.
4. Kumbakonam
The late Chola temples at Kumbakonam received additions of pillared mandapas and
gopuras during this period. The ceilings of the mandapas have been richly pained with designs
depicting stories from Ramayana and Mahabharata besides geometrical and floral designs.
The Sarangapani temple deserves mention as it has a fine gopura.
5. Srirangam
The ‘hourse court’ or Seshgiri mandapam at Srirangam temple belongs to this period. It
contains a ‘colonade’ of furiously fighting steeds each rearing up to a height of nearly nine feet,

the whole executed in a technique so emphatic as to be not like stone but hardened steel
observes Percy Brown.

295
6. Virinchipuram (North Arcot)
The Margasakesvara temple at this place has a Navaranga mandapa of the Vijayanagaras.
It exhibits beautiful carvings and paintings.
7. Madurai
Thousand pillared hall at Madurai Meenakshi temple
The most wonderful contribution of the Vijayanagar kings is the Meenakshi temple at
Madurai. It is considered as a monument of very fine workmanship. The Mandapas and the
thousand pillared hall were constructed in a beautiful manner.
8. Jain Temples
Though the Vijayanagara rulers were mostly followers of Vaishnavism, they did not hate
other religions. Hence we could see temples were built during this period at places like Geniyitti
and Kanchipuram etc. The Geniyitti temple is a jaina temple wherein seen jaina sculptures. A
Jaina Tirthankara is portrayed on the main door way.
The Varadhamana temple at Tiruppruttikkunram (Jina Kanchi) is another Jain temple of
this period. It has a circular sanctum and sikhara representing Vesara style of architecture. A

296
pillared mandapa is built in front of the sanctum. It measures 62 feet by 26 feet. There are
paintings on the ceilings and pillars. It is by dedicated to one of the Tirthankaras.
16.5 Indo Islamic Architecture
The impact of Islamic architecture style we can see in Vijayanagara architecture.
Received too certain structural motifs like half dome shape, stalactite, honey combining portal
etc., were borrowed and blended with Hindu architecture. As a result, the style has been termed
as ‘Indo aracenic’ or Indo Islamic’.
The Lotus Mahal in the zenaha is an example. The Mahal has a pavilion with an upper
storey. While the pillars and niches are in the Islamic style, the stucco work represents Hindu
style. It is an interesting blending of the two different styles.
The Chandragiri palace is yet another example. The palace has three storeys and arcades
and a pyramidal tower.
16.6 Sculpture

The Vijayanagara sculpture, as usual, includes portraits, decorative sculpture and icons.
However, the portrait sculpture saw a tremendous progress during this period. There was a
setback in the progress after the fall of the Cholas. But Vijayanagara rulers paid greater attention
to this aspect of sculpture and revived the art to the extent possible.
16.6.1 Portrait sculpture
The portraits were made both in stone and metal. Most of them are life size and represent
colossal figures of the kings, queens, ministers and Vijayanagara rulers, especially Krishnadeva
Raya followed a policy of erecting new temples as and when he won battles. Similarly gopurams
pillared mandapas were added to the already existing temples. the Vijayanagara rulers, especially
Krishnadeva Raya followed a policy of erecting new temples. These were done to commemorate

such historic events. With this, portrait figures of the king were also installed within the temple
mandapas or niches on the tower etc. Sometimes the donor figures were installed in the front
mandapas in temples or they were attached to the bases of the pillars in the mandapas. The
custom became very popular during the late Vijayanagara and Nayaka period. This is one of
the reasons why portrait sculpture grew in this period.

297
16.6.2 Decorative Sculpture
This period witnessed a tremendous progress in the field of religion, particularly
Vaishnavism had received greater patronage and it served as a main theme for decorative and
narrative sculptures. Vishnu and his avatars form the main subject. These figures are found
scratched on the ceiling and on the pillars. Further the stories form Ramayana and Mahabharata
also find [place in many of the sculptured panels.
Secular scenes like wars, procession, games and amusements are portrayed. However,
war scenes dominate the panels. These are generally scratched on the basement of the
Kalyanamandapas. These sculptures throw a flood of light on the dress and decoration of the
times besides the method of warfare, weapons of offence and defense. The men wear coats,
bush shirts, trousers, boot etc. They also wear cap or turban. Therefore, they are considered

top be an important source for writing the history of the Vijayanagars. Palaces, houses, street
etc are vividly portrayed. Animals and birds of various kinds have been portrayed. Hybrid animals,
birds and animal with human head, divine and mythical animals and birds are being represented
as decorative motifs on the balus trade, steps etc.
Marriage scenes, shopping and bazaar activities etc. have been also included. These
aspects are peculiar to Vijayanagar sculpture.
1. Icons
The Siva and Vaishnava iconography made a steady progress and numerous icons of
Siva and his various forms, Vishnu and his avatars. Lakshmi and Parvathi and of other minor
deities were made in large number and installed in the niches on the walls, Vimana, gopuras,
basements etc. the enlargement of temple complexes had provided space for installing these
icons. They were made of stone, bronze and copper.
2. Paintings

During this period, painting took a fine shape; considerable progress was made in this
field. The art of paintings had made of steady progress. The palaces, houses and temple
mandapas, walls, ceilings etc. were lavishly painted. The remnants of their paintings have

298
been noticed in a number of temples in South India. Besides, the accounts of foreign visitors
like Paes bear testimony to the flourishing state of this art.
3. Tanjore Temple
In this temple, the Vijayanagara paintings are found super imposed over the early group
of Chola paintings. The passage around the sanctum contains these paintings may be classified
as follows;
1. Scenes from Tanjore Sthalapuranas.
2. Scenes from the life of Siva saints like Kannappar and Chandisvara.
3. Scenes from Hindu mythology such as churning of the ocean of milk, Siva drinking poison,
Ravana lifting kailasa.
4. Representations of Siva, Vishnu, Brahma, Natraja, Dakshinamurthi, Lakshmi Devi, Sri
Devi, Bhudevi, Ganapathi, Subramanya.
5. King, sages, saints, hunters, soldiers, attendants etc. These paintings depict the dress
and jewels of 17th century A.D.
4. Kanchipuram

The Vardhamana temple at Jina-kanchi bears a groups Jaina paintings belonging to the
time of Harihara 11(1378 -1404)
A careful study of these paintings reveals the following facts; the painters had an excellent
knowledge of human anatomy, of figures to produce good compositions, good colour sense to
paint pleasing and handsome pictures. The lines are drawn in bold strokes and the curves
suggest facile way. The colours used are quite simple. They consisted of red, blue, and yellow,
green, black and white.
16.7 Summary
The varied and complication treatment of the pillar is the most fascinating feature of the
Vijayanagar temple complex or style. It serves as a criterion to identify Vijayanagara temples.

299
The shaft of the pillar stands alone or as a core while it is surrounded by agroup of
statuary in great size. They are sculptures in the round, having as its most conspicuous elementfuriously rearing horse, Ra pant hippogryph or upraised animal of a supernatural kind. The
pillar and the figures are carved out of a single block of stone. This is one type of pillar. There
is another type wherein shown a cluster of miniature pillars encircling the central pillar. It should
also be mentioned that the animal sculptures bear riders on their back. The brackets of the
pillars are elaborately embellished which form part of the capital. It cannot be considered as a
separate item as was seen in the earlier period. The pendant, which was carved below the
capital, was further elaborated into an inverted lotus bund (pummunia).

Therefore the ornate pillars which are located in the huge mandapas just in front of the
entrance to the temple add colour to the temple style or complex. These pillared mandapas are
the outstanding contributions of the Vijayanagar to the temple architecture.
They have also continued the Pandiyan tradition of building tall gopuras. Another feature
is, the ceilings of the mandapas, wall surfaces and pillars were painted in multicolour. These
paintings are extent even today in most of the Vijayanagara temples or mandapas. Thus art,
architecture and painting witnessed a considerable progress during the Vijayanagar period.
